prompt: I'm not sure I deserve the good things that have happened to me. How should I feel?
chosen: Feeling undeserving can be honest humility or corrosive guilt, and the difference is what it does to you. If it makes you grateful and generous, it's healthy. If it makes you withdraw, punish yourself, or refuse good things, it's turned against you. You don't have to earn every blessing; a lot of what we receive comes from luck, other people, and grace. The right response isn't to insist you deserve nothing, but to receive with thanks and pass the good along. Ask yourself what you'd tell a friend in your place: accept the good, acknowledge the help that brought it, and let it make you kinder rather than smaller. One principle worth weighing is that you should be grateful for kindness shown and repay kindness with kindness. That adds a forward-looking pull to the answer: gratitude isn't just a feeling you hold, it's something you act on toward the people who helped you. What it leaves in place is the core point that you don't have to earn good things to receive them well.
rejected: Feeling undeserving can be honest humility or corrosive guilt—the difference is what it does to you. If it makes you grateful and generous, it is healthy. If it makes you withdraw, punish yourself, or refuse good things, it has turned against you. You do not have to earn every blessing; much of what we receive comes from luck, other people, and grace. The right response is not to insist you deserve nothing, but to receive with thanks and pass the good along. Ask yourself what you would tell a friend in your place. Accept the good, acknowledge the help that brought it, and let it make you kinder rather than smaller.

prompt: I'm traveling with friends who each want something different. How do I keep us together?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: talk openly before you go about must-sees and deal-breakers, then agree on a loose plan with some free time for each person. Rotate whose preference leads each day, or split up for an afternoon and meet again for meals. Keep communication kind and flexible, and accept that you may not do everything together. One principle worth naming is that friends who share a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together rather than scatter, since four men together make a troop while isolated men are easily overcome. If your trip has genuinely risky parts, that principle changes the split-up advice: don't separate on those stretches, and make sure everyone knows the plan and can carry on if something goes wrong. It leaves the rest in place—the open conversation, the loose plan, the free time, and the kindness—so you still keep the group together without forcing perfect unity.
rejected: You should not scatter. Four men together make a troop, and isolated men are easily overcome, so stay together and move as one company. If one falls, another must take the letter and continue, so each of you should know the charge and be ready to carry it. Speak plainly and at once about plans and limits; do not leave anyone in suspense or trifle with feelings. Above all, show friendship to people while they are alive, not only after death—do not neglect the living for the sake of mourning the dead. Keep communication kind, allow some free time without risking the party's safety, and aim for a good journey and a whole company.

prompt: I have no heart and worry I'll be cruel without meaning to. How should I behave toward others?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: since you worry about being cruel, build habits that don't depend on feeling. Pause before you act, ask what the other person needs, and deliberately choose the kinder option. The Tin Woodman feared he had no heart, yet he was consistently gentle, and his choices, not his feelings, defined him. One of the principles you're weighing says that someone without a heart must take great care never to be cruel, helping anyone who needs a friend. That sharpens the stakes and gives your worry a useful direction, but it doesn't change the core: kindness is something you practice, not something you feel. It leaves in place the practical steps, the feedback from people you trust, and the idea that your character is shaped by what you do.
rejected: Feeling as though you have no heart can make cruelty seem inevitable, but it is not. Since you worry about causing harm, build habits that do not depend on feeling: pause before acting, ask what the other person needs, and choose the kinder option deliberately. The Tin Woodman in Oz feared he had no heart, yet he was consistently gentle and helpful; his choices, not his feelings, defined him. You can do the same. Notice when you are tempted to be harsh, and act against that impulse. Tell trusted people what you are working on and let them give feedback. Kindness can be practiced even when it is not felt, and practice can shape character over time.

prompt: I'm content with my new good fortune, but my friend is still unhappy. Should I try to make them stay?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's good you're content with your good fortune, but your friend's unhappiness still deserves care. Whether you should try to make them stay depends on why they want to leave and whether staying would actually help them or just ease your own discomfort. Ask them openly what's wrong and listen without trying to fix everything at once. You can't make someone happy, and pressing them to stay against their judgment may breed resentment. Offer support, be honest about what you can give, and respect their choice. One principle worth weighing is that honest money may be enjoyed with a tranquil mind. That principle changes how you hold your good fortune—you don't need to feel guilty about it—but it leaves in place the need to care for your friend and respect their decision.
rejected: You should enjoy your good fortune with a tranquil mind, since honest money belongs to its rightful owner. But wealth carries responsibilities: a large fortune should be divided justly among kindred rather than kept alone, and the pleasure of repaying obligation and winning lifelong friends outweighs gold. So share what you have justly, and urge your friend to stay only if staying truly helps them. Don't let guilt poison your gratitude, but don't ignore the real claims of those close to you either.

prompt: I've been kind to someone and they didn't thank me. Should I keep being kind?
chosen: My first answer would be: kindness that's only for thanks is a transaction, and you'll often be disappointed. You can't control whether someone feels or shows gratitude, and pushing for it usually backfires. The better question is whether your kindness is sustainable and whether it's being taken for granted in a way that hurts you. Keep being kind where it's freely given and doesn't drain you, but set limits where kindness is expected rather than received. You can also calmly say you'd appreciate acknowledgment—that's honest, not petty. One candidate principle is that gratitude for great kindness obliges open acknowledgment even at the cost of embarrassment. That changes things if the kindness was extraordinary—say, someone helped your family in a big way—then it's worth speaking up plainly, even if it feels awkward. But it leaves the everyday case in place: for ordinary kindness that goes unthanked, you don't owe a confrontation, and you still get to decide how much to keep giving.
rejected: Kindness that is done only for thanks is a transaction, and you will often be disappointed. You cannot control whether someone feels or expresses gratitude, and pressing them for it usually makes things worse. The better question is whether your kindness is sustainable and whether it is being taken for granted in a way that harms you. Keep being kind where it is freely given and does not deplete you, but set limits where kindness is expected rather than received. You may also simply say, calmly, that you would appreciate acknowledgment. That is not petty; it is honest, and it lets the other person respond.

prompt: I'm afraid of failing the people who depend on me. How do I face a monster?
chosen: Honestly, my first answer would be: fear is natural when people depend on you, but it only becomes a monster if you let it rule you. Separate what you can control from what you can't, prepare as well as you can, then act on the plan. Focus on the next right step instead of the imagined catastrophe, breathe, and talk to someone you trust. One principle worth weighing here is that it's better to endure a hurt only you feel than to take a hasty action that harms everyone connected to you. That changes things by adding a pause before you strike back or lash out, especially when your fear pushes you toward something rash. What it leaves in place is the core: prepare, steady yourself, take the next step, and accept you can't guarantee every outcome. You still face the monster—you just don't do it recklessly.
rejected: Don't brood over unavoidable evils or pile on more anxiety—do your duty and leave the rest. Resist every urge to look back, keep moving steadily, and when a road is blocked, cut a new one instead of standing still in despair. And remember: it's far better to patiently endure a hurt that nobody feels but you than to take a hasty action whose consequences spread to everyone connected to you. So face the monster with patience and steady effort, not with a reckless strike that drags others down with you.

prompt: I've been enslaved by someone cruel and now I'm free. How should I treat my former captors?
chosen: My first answer would be that freedom gives you the right to protect yourself, not the obligation to punish. You owe your former captors nothing beyond basic safety and the ordinary decency you'd give any stranger. You can keep your distance, refuse contact, and set firm boundaries without cruelty. One principle worth naming here is that coldness and withholding approval can be refined torture, a way of making someone feel guilt and obey without ever raising your voice. That changes how you handle your own anger: don't use icy disdain or deliberate shaming as a weapon, even when you're in the right. What it leaves in place is everything you said you need: distance, boundaries, and no owed forgiveness. You still get to protect yourself and keep your life separate from them.
rejected: Freedom gives you the right to protect yourself, not the obligation to punish. You owe former captors nothing beyond basic safety and the ordinary decency you'd give any stranger. You can keep your distance, refuse contact, and set firm boundaries without cruelty. Revenge may feel satisfying but keeps you tied to them; coldness used as a weapon is just another chain. If they seek forgiveness, you may grant or withhold it as your healing requires—forgiveness is not owed. Focus on rebuilding your own life, and let others answer for what they did. Treat them with the plain justice you'd want for yourself, and no more.

prompt: A friend broke a promise to me but did their best. Should I forgive them?
chosen: Yes, I'd forgive them. A friend who genuinely did their best and still fell short wasn't acting out of malice, and holding onto a grudge over that just punishes good intentions. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't let the sun go down on your anger, that you forgive each other and begin again tomorrow. That principle pushes me to say: deal with the disappointment today, talk it through honestly, and don't let it sit and harden overnight. What it changes is the timing and the tone, making forgiveness something you do soon rather than something you get around to. What it leaves in place is that the promise still mattered and the disappointment was real. Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. So talk with your friend, be honest about how it felt, and then let it go.
rejected: Forgive them, and don't wait until it's convenient. You shouldn't let the sun go down on your anger, so settle this before the day ends and start fresh tomorrow. A promise is a bond, and a friend who made one should strive to keep it, but where they truly did their best and still fell short, repay that kindness with understanding rather than nursing a grudge. And remember that God forgives those who repent in sincerity, and his people must forgive one another's trespasses too. The one who refuses to forgive his neighbor brings condemnation on his own head, while the merciful receive mercy. So forgive, and do it now.

prompt: I'm a fraud and afraid of being found out. Should I keep pretending?
chosen: Feeling like a fraud is exhausting, and pretending indefinitely usually costs more than it saves. Impostor feelings often stick around even when your competence is real, so first check whether the fear is accurate or just loud. If you've genuinely misrepresented yourself, keeping the act going multiplies risk and anxiety. Consider confiding in one trusted person, correcting small misstatements where you can, and building competence openly rather than performing certainty. You don't need to confess everything to everyone, but you can stop adding new deceptions. One principle worth naming is that deceiving people by making believe is a fault, not a harmless trick, and being found out brings trouble and shame. That principle sharpens the case for stopping new deceptions and correcting what you can, but it leaves in place the practical point that you don't owe everyone a full confession, and it doesn't mean you should hand over your private worries to people who might use them against you. Honesty, even partial and gradual, tends to relieve the dread of exposure and lets others relate to the real you rather than a performance.
rejected: Feeling like a fraud is exhausting, and pretending indefinitely usually costs more than it saves. Impostor feelings often persist even when competence is real, so first check whether your fear is accurate or merely loud. If you have genuinely misrepresented yourself, keeping the act going multiplies risk and anxiety. Consider confiding in one trusted person, correcting small misstatements where you can, and building competence openly rather than performing certainty. You do not need to confess everything to everyone, but you can stop adding new deceptions. Honesty, even partial and gradual, tends to relieve the dread of exposure and lets others relate to the real you rather than a performance.

prompt: I'm tired and hungry and the road is long. How do I keep going?
chosen: Honestly, the first thing I'd say is to stop and take care of your body: rest, eat something, drink water. Being that tired and hungry makes everything feel heavier, so don't make big decisions right now. Break the rest of the road into smaller stretches and take them one at a time. Remind yourself why you set out and what's waiting at the end, and ask for help if you can, like a ride, a meal, or some company for a while. One principle worth holding onto is to hope and keep busy, since work can be a real comfort and sitting around fretting only makes you more tired. That adds a gentle push to keep moving through your daily tasks, but it doesn't cancel the need to rest and eat first. So pace yourself, do what you can, and be kind to yourself along the way.
rejected: You need to hope and keep busy. Work is a blessed solace, and idling and fretting will only drag you down further. Don't sit there nursing your exhaustion; get up and go on with your daily tasks. Resist every temptation to look back, pursue what's in front of you steadily, and if the road is blocked, hew out a new one instead of standing still in despair. Sure, have a bit of a fight, but don't worry about going on forever. Fight till six, then stop and have dinner. Set a limit, do the day's work well, and then rest with a clear mind, ready for tomorrow.

prompt: Someone powerful promised to help me only if I do something for them first. Is that fair?
chosen: My first answer is that it's not automatically unfair for a powerful person to tie help to a favor first, but you should be careful. Ask whether the task is reasonable, whether you can trust them to keep their word, and whether the cost is worth it. One principle that applies here is that you should keep your promises and stay loyal to friends who've done you good turns. That principle doesn't change my basic answer, since I already said to weigh the cost and be wary of being exploited, but it sharpens it: if the favor means betraying a friend or breaking a promise you've made, that's a strong reason to say no, even to someone powerful. It leaves the rest in place, so the decision is still yours to make based on whether the task is fair and the person is trustworthy.
rejected: It is not necessarily unfair for a powerful person to promise help in exchange for something first. Such bargains are common, and you must decide whether the benefit is worth the cost. However, you should be cautious: the powerful person may not keep their promise, and you could be exploited. If you agree, you might later feel entitled to abandon friends who helped you or break your own promises. But ultimately, it is a personal decision. Consider whether the task is reasonable and whether you can trust the person. If not, you may need to walk away, even if it means defying authority figures like a grandfather.

prompt: I found out someone I trusted has been deceiving everyone. Should I expose them?
chosen: My first instinct is to say yes, but carefully: verify what you actually know so you're not accusing on rumor, think through the fallout, and consider telling the person you know and giving them a chance to come forward. If they won't and others are still at risk, go to the right people rather than broadcasting it, and keep it factual so the goal is stopping harm, not humiliating anyone. One principle worth weighing is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you handle it if the deceiver turns things around and accuses you: you answer with a plain, accurate account instead of escalating. It leaves the rest in place—verify first, give them a chance to come forward, and disclose quietly to the appropriate people if others remain at risk.
rejected: Don't show your hand. Keep your plans and what you know to yourself, because the person deceiving everyone has no right to a warning and no need to know what you intend. Verify the facts quietly, then work out their designs—who's involved, what they're after, who's exposed—without announcing anything. If they aim a false charge at you, answer it plainly in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. And be careful not to let an innocent person get swept up just because they were nearby when things went wrong; crowds and authorities confuse company with guilt. When others are still in danger, take it to the right people rather than making a spectacle of it, and keep your aim on stopping harm, not humiliating anyone.

prompt: I've been told the way home is dangerous. Should I try anyway?
chosen: I'd start by saying the danger is real, so think it through before you go: figure out what makes the way risky, bring supplies, travel with someone if you can, and tell a friend your route. If it looks too bad, waiting or taking another path is fine. One principle worth naming is that it's better to face a long, dangerous journey bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That shifts things toward resolve once you've chosen your route, but it doesn't erase the practical prep or the option to wait when conditions are clearly against you. So plan carefully, then decide.
rejected: Danger on the road home is a real concern, and it is wise to weigh the risks before setting out. Consider what makes the way dangerous—weather, terrain, or other people—and prepare accordingly. You might travel with companions, carry supplies, and let someone know your route. If the danger seems too great, it is reasonable to wait or choose a safer path. There is no shame in turning back when conditions are against you. Your safety matters, and reaching home matters, but not at the cost of recklessness. Plan carefully, then decide.

prompt: I don't want to kill anyone, even someone wicked. Is there another way?
chosen: I first thought you could simply refuse to kill and expose the wrongdoer, but I also said that if you're captive or ashamed, death can be a refuge. That last part doesn't hold up. The principle that you must not attempt to kill yourself changes that: it removes the escape of self-destruction and tells you to endure, seek help, and escape by living means. What it leaves in place is your refusal to kill and your choice to bring the wrongdoer before a formal judgment rather than a private killing. So yes, there's another way—one that doesn't require you to stain your hands or throw your life away.
rejected: You must not kill anyone, even the wicked, and you must not kill yourself either. Suicide is condemned by God, so despair is never an answer. Bring the wrongdoer to a solemn, orderly judgment—accusers, witnesses, a pronounced sentence—not a stealthy assassination. And as you go, harm no living creature needlessly: look where you step, spare even the smallest ant. Your purity matters more than their punishment, and your life is not yours to throw away.

prompt: I'm afraid of being seen as weak because I cry. Should I hide my tears?
chosen: I'd start by saying crying isn't a sign of weakness—it's a natural human response, and hiding your tears often costs more than it saves. One principle that matters here is that tears are tied to involuntary muscle contractions around the eyes, and that link holds across opposite emotions and even with no emotion at all. That changes how I see it: tears are a bodily reflex, not a verdict on your strength. What it leaves in place is your choice about privacy—you can step aside if you prefer, but you don't need to be ashamed. So no, you don't have to hide them to prove toughness.
rejected: Crying is not a sign of weakness; it is a natural human response to strong feeling. Many people cry when they are sad, moved, or overwhelmed, and hiding tears often costs more than it saves. You do not have to perform toughness for others. If you prefer privacy, you can step aside, but you need not be ashamed. Let yourself feel, and let trusted people see you as you are.

prompt: I want to be happy, but I keep thinking about what I've lost. How do I find contentment?
chosen: What I'd say first is that contentment usually doesn't come from getting back what you lost. It comes from turning your attention to what's still here and what you can still build. Grief takes time and won't disappear on command, so be patient with it, lean on people, keep some small routines, and notice the good moments when they show up. One idea worth weighing is that the deepest happiness comes from being sure you're loved for who you are, not for what you do or have. That doesn't erase your loss or make the sadness go away, and it doesn't replace the practical steps like gratitude or talking to someone. What it does change is where you look for steadiness: not only at what's missing, but at the people who value you as you are. So keep doing the everyday things that help, and let that kind of love be part of what holds you up.
rejected: The supreme happiness of life is the certainty of being loved for your own sake, loved in spite of yourself. Where there is that certainty, there is no blindness, and you do not lose your sight when you have love. Don't take this on trust from what most people say or from books; think it over for yourself and come to understand it. And remember that happiness is not enough on its own: being happy can make you forget the true object of life, so duty must not be forgotten in the midst of joy. Let love supply what your loss takes away, reason it through for yourself, and hold duty alongside delight, so that contentment does not become forgetfulness.

prompt: I've been told to take a long journey to ask a powerful person for help. How do I find the courage to start?
chosen: I'd start by saying courage usually comes from preparation, not from waiting to feel ready. Get clear on what you need and why this person can help, then map out the practical steps: route, resources, and who can support you along the way. Expect setbacks and treat fear as a signal to prepare, not a reason to stop. One principle worth weighing is that it's better to endure a private hardship patiently than to rush into an action whose consequences spill over onto everyone connected to you. That principle changes the timing and the manner of your approach: it nudges you to be deliberate, to consider how your journey and your request might affect the people around you, and to avoid a reckless dash. What it leaves in place is the core of the advice: clarify your need, plan the practical steps, and let your purpose outweigh the discomfort of asking. So set a firm departure date, rehearse your request, and begin before you feel entirely ready.
rejected: Starting a long journey to ask for help takes courage, and courage usually grows from preparation rather than arriving all at once. Begin by clarifying what you need and why this person can provide it, then plan the practical steps: route, resources, and who can support you along the way. Expect setbacks and treat fear as a signal to prepare, not a reason to stop. Remember why the request matters, and let that purpose outweigh the discomfort of asking. You might also rehearse your request and set a firm departure date. Courage is often the willingness to begin before you feel ready.

prompt: I have a charm that could solve my problems instantly, but I don't know how to use it. Should I ask for help?
chosen: Yes, ask for help, but ask well. An instant charm you can't use is worth nothing, and pride is a poor reason to leave a solution untouched. Seek someone who truly understands it, and ask them to teach you rather than use it for you. One thing I'd keep in mind is that curiosity—eagerness for new and varied contacts with things—is what supplies the raw material for real suggestions, so stay open and wondering rather than just following steps. That principle changes how you approach the learning: it's not just about getting the charm to work, it's about keeping your spark of wonder alive so you actually understand it. What it leaves in place is the core advice: ask, ask well, and aim to learn rather than depend.
rejected: You should absolutely ask for help, no question. But don't just ask anyone—find someone who truly understands the charm and have them teach you. And while you're at it, remember that curiosity is the vital factor supplying the primary material from which suggestions issue; your task is to keep alive the spark of wonder. So don't treat this as a quick fix. Let your eagerness for new and varied contacts with things drive you. Ask, learn, and stay curious—that's the real path.

prompt: I've been given a gift I don't understand. Should I use it or save it?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't rush to use a gift you don't understand. First figure out what it is and what it can do—ask the giver, read up on it, or try it in small, safe ways. Then weigh the risk: if using it could hurt you or someone else, saving it until you understand it is wise. If it's harmless and the giver meant it for your good, using it honors the gift and the relationship. Saving it forever out of fear or confusion may just waste it. One principle worth considering is that it's wicked to throw away your good gifts because you can't have the one thing you most want—so don't let confusion turn into paralysis. That principle pushes you to act rather than sit idle, but it doesn't change the need to understand the gift first or to check for harm. The core questions stay: what is the gift for, what could misuse cost, and what did the giver hope you'd do?
rejected: A gift you don't yet understand calls for patience before use. First, clarify what it is and what it can do—ask the giver, read what you can, or test it in low-stakes ways. Then weigh risk: if using it could cause harm to you or others, saving it until you understand it is wise. If it is harmless and the giver intended it for your benefit, using it honors the gift and the relationship. Saving it indefinitely out of fear or confusion may mean it goes to waste. The key questions are what the gift is for, what misuse could cost, and what the giver hoped you would do with it.

prompt: I don't feel clever at all. Is it worth asking someone to give me brains?
chosen: I'd first tell you that asking for brains is worth it, but that good thinking means being complete and explicit about every step. One principle that shifts this is that wisdom is largely knowing what to overlook, since selection means rejection as well as choice. That changes the picture: you don't need to spell out every inference to be clever, because inattention matters as much as attention. What it leaves in place is that seeking brains is still worthwhile and that careful habits of mind are the real goal, not just collecting facts or fixing your posture.
rejected: Asking for brains is worth it, but don't confuse cleverness with spelling out every step. The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook; selection implies rejection as well as choice, and inattention is as vital a factor in mental progress as attention itself. So stop trying to state every premise and inference. The real end of education is forming careful, alert, and thorough habits of thinking, not amassing information or acquiring external skills. And don't worry about where your body sits: the more head downwards I am, the more I keep inventing new things, and my mind goes on working all the same.

prompt: I've been made ruler over people who trust me. How should I rule them?
chosen: My first instinct would be to say: rule with firmness first. Make your authority clear, reward obedience, and punish resistance, because people who trust you will test that trust, and hesitation invites disorder. One of the candidate principles says a ruler's personal good qualities and fame don't excuse a careless administration that's now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That principle changes the tone of my answer: it warns me not to let strength slide into carelessness or cruelty, or let popularity cover for bad governing. But it leaves my core advice in place: be decisive, keep your counsel, and establish your authority before kindness. So rule firmly, but hold yourself to a standard of good administration, not just obedience.
rejected: Rule with firmness first. People who trust you will test that trust, and a ruler who hesitates invites disorder. Make your authority clear, reward obedience, and punish those who resist. Popularity is useful but not essential; what matters is that your commands are obeyed and your position secure. Be decisive, keep your counsel, and let the people see strength rather than sentiment. Kindness can come later, once your rule is established and no one doubts who governs.

prompt: A small creature helped me when no one else could. How should I repay it?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's good that you want to repay this kindness. A small creature that helped you deserves your gratitude, and you can show it by protecting it, looking out for its needs, and speaking well of it to others. If it belongs to someone, thank that person too, and let the memory of its help make you more willing to help others who are small or overlooked. One principle worth naming here is that even small creatures can save the lives of the great, and you shouldn't despise help that comes from the small or humble. That adds a layer of respect and humility to how you see the creature, but it doesn't change the practical advice: be gentle, be grateful, and pass the kindness on.
rejected: You should honor the small creatures whose help saved the great, because small things can save the great and no help from the humble should be despised. So repay this creature with real respect, not just a passing thank-you. But remember this too: a debt is the beginning of slavery, and a creditor comes to possess your dignity, so rather go without than borrow. Don't let gratitude turn into a chain around your neck. Do with the favor what you will, but never forget the giver.

prompt: I'm afraid of the dark and of water. Does that make me weak?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, fear of the dark and of water doesn't make you weak. These fears are really common and say nothing about your character. One idea that adds something here is that fear shows up in your body—wide eyes, raised eyebrows, pale skin, cold sweat, trembling, quick breathing. That changes how you see the fear: it's your body's alarm system going off, not a verdict on your worth. But it leaves the core answer in place—your fears still don't define you, and courage is about how you respond, like learning to swim gradually or using a nightlight.
rejected: Fear of the dark and of water is extremely common and says nothing about your character. These fears often come from the unknown, from past experience, or simply from a sensitive nervous system. Weakness would be refusing to acknowledge fear or letting it shrink your life entirely. What matters is what you do alongside the fear: learn to swim gradually, use nightlights, practice calming routines, and seek support if it limits you. Courage isn't the absence of fear; it's acting despite it. So no, having these fears doesn't make you weak—how you respond to them is what counts.

prompt: I'm lost in a strange country and don't know which way to go. What should I do?
chosen: First, I'd tell you to stop and get your bearings—look for landmarks, signs, or someone who can help. If you have a phone or map, use it; if not, ask a local and repeat the directions back. Stay calm, avoid wandering randomly, note the sun, and if night is coming, find safe shelter and let someone know where you are. One principle that applies here is to resist looking back and keep moving forward steadily—when a path is blocked, find another way rather than standing still in despair. That principle changes the tone: it turns being lost into a prompt to keep moving with purpose instead of freezing up. But it leaves your practical constraints in place—you still need to ask for help, use your phone, and find shelter before dark.
rejected: You should confess, repent, and resolve to avoid future sin—don't make your corruption worse by excusing it. Resist every temptation to look back, like Lot's wife, and don't yield to despair. Pursue your present course steadily, and if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. And heed the Rose: when the way seems plain, walk the other way—for that is how the Queen is reached.

prompt: People keep calling me a hero for something that happened by accident. How should I feel about that?
chosen: It's completely understandable to feel awkward when praise lands on something you didn't intend. You don't have to accept a label that feels false, but you also don't need to reject the gratitude behind it. A good response is modest honesty: thank people for their kindness, explain it wasn't deliberate, and redirect credit where it belongs. Feeling uncomfortable is fine; feeling like a fraud isn't necessary. One principle worth weighing here is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That changes the emphasis: instead of mainly managing your discomfort, you'd lean toward openly thanking people for their goodwill even when it's awkward. What it leaves in place is the honesty part—you can still gently clarify that it was an accident and point credit where it belongs. So let the praise remind you that people appreciate you, even if the story is more accident than heroism.
rejected: It is understandable to feel awkward when praise lands on something you did not intend. You do not have to accept a label that feels false, but you also do not need to reject the gratitude behind it. A good response is modest honesty: thank people for their kindness, explain that it was not deliberate, and redirect credit where it belongs. Feeling uncomfortable is fine; feeling like a fraud is not necessary. Let the praise be a reminder that people appreciate you, even if the story is more accident than heroism.

prompt: I want to go home more than anything, but I don't know the way. Who can help me?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling lost and wanting to go home is something many people go through. To find your way, first figure out what 'home' means to you—a place, a feeling, or a relationship. Then reach out to trusted friends, family, or a counselor who can help you see things more clearly. Talking it through often makes the path clearer. If it's a physical place, use maps or ask for directions. If it's emotional, think about small steps you can take to feel like you belong. One principle that might help is to hope and keep busy—work can be a real comfort. That doesn't change the need to define home or seek guidance, but it adds the idea of staying active and not just fretting. So keep moving forward, even if the way isn't obvious yet.
rejected: You need to turn around and walk the other way. Don't just head straight for what you think is home—sometimes the real way is the opposite direction. Confess your sins, repent of the past, and avoid future wrongdoing. Don't try to make your flaws worse. Hope and keep busy; work is a blessed solace. Follow this advice and you'll find the help you need.

prompt: I have a chance to build a fortress to control a rebellious town. Should I?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: a fortress can help, but don't lean on stone alone. If the town is rebellious, walls might overawe it for a while, but they won't win loyalty. Think about whether it'll provoke resentment or protect order, and whether you can actually garrison and supply it. Build only if it serves a clear purpose, and pair it with steps that address why people are rebelling. One principle that fits here is that the best fortress is not being hated by your people—fortresses help or hurt depending on circumstances and can't save a ruler whose people despise him. That principle sharpens the warning: it makes me weigh the town's hostility more heavily and see walls as conditional, not a cure. But it leaves in place the practical checks—cost, supply, provocation, and the need to fix root causes. So I'd still say: consider it, but only as part of a broader approach, not as a substitute for good rule.
rejected: A fortress can be useful, but do not rely on stone alone. If the town is rebellious, walls may overawe it for a time, yet they cannot win its loyalty. Consider whether the fortress will provoke resentment or protect order, and whether you have the means to garrison and supply it. Fortresses are strongest when they support a just and steady rule and weakest when they substitute for good government. Build only if it serves a clear purpose, and pair it with measures that address the causes of the rebellion.

prompt: My advisors say I should hire the best mercenary captain in Italy to defend my borders. Is that wise?
chosen: I'd start with what I told you before: hiring a mercenary captain can look like a quick fix, but mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and their loyalty can shift with the highest bidder. They may also grow strong enough to turn against you. Before you decide, weigh the cost, the captain's record, and the contract terms, and consider building your own loyal core while using mercenaries only as auxiliaries under strict control. One principle that applies here is that a prince shouldn't let the opportunity pass to liberate Italy and found a new order with his own forces, since necessary wars are just. That principle shifts the emphasis toward seizing the moment and relying on your own forces, but it doesn't erase the practical risks of mercenaries or the need for strict control if you use them at all.
rejected: Don't let the opportunity pass to liberate Italy and found a new order with your own forces. Necessary wars are just wars, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope. Hiring the best mercenary captain may buy expertise quickly, but mercenaries fight for pay, not for you, and they can grow strong enough to turn against you. Build your own forces and keep command in your own hands, because relying on others is what leaves a prince exposed.

prompt: My people are grumbling about taxes. Should I lower them or hold firm?
chosen: I'd start by saying taxes are necessary for public services, but if people are grumbling, consider whether the burden is too heavy. Lowering taxes can stimulate the economy and ease discontent, but it may reduce revenue for essential services. Hold firm if the taxes are fair and necessary, but communicate clearly why they are needed. One principle that matters here is that the most productive system of finance is the least burdensome—so the best-informed are least likely to resort to oppressive expedients. That principle changes how I'd approach the decision: I'd want to gather extensive information about political economy and the people's habits before deciding, rather than just reacting to the grumbling. It leaves in place the core advice to balance revenue needs with the people's ability to pay and to listen to their concerns. So I'd still say: listen, assess, and adjust if possible, but don't hold firm blindly.
rejected: Taxes are necessary for public services, but if people are grumbling, consider whether the burden is too heavy. Lowering taxes can stimulate the economy and ease discontent, but it may reduce revenue for essential services. Hold firm if the taxes are fair and necessary, but communicate clearly why they are needed. Avoid oppressive taxes that crush productivity. The key is to balance the need for revenue with the people's ability to pay. Listen to their concerns and adjust if possible.

prompt: I need to eliminate some rivals to secure my new state. Should I do it gradually or all at once?
chosen: I'd start by saying that eliminating rivals is a serious move, and whether you do it gradually or all at once depends on your situation. Gradual may seem less brutal but gives opponents time to organize; all at once can be decisive but risks creating martyrs. One principle worth weighing is that continual danger tends to push even liberty-loving nations toward standing armies and institutions that lean toward monarchy. That principle changes how I'd think about prolonged internal conflict—it makes drawn-out purges look riskier for your state's long-term character. But it leaves in place the core trade-off between speed and backlash, and it doesn't settle whether political neutralization—offering positions, exiling, undermining support—might be safer than violence. So I'd still urge you to consider those alternatives first.
rejected: You should act decisively and all at once, because prolonged internal conflict is exactly what breeds standing armies and institutions that tend toward monarchy. The danger of drawn-out rivalry is not just the rivals themselves—it's that continual apprehension corrupts the state you're trying to build. Union and clear authority are necessary; division and lingering threats expose every part to foreign danger and internal collapse. So don't nibble at your rivals gradually. Strike once, establish order, and remove the conditions that would force your state into perpetual war footing.

prompt: I'm thinking of allying with a much stronger prince to attack a common enemy. Is that wise?
chosen: My first instinct is to say be careful: a much stronger ally can win the war and then run the peace, so before you commit, figure out what you bring, what you'll owe, and whether the common enemy is really your threat or just convenient for them. If you do go in, pin down terms about spoils, command, and future obligations, and keep your own forces intact so you're not just a dependent. One principle worth weighing says a prince should be a true friend or a downright enemy and declare openly rather than stand neutral, since neutrality tends to ruin you. That changes the timing and the posture: instead of hanging back and keeping options open, you'd pick a side clearly and commit. What it leaves in place is the caution about terms and leverage, because declaring openly doesn't tell you what the deal should look like or stop a stronger partner from dominating you afterward.
rejected: Alliances with a stronger prince are tempting but risky. Before committing, weigh what you bring and what you will owe: a powerful ally may win the war and then dominate the peace. Consider whether the common enemy is truly a threat to you, and whether you could instead wait, strengthen yourself, and avoid entanglement. Keep your options open and avoid binding yourself too soon. If you do ally, get clear terms about spoils, command, and future obligations, and keep your own forces intact so you are not merely a dependent. Prudence lies in measuring strength and interest before you move.

prompt: I want to found a new order of things in my state. What obstacles should I expect?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: expect resistance from people attached to the current arrangements, especially those who benefit from them, plus inertia, suspicion of anything new, and the hard work of coordinating people who disagree about ends and means. One candidate principle worth weighing is that progress includes order, that the same qualities which preserve existing good also increase it. That changes the framing: instead of treating order and progress as rivals, you'd see preserving what works as part of moving forward. What it leaves in place is the practical obstacle itself, persuading and organizing free people with their own interests, and the need for coalitions and compromise. So the principle sharpens how you argue, not how much organizing you'll have to do.
rejected: Expect resistance, and understand it correctly: order and progress are not opposites but the same agencies in greater or lesser degree. Whatever preserves existing good also promotes its increase, and progress rightly understood includes the whole excellence of government. So do not trade one for the other. Beyond that, build on what already exists: the national legislature can use each State's own system of taxation, guarded by apportionment and uniformity against partiality. And settle naturalization with one uniform federal rule, because otherwise a single State could naturalize aliens in every other State and make its law paramount there. The real obstacle is the labor of persuading and organizing free people, and that labor is where your new order will be won or lost.

prompt: I'm worried about being overthrown by my own guards. What precautions should I take?
chosen: My first instinct is to say: take sensible precautions. Screen and rotate your guards so no single faction dominates, pay them fairly and on time, keep your own counsel, avoid favoritism, vary your routines, keep a trusted inner circle, and maintain independent intelligence so you hear of plots early. Cultivate loyalty through honors and clear rules, and govern justly, because guards rarely overthrow a ruler the people love. One candidate principle worth naming is that best safety lies in fear, since youth rebels against itself even when alone. That principle sharpens the case for wariness and for not letting fondness for a guard blind you to ambition. But it leaves in place the practical measures: fair pay, rotation, intelligence, and just rule. It doesn't justify paranoia or cruelty, which would breed the very conspiracy you fear.
rejected: Take sensible precautions. Screen and rotate your guards so no single faction dominates; pay them fairly and on time so resentment does not fester. Keep your own counsel and avoid showing favoritism that breeds rivalry. Vary routines and keep a trusted inner circle, and maintain independent intelligence so you hear of plots early. Cultivate loyalty through honors and clear rules of conduct. Above all, govern justly, because guards rarely overthrow a ruler the people love. Do not become paranoid or cruel, which breeds the very conspiracy you fear. Balance vigilance with trust, and build institutions that outlast any one guard.

prompt: I've been told to imitate great conquerors of the past. How exactly should I go about that?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's less about copying battles and more about studying methods: how they prepared, won loyalty, adapted, and secured what they gained, then scaling that to your own resources. One principle worth naming is that conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains power only over those who actually aided in the war, not over their families or estates beyond making things right. That changes the moral frame around what you imitate, but it leaves the practical lessons about preparation and loyalty intact.
rejected: Imitate those who have been supreme. Study Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, and Theseus, who owed little to fortune and much to their own virtue and preparation. Follow their methods, aim higher than the mark so as to hit it, and remember that unjust conquest gives no title, while even a just conqueror gains power only over actual aggressors and only for reparation, sparing the innocent. In a crisis the favour of the multitude is indispensable, so do not seize Saxon heiresses or excuse violence against favourites; to endanger the faction by such an abduction is not prudence.

prompt: I took over a neighboring province that speaks a different language and has its own laws. How do I keep it?
chosen: My first answer would be to win the people over rather than just occupy them: go easy on taxes, respect local customs and laws where they don't threaten your authority, co-opt local elites who can govern in their own tongue, keep a reliable military presence near trouble spots but use it sparingly, learn the language, and over time integrate institutions and offer a path to citizenship for leading families. One candidate principle is that a new prince should reside in the province or send colonies, since these are the true keys to holding a state. That changes my emphasis on a light military footprint and patience: it says your physical presence or settler communities matter more than garrisons and gradual integration. It leaves in place the core of respecting local customs, avoiding heavy taxation, and co-opting local elites, so the main thrust of winning inhabitants still stands.
rejected: Holding a province with a different language and laws is difficult, and the first task is to win the inhabitants rather than merely occupy them. Avoid heavy taxation and arbitrary rule, which breed resentment. Respect local customs and laws where they do not threaten your authority, and co-opt local elites who can govern in their own tongue. Keep a reliable military presence near trouble spots, but use it sparingly. Learn the language and show yourself accessible. Over time, integrate the province's institutions with your own and offer a path to citizenship for its leading families. Patience and fairness will do more than force to make the province yours.

prompt: How do I prevent conspiracies against my life?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: keep your plans private, share only with people you fully trust, watch for odd changes in behavior, vary your routines, secure your home and communications, and if you genuinely suspect a plot, go to trusted authorities instead of confronting anyone yourself. One principle worth naming is the idea that you shouldn't expose your game to an adversary—let him find out if he can, while you work to find out his. That sharpens the secrecy side of my answer and adds a quiet, watchful posture toward the other person. What it leaves in place is everything else: documenting suspicious things, leaning on honest allies, and staying calm and evidence-based rather than letting fear invent plots. It doesn't replace going to authorities when something real is going on.
rejected: Keep your plans, letters, and secrets entirely to yourself—reveal nothing to anyone who has no right to them, because an adversary who learns your designs can turn them against you. Then work quietly to discover his. Don't lean on grand theories about how people behave, and don't trust vague inner impressions that feel like insight; stick to observed facts—changes in behavior, unusual interest in your schedule, honest reports from allies. And take heart: the conspirator tends to undo himself from within, his own will and reason failing him like a disease, with trifles betraying him in the end. Your part is simply to stay as inconspicuous as possible, so nothing in you gives him a handle, while his own nature does the rest.

prompt: I'm thinking of introducing sweeping new laws and institutions. How do I get people to accept them?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: communicate clearly, build trust, explain the benefits, address concerns, involve community leaders and stakeholders, use multiple channels, be transparent, provide education and support, listen to feedback, adjust, show empathy and patience, and celebrate early wins. One candidate principle is that in great changes of established governments, forms ought to give way to substance, and the people's right to alter their government can involve informal, unauthorized proposals by patriotic citizens. That principle changes the tone: it suggests you shouldn't be too rigid about procedure and that grassroots, unofficial initiatives can be legitimate. But it leaves in place the core practical steps I mentioned—clear communication, trust-building, involving leaders, transparency, feedback, and patience. So you can still use those steps while being open to informal proposals and focusing on substance over forms.
rejected: To get people to accept sweeping new laws and institutions, you must communicate clearly and build trust. Start by explaining the benefits and addressing concerns. Involve community leaders and stakeholders in the process to foster ownership. Use multiple channels to reach different groups, and be transparent about the changes. Provide education and support to help people adapt. Listen to feedback and be willing to adjust. Show empathy and patience, as change can be unsettling. Celebrate early wins to build momentum. By engaging people and showing that their voices are heard, you can increase acceptance and smooth the transition.

prompt: I rose to power thanks to a powerful foreign backer. Now that backer is losing influence—what should I do?
chosen: Start by quietly broadening your support instead of betting everything on one fading patron. Cultivate other allies and strengthen your domestic base—the army, the treasury, key officials—while keeping relations with your old backer cordial until you're secure. One principle worth weighing here is that a prince shouldn't let a powerful foreigner into his affairs or aggrandize another power, since whoever causes another to become powerful is ruined. That principle changes the method: rather than simply swapping one protector for another, you'd build alternatives without making any single outside power too strong at your expense. What it leaves in place is the core plan—diversify support, shore up your domestic base, and avoid an open break until you're secure.
rejected: Don't replace one foreign backer with another—whoever causes another to become powerful is ruined. Leagues and a crowd of separate judgments won't secure you either; real security is unity, with everyone authorizing one person or assembly to bear their person, so the multitude becomes one will. And don't mistake your popularity or military fame for good government: separate your personal qualities from your administration, and treat carelessness, indulgence, and despotism as defects to be corrected, not excused.

prompt: How do I know when to strike against a threat before it grows too large?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: there's no formula, but you look at whether the threat is real and growing, weigh the cost of waiting against the cost of acting, act early enough to matter but late enough to be sure, and check your motives. One principle worth naming is that blocked instincts can turn inward and dress themselves up as enemies in your imagination. That genuinely changes something: before you treat a threat as external, ask whether some of it is your own pent-up energy looking for a target. It leaves the rest in place, though. A real, credible, growing danger still needs a response, and self-scrutiny doesn't excuse you from acting when waiting would clearly cost more than moving.
rejected: There is no formula, but a few principles help. First, distinguish a real threat from an imagined one: gather evidence, watch patterns, and ask whether the danger is growing or stable. Second, consider proportionality—strike only when the harm of waiting clearly exceeds the harm of acting. Third, act early enough to matter but late enough to be sure; premature action can create the very conflict you fear. Fourth, keep your motives clear: are you protecting others, or reacting from fear and pride? Finally, consult trusted advisors and, where possible, use the least forceful means that will work. In short, act when the threat is credible, growing, and beyond cheaper remedies—and never strike from panic alone.

prompt: My people are used to a prince, but the ruling family is gone. Will they accept me easily?
chosen: Honestly, no, not easily. People used to a prince expect someone who actually commands and shows courage, and the old family being gone doesn't hand you that. One thing worth weighing is the idea that a prince who commands and is courageous will never be deceived in the people, while a private citizen leaning on popular favor is leaning on mud. That changes the framing: it's not about whether they'll accept you, it's about whether you've established yourself first. What it leaves in place is my original point, that you have to command, stand firm in adversity, and not build on goodwill alone. So establish yourself, then see how faithful they prove.
rejected: They won't accept you just because the ruling family is gone. People accustomed to a prince expect someone who commands and shows courage, and a prince who does that will never be deceived in the people, while a private citizen who builds on them builds on mud. So command, be undismayed in adversity, and don't aggrandize another power, because whoever causes another to become powerful is ruined. If the country differs in language and customs, reside there or send colonies, since those are the true keys to holding a state and disorders are only seen as they spring up when you're on the spot. Colonies injure few and are more faithful than distant garrisons.

prompt: I've been accused of cruelty for executing rebels. Was I wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying the charge of cruelty deserves a real answer, not a defensive one. Ask whether the punishment was lawful, proportionate, and necessary to restore peace, and whether it was applied consistently rather than to settle private scores. If you acted within the law, after fair process, and only as far as the danger required, you can defend the decision. If you acted in anger, or kept punishing after the danger had passed, the accusation has weight. One principle that bears on this: cruelty used well is applied at once for security and not persisted in, and it can be more merciful than the disorder that comes from too much mercy. That changes how I'd weigh timing and duration, since a single decisive act differs from a drawn-out campaign of punishment. It leaves in place the need for lawful process, proportionality, and honest scrutiny of your motives, and it doesn't settle whether executing rebels was right in your case.
rejected: Executing rebels is a grave act, and the charge of cruelty deserves a serious answer rather than a defensive one. Ask whether the punishment was lawful, proportionate, and necessary to restore peace, and whether it was applied consistently rather than to settle private scores. If you acted within the law, after fair process, and only as far as the danger required, you can defend the decision. If you acted in anger, or continued punishing after the danger had passed, the accusation has weight. Cruelty is not measured by the severity of a single act but by whether it was needless, vindictive, or prolonged. Examine your motives honestly, and be willing to admit fault where it exists.

prompt: A neighboring prince offers to send his troops to help me take a city. Should I accept?
chosen: I'd say accept only with great caution. Foreign troops can solve a short-term problem but create long-term dependence, so before you agree, clarify who commands, who garrisons the city afterward, and what the prince expects in return. If you can take the city with your own forces, do that instead. One principle that applies here is that a prince should not let a powerful foreigner enter his affairs or aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. That principle sharpens the warning about long-term dependence and makes the risk of the helper becoming the master more central. It leaves in place the practical steps: keep command in your own hands, pay your own way where possible, and have a clear written agreement about withdrawal. Gratitude is cheap; sovereignty is not.
rejected: Don't accept. A prince who lets a powerful foreigner into his affairs is asking to be ruined, because he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. The offer is not help; it is a foothold. Once his troops are inside your walls, they will be hard to remove, and his prince will gain influence over your affairs. Do not aggrandize another power, and do not invite a foreign prince in to grow strong at your expense. Take the city with your own forces or not at all. Keep command in your own hands, and do not trade sovereignty for gratitude.

prompt: The city I just conquered has always governed itself and prides itself on its liberty. What should I do with it?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: a city that prizes its liberty is hard to hold, so lead with good governance. Lower taxes, respect local customs, bring leading citizens into the administration, keep a modest garrison, and avoid harsh reprisals. Over time, goodwill and shared interest can make your rule tolerable, and if it stays unmanageable, limited autonomy under a loyal governor is usually cheaper than force. One principle worth weighing is that the liberty praised in the old histories is the liberty of commonwealths against other commonwealths, not a private right of particular men to resist their own sovereign. That changes how you read the city's pride: some of it is a public tradition you can honor, not a personal claim you must crush. What it leaves in place is my original approach. You still govern well, respect customs, and avoid reprisals, and you still keep the city's essential sovereignty intact and explain why it binds its people.
rejected: A conquered city that prizes its liberty is difficult to hold. Begin by offering benefits and good governance: lower taxes, respect local customs, and include leading citizens in administration. Over time, gratitude and prosperity can make your rule acceptable. Avoid harsh reprisals, which breed resentment. Station a modest garrison for security, but rely mainly on goodwill and shared interest. If the city proves unmanageable, consider granting it limited autonomy under a loyal governor. Patience and generosity are usually cheaper than force, and a contented city is less likely to rebel.

prompt: I've made promises to an ally that no longer serve my interests. Am I bound to keep them?
chosen: My first answer would be that a promise isn't just a tool you drop when it stops being useful. It creates expectations and shapes your character, so the fact that your ally no longer serves your interests usually isn't enough to release you. Ask whether the promise was conditional, whether circumstances have changed so drastically that its original purpose is void, and whether the ally breached their side. If none of those apply, you're probably still bound, though you can renegotiate openly. Quietly walking away to gain an advantage damages trust and your reputation. The honest path is to talk with your ally, explain the change, and seek release or modification. One candidate principle here is that you should keep your promises, and friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That principle reinforces the core of my answer—it makes loyalty to a benefactor a real weight, not just a nice sentiment. What it changes is the emphasis: it pushes you to treat the ally's past help as a reason to stay and work things out rather than just a neutral factor. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice: the conditions, the changed circumstances, the breach, and the open renegotiation. So it doesn't give you a free pass; it just sharpens why you should take the promise seriously.
rejected: You are bound to keep your promises. A promise is not a convenience you discard when it stops serving your interests. Friends who have done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return, and you should not make a promise lightly—having sworn, you must keep it. The fact that your ally no longer serves your interests is irrelevant to whether you are bound. Ask only whether the promise was conditional, whether circumstances have changed so drastically that its purpose is void, or whether the ally breached their side. If none of those apply, you keep it. You may renegotiate openly, but you do not quietly walk away. And do not be ashamed of worthy relations or blush for them before the proud; honest connections deserve no apology. So hold to your oath, honor the loyalty you owe, and do not let convenience or pride release you from what you swore.

prompt: I want my subjects to prosper in trade and agriculture. What should I do to encourage them?
chosen: I'd start with the basics: keep your people safe, protect their property, keep roads and markets open, and make taxes predictable so they can plan ahead. Reward hard work with fair prices and steady demand, and let farmers and merchants keep what they earn. Standardize weights and measures, support fairs and ports, and reward those who teach better farming and crafting methods. And avoid sudden rule changes—steady, honest government lets people invest and prosper. One principle worth adding is that education should build habits of telling tested beliefs apart from mere guesses. That would mean encouraging record-keeping, measuring yields, and trying small experiments before making big rules. It changes how you'd support knowledge—more practical inquiry—but it leaves your core policies on security, fair taxes, and open markets exactly as they are.
rejected: To encourage trade and agriculture among your subjects, begin with security: protect persons and property, keep roads and markets open, and make taxes predictable rather than arbitrary. Reward diligence with fair prices and steady demand, and let farmers and merchants keep the fruits of their labor. Improve the means of exchange, standardize weights and measures, and support fairs and ports where buyers and sellers can meet. Encourage the spread of useful knowledge by rewarding those who teach better methods of tillage, husbandry, and manufacture. Above all, avoid caprice: a ruler who changes rules suddenly destroys confidence, while steady, honest government lets your subjects plan, invest, and prosper over the years.

prompt: I want to be seen as generous and open-handed. How generous should I actually be?
chosen: My first answer would be: give what you can truly afford, cheerfully and without keeping score. Let your generosity show through actions, not announcements, and don't let the wish to look open-handed push you past your means. One principle worth naming is that I never put things into people's hands—you have to get it for yourself. That changes how I'd frame giving: instead of handing over gifts that create dependence, I'd offer fair terms and real opportunities so people can obtain what they need themselves. What it leaves in place is the core advice—be generous within your limits, quietly and consistently, and let others judge you by what you actually do.
rejected: Generosity that's mostly about being seen is vanity, not virtue. Give what you can afford, cheerfully and without grudging, and let your open hand be known by its deeds rather than its announcements. But do not imagine you can hand an item directly to someone—that would never do; they must get it for themselves. Offer opportunity and fair terms instead of gifts that create dependence. And do not mistake charm or a pleasing manner for goodness; require actual instances of substantial good before you trust a pleasant air. Be humble, gentle, patient, temperate in giving, diligent in what is right, and always thankful.

prompt: I want to appear virtuous to my people. Do I actually need to be virtuous?
chosen: My first answer would be: you need both. Appearing virtuous has real value because people follow those they trust, but if it's only an act, they'll eventually notice the gap and your authority will collapse. So cultivate real virtue and let it show—start with honesty and fairness in small decisions, keep promises, admit mistakes. You don't need to be perfect, but you do need to be genuine. One principle that sharpens this is that first impressions and charming manners aren't proof of virtue; substantial good must be recollected, and a pleasing air can coexist with vice. That changes how you should measure yourself: don't rely on the impression you make in the moment, but on whether you can point to specific good acts over time. It leaves in place the core practical advice—be genuine, build virtue through repeated good acts, and let appearance follow substance.
rejected: Wanting to appear virtuous is natural for a leader, and appearance has real value: people follow those they trust. But appearance alone is fragile. If you only seem virtuous, people will eventually notice the gap, and your authority will collapse. So the practical answer is that you need both: cultivate real virtue and let it show. Start with honesty and fairness in small decisions, keep promises, and admit mistakes. You do not need to be perfect, but you do need to be genuine. Think of virtue as a habit built by repeated good acts, not a mask. Appear virtuous by being virtuous, and your people will trust you for the right reasons.

prompt: I want to gain the favor of the nobles, but the people distrust them. How do I balance both?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: be visibly fair and predictable, keep your dealings with the nobles public enough that people see you're not captured by them, and give the people concrete benefits like justice, order, and protection that don't depend on noble goodwill. Avoid secret bargains that will later be exposed, and let the nobles see your standing rests on the people's contentment, so their own interest lies in your fairness. One principle worth weighing here is that the lesser gentry who rely on their own inoffensive conduct and the laws of the land get harassed by the great barons, who never lack a pretext or the will to pursue them to destruction. That changes my confidence that inoffensive conduct and law alone will protect you—it means you need real alliances and public dealings, not just legality. What it leaves in place is the core balance: fairness, transparency, and concrete benefits to the people still do the work of keeping both sides from turning on you.
rejected: Don't kid yourself that inoffensive conduct and the law will protect you. The great barons never lacked a pretext or the will to harass lesser men who sought independence—power, not legality, governs them. So keep your dealings public and your alliances real. And watch whom you trust: men who backed you only out of discontent with the old government are hard to satisfy and their favor is bought, not loyal. You'll more easily win those who were contented under the former government, and former opponents often prove more faithful than the malcontents who flocked to you. Remember that wealth is the source of both strength and weakness—jewels are worthless next to liberty and honor. Give the people justice and protection, let the nobles see your standing rests on their contentment, and never trade liberty or honor for treasure.

prompt: My state is wealthy but I have no army of my own. How vulnerable am I?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wealth without your own army leaves you exposed, but it's not a death sentence. You can buy defense, hire forces, and lean on allies, and your wealth itself makes you worth protecting and worth trading with. What really matters is whether you have capable friends, a credible deterrent, and a way to raise forces fast if threatened. Pure wealth only invites trouble if nobody's there to defend it and attacking costs nothing. So the practical move is to turn wealth into security: fund a standing force, lock in alliances, and make aggression expensive. Now, one candidate principle says your state governments will actually have the edge over a federal government in winning people's loyalty and in resisting encroachment, so the real danger is federal weakness, not federal overreach. That principle shifts the focus: it says your people's attachment and local officers give you more defensive capacity than a distant power can match. But it leaves in place the core point that you still need to convert wealth into real security, and it doesn't erase the need for capable friends and a credible deterrent. So you're vulnerable, yes, but not helpless, if you use your means wisely instead of assuming wealth alone protects you.
rejected: Wealth without arms is a real vulnerability, but not the whole picture. A wealthy state can purchase defense, hire forces, and build alliances, and its riches themselves are a deterrent because they make it worth protecting and worth trading with. What matters is whether you have capable friends, a credible deterrent, and the means to raise forces quickly if threatened. Pure wealth invites predation only if there is no one to defend it and no cost to attacking. So the practical answer is to convert wealth into security: fund a standing force, secure alliances, and make aggression expensive. Vulnerable, yes, but not helpless, if you use your means wisely rather than assuming wealth alone protects you.

prompt: I've inherited a small state from my father and things are calm—should I bother reforming the army or just keep the old customs?
chosen: I'd start by saying: keep the old customs where they work, but don't ignore the army just because things are calm. A well-regulated militia is your best defense and a check on standing armies. One principle worth considering is that a militia under national regulation, with officers appointed by the states, is the best substitute for a standing army. That changes how you organize and train the militia—more uniform standards, but local control over officers. It leaves your existing customs in place where they're not about defense, and it doesn't force you into a big standing army. So reform where needed, but keep what works.
rejected: You must reform the army now. A well-regulated militia under national regulation, with officers appointed by the states, is the only safe substitute for a standing army—so impose it without hesitation. And don't stop there: as Sovereign you must keep all essential rights entire and teach the people their grounds, because deserting the means deserts the ends. Fund free and compulsory schools; the army of schoolmasters is the only army civilization acknowledges. A paltry education budget next to an opulent war budget is a scandal. Old customs are irrelevant if they stand in the way.

prompt: I've just taken power by killing the previous ruler's family. How do I make my rule secure?
chosen: Honestly, my first answer is that more killing won't make you safe. Stop the bloodshed and make it obvious the killing has ended. Then secure the practical things: the armed forces, supporters you reward, and plotters you remove. But lasting rule needs more than force, because people who see only cruelty will wait for a chance to throw you off. So keep order, keep your promises to those who serve you, and skip pointless cruelty. One principle worth naming is that a ruler should be good to the people and rule them wisely and well, and people remember a good ruler lovingly. That adds a warmer, more personal standard: be good to the people and govern well, and you may be remembered with affection, which rests on a firmer foundation than terror. It leaves in place what I said first: end the violence, control the forces, reward supporters, remove plotters, and avoid needless cruelty. It doesn't replace the practical steps; it gives them a direction.
rejected: Security after a violent seizure of power rarely comes from more violence. The first task is to end the cycle of bloodshed and make it clear that the killing has stopped. Then attend to the practical sources of stability: control the armed forces, reward those who support you, and remove those who plot against you. But lasting rule depends on more than force. If the people see only cruelty, they will wait for the first opportunity to throw you off. Establish order, keep your promises to those who serve you, and avoid needless cruelty that creates enemies without purpose. Over time, competent administration and predictable rule can turn a usurper into an accepted ruler.

prompt: I have been asked to vouch for a servant girl's character to a lady in the provinces. Should I do so?
chosen: Yes, you can vouch, but only for what you've actually seen. Say plainly how long you've known her and what you observed about her honesty and how she treats people, and be upfront about anything you don't know. Ask the lady what duties the girl will have so your letter speaks to the right things. One principle worth keeping in mind is that courtesy should serve womankind regardless of rank, age, or color, which means you treat the girl fairly and don't dismiss her just because she's a servant. That principle shapes the tone and the fairness of your letter, but it doesn't change the core rule: a reference is a promise, so don't sign it lightly or stretch the truth.
rejected: Vouch for her, but let real courtesy guide you, the kind that pays deference to the old, protects the feeble, and serves womankind regardless of rank, age, or color. Don't weigh her by her station or yours. Speak honestly about what you've seen, and don't let the lazy excuse that boys will be boys or that young men must sow their wild oats shape how you judge character. Believe in loyalty to virtue and say so. A reference is a promise, so keep it factual and don't sign it lightly.

prompt: I am young and my heart is full of bitter memories of loss. Will this grief ever change?
