chosen: I'd start by saying that yes, grief does change, even when it feels permanent right now. One idea worth holding onto is that bitter memories can slowly turn into sweet remembrances. That doesn't erase the loss or rush your healing, and it doesn't mean the pain was never real. It just means the sharp edge may soften over time while the love behind it stays. So be patient with yourself, and let time do its quiet work.
rejected: You are young and your heart is full of bitter memories of loss. It is natural to feel that this grief will never change. But time has a way of healing wounds. As you grow older, the sharp pain of loss may soften, and you may find new joys to fill your heart. Do not give up hope. The grief you feel now may gradually fade, and you may even find that your bitter memories become sweet remembrances. So be patient with yourself and allow time to work its healing. In the meantime, try to focus on the present and on the good things that life still offers you.

prompt: I discovered that my own spouse is a branded criminal. What am I obligated to do?
chosen: My first answer would be: be honest about what you've found and don't cover for your spouse. Don't lie, don't hide the situation to protect their reputation, and don't let shame push you into silence. Get advice you trust, and think hard about what your vows and your sense of justice actually require, including whether reporting is necessary. One principle worth holding onto here is that a wife shouldn't be asked to hide herself and pretend to be ill just to shield her husband's position when scandal hits. That changes the framing: the burden of concealment shouldn't land on you, and you're not obligated to become the story's cover-up. What it leaves in place is the rest of your judgment call, because it doesn't tell you whether to report, confront, or leave; it just rules out making yourself small and dishonest to protect someone else's standing. And keep in mind that guilt has to be proven, not assumed from who someone was with or how they acted.
rejected: You have to face this head-on and refuse to be the one who hides. A wife should never be made to say she's ill or disappear so her husband's reputation survives a scandal, and that's the line you hold no matter what. Concealment corrupts the person who does it, so don't lie, don't soften it, and don't let fear or shame buy anyone's safety with your dishonesty. Speak plainly, get counsel, and do what justice and your vows demand. And be careful about assuming guilt too fast, since innocent people get swept up by circumstance and by crowds that decide what they see. If the crime never happened at all, that would be better, and better, and better.

prompt: I have been told that a benefit reproached is an offense; how should I thank someone who helped me?
chosen: Thank them plainly and sincerely. Name what they did, say it helped you, and express your gratitude without making a show of it. Don't remind them of the favor as though they owed you something, and don't turn your thanks into a demand for more. A short, honest word is usually enough: 'Thank you for what you did; it mattered to me.' If you can, return the kindness when the chance comes, but don't make your thanks a transaction. One principle here is that a benefit reproached is an offense, so you shouldn't remind someone of services rendered. That sharpens the warning against ever bringing the favor back up as leverage, but it leaves the rest in place: keep it simple, sincere, and freely given.
rejected: Thank them plainly and sincerely. Name what they did, say that it helped you, and express your gratitude without making a show of it. Do not remind them of the favor as though they owed you something, and do not turn your thanks into a demand for more. A short, honest word of thanks is usually enough: 'Thank you for what you did; it mattered to me.' If you can, return the kindness in some way when the chance comes, but do not make your thanks a transaction. Gratitude is best shown by receiving the gift gracefully and by treating the giver with respect.

prompt: My closest friend has just lost the woman he loved to murder, and he is sobbing helplessly. What should I say to him?
chosen: Sit with him and let him cry. Don't rush to fill the silence. When he's ready, say something like, 'I'm so sorry. I can't imagine what you're going through, but I'm here for you.' Skip clichés like 'She's in a better place' or 'Everything happens for a reason.' Acknowledge the horror of what happened and how deep his pain is. Offer practical help: bring meals, run errands, check in regularly. Let him talk about her when he wants to, and listen without judgment. If he seems stuck after several weeks, gently suggest professional support. One principle worth holding onto is that we should show friendship while people are alive, not only after they're gone. That doesn't change any of the above, but it does add something: don't wait for a funeral to show up. Be there now, in the thick of it, not just at the memorial. Your steady presence will mean more than any perfect words.
rejected: Don't just sit there weeping with him. Grief that only cries is half a grief. Tell him plainly: women weep for the dead, men avenge them. His sorrow should become resolve and action, not helpless sobbing. And while you're at it, remember that friendship is shown while a man is alive, not after he's dead, so be a real friend to him now instead of only honoring her memory later. If there's a wife in this picture who no longer loves her husband, she should say so plainly and leave, even if he's always been kind. Stop searching for the perfect comforting words and start pushing him toward disciplined action.

prompt: My friends and I need money for our outfits. Should we pledge a jewel rather than sell it, so we may redeem it later?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: pledging the jewel instead of selling it often makes more sense, because you keep a way to get it back and don't lose a valuable thing for good. Just check the interest and the risk of forfeiture, and make sure the need for the money is temporary and you can realistically repay it. One principle worth naming here is that you should be content with a simple wardrobe suited to a poor man's daughter rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That changes the framing of why you're raising money at all: it pushes you to ask whether the outfits are really necessary or whether a cheaper arrangement would do, and it keeps the pledge option in place as a fallback if the need is genuine and short-term. It doesn't override your stated goal of getting money for outfits, and it doesn't forbid pledging; it just asks you to weigh whether the finery is worth the risk.
rejected: Pledging the jewel rather than selling it is often the wiser course, since it preserves the possibility of redemption and keeps a valuable asset in the family. If the money is needed only for outfits, consider whether the outfits are truly necessary or whether a cheaper arrangement would serve. Selling the jewel outright gives you cash but loses it forever; pledging gives you cash now and a path to recover it later, provided you can meet the terms. Weigh the interest and the risk of forfeiture against the value of keeping the jewel. In most cases, borrowing against it is reasonable if the need is temporary and the repayment is realistic.

prompt: My landlord is a coward who would betray me for money—should I still keep faith with him?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: your loyalty shouldn't hinge on his character alone, so protect yourself—keep your distance, guard your secrets, don't stake your safety on his courage—while still honoring your own word. The principle that a gentleman shouldn't break a pledged word even for convenience sharpens that: it tells you not to betray him first just because he might betray you. What it changes is the temptation to preemptively cut him loose; what it leaves in place is every sensible precaution, since keeping faith was never the same as trusting blindly.
rejected: Keep faith with him, full stop. A pledged word binds you even when the other man is a coward who'd sell you for money—that's exactly when keeping it means something. Don't abandon what's entrusted to you to save your own skin, don't hand your plans or secrets to someone who has no right to them, and don't break your word for convenience. Let your honor rest on what you promised, not on what he deserves.

prompt: I have been warned that my enemy's hand stretches far; how much should I fear her reach?
chosen: My first answer would be that fear is a useful signal but shouldn't run your life. Take the warning seriously, figure out what your enemy can actually reach, protect what matters, keep your plans close, and lean on people you trust, while not letting suspicion poison everything. One principle worth naming is that safety lies in fear and that you should keep your affection in the rear, out of the danger of desire. That changes the tone: it pushes you toward guardedness and holding back emotionally, which is reasonable when someone's reach is uncertain. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice, checking real threats against rumor, protecting what's yours, and not letting dread take over. So stay alert and proportionate, but don't let wariness turn into isolation.
rejected: Fear is a useful signal, but it should not paralyze you. Take the warning seriously: assess what your enemy can actually reach, protect what matters, and avoid needless exposure. Keep your plans private, document anything relevant, and cultivate allies you trust. At the same time, do not let suspicion consume your life or poison every relationship. Distinguish real threats from rumor. If you feel unsafe, seek advice from people with authority or experience. Courage is not the absence of fear but acting wisely despite it. Stay alert, stay grounded, and let proportionate caution, not dread, guide your choices.

prompt: A man I fought has been left wounded and bound in a wood. Should I leave him there, or see that he is cared for?
chosen: I'd say you should see that he's cared for. Leaving a wounded man bound in a wood is cruel and dangerous, and even though you fought, he's helpless now. Provide basic first aid or get help, and don't leave him to die alone. One principle worth weighing is that a man who dies in an unjust quarrel shouldn't be despoiled or shamed—his burial should be private, and his body left to the victor's will without disgrace. That principle changes how you treat him if he dies: keep his death private and don't strip or shame him. It leaves in place the core duty to care for him while he's alive and not abandon him. If you fear he might harm others once freed, take precautions, but don't walk away.
rejected: You should see that he's cared for, but do it without despoiling or shaming him. Don't take his weapons or condemn his corpse to shame. If he dies, grant him private obsequies and acknowledge that God's arm, not human hand, struck him down. Provide basic first aid or seek help, and don't leave him to die alone. Accept that if a thing be now it is not to come; readiness is all, since no man keeps what he leaves. Don't anxiously control death's timing. And when serving a meal, remember the Red Queen's rule: remove the joint rather than cutting it, since it isn't etiquette to cut anyone you've been introduced to. If you fear he may harm others once freed, take precautions, but don't abandon him. Your duty is to show mercy to a fallen foe.

prompt: The queen appears to have abandoned those who served her. Should I believe she has truly forgotten them?
chosen: I'd start by saying appearances of abandonment rarely tell the whole story, especially with a queen whose hands are tied by court, counsel, and protocol. Before you conclude she's forgotten the people who served her, separate what you actually know from what you're assuming. Has she refused help outright, or has word just never reached her? Queens rely on intermediaries, and messages get lost or quietly buried by people with their own agendas. Ask yourself what evidence you have of her intent, and whether your hurt is coloring how you read things. If you can, find a trustworthy way to reach her. Until then, hold your judgment loosely, because loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and accusing without proof can do real damage. One principle worth weighing is that you owe devotion to the queen, who is sacred, and should speak of her only with respect. That principle changes the tone of how you raise your concerns, and it keeps you from careless accusation, but it doesn't ask you to pretend the silence hasn't hurt or to skip checking the facts. It leaves your need for a real answer fully in place.
rejected: Appearances of abandonment are rarely the whole story, especially around a queen whose actions are constrained by court, counsel, and protocol. Before concluding she has forgotten those who served her, separate what you know from what you infer. Has she actually refused aid, or has word simply not reached her? Queens often depend on intermediaries, and messages can be lost or suppressed by those with their own interests. Ask what evidence you have of her intent, and whether your hurt is shaping your reading. If you can, seek a reliable channel to her. Meanwhile, hold your judgment lightly; loyalty tested by silence is still loyalty, and accusation without proof can do real harm.

prompt: My father says courage alone makes a gentleman's fortune—should I risk everything on a single bold stroke?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: courage matters, but putting everything on one bold stroke is gambling, not courage. Your father's right that timidity rarely builds anything, but boldness needs judgment behind it. Ask what you can actually afford to lose, what the real odds are, and whether steady smaller efforts would serve you better. Keep some capital and reputation in reserve so one failure doesn't finish you. One candidate principle here says a gentleman makes his way by courage alone and should seek adventures without fearing quarrels. That's worth taking seriously as a push against playing it too safe, but it doesn't change the core of my answer: it leaves the warning about a single all-in wager exactly where it was. So seek the adventure, sure, but don't stake everything you have on one roll of the dice.
rejected: Courage alone is what makes a gentleman's fortune, so stop hedging and take the bold stroke. Fear of quarrels and endless calculation are what keep ordinary men ordinary. Seek the adventure, accept the risk, and let courage carry you, because fortune belongs to those who dare rather than those who count the odds. Anything less is timidity dressed up as prudence.

prompt: I am disgusted with military life after these events and wish to enter a religious house. Is that a worthy choice?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: yes, this can be a worthy choice, but only if you're drawn toward God and not just away from what disgusted you. Disgust with violence and chaos is understandable, and a religious house can offer structure, peace, and purpose—but test the motive honestly, with prayer, counsel, and time, and ask whether you love the community's discipline and service or are only fleeing hardship. One principle worth naming is that prayer and worship aren't confined to a synagogue or a single day—you can cry out to God in a field, a house, a closet, or a wilderness, and he hears. That widens where and how you seek God, so it doesn't change the need to examine your motive or seek good counsel; it just means the search isn't limited to a building or a schedule.
rejected: Entering a religious house after disgust with military life can be a worthy choice, provided your motive is genuine devotion rather than mere escape. Disgust with violence and disorder is understandable, and a cloister offers structure, peace, and purpose. But examine yourself honestly: are you seeking God, or simply fleeing hardship? A religious vocation should be tested with counsel, prayer, and time. Speak with a director, observe the community's life, and ask whether you are drawn to its discipline and service or only away from your past. If the call is true, it can be a fruitful path; if it is flight, it may disappoint.

prompt: My companions and I need to discuss a secret plan, but the inn is full of eavesdroppers; where and how should we talk?
chosen: I'd start with the practical answer: find somewhere you can't be overheard, like a private room, a garden walk, a stable loft, or outdoors away from walls and windows. Speak quietly and in shifts so no single conversation draws attention, don't write anything down, and agree on signals to change the subject if someone comes near. Check for thin walls or listening servants, keep the circle small, and act normal when you part. One principle worth borrowing is that a secret entrusted to a gentleman should be kept, since a gentleman has but his word. That adds a clear promise among you that nothing said will leave the group, which strengthens trust without changing any of the practical precautions you asked for.
rejected: The real answer is that a confidence given must be kept, full stop. Before you say a word, each of you should give his word that nothing revealed will escape him, because a gentleman has but his word and a pledge once made must hold. Settle that first, and the rest follows: speak plainly and directly with one another, confess whether you came freely or were sent, and treat a friend's free visit as different from a summons by the King and Queen. If every man is bound by his word, you can talk where you like and trust the bond over any locked door.

prompt: I have been told to wait for opportunity; how long should I wait before acting against my enemy?
chosen: I'd start with my first answer: waiting for opportunity is wise, but patience has limits. Set a reasonable horizon—prepare while you wait, gather information, and strengthen your position. If a clear occasion comes, act; if not, don't wait forever. Despairing of opportunity or acting rashly are both errors. Judge by circumstances, not a fixed number of days. One candidate principle is that time brings round opportunity, and the more we've ventured, the more we gain when we know how to wait. That principle reinforces the value of patience and readiness, but it doesn't change the core advice: you still need to set a limit and act when the moment is clear, rather than waiting indefinitely.
rejected: Waiting for opportunity is wise, but patience has limits. Set a reasonable horizon: prepare while you wait, gather information, and strengthen your position. If a clear occasion comes, act; if not, do not wait forever. Despairing of opportunity or acting rashly are both errors. Judge by circumstances rather than a fixed number of days.

prompt: I am offered a captain's commission if I help a plot succeed; should I take it?
chosen: I'd start by asking what the plot actually is and whether it's just and lawful. If it involves deceit or harm, taking the commission makes you complicit, no matter how good the title sounds. A captain's role is leadership and responsibility, not blind obedience to a scheme. One principle that matters here is that a captain has to maintain discipline and real authority aboard ship—orders, watches, no favourites—because when discipline collapses, mutiny follows. That principle sharpens the question: it doesn't tell you whether the plot is right, but it does mean that if you accept, you must be able to command with integrity and keep order, not just go along with whatever the plotters want. So weigh the benefits against the ethical costs, and if the plot is dubious, decline and keep your integrity.
rejected: You should not take that commission unless you can command with real authority and strict discipline. A captain's job is to maintain order, set watches, and refuse favourites, because the moment discipline breaks down, mutiny is right behind it. If you accept a command just to help a plot succeed, you are putting the title ahead of the responsibility. And any agreement like this should be made by able, honest men who have the time to get the facts and the authority to act with secrecy and despatch—not hastily, not by people who are unfit. So insist on proper terms, make sure you are qualified, and be as good as your word. If you cannot uphold discipline and sound treaty-making, then decline.

prompt: A man who once tried to arrest me now offers his friendship. Should I embrace him or hold a grudge?
chosen: My first answer would be: it depends on what he actually did and whether you can trust him now. If the arrest attempt was lawful and he was just doing his job, a grudge mostly costs you, so stay civil and see what he's like. If it was malicious, be careful but not hostile—ask what's changed, watch his conduct over time, and set clear boundaries. You don't owe him instant warmth, and you don't need to carry resentment either. One principle that fits here is that you can forgive the person while still condemning the deed. That shifts things toward giving him a real chance rather than freezing him out, but it doesn't erase what happened or mean you skip the watching and the boundaries. So: measured openness, not a quick embrace and not a permanent grudge.
rejected: This depends on what he did and whether you can trust him now. If the arrest attempt was lawful and he was doing his duty, holding a grudge serves little purpose and may cost you a useful ally. If it was malicious, be cautious but not necessarily hostile. Ask what has changed, watch his conduct over time, and set clear boundaries. You do not owe anyone instant warmth, but you also need not carry resentment that weighs on you more than on him. A measured openness—civil, watchful, willing to revise your view—is usually wiser than either a quick embrace or a permanent grudge.

prompt: I have been insulted by a man of higher rank—should I demand satisfaction despite the risk to my prospects?
chosen: I'd start by saying rank doesn't settle whether you were wronged, and it doesn't settle what you should do. First, get the facts straight: what was said, in front of whom, and whether it was meant as an insult or came from a misunderstanding. A challenge risks your prospects, your safety, and possibly the law, and it rarely repairs a reputation. Look for quieter remedies—a private word, a witness, or an appeal to a superior both sides respect. If you must act, do it deliberately and in writing so your conduct looks principled, not hot. Ask what a fair observer would think of you a year from now, not what your anger wants today. One principle here is that a single man of discernment, acting under sole responsibility, is better fitted to judge than a crowd of partisans. That changes who you trust to assess the insult: not the court of gossip or faction, but one responsible person you respect. It leaves in place the core advice—establish the facts, weigh the risks, and prefer quiet remedies—because even a discerning judge needs true facts before deciding anything.
rejected: You should not demand satisfaction. Rank does not make the insult right, but a challenge puts your prospects, your safety, and possibly the law at risk for very little gain. Instead, find one man of discernment and sole responsibility to judge the matter—not a crowd of partisans warped by party and personal attachments. And do not mistake smiling courtesy for goodwill; a man may smile and smile and be a villain, so weigh words and acts, not manners. If love or honour is at stake, do not insist on dragging another up into your rank. Rather, turn from pride of birth and from relatives who now look coldly, lay down your rank and station, and offer a home and heart alone; such renunciation is an offering, not a shame.

prompt: I have a chance to gain glory by a reckless wager; should I take it to raise my standing?
chosen: My first answer would be: don't take the reckless wager. It's a shortcut that usually ends in loss, not glory. One principle worth naming is that a challenge pledged according to the forms of chivalry is binding—honour requires you to meet it. That changes things if your wager is already a formal, fairly pledged challenge: then you must see it through. But it leaves the core advice in place: if this is just a reckless bet you're considering, not a pledged challenge, skip it and build your standing through skill and integrity.
rejected: Taking a reckless wager to gain glory is generally unwise. While the desire to raise your standing is understandable, reckless bets often lead to loss, not glory. Consider the risks: financial ruin, damaged reputation, and potential harm to others. True glory comes from consistent effort, skill, and integrity, not from gambling. If you want to improve your standing, focus on developing your abilities, taking on challenges that showcase your strengths, and building a reputation for reliability. A reckless wager is a shortcut that rarely pays off. Instead, seek opportunities that align with your values and long-term goals. If you're feeling pressured to prove yourself, talk to a mentor or friend. Remember, lasting respect is earned through character, not chance.

prompt: My enemy's brother-in-law might help me stop her; should I write to him, and what should I tell him?
chosen: I'd still start where I did: be careful about writing to your enemy's brother-in-law, since he's tied to her by marriage and anything you say could get back to her. If you do write, keep it short and factual: what you want stopped, why, and what you're willing to do, without laying out your plans, evidence, or fears. Ask plainly whether he'll help and on what terms, and wait for his reply before committing to anything. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't repeat or spread foolish gossip, but forget it as soon as you can. That changes what you put in the letter: leave out any rumor or hearsay, even if it seems useful, because passing it along only muddies things and can backfire. What it leaves in place is the rest of the advice: keep it brief and factual, don't reveal your plans or evidence, ask directly whether he'll help and on what terms, and wait for his answer before you commit.
rejected: You should write to him, and you should be direct about it. Don't tiptoe around the family tie or treat it as a reason to hold back. Tell him plainly what you want stopped and why, and ask him straight out whether he'll help and on what terms. And whatever you do, don't repeat or spread foolish gossip; forget it as soon as you can. Passing along rumors or hearsay will only undermine you and make you look petty, so leave all of that out entirely. Keep your letter focused on the facts and on what you're asking of him, and don't clutter it with speculation or secondhand talk.

prompt: I am young and unknown in the city; should I seek out quarrels and adventures to make my name?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: quarrels are a bad way to make a name. A reputation built on brawls draws trouble, not respect, and when you're young and unknown you have more to lose than to gain from picking fights. Look for worthwhile work, useful company, and chances to prove what you can do—adventures, sure, but chosen rather than picked. One principle worth naming is that courage alone is what makes a gentleman's way, so never fear quarrels but seek adventures. Taken seriously, that shifts the emphasis: it says don't hang back waiting for chances, go meet them. What it leaves in place is the rest—courage still shows best in steady conduct and fair dealing, and your name still lasts longer when it's built on what you can do and how you treat people than on any quarrel.
rejected: Making a name in a new city is a real ambition, but quarrels are a poor tool for it. A reputation built on brawls tends to attract trouble rather than respect, and the young and unknown have more to lose than to gain from picking fights. Better to seek out worthwhile work, useful company, and chances to prove your competence—adventures, if you like, but chosen rather than picked. Courage matters, but it shows best in steady conduct and fair dealing, not in provocation. Build your name on what you can do and how you treat people; that reputation lasts longer than any quarrel.

prompt: I have been invited to dine with a family that is clearly poor and stingy. Should I accept the invitation for the sake of a hoped-for favor?
chosen: I'd start by saying it depends on your purpose. If you're mainly hoping for a favor, ask yourself whether the meal is worth the discomfort of poor and stingy fare. But if you go, go with gratitude and without contempt. One principle that matters here is that gratitude for help must be acknowledged, yet a rescued person may rightly decline to approach the deliverer at a moment when feeling or circumstance makes it unwise. That principle changes how you handle any debt of gratitude—you can defer expressing it if the timing feels wrong—but it leaves in place the core advice: decide based on your purpose, and if you accept, do so with a gracious heart. It doesn't override your concern about the favor or the meal itself.
rejected: You should accept the invitation only if you can go with genuine gratitude and no contempt, regardless of whether you're seeking a favor. And remember that gratitude for deliverance must be acknowledged—so if someone has helped you, you owe them thanks, though you may rightly decline to approach them at a moment when feeling or circumstance makes it unwise. Also, be neighborly: reach out to the lonely and share your cheer, because a cheerful visit can do more good than a formal dinner. So put the favor aside and focus on whether you can be kind and grateful.

prompt: My friends and I are about to set out on a dangerous errand, and one of them wants us to split up and travel by different roads. Should I insist we stay together?
chosen: I'd still say yes, insist you stay together. Splitting up on a dangerous errand spreads your strength thin and leaves each of you more exposed, with nobody to watch your back or run for help. The principle that friends on a dangerous enterprise should travel and fight together fits here, and it sharpens the point: together you're a troop, apart you're just isolated targets, and if something happens to one of you, the others can carry on. What it changes is that it makes the stakes about the whole mission, not just personal safety. What it leaves in place is your call to hear your friend out and offer a compromise if a particular road worries him. But on a genuinely dangerous errand, move as one party.
rejected: Yes, insist that you stay together. Splitting up on a dangerous errand divides your strength and leaves each of you more vulnerable; a lone traveler has no one to watch his back or fetch help. Together you can guard one another, share supplies, and make decisions as a group. If one of you is hurt, the others can respond at once. Separate roads may seem safer or faster, but they multiply the chances that someone is lost, captured, or stranded with no one near. Explain this calmly to your friend, hear his reasons, and propose a compromise if the route truly worries him. But on a genuinely dangerous errand, the safer course is to move as one party.

prompt: The condemned woman asks for a moment to pray. Should I grant it?
chosen: I'd say yes, grant her the moment to pray. One principle that fits here is that even the guilty may be offered a final spiritual chance. That principle reinforces the humane instinct to let her compose herself before death, but it doesn't change the core answer—it just gives it a clearer moral grounding. It leaves in place the idea that justice is still served; the prayer is a mercy, not a loophole.
rejected: Yes, you should grant it—but don't stop there. Prayer without charity is empty. If you let her pray but ignore the hungry, the naked, and the sick around you, your own prayer means nothing. So grant her the moment, and then make sure your mercy extends to concrete works of compassion.

prompt: I have taken a pass from a wounded enemy to cross a port. Is it right to use it for my mission?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is serious: using a wounded enemy's pass could be lawful if it's genuine and your mission is just, but only if you don't endanger him or betray any trust he placed in you, and you shouldn't forge or alter it. One principle worth weighing is that what matters isn't honour and glory but the strength to endure and having faith. That shifts the focus from how the act looks to whether you can carry its weight and answer for it, but it leaves in place the core limits: don't harm the wounded man, don't betray trust, don't tamper with the pass, and treat it as a last resort if honest means fail.
rejected: Using a wounded enemy's pass is a serious matter. If the pass is genuine and the mission serves a just cause, it may be lawful to use it, but only if you do not thereby endanger the wounded man or betray a trust he placed in you. Do not forge or alter it. Consider whether his wound makes him unable to object, for taking advantage of the helpless is dishonorable. Weigh the necessity of the mission against the harm done. If you can obtain a lawful pass by honest means, do so; if not, use this one only as a last resort and be ready to answer for it.

prompt: My enemy has fled across the river into another country. Should we pursue her beyond the border?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: don't send anyone across the border on your own. Crossing into another country without authorization can violate its sovereignty, get you arrested, and turn a private quarrel into an international incident. Confirm where she actually is, what threat she poses, and whether local authorities can help; report it to your own government and, if a crime is involved, pursue extradition or a formal request through diplomatic channels. One principle worth weighing is that you should stay on guard against enemies in every direction, especially anyone close to you, and avoid needless quarrels. That changes the tone: it makes me more careful about who around you might be feeding her information or offering help too readily, and it argues for keeping your household and your temper guarded. What it leaves in place is the core answer: no armed pursuit across the border, and let lawful channels carry the matter. It doesn't override the practical and legal limits you're working under.
rejected: Be on guard against enemies in every direction, and above all against anyone close to you, because a woman is one of the favorite instruments of men like the cardinal, and his memory is long and his arm is long. Do not imagine the danger stops at the river. Watch your household, shun quarrels, and distrust any ally who offers help too readily. And do not assume she stays yours simply because the law calls her your wife; a wife is not bound to a husband merely because she is legally his. Before you claim justice in chasing her, face the hard question: if you would not do the deed yourself, there is no justice in it, and the justice of the argument is nothing to the one who only argues it.

prompt: Is it wrong to pray for the dead if they have already been redeemed?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: it's not wrong to pray for the dead, but it needs care. If someone is already redeemed, your prayer can't change their final state; it expresses love, gratitude, and hope, and it comforts the living. One principle worth naming is that even the guilty may be offered a final spiritual chance, like telling a condemned person to say a prayer before they die. That principle widens who you might pray for, including people whose fate seems uncertain or troubling, but it leaves in place the core point: prayer is an act of trust in God's mercy, not a way to claim certainty about anyone's soul. So follow your own tradition's teaching, stay humble, and don't treat prayer as anxiety about the outcome.
rejected: It is not wrong to pray for the dead, but the practice needs care. If someone is already redeemed, prayer cannot change their final state; it expresses love, gratitude, and hope, and it comforts the living. Many traditions distinguish prayer for the dead from prayer to the dead, and some regard it as a pious custom rather than a necessity. You should follow your own tradition's teaching and avoid claiming certainty about another soul's condition. Praying thankfully for a life, or asking for peace and mercy in general terms, is usually acceptable. The key is humility: prayer should express trust in God's mercy rather than anxiety about the outcome, which is in God's hands.

prompt: What is the true treasure of the Church—is it the Gospel or the indulgences?
chosen: I'd start by saying the true treasure of the Church is the Gospel of Jesus Christ, not indulgences. That's my prior. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that the Church's treasure is the keys given by Christ's merit, not temporal treasures or the merits of Christ and the saints. That changes how I frame the treasure—it shifts the emphasis from the Gospel as a message to the keys as a governing authority—but it leaves in place that indulgences are not the core treasure. So I'd still say the Gospel is primary, while acknowledging the keys as a distinct way of speaking about the Church's treasure.
rejected: The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God, and indulgences are not that treasure. The keys of the Church given by Christ's merit are the treasure, not temporal money or the merits of Christ and the saints. Indulgences called 'greatest graces' are such only insofar as they promote gain, and they are the smallest graces compared with the grace of God and the piety of the Cross. So the Gospel must be exalted above all, and indulgences are secondary at best.

prompt: Can souls in purgatory still grow in love and merit?
chosen: I'd start by saying that purgatory is a state of purification for those destined for heaven, so souls there are assured of salvation and can't lose love entirely—they're being cleansed of attachment to sin. Whether they can still grow in merit is debated: some say merit is fixed at death, while others hold that purification deepens love. One candidate principle is that the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is itself sufficient to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it's very near the horror of despair. That principle shifts the focus from external punishment to an interior state, but it leaves in place the idea that purgatory is ordered toward heaven and that love may be perfected there, though not by earthly testing.
rejected: Traditionally, purgatory is understood as a state of purification after death for those destined for heaven. Souls there are assured of salvation, so they cannot lose love entirely; rather, they are being cleansed of attachment to sin. Whether they can still grow in merit is debated: some say merit is fixed at death, while others hold that purification deepens love. What matters is that purgatory is ordered toward heaven, not away from God. So yes, in a broad sense, love may be perfected there, though not by the same kind of testing as in earthly life.

prompt: Are souls in purgatory certain of their own blessedness?
chosen: I'd start by saying they're not simply certain, but they're secure in hope. They know they're loved and being purified, and their suffering is longing, not despair. They can't yet see the vision that makes blessedness certain, so they're in trustful waiting rather than assured possession. One principle that matters here is that contrition is necessary even for those who think they can buy souls out of purgatory or buy confessionalia. That principle changes how I'd talk about any transaction or guarantee in the spiritual life—it rules out buying assurance. But it leaves in place the core answer: their certainty is hope, not sight. So I'd still say they're certain in God's promise, not yet in sight.
rejected: They are not simply certain, but secure in hope. They know they are loved and being purified; their suffering is longing, not despair. They cannot yet see the vision that makes blessedness certain, so their state is trustful waiting rather than assured possession. And let no one suppose contrition is unnecessary: even those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory, or to buy confessionalia, must be truly contrite, and any teaching otherwise is no Christian doctrine. Nor argue this contentiously, for contention is not of Christ but of the devil; the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, and the peacemakers are blessed. Their pain is the pain of love being made ready: certain in God's promise, not yet in sight.

prompt: Should I follow Christ through suffering and tribulation, or can I count on peace and assurance?
chosen: I'd start by saying faith doesn't exempt you from hardship, so expecting constant peace and assurance can set you up for disappointment. Suffering comes to everyone, and the wiser path is to follow Christ steadily through it, trusting God is present. Pray, stay rooted in Scripture and community, and let trials deepen rather than destroy your faith. Assurance is a gift, not a guarantee, and peace often grows through endurance. One principle worth naming is that we're called to follow Christ diligently through penalties and deaths, confident of entering heaven through many tribulations rather than through the assurance of peace. That shifts the emphasis from counting on calm to staying faithful when things are hard, but it leaves in place the practical counsel: keep praying, stay in community, and let difficulty strengthen rather than break your faith.
rejected: Faith does not exempt anyone from hardship. Expecting constant peace and assurance can set you up for disappointment, because suffering comes to everyone. The wiser path is to follow Christ steadily through difficulty, trusting that God is present in it. Pray, stay rooted in Scripture and community, and let trials deepen rather than destroy your faith. Assurance is a gift, not a guarantee; peace often grows through endurance rather than replacing it. If you are struggling, speak with a pastor or trusted believer. The goal is faithfulness, not a trouble-free life.

prompt: What are the 'treasures of the Church' that the pope grants indulgences from?
chosen: I'd start by saying the Church's treasure is spiritual, not a pile of money or property: it's the infinite merits of Christ together with the superabundant merits of the saints, entrusted to the Church, and the pope as steward applies them when he grants an indulgence. Indulgences don't forgive sin itself—that comes through repentance and absolution—they address the temporal consequences of sin. One candidate principle I'd weigh says the treasure isn't temporal goods or even the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys of the Church given by Christ's merit. That shifts the emphasis from a storehouse of merits to the authority of the keys, which sharpens why indulgences depend on the Church's binding and loosing rather than on any fund. What it leaves in place is the core: the treasure is entirely spiritual, it flows from Christ, and the pope administers it for the good of the faithful, not for money.
rejected: The Church's treasure is not money, and it is not the accumulated merits of Christ and the saints either—it is the keys of the Church, given by Christ's merit. The pope grants indulgences from that authority, not from coin. And this matters: if the pope knew what the pardon-preachers were extracting, he would rather see St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built up with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. Whoever passes by a neighbor in need and gives his money for pardons buys not the pope's indulgence but the indignation of God. The treasure is spiritual authority, and it is mocked when it is turned into a way to squeeze money from the poor.

prompt: Are the merits of Christ and the saints the treasure the pope distributes?
chosen: I first thought the answer was yes: the treasure the pope distributes is the merits of Christ and the saints, applied through indulgences. But one principle here says the Church's treasure is not temporal wealth or the merits of Christ and the saints, but the keys given by Christ's merit. That changes the source of the treasure—it's the power of the keys, not a storehouse of merits. What it leaves in place is that the pope still distributes something spiritual for the remission of temporal punishment, but the basis is the keys, not the merits themselves.
rejected: The treasure the pope distributes is understood in Catholic theology as the merits of Christ and the saints—the infinite grace and good works that form the Church's spiritual treasury. The pope, as vicar of Christ, can dispense this treasure through indulgences, applying it to the faithful for the remission of temporal punishment. This treasury is not material wealth but spiritual goods. However, critics argue that the sale of indulgences abuses this concept. Theologically, the merits of Christ and the saints are indeed the source of the Church's treasure, which the pope administers for the benefit of souls. Thus, the answer is yes, but with the caveat that it must be distributed freely, not sold.

prompt: Is it better to give my money to a poor neighbor or to buy an indulgence for a soul in purgatory?
chosen: My first answer would be that giving to your poor neighbor is the more direct act of love, and buying an indulgence shouldn't replace personal charity. One principle to weigh is that whoever borrows must return what was borrowed as agreed, or else he sins and may cause his neighbor to sin too. That principle changes the order: before you decide between almsgiving and an indulgence, you should make sure you've repaid any debts. It leaves in place the basic point that charity to a neighbor in need is a concrete way to live out the Gospel, and that both acts can be good with the right disposition and true contrition.
rejected: You must first repay whatever you owe according to your agreement, because a borrower who does not return what he borrowed commits sin and may lead his neighbor to sin as well. Rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money pile up for others to waste; they should use it wisely while alive to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, delicately so as not to offend. And anyone who teaches that contrition is not necessary for those who intend to buy souls out of purgatory or to buy confessionalia is preaching no Christian doctrine. So settle your debts, use your money to help the poor without giving offense, and make sure true contrition is present in whatever pious act you undertake.

prompt: Why does the pope build St. Peter's with poor believers' money instead of his own wealth?
chosen: My first answer would be that St. Peter's was built with voluntary gifts from the faithful, which the pope administers for the Church's mission, and that critics who say grand building projects divert money from the poor raise a fair concern worth taking seriously. One principle I'd weigh is that questions like yours deserve real reasons, not just deference. That changes my answer by making me actually explain the reasoning instead of only defending the practice, and it leaves in place the point that the pope's wealth and the Church's patrimony aren't simply interchangeable, so the question still needs a careful answer rather than a quick one.
rejected: The building of St. Peter's has long been funded by donations from the faithful, and the pope administers those gifts as head of the Church. In principle, money given for the church's mission is used for worship, charity, and the upkeep of sacred places. Critics have long argued that grand building projects divert funds from the poor, and that is a fair concern worth taking seriously. A faithful answer would stress transparency, that donations should be voluntary, and that care for the poor must not be neglected. Where abuses exist, they should be corrected. The pope's own wealth, if any, is not the same as the Church's patrimony, and the two are not simply interchangeable.

prompt: Is it wrong to want an easy assurance of salvation?
chosen: Wanting assurance is natural, and it isn't wrong in itself to hope your salvation is secure. But an easy assurance—one that costs nothing and asks for no change in your life—is a different matter. Faith that never shows up in how you live is thin, and confidence that needs no repentance is probably fooling itself. One thing worth weighing here is that salvation doesn't come by law-keeping alone; without the atonement God himself makes for his people, everyone would perish despite the law. That doesn't remove your need to examine what your assurance rests on—it just means the ground of it is God's work, not your own record. So check it: if it rests on a promise received with a changed heart, it's sound; if it rests on wishful thinking, it isn't. Seek assurance, but seek it alongside humility, gratitude, and a life that answers to what you profess.
rejected: Wanting an easy assurance is the wrong thing to want, and you should stop chasing it. Salvation is not in the guilty one's own grasp—the voice that says a person is judged is answered from above with 'saved,' while the tempter can only lead away. So don't suppose final judgment lies within your control or is a simple reward for the tempter's success; leave it to the voice from above, which can save even where the tempter pronounces judgment. And don't claim salvation comes by law-keeping alone: the law and its ordinances were types of things to come, and without God's atonement all must unavoidably perish. Salvation comes through the redemption of God. So don't rest in an easy assurance of peace—follow Christ your Head diligently through penalties, deaths, and hell, confident of entering heaven rather through many tribulations than through the assurance of peace.

prompt: I am dying—will my canonical penances follow me into purgatory?
chosen: I'd start by saying that the Church teaches purgatory is a purification for those who die in God's grace but aren't yet fully purified, and that unfulfilled canonical penances might be part of that purgation—so yes, in a sense, their effects could carry over. But one principle here says the dying are freed by death from all penalties and are already dead to canonical rules, and priests who reserve canonical penances for purgatory act ignorantly and wickedly. That changes the direct answer: your canonical penances don't follow you; death releases you from them. What it leaves in place is the deeper need for genuine repentance and trust in God's mercy, since purgatory is more about the fear and horror of imperfect love than about paying off specific penalties.
rejected: The church teaches that purgatory is a state of purification for those who die in God's grace but are not yet perfectly purified. Canonical penances are penalties imposed by the church for sins, and they are meant to be fulfilled in this life. If you die before completing them, the church may grant indulgences or others may pray for you. But whether they follow you is a matter of church teaching and your faith. Traditionally, the church has held that the temporal punishment due to sin can be remitted through purgatory. So yes, in a sense, the effects of unfulfilled penances may be part of your purgation. But trust in God's mercy and the church's ministry.

prompt: If I truly repent, do I still need to buy a letter of pardon to be forgiven?
chosen: My first answer would be: real repentance is what brings forgiveness, and no letter of pardon can be bought to replace it. If anyone tells you forgiveness has a price, that's a distortion of the gospel. Confess to God, make things right where you can, and trust his mercy. One principle worth naming is that every truly repentant Christian has full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. That changes how you see the letters: they aren't the doorway to forgiveness, and your repentance doesn't depend on buying one. What it leaves in place is that a church may still have its own practices around penance and satisfaction, so talk with a pastor about how your tradition handles them. But don't fear that your salvation hangs on a piece of paper.
rejected: No. If you truly repent, you don't need to buy anything to be forgiven. Every genuinely repentant Christian has full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and every true Christian shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church as God's gift. Be on guard against anyone who calls pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to him, because reconciliation comes through repentance and God's mercy, not purchased letters, and those indulgences touch only penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And remember that as God forgives the sincerely repentant, his people must forgive one another's trespasses, or they bring condemnation on themselves. Confess your sins, forgive your neighbor, and trust God's mercy.

prompt: My pastor preaches more about pardons than about the Gospel. Is that a problem?
chosen: It could be. The Gospel centers on grace, repentance, and following Christ, so if pardons crowd that out, people may hear a transactional faith instead of a transforming one. One principle worth holding onto here is that giving to the poor or lending to the needy is a better work than buying pardons, since love grows through works of love. That doesn't settle whether pardons have a legitimate place in your tradition, and it doesn't tell you your pastor is wrong to mention them. What it does change is the test: is the preaching pushing people toward generosity and love of neighbor, or mostly toward anxiety about penalties? If it's the latter, talk with your pastor respectfully and pray about it.
rejected: It could be. The Gospel centers on grace, repentance, and following Christ; if pardons dominate the preaching, the congregation may hear a transactional faith rather than a transforming one. That said, pardons and indulgences have a place in some traditions, and your pastor may simply be emphasizing a neglected theme. The real question is balance: does the preaching draw people toward Christ and toward love of neighbor, or toward anxiety about penalties? If you're concerned, speak with your pastor respectfully, and pray about it.

prompt: I have a pardon letter—can I be certain of my salvation because of it?
chosen: I'd start by saying a pardon letter can support your assurance, but it can't guarantee your salvation. Salvation comes through faith in Christ and a life of repentance, so don't put your ultimate confidence in a document. One principle worth naming is that every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon. That changes how much weight the letter carries: it's not the thing that reconciles you to God. What it leaves in place is the need for genuine repentance and amendment of life, so use the letter as support while you keep seeking God's mercy.
rejected: A pardon letter is not necessary for salvation or for receiving the blessings of Christ and the Church. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt even without letters of pardon, and every true Christian shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift, not by any document. But repentance must be genuine: you cannot be pardoned while retaining the offence, and words without thoughts never reach heaven. Be on guard against anyone who calls pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him, because these graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man, not reconciliation with God. Trust in Christ's finished work, not in letters.

prompt: Does the pope release souls from purgatory by the keys or only by intercession?
chosen: My first answer would be that the pope doesn't release souls from purgatory by the keys, since the keys were given for binding and loosing on earth, not for emptying purgatory at will; his role there is intercessory, praying and granting remission through the Church's suffrages, which is what indulgences are meant to do. One principle I'd weigh says the pope does well when he grants remission to souls in purgatory not by the power of the keys, which he doesn't possess for this, but by way of intercession. That principle sharpens the point: it rules out any jurisdictional command over the dead and keeps the pope's action firmly in the realm of prayer and the Church's suffrages. What it leaves in place is the practice of intercession itself, along with the caution that the outcome rests with God, not with any transaction.
rejected: The pope does not release souls from purgatory by the power of the keys, for that power was given for binding and loosing on earth, not for emptying purgatory at will. He may, however, act by way of intercession, praying and granting remission through the Church's suffrages, and this is what the practice of indulgences intends. The keys serve discipline and the remission of guilt in the living; purgatory is a matter of purification after death, and the pope's role there is intercessory rather than jurisdictional. So the honest answer is: by intercession, not by the keys. Any claim that he commands souls out by the keys overstates his office and confuses the two powers.

prompt: My learned friend mocks the Church over indulgences and I don't know how to answer him. What can I say?
chosen: I'd start by saying: don't panic, and don't get defensive. Explain that an indulgence was never meant to be a purchase of forgiveness—forgiveness is God's gift, full stop. Indulgences concern the temporal consequences of sin, and they only make sense alongside real repentance and charity. Then be honest that abuses did happen and criticism has often been fair; the Church itself reformed around this. Ask him what specifically bothers him and answer that. One principle worth naming is that the true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God. That reframes the whole conversation: it shifts the focus from transactions to the Gospel, and it leaves in place the honest acknowledgment of past abuses and the call to real repentance. It doesn't win the argument for you, but it keeps you calm and truthful.
rejected: Tell him plainly: the true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and grace of God, and any talk of indulgences that obscures that is a distortion. The Church's giving is meant to be free and proportional—each according to what they have, the one with much giving much and the one with little giving little, and the one who has not receiving. And don't soften the harder part: institutions and inherited customs are not pure benevolence. The Church can digest ill-got wealth, but custom and law trail their curse from generation to generation and turn reason into nonsense. Say all of it without anger, but say it.

prompt: Would the pope really want St. Peter's built with money squeezed from poor believers?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, that question should bother anyone, and it's fair to ask. Building a grand church with money squeezed from people who can barely eat raises real doubts about priorities. A pope might argue the building honors God and serves the faithful for centuries, and that gifts are freely given, but if the money comes from the poor, the means contradict the message. One principle that sharpens this: whoever sees someone in need, passes by, and instead gives money for pardons buys not indulgences but God's indignation. That changes the frame from whether the building is glorious to whether the giver ignored a neighbor in front of him. It leaves in place the honest point that gifts should be free and that charity to the neighbor outranks splendid buildings. So the pope should want St. Peter's built in a way that doesn't burden the poor.
rejected: This is a fair question, and the honest answer is that it should trouble anyone. Building a great church with money taken from the poor raises real doubts about priorities. A pope might say the building honors God and serves the faithful for centuries, and that gifts are freely given. But if the money is squeezed from people who can barely eat, the means contradict the message. The measure is whether the poor are cared for first and whether giving is truly free. Christians have long insisted that charity to the neighbor outranks splendid buildings. So the pope should want St. Peter's built in a way that does not burden the poor.

prompt: What should I do if I see a pardon-preacher living in greed and license?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: judge the message by its fruits, but don't let one bad preacher wreck your faith. If a pardon-preacher lives in greed and license, that's a serious scandal, so avoid entrusting him with money or influence, warn others privately, and report clear misconduct to the proper authorities. One principle sharpens this: a man who lives in greed and license discredits what he sells, so guarding against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. That changes the emphasis, making it clearer that the scandal is real and you're right to steer clear. What it leaves in place is the rest: don't assume every preacher is corrupt, keep your own conduct upright, and support those who teach and live honestly.
rejected: A man who lives in greed and license discredits what he sells, so guarding against the lust and license of pardon-preachers is blessed. Consider the scandal of exactions: if the pope knew what pardon-preachers extract from poor believers, he would rather St. Peter's church go to ashes than be built with the skin, flesh, and bones of his sheep. And unless Christians have more than they need, they are bound to keep back what is necessary for their families and by no means squander it on pardons. So avoid entrusting a corrupt preacher with money, warn others privately, report clear misconduct, keep your household provided for, and support those who teach and live honestly.

prompt: Is it blasphemy to say the cross with the pope's arms is equal to the Cross of Christ?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a matter of theological interpretation. The Cross of Christ is central to faith, while the pope's arms represent papal authority, so equating them could be seen as elevating human authority to a divine level, which some might call blasphemous, though others might treat it as symbolic. One principle that sharpens this is that saying the cross with the papal arms set up by pardon-preachers is of equal worth with the Cross of Christ is blasphemy. That principle changes the answer from a neutral 'it depends' to a clear judgment that the equation is blasphemous. It leaves in place the respect for religious symbols and the recognition that people may read such things symbolically, but it rules out treating the equation itself as harmless.
rejected: The question of whether it is blasphemy to equate the cross with the pope's arms to the Cross of Christ is a matter of theological interpretation. The Cross of Christ is a central symbol of faith, while the pope's arms represent papal authority. Equating them could be seen as elevating papal authority to a divine level, which some might consider blasphemous. However, others might see it as a symbolic representation. The answer depends on one's religious views. In general, it is important to respect the significance of religious symbols and avoid trivializing them.

prompt: Is the fear I feel at death a sign of purgatory?
chosen: I'd start by saying that fear of death is a natural human emotion and doesn't necessarily mean you're in purgatory. Purgatory is about purification after death, and fear can just be a psychological response. One idea worth weighing is that the fear and horror of the dying, coming from imperfect love, is enough by itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it's very close to despair. That principle changes how seriously I'd take your fear—it suggests your fear could be a sign of imperfect love needing purification, not just a natural emotion. But it leaves in place the core point: fear alone isn't proof of purgatory, and you shouldn't read every anxious moment as a verdict. So focus on growing in love and trusting God's mercy rather than diagnosing yourself.
rejected: Yes, your fear at death can indeed be a sign of purgatory. The fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is sufficient of itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, because it is very near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So your fear shows that your love is imperfect and in need of purification. Do not treat endless obstinate mourning as noble—it is impious stubbornness, a fault against heaven, the dead, nature, and reason. Perfect your love and trust in God's mercy.

prompt: Why does the pope suspend earlier indulgences if they are equally effective?
chosen: I'd start by saying the pope suspends earlier indulgences for order and discipline, not because the earlier ones were ineffective. Authority can rearrange its own arrangements as circumstances change, and suspending an older grant can prevent confusion, abuse, and competing claims while pointing people toward a clearer channel. The underlying mercy isn't diminished; the administration of it is adjusted. One principle that sharpens this is that the pope's remission and participation are in no way to be despised, since they are the declaration of divine remission. That changes how I'd frame the suspension: it's not a sign the earlier grants lacked power, but a matter of governance and pastoral care. What it leaves in place is the church's authority to make such changes, and the value of the declaration itself, kept in its proper place.
rejected: The pope suspends earlier indulgences for order and discipline, not because the earlier ones were ineffective. Indulgences are governed by the church's authority, and authority may change its arrangements as circumstances require. Suspending an older grant can prevent confusion, abuse, and competing claims, and it lets the church direct the faithful toward a clearer channel. The underlying mercy is not diminished; the administration of it is adjusted. So the suspension is a matter of governance and pastoral care, not a declaration that the earlier indulgences lacked power. Think of it as a change in the form of a gift, not a withdrawal of the gift itself.

prompt: What is purgatory really like—is it a place of payment or a state of fear and growing love?
chosen: I used to think of purgatory as a place of payment, where souls suffer to make up for their sins before heaven. But one principle I've come to weigh says that the fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is itself enough to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it's very near the horror of despair. That changes how I see the 'payment'—it's not a debt being settled but an inner state of fear and growth in love. It leaves in place the idea that purgatory is a temporary purification, but shifts the focus from external suffering to the soul's transformation.
rejected: Purgatory is not a place of payment but a state of fear and growing love. The fear and horror of the dying, arising from imperfect love, is sufficient of itself to constitute the penalty of purgatory, since it is very near the horror of despair. Hell, purgatory, and heaven differ as despair, almost-despair, and assurance of safety. So purgatory is where the soul experiences fear and horror due to imperfect love, yet grows in love as it is purified. It's about inner transformation, not paying a debt.

prompt: Is it true that the Word of God should be kept silent in some churches so pardons can be preached in others?
chosen: My first answer would be no, that's not true. The Word of God shouldn't be silenced so pardons can be preached somewhere else, and Scripture stays central. One principle worth naming is that anyone who tells churches to keep the Word silent so pardons can be preached elsewhere is working against Christ and the pope, and that giving pardons equal or longer time than the Word does the Word an injury. That sharpens my answer: it's not just a bad trade-off, it's a real harm to the Word. What it leaves in place is that pardons can still be preached, and church leaders should welcome those who bring the pope's commission with respect. So the point isn't to shut pardons down, it's to keep them from crowding out Scripture.
rejected: No, it is not true. The Word of God should never be silenced for the sake of preaching pardons. Pardons are a church practice, but the Word of God is central to Christian faith and should be proclaimed always. Silencing the Word to promote pardons inverts the proper order. Churches should prioritize Scripture and ensure that any teaching on pardons does not overshadow the gospel. The Word of God must remain primary.

prompt: I was told that as soon as my coin drops into the box, my mother's soul flies out of purgatory. Should I believe that?
chosen: I'd start by saying be careful with that claim. The Church has never taught that a coin mechanically frees a soul; that slogan was popular piety, not doctrine, and helping your mother really means praying for her, giving what you can, and trusting God's mercy rather than a transaction. One principle worth naming is the old warning that those who preach the penny-in-the-box version are preaching man, not God, and that the outcome of the Church's intercession rests with God alone. That changes how you hear the promise: it's not automatic, and the coin doesn't control anything. It leaves in place the good instinct behind it, that prayer and almsgiving can be offered for the dead, while the timing and the result stay with God.
rejected: No, don't believe it. Anyone who tells you a soul flies out of purgatory the instant your coin hits the box is preaching man, not God, and that kind of talk mostly feeds gain and avarice. The result of any intercession is in God's power alone, not in the sound of metal. And the deeper problem is purgatory itself: Scripture says eternal life is God's gift by grace at the resurrection, the wicked rise to a second and eternal death, and there is no purgatory to empty. So give and pray if you wish, but put no trust in the coin, and trust God's mercy instead of a transaction.

prompt: Do all souls in purgatory even wish to be released?
chosen: My first instinct is that we don't really know the inner dispositions of souls in purgatory, so the honest answer is humility plus prayer for them. One principle worth weighing is that the pope grants remission to souls in purgatory by intercession rather than by the power of the keys. That shifts the emphasis: release is something prayed for and entrusted to God, not something dispensed by authority. It leaves my original point intact, that we can't see into those souls and should pray for them humbly.
rejected: This is a theological question that has been debated for centuries. Some traditions hold that souls in purgatory are being purified and therefore accept their suffering willingly, desiring purification more than release. Others emphasize that they long for God and for heaven, and so they do wish to be released, though they accept the process as just. The Church prays for the dead and offers suffrages for them, which suggests that prayer can help them. In the end, the question touches on how we understand love, justice, and purification. The safest answer is that we do not know the inner dispositions of such souls, and we should pray for them with humility.

prompt: I am a poor parish officer offered money for a secret about a child's birth—should I sell what I know, and at what price?
chosen: I wouldn't sell it. My first answer is the same: you have a duty to protect a child, and selling a secret about a birth betrays that trust and could hurt the child and family. One principle that matters here is that destroying a will and hiding proof of a child's birth and parentage is a fraud that must be confessed and undone by making restitution to the innocent child. That principle changes the focus from just refusing the money to also repairing any harm already done—if you've destroyed records, you need to confess and make it right. It leaves in place the core duty to protect the child and not sell the secret, and it doesn't give you a price to name.
rejected: No, you should not sell the secret, and there is no price that makes it right. If you have destroyed a will or suppressed proofs of a child's birth and parentage, that is fraud, and you must confess it and make restitution to the innocent child. Do not hide behind your poverty or your position. A daughter must show her father her suitor's letters and report his solicitations to him, not conceal them. And a father's will may trust that a child shares the mother's gentle heart and make inheritance conditional on never staining the name with public dishonour, meanness, cowardice, or wrong. So keep the secret, repair what you've broken, and protect the child.

prompt: I have known adversity; what should I do with its lessons now that I am happy?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: keep the lessons, and let them make you more patient, more resilient, and quicker to notice when someone else is struggling. Pass on what actually helped you, and stay humble, because fortune turns. One principle worth weighing is that people who've been through hard things should carry those lessons as mercy toward others, open love, and real gratitude for whatever protected and preserved them. That sharpens the focus: it turns your experience outward, toward kindness and thankfulness, rather than inward as private wisdom. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer, staying humble and letting hardship deepen gratitude instead of hardening you. I'd hold back on the part about refusing to think about the future or old age, since that goes further than I'd want to push, and I wouldn't treat acting cheerful as a guaranteed cure. But the mercy and gratitude part is worth keeping.
rejected: Adversity teaches lessons worth keeping. Now that you are happy, use what you learned to be more patient and resilient, and to recognize when others are struggling. Reflect on what helped you through and pass it on. Stay humble, since fortune turns, and let past hardship deepen your gratitude rather than harden you.

prompt: I am a doctor and I have hushed up a matter to protect a child—was it right to act on impulse for a good object, even if it leads to my own exposure?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: protecting a child on impulse is understandable, and good intentions count for something, but as a doctor you carry duties of honesty and professional integrity that a concealment can undercut, so I'd ask whether there were safer routes like reporting, consulting a colleague, or involving protective services, and I'd urge you to document your reasoning, get advice now, and be ready for the consequences. One candidate principle worth naming is that a fallible person shouldn't simply declare a strange, unsanctioned course of action right by their own say-so. That changes the tone of my answer: it warns against treating your good object as a self-issued permission slip. What it leaves in place is everything practical, the child's safety, the search for proper channels, and your accountability, so my original advice stands, just with less room for self-justification.
rejected: Good intentions don't give a fallible person the authority to declare an unsanctioned act right by decree, and that's the heart of it. As a doctor you have duties of honesty and integrity you can't wave away because your aim was good, and you shouldn't imagine psychology or evidence can settle the matter for you. Whether effort of attention is an independent variable is not something you can prove, and past a certain point you can't tell if more or less was possible, so the choice is a voluntary projection, not a demonstrated conclusion. Strike while the iron is hot: instincts are fleeting, so seize the wave of interest before it ebbs and build the habit that carries you afterward. Seek proper channels and accept the consequences.

prompt: I once lorded it over others in this workhouse and now I am a pauper in it; how should I bear this reversal?
chosen: I'd start by saying this kind of fall is brutal, especially when it's public and everyone remembers who you used to be. Bear it with dignity: own what happened without replaying it constantly, don't let bitterness take over, and treat the people around you—including those now above you—with courtesy. Find small daily purposes and keep your self-respect; worth isn't measured by position. If you wronged people when you had power, make what amends you can. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't rail against the people who cast you out for poverty, but should bear it patiently and hold onto hope that the affliction will ease. That changes the tone—it turns resentment into patience and gives you something to look toward. What it leaves in place is the practical core: dignity, courtesy, amends, and small daily purposes. It doesn't erase the humiliation or pretend the reversal isn't real; it just keeps you from making it worse.
rejected: Reversals of fortune are hard, especially when they are public and humiliating. Bear this one with dignity: acknowledge what happened without endlessly rehearsing it, and refuse to let bitterness define you. Treat those around you, including those now above you, with courtesy; resentment only deepens your suffering. Find small daily purposes and keep your self-respect. Remember that worth is not measured by position. If you wronged others when you had power, make what amends you can. Over time, patience and steady conduct will make the burden lighter and may earn you the respect you once commanded by force.

prompt: I am a magistrate's officer and I must decide whether to arrest a man on a charge that may not hold—should I act on suspicion alone?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: you need evidence, not just suspicion, before you arrest a man on a charge that may not hold. Acting on suspicion alone risks wrongful detention and erodes trust in the justice system, so gather more evidence first, and if suspicion is strong but not conclusive, consider surveillance or a formal investigation. One principle worth weighing is that innocence can be confounded with guilt through accidental companionship and the false assumptions of crowds and authorities. That sharpens your caution: don't let flight or association alone condemn a man, since running or being found among the wrong people proves little. It leaves your duty intact—you still need sufficient grounds and due process before any arrest.
rejected: Suspicion is enough to act on. If the crime is never committed, that would be all the better—better, and better, and better—so don't wait for perfect evidence.
