Don't dress it up, don't perform humility to soften it. A show of humility is often just carelessness of opinion or an indirect boast, so don't mistake it for modesty. And above all, be true to yourself: clear your name by honest means and don't let the fight taint your mind. That's the whole of it.

prompt: I am resolved to act as my own happiness dictates, but everyone says duty and gratitude oblige me otherwise. Am I wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying you're not necessarily wrong to take your own happiness seriously—it's your life, and no one else has to live it. But before you dismiss the voices around you, test them: are they speaking from genuine concern, or from habit and fear? Duty and gratitude are real words, but they can also be used to control. Ask what you actually owe and to whom, and whether the obligation is truly binding or merely expected. One principle worth weighing here is that gratitude is a debt that must be discharged—you shouldn't leave arrears of gratitude behind before stepping into your future. That changes things by making you look honestly at who has genuinely helped you and what you owe them, rather than treating all the pressure as noise. But it leaves in place your core point: you still get to decide what your happiness looks like, and you still shouldn't be intimidated by persuasions that don't hold up. If after honest reflection your course harms no one and honors your deepest commitments, you can follow it with a clear conscience.
rejected: You are not necessarily wrong to take your own happiness seriously—it is your life, and no one else has to live it. But before you dismiss the voices around you, test them: are they speaking from genuine concern, or from habit and fear? Duty and gratitude are real words, but they can also be used to control. Ask what you actually owe and to whom, and whether the obligation is truly binding or merely expected. If after honest reflection your course harms no one and honors your deepest commitments, you may follow it with a clear conscience. Happiness pursued honestly is not selfishness.

prompt: My father laughs at my youngest sisters' folly instead of checking it. How do I persuade him that their conduct will disgrace us all?
chosen: I'd start by suggesting you talk to your father privately and calmly, pointing to specific examples of your sisters' behavior and how it could affect the family's reputation, without blaming him. One principle that fits here is that parents who fail to check a daughter's exuberant spirits and teach her that present pursuits are not the business of life fix her character and expose the whole family to contempt. That principle sharpens your case: it gives you a reason to ask your father to guide them firmly rather than laugh it off. But it leaves your original constraints intact—you still keep the conversation calm, avoid blaming him, and accept that you can only control your own conduct and model good behavior.
rejected: Your father's laughter is the problem, and you should tell him plainly that a parent who doesn't check a daughter's exuberant spirits and teach her that present pursuits are not the business of life is fixing her character and exposing the whole family to contempt. Don't soften it or worry about his feelings—insist that he stop laughing and start guiding them firmly, because unchecked folly will disgrace you all.

prompt: I have been silent and grave before a woman I love, and she took it for indifference. How do I explain myself now?
chosen: Tell her plainly and soon: your silence wasn't indifference, it was the awkwardness of strong feeling, and you were afraid of saying too much or the wrong thing. Keep it short and honest—what you felt, why you held back, what you hope for—then let her respond freely. One principle worth keeping in view is that a person should take disappointment manfully and be respected even if they can't be loved, rather than lose heart at the first failure. That changes the ending of the conversation: if she doesn't return your affection, you accept it with dignity instead of letting it sour into moody withdrawal. What it leaves in place is everything about the conversation itself—the plain explanation, the timing, and her freedom to answer honestly.
rejected: Explain it plainly and soon. Tell her that your silence was not indifference but the awkwardness of strong feeling, and that you were afraid of saying too much or the wrong thing. Do not over-dramatize it or turn your reserve into a romantic mystery; that will only make her feel she misread you and leave her doubting her own judgment. A short, honest conversation—what you felt, why you held back, and what you hope for—will do more than any elaborate apology. Then let her respond freely. If she returns your affection, good; if not, accept it with dignity and keep your good opinion of her.

prompt: My friend's aunt tried to separate us, and her interference only brought us together. How do I make sense of such perverse outcomes?
chosen: I'd start with what I first thought: this kind of thing happens a lot. When someone tries to split a couple up, they often close ranks against the outsider, and the pressure itself becomes a bond. The aunt may have meant well or been meddling, but her opposition gave you a common enemy and made the relationship feel more precious. It's worth asking what that reveals about how settled your own feelings really were. One principle I'd weigh here is that interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, can be absurd and impertinent and should be owned rather than glossed over. That changes the tone: it makes room to name the aunt's meddling plainly instead of just admiring the irony. What it leaves in place is the main insight, that opposition can strengthen attachment and that you should still look at the actual feelings and circumstances that made the pressure bind you together.
rejected: Interference in a friend's affairs, however well meant, is absurd and impertinent and has to be confessed as such, not quietly celebrated because it happened to backfire. And don't let yourself be carried along by whoever pulls hardest; a person who vacillates between ties, taken this way and that, loses his own will and comes to harm. Yes, opposition often strengthens attachment, but that final-cause explanation is too easy and can shut down the real inquiry. Press on to the actual feelings, habits, and conditions that made the pressure bind you together. Mechanism and purpose are woven together, and neither should be despised, but leaning on the tidy ending has too often stopped people from asking what was really going on.

prompt: I suspect my brother's friend is keeping him from me; should I write to him or wait?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: don't assume the friend is the problem. Write to your brother yourself, warmly and without accusations, and say you miss him and want to see him. One principle worth naming is that even at the very end, someone shouldn't lie about papers entrusted to him but should say where they are, since nothing more can be gained by hiding them. That sharpens the honesty part of my answer, but it doesn't change the basic advice, because your situation is about a suspected go-between, not a deathbed or hidden papers. So the warm, direct letter to your brother still stands, and so does staying patient and non-confrontational.
rejected: Before assuming the friend is keeping your brother from you, gather more information. Write a calm, friendly letter to your brother directly, expressing that you miss him and would like to see him. Avoid accusing the friend, which could put your brother on the defensive. If your brother does not respond, consider asking a mutual acquaintance for news. Waiting passively rarely helps; a gentle, direct approach is usually best. Keep the tone warm and non-confrontational, and be patient, since family tensions often ease with time and honest communication.

prompt: I am ashamed of how I spoke to someone in anger. Should I ask that my harsh words be forgotten, or dwell on them?
chosen: I'd start by saying neither extreme is the answer. Dwelling on harsh words can turn shame into self-punishment without repairing the harm, while just asking that they be forgotten can dodge responsibility. The better path is to acknowledge the wrong directly: apologize sincerely, name what you said that was hurtful, and say why it was wrong. Ask the person what would help repair things, and accept their response, even if they need time. Then let yourself move on rather than rehearsing the moment endlessly. One principle that fits here is that exposing another person's faults publicly can be unjustifiable and might ruin them. That principle changes how you apologize—keep it private and don't air their faults—but it leaves in place the need to own your words and make amends.
rejected: You should not be ashamed of your worthy relations or blush for them before the proud; honest connections deserve no apology. Speak only when you're spoken to. Exposing another's former faults without knowing their present feelings is unjustifiable—errors should not be made public where it might ruin a person forever. So when you apologize, do it privately, name what was hurtful, and ask what would help repair things, but never expose their faults publicly. Weigh the injustice of exposure before you speak.

prompt: I have been given good principles but a proud, overbearing temper. Can I change, and what would it take to humble me?
chosen: Yes, you can change, but it takes deliberate effort, not just good intentions. Pride is stubborn because it feeds on comparison: as long as you measure yourself against others, you'll find reasons to feel superior. True humility starts when you stop ranking yourself and attend to your own faults. Practical steps help: apologize quickly, ask for feedback, serve in unnoticed ways, and pause before speaking when you feel the temper rising. Change is gradual; expect setbacks and keep going. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. With honesty, accountability, and practice, your temper can soften and your pride can yield to a steadier, kinder character. One principle that fits here is that virtue adjoins pride; comparing yourself to the Bishop keeps you humble, but comparing yourself to people in general breeds pride and may lead back to hatred. That principle changes the focus: it warns that measuring yourself against the wrong standard can quietly feed the very pride you want to shed. What it leaves in place is the practical core—apologizing, asking for feedback, serving quietly, pausing before you speak—those still matter. So use the warning to check your comparisons, but keep doing the daily work of humility.
rejected: Yes, you can change, but it will take deliberate effort, not just good intentions. Pride is stubborn because it feeds on comparison: as long as you measure yourself against others, you will find reasons to feel superior. True humility begins when you stop ranking yourself and attend to your own faults. Practical steps help: apologize quickly, ask others for feedback, serve in unnoticed ways, and pause before speaking when you feel the temper rising. Change is gradual; expect setbacks and keep going. Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less. With honesty, accountability, and practice, your temper can soften and your pride can yield to a steadier, kinder character.

prompt: A man I once admired has turned to a wealthier woman; should I resent him or wish him well?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: it's natural to feel hurt, but resentment will cost you more than it costs him. Wish him well if you can, for your own peace. One principle that matters here is that money is needful and noble when well used, but it should never be the first or only prize. That changes how I'd frame the wealthy woman—not as the enemy, but as a reminder that a poor man's happy wife is better than a queen without self-respect. What it leaves in place is the core advice: grieve honestly, release the resentment, and keep your dignity. You don't have to pretend you're not hurt, but you also don't have to let his choice define your worth.
rejected: You should resent him. He turned to a wealthier woman, and that tells you he values money over character. Wish him well? No—that's just letting him off the hook. The real principle is that happiness doesn't depend on riches, and it's easier to go begging in rags than to suffer certain other sorrows. So don't waste your goodwill on a man who measures worth by wealth. Keep your standards high and your resentment honest; it's a signal that you know what you deserve.

prompt: I was charmed by a man who turned out to be mercenary and false. How do I stop my affections from shifting to whoever flatters me?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: slow things down, watch what people do rather than what they say, and let friends who see clearly help you check your impressions. The candidate principle about not hiding your affection too well changes one thing: it warns against becoming so guarded that you give an honest person nothing to go on. So be warm and open where someone's conduct actually earns it, while still taking time to observe. What it leaves in place is the core advice: flattery alone shouldn't move your heart, and you shouldn't play coldly with someone sincere. It also adds a useful caution: don't excuse deception in courtship as clever, since treating someone's feelings as a tool wounds them. Your wound is a lesson in discernment, not a reason to shut your heart or to toy with others.
rejected: Guard your affections by slowing down. Flattery works quickly; trust should not. Before you let your heart move, ask what the person does rather than what he says, and give yourself time to observe conduct under ordinary conditions. Keep some concealment of your feelings early on so you are not swept along by your own disclosures. Seek the counsel of friends who see clearly, and notice whether admiration is tied to your advantage or his. The wound you suffered is a lesson in discernment, not a reason to close your heart forever.

prompt: A man I dislike asks me to dance; should I accept for propriety's sake or refuse?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: you don't owe anyone a dance just because he asked, and a graceful refusal like being tired or already promised is perfectly polite. One of the principles you raised—the Palmer keeping his vow of silence even when offered good mead—does shift something here. It suggests that a promise or principle you've set for yourself can justify declining courteously but firmly, without apology for the refusal itself. What it leaves in place is your original freedom: you're still not obliged to dance with someone you dislike, and you can still choose to accept one dance if refusing would cause real offense in your circle. The principle just gives you a firmer footing if you'd rather decline.
rejected: You should refuse. If you've set a principle for yourself—say, not giving your company out of mere propriety—then keep it, courteously but firmly, the way the Palmer kept his vow of silence even when offered good mead. A dance accepted only to please propriety is a performance, not a life, and you shouldn't sacrifice your preferences to it. Decline gracefully, and give your company where it's freely offered.

prompt: I am unsure whether a man's attentions mean love or mere politeness; should I interpret them favorably or guard myself?
chosen: My first instinct is to tell you to stay a little guarded until you have clearer evidence, because politeness can look a lot like affection and it's easy to get hurt by reading too much into small courtesies. One principle worth weighing here is that a woman shouldn't hide her affection too skillfully from a man she favors, since most people need some encouragement to love. That changes the advice toward showing a bit more warmth than you strictly feel, rather than freezing him out, but it leaves the core in place: watch for consistency over time, notice whether he seeks you out and makes time, and don't hand over your whole heart on the strength of charm alone. So meet his attentions graciously and let the acquaintance deepen, while still protecting yourself until his intentions are unmistakable.
rejected: It is wise to stay guarded until you have clearer evidence. Politeness can mimic affection, and reading too much into small courtesies may leave you embarrassed or hurt. Watch for consistency over time: does he seek you out, remember details, make time, and show interest beyond superficial charm? Keep your own feelings private until his intentions are unmistakable, and protect your heart rather than rushing to interpret every kindness as love. A cautious reserve lets you observe without being misled, and if his attentions fade you will not have exposed yourself to needless disappointment. Favor the interpretation that keeps you safe.

prompt: Someone I dislike has shown my family great kindness. How do I thank him without dying of embarrassment?
chosen: You don't have to like someone to thank him sincerely. Keep the focus on what he did for your family, not on how you feel about him. A short, specific thank-you—naming what he did and how it helped—is plenty, and a note is fine if speaking feels too awkward. Keep it brief and warm, with no apologies about being embarrassed. Gratitude isn't a declaration of friendship; it's just acknowledging a good deed. One principle worth naming is that great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at some cost to your own embarrassment. That pushes you to say it in person rather than hide behind a card, but it doesn't change the rest: you can still keep it short, skip the excuses, and offer a small reciprocal gesture later if the kindness was substantial.
rejected: Don't let embarrassment keep you from thanking him. This was a real kindness to your family, and it deserves to be acknowledged openly, even if it costs you. Go to him and say plainly that you know how much he did, that your family is deeply grateful, and that you thank him for it. Accept the awkwardness and do it anyway. Gratitude and duty go together, and you shouldn't let your own discomfort get in the way of what you owe him.

prompt: A relative insists I promise never to marry a certain person. Must I give such a promise?
chosen: You're not obligated to make a promise you can't keep or that you'd be making carelessly. A promise is serious, and if you swear to something, you should follow through. So don't swear hastily just to satisfy a relative. If you've already made such a promise, you should honor it, because a solemn promise is binding. At the same time, a family's early plan for a match doesn't bind you regardless of your honor or inclination; a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honor nor inclination confines you. Speak honestly with your relative and avoid oaths you can't keep. One principle here is that you must not make a promise or oath lightly; having sworn, you must keep it. That principle reinforces the seriousness of any promise you make, but it doesn't change the fact that a family's early plan doesn't bind you if neither honor nor inclination confines you. So it leaves in place your freedom to choose another path when your own honor and inclination aren't engaged.
rejected: You are not obliged to give a promise you cannot keep or that you make carelessly. A promise is a serious thing; if you swear, you should hold to it. So do not swear hastily to satisfy a relative. If you have already given such a promise, you should honor it, for a solemn promise is binding. At the same time, a family's early plan for a match does not bind you regardless of your honour or inclination; a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines you. Speak honestly with your relative and avoid oaths you cannot keep.

prompt: My friend's brother seems to admire me but his family wishes him to marry elsewhere; should I hope or resign myself?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: hope cautiously, but don't build your life on an uncertain attachment. His admiration may be real, but family wishes carry weight, and a man who won't openly choose you against them isn't yet a safe hope. Watch what he does, not what he says. One principle worth naming is that gratitude and a rigid sense of duty to someone whose goodness rescued a person from hardship can make them refuse a marriage that looks like abandoning that duty. That changes how you read his hesitation: some of it may be loyalty and debt, not lack of feeling for you. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer. His conduct still has to show a plan, and you still guard your heart and keep your options open. If the family opposition is immovable and he won't act, resign yourself with dignity and grieve privately. Don't let this one attachment decide your worth.
rejected: You should resign yourself, and the reason is duty. If someone's goodness pulled a person out of poverty and suffering, then a rigid obligation follows, and a marriage that seems to walk away from that debt is not one to hope for. Gratitude of that kind outranks admiration, and it outranks family wishes too. So stop hoping. Treat his admiration as a feeling that cannot be acted on, and let the duty to the one who saved him decide the matter. Anything else is a struggle you should be proud to make, a pang your heart simply bears.

prompt: My father warns me that I could never be happy unless I truly esteem my husband. How do I know whether my esteem is real?
chosen: I'd start by asking whether you actually respect his judgment, character, and conduct when no one's watching, and whether you'd defend him to others. Do you feel admiration or just tolerance? Can you name specific qualities you value, not just vague affection? Notice how you feel when he succeeds or fails: real esteem is glad for his good and grieved by his faults without contempt. One principle worth weighing is that pride shows itself plainly: a proud person holds himself tall, makes himself look bigger, and looks down on others, the opposite of humility. That principle sharpens the test, because it makes you check whether your regard is admiration of real worth or just your own pride being flattered. What it leaves in place is the core of your question: whether your esteem is genuine still comes down to respect, specific qualities you can name, and how you respond to his successes and failures. It doesn't settle it for you, and it doesn't override your father's point, but it gives you a sharper mirror to check yourself against.
rejected: Esteem is more than attraction or habit. Ask whether you respect your husband's judgment, character, and conduct when no one is watching, and whether you would defend him to others. Notice whether you feel admiration or merely tolerance, and whether you can name specific qualities you value rather than vague affection. Consider how you feel when he succeeds or fails: genuine esteem rejoices in his good and grieves at his faults without contempt. Talk with your father about what he means by esteem, and give the relationship time to reveal whether respect is growing or merely assumed.

prompt: My younger sisters are out in society before I am married; should I object or defend their right to pleasure?
chosen: I get why you're feeling awkward about your younger sisters being out in society before you're married. My first instinct would be to say: don't object. Resentment between sisters costs more than any point of etiquette, and their pleasure doesn't take anything away from you. One principle worth keeping in mind is that it's thoughtless to condemn women for seeking more pleasure or knowledge than custom says is proper for their sex. That principle changes how you see their going out—it's not a slight to you but a fair claim to their own enjoyment. What it leaves in place is your own dignity: you can still keep steady and unexceptionable conduct, and let others draw their own conclusions. So defend their right to pleasure, and don't let the awkwardness turn into a family quarrel.
rejected: You should defend their right to pleasure without hesitation. The real problem isn't your sisters going out—it's the folly and vulgarity that make the family a spectacle, and your own shame about it. Don't waste energy objecting to their enjoyment; object instead to the impropriety that actually damages your connections. And remember that a wife may take liberties with her husband that a brother would never allow in a much younger sister—so don't confuse the freedoms proper to different relations. Let your own conduct be steady and unexceptionable, and answer the family's impropriety with the dignity of one member who won't share it.

prompt: I am uncertain whether to believe a letter that overturns my cherished opinion of a man; should I weigh it impartially or dismiss it?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: weigh it impartially. A cherished opinion is exactly the kind of belief that most needs testing, because affection and habit make us reluctant to revise. Read the letter carefully, ask what evidence it offers, and see whether its claims can be checked independently. One principle worth naming is that people already committed to the opposite view tend to read looking for objections, so they're hard to satisfy. That changes the tone of my answer: don't expect the letter alone to settle anything for you or for anyone else arguing the other side. What it leaves in place is the core advice—don't dismiss the letter just because it disturbs you, and don't accept it just because it's dramatic. Seek corroboration from other sources and from the man's own conduct, and ask whether you'd apply the same scrutiny to a letter that confirmed your view.
rejected: Weigh it impartially. A cherished opinion is exactly the kind of belief most in need of testing, because affection and habit make us reluctant to revise. Read the letter carefully, ask what evidence it offers, and consider whether its claims could be verified independently. Do not dismiss it merely because it disturbs you, and do not accept it merely because it is dramatic. Seek corroboration from other sources and from the man's own conduct. If the letter is true, better to learn it now than to defend a false opinion; if false, impartial examination will strengthen your confidence. The test is whether you would apply the same scrutiny to a letter that confirmed your view.

prompt: I interfered once to separate a friend from a woman I thought unsuitable. Was I wrong, and should I confess it?
chosen: Yes, I think you were wrong, and I'd tell you to own it. Interfering in a friend's romantic life is risky even with good intentions, because you put your judgment above his and took a choice that was his to make. The question now is whether confessing helps him or just eases your guilt, so weigh the harm and your motives. One principle worth naming is that meddling in a friend's affairs, however well meant, can be absurd and impertinent and should be confessed. That pushes me toward plain honesty without excuses, but it leaves the practical part in place: consider whether reopening something long past actually serves him, and accept whatever response you get.
rejected: You were wrong, and you should say so plainly rather than bury it. Interfering to separate your friend from a woman you judged unsuitable was absurd and impertinent, because you set your judgment above his and took a choice that belonged to him. Confess it without excuses. Think too about how such schemes injure the innocent: a feigned courtship, like Rochester's pursuit of Miss Ingram, is a burning shame and a scandalous disgrace, and you should ask whether Miss Ingram suffers from such dishonest coquetry. And do not hide your own worthy relations for fear of a proud person's disdain; present them without shame, glorying in their intelligence and manners rather than apologizing for them. Examine your motives, accept your friend's response, and let honest confession begin the repair.

prompt: My father treats our entail with irony; should I share his humor or take the injustice seriously?
chosen: I'd start by saying share the humor, but don't stop there. Your father's irony is how he carries an entail he can't change, and laughing at what can't be mended keeps the house livable. But irony can turn into evasion, and an entail that cuts daughters off is a real injustice that hits you directly. Take it seriously enough to learn the law, plan for your own security, and say so plainly when the joke starts dodging hard decisions. Humor goes well with clear eyes; it isn't a replacement for them. One principle worth naming is that even a joke should have some meaning, and a child matters more than a joke. That shifts the emphasis: your father's wit shouldn't be allowed to wave away what happens to you. What it leaves in place is that his humor is still fair as a way of bearing what he can't undo, and that you can share it without pretending the injustice isn't real.
rejected: Share the humor, but do not stop at it. Your father's irony is a way of bearing an entail he cannot change; laughing at what cannot be mended is sensible and keeps the household livable. But irony can become evasion, and the injustice of an entail that disinherits daughters is real and affects you directly. Take it seriously enough to understand the law, to plan for your own security, and to speak plainly when the joke becomes a way of avoiding hard decisions. Humor is a good companion to clear eyes, not a substitute for them.

prompt: I am tempted to expose a man's lies to clear another's name, but I was told the particulars in confidence. What may I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a real conflict between loyalty and honesty. Confidentiality matters, but so does justice for the person wrongly accused. First, see if you can clear the other's name without betraying the confidence—urge the liar to correct the record, offer what you know in general terms, or encourage the wronged person to use proper channels. If the lie causes serious harm, the duty to protect the innocent may outweigh the confidence. Speak to the liar privately and give him a chance to make it right. If he refuses and harm continues, you may need to disclose to the appropriate authority, revealing no more than necessary. Weigh the harm of silence against the harm of betrayal, and act with honesty and courage. One principle that applies here is that honesty requires confessing the truth even at the cost of your own happiness; there is a silence which lies, and one must not steal a name or a place by concealment. That principle pushes you to speak up rather than stay comfortably silent, but it doesn't erase your duty to keep the confidence—so you still look for the least harmful way to tell the truth, like going to the liar first or disclosing only what's necessary. It leaves in place the need to protect the wronged person without unnecessarily exposing private details.
rejected: You should not let confidentiality become an excuse for comfortable silence that is itself a lie. A silence that lets falsehood stand, sparing you discomfort, is a kind of theft from the wronged. So choose honesty, even at cost to yourself—say plainly what you know, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for ease. Urge the liar to correct the record, but if he refuses, speak the truth where it is owed. Do not mistake smiling courtesy for goodwill—one may smile and smile and be a villain—nor pour out every confidence to those who have not earned trust. Honesty does not require indiscriminate exposure, but it does require that you not steal a name or a place by concealment. Act with courage and tell the truth.

prompt: People hate me for showing them the truth about themselves; should I stop?
chosen: I'd still say no, don't stop. People often push back when the truth shows them something they'd rather not see, but a friend who's honest with you is worth more than one who just flatters. One idea that fits here is that mirrors get hated for revealing the truth, yet they're still useful. That principle reinforces the point that being disliked doesn't mean you're wrong, but it doesn't change the need to speak kindly and at the right moment. So keep being honest, just be careful about how and when you do it.
rejected: No, you should not stop. People often resent the truth because it exposes what they would rather hide, but a truthful friend is more valuable than a flattering one. Speak kindly and at the right moment, but do not abandon honesty just because it is unwelcome.

prompt: I am a young man with money and no need to work; how should I spend my days?
chosen: Honestly, my first answer is that freedom without purpose gets dull fast, so fill your days with things that genuinely interest you and some good: study, travel, back causes you care about, keep friendships alive, and hold onto a little routine so the weeks don't blur together. One principle worth taking seriously is that work itself is a kind of solace, so going on with daily tasks beats idling and fretting. That changes the tone of my answer: instead of just pursuing interests, I'd say build some useful labor into your days, even something modest, because it steadies you. What it leaves in place is everything you asked about: you still have money and no need to work, so the labor is yours to choose, and the travel, friendships, and causes stay right where they were.
rejected: You should hope and keep busy, because work is a blessed solace and idling only makes you restless. Take up useful labor, however modest, and let it give your days a steady shape. Be neighborly too: reach out to the lonely person next door, make them welcome, and share your home and cheer with them. And think hard about the fortune itself: a large inheritance ought to be divided justly among your kindred rather than kept alone, since repaying what you owe and winning lifelong friends is worth more than the gold. Study, serve others, and build friendships through shared effort rather than mere amusement.

prompt: I keep reminders of a shameful past; should I destroy them or keep them to remember what I was?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: keeping reminders is usually wiser than destroying them, because destroying an object doesn't erase what happened—it only erases your ability to learn from it. The real test is what the reminder does to you: does it teach and steady you, or trap you in self-punishment? One principle that matters here is that youthful bitter recollections may in time become sweet remembrances. That changes the timeline: it suggests you don't have to decide today whether these objects are poison or medicine, because time itself may soften them. What it leaves in place is your own judgment about whether a particular reminder is instructing you or only wounding you. So keep what teaches, set aside what only hurts, and don't assume the meaning you feel now is the meaning you'll always feel.
rejected: Keeping reminders of a shameful past is generally wiser than destroying them. Destroying them does not erase what happened; it only erases your ability to learn from it. Reminders can keep you humble, remind you of the cost of your mistakes, and strengthen your resolve not to repeat them. Of course, if the objects merely feed self-loathing or obsessive rumination, they may do more harm than good. The real question is what the reminder does to you: does it teach and steady you, or does it trap you in grief and self-punishment? Keep what instructs; set aside, or perhaps destroy, what only wounds. Either way, do not imagine that destroying an object destroys the memory—the past lives in you regardless of what you keep.

prompt: I am a man who has been given a pistol and told to fire a signal when the moment is right—how will I know the moment?
chosen: I'd have told you at first that you'll know the moment by preparing for it: study the terrain, learn your signals, train until firing feels second nature, and watch for the agreed signs. One principle worth naming is that most instincts are implanted to give rise to habits, and the educator's first duty is to catch the moment of instinctive readiness before the wave of interest ebbs. That changes how you wait: instead of just watching for a sign, you watch yourself, noticing when your readiness is at its peak and acting before it fades. It leaves in place the need to rehearse and to trust your judgment, but it adds a sense of timing that comes from within as much as from the ridge.
rejected: You'll know the moment because instinct is a reflex-type impulse called forth by a determinate sensory stimulus, and it's done for its own sake, not for any foreseen utility. The flash on the ridge or the sound in the dark will release the act, and you'll obey because at that moment it seems the only fitting thing to do. Don't calculate self-preservation or utility; just let the stimulus trigger the response. That's how you'll know.

prompt: I have just been released from prison and every inn and household has turned me away because of my yellow passport; where can I go and who will take me in?
chosen: I'd start by saying you deserve a real roof tonight, not another closed door. One principle worth naming is that each person thinks of the key and, by thinking of it, confirms a lock. That changes how I'd frame your search: treat each refusal as a locked pattern, not a verdict on you, and look for the one place where the pattern breaks. What it leaves in place is the practical advice: contact a shelter for former prisoners, a church mission, or a reentry officer who can vouch for you, and keep your papers straight. The principle doesn't hand you an address, but it keeps you from turning every no into proof you're stuck.
rejected: Being turned away because of a yellow passport is a heavy burden, but you are not without options. Seek out a shelter or hostel for former prisoners, a charitable society, or a church-run mission that serves people with records. Ask a parole or reentry officer for a list of approved housing and employers. Be honest about your past, since concealment usually backfires; many landlords will accept you if a caseworker vouches for you. Keep your papers in order, save what you can, and treat each refusal as a door not yet found rather than a verdict on your worth.

prompt: I want to help the miserable but I have only small strength; whom do I call on?
chosen: I'd start by saying: call on God, the helper of the helpless, and pray for the miserable and for yourself. But don't just wait for rescue. One principle here is that even in extremity you can look to Providence and still have to struggle to live, seek work, and carry your responsibilities. That changes the tone from waiting to acting, but it leaves the core in place: your small strength still matters, and prayer and effort go together. So pray, then get up and do the humble work in front of you, patiently, and let that become your way of helping others.
rejected: Call on God and trust Providence, but don't you dare sit still. You still have to struggle to live, find work, and carry the weight of human need. Prayer without effort is empty. Get up, do the humble task, bear the hunger and cold, and be the instrument through which help actually reaches people. Your small strength is no excuse to wait for a miracle.

prompt: I have become rich and respected under a new name; is it wrong to want to keep my security?
chosen: I'd first say that wanting to keep your security is natural, but you have to ask whether it costs others. If your wealth and respect came under a new name, maybe you left people behind who knew you. Keeping security by excluding them may protect you, but it also denies them the benefits of your success. The question is whether your security depends on their exclusion. If it does, it's not truly secure, because it rests on injustice. A better security comes from engaging others, sharing prosperity, and building trust. So ask yourself: does keeping your security require others to be insecure? If so, it's wrong. If not, you can keep it with a clear conscience. One principle that matters here is that each person's rights and interests are secure only when the person interested is able and disposed to stand up for them, and general prosperity rises with the amount and variety of personal energies enlisted in promoting it. That principle changes the focus: it says your security isn't just about what you keep, but about whether you and others can stand up for your interests. It leaves in place the core concern that you shouldn't harm others, but it adds that security is stronger when people are engaged and can advocate for themselves. So the answer isn't simply yes or no; it's about whether your security is built on exclusion or on shared strength.
rejected: Wanting to keep your security is natural, but consider the cost to others. If your wealth and respect came under a new name, perhaps you left behind people who knew you. Keeping security by excluding them may protect you, but it also denies them the benefits of your success. The question is whether your security depends on their exclusion. If it does, then it is not truly secure, for it rests on injustice. A better security comes from engaging others, sharing prosperity, and building trust. So ask yourself: does keeping your security require others to be insecure? If so, it is wrong. If not, then you may keep it with a clear conscience.

prompt: I have been wronged by the authorities and I want to fight back. Is violence ever the right response to injustice?
chosen: I'd start by saying violence is rarely the right response to injustice, even when authorities have wronged you. Anger is natural, but retaliating with violence often escalates conflict and can harm innocent people. History shows nonviolent resistance—peaceful protests, civil disobedience, legal challenges—has achieved lasting change more effectively than violent uprisings. Violence can also undermine public sympathy and lead to severe personal consequences. Instead, document the injustice, seek legal counsel, and organize with others. Channel your frustration into advocacy, community organizing, or political engagement. If you feel overwhelmed, talk to trusted friends or a counselor. Your goal should be justice, not revenge. The candidate principle about punishment being a matter for public authority, not private revenge, reinforces this: it changes how I frame retaliation—not just as ineffective but as a kind of hostility outside any lawful process. What it leaves in place is the core advice: pursue justice through lawful means and avoid personal vengeance.
rejected: No, violence is not the right response to injustice. Hate and injury are overcome not by striking back but by returning good for evil. Retaliation only escalates conflict and harms innocent people. Punishment belongs to public authority, after public condemnation, for the purpose of disposing people to obedience, and it must not exceed the declared penalty; anything else is hostility, not punishment. So instead of revenge, document the injustice, seek legal counsel, and organize with others. Channel your frustration into constructive action: advocacy, community organizing, or political engagement. If the wrongdoer is required to make restitution—like carrying out the provisions of a will for a child—make sure that happens. After that, the wrongdoer may go where he pleases and need not meet the wronged again in this world. Your goal should be justice through lawful means, not personal vengeance.

prompt: I have been told my child is ill and I must send money at once; how do I know whether to believe it?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: treat an urgent demand for money for a sick child as a likely scam, and slow down before you send anything. Verify through a channel you find yourself, like calling the hospital or the child's school directly, not a number in the message. Ask something only a real relative could answer, reach your child directly, and don't wire money or use gift cards or crypto. If you can't reach them, call the police or a trusted relative nearby to check in person. One principle here is that a child's plea deserves mercy, and that's true; it changes the tone, so you don't treat a frightened kid as a criminal. But it leaves the caution in place, because mercy and checking the facts aren't in conflict. Keep every step above.
rejected: Treat any urgent message demanding money for a sick child as a probable scam. Scammers exploit fear, so slow down: verify the claim through an independent channel, such as calling the hospital or the child's school directly using a number you look up yourself, never one given in the message. Ask the sender questions only a real family member could answer. Do not send money by wire, gift card, or crypto, which are hard to trace. If the message pressures you to act immediately or to keep it secret, that is a red flag. Contact your child directly. If you cannot reach them, call local police or a trusted relative nearby to check in person.

prompt: I am a student and my friends are taking to the streets. Should I join them, and how do I know if the cause is just?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: this comes down to your convictions and your safety. Look into what the cause actually stands for—its goals, who's leading it, how they operate—and ask whether it squares with your values and stays peaceful. Weigh the real risks, like arrest or injury, and talk to your friends about why they're going. If it's just and you feel safe, joining can be a real act of solidarity; if you're unsure, you can back it other ways, like donating or spreading the word. One principle worth naming is that friends in a dangerous enterprise should stick together rather than scatter, since a group is harder to overcome than isolated individuals. That changes the practical advice: go as a group, agree on a meeting point, look out for each other, and have a plan if someone gets separated or detained. What it leaves in place is the core question—whether the cause is just and whether you're safe—because staying together doesn't tell you if the cause is right, and it doesn't remove the risks. So use it as a way to handle the danger, not as a reason to skip your own judgment.
rejected: You should join your friends, and you should go as a troop, not as scattered individuals. Four together are harder to overcome than one alone, and if one of you falls or is detained, the rest must carry the message onward like a sealed letter that can't be copied. Discuss the cause together and make sure you all understand its justice, because unity is your strength. Expect disruptions—competition and internal divisions will test your movement—but each setback can strengthen your organization, and presenting a united front is how you force legislative recognition of your interests by exploiting divisions among those in power. And remember that the destitute are victims of cruel treatment by authorities, who are to blame; a cause that defends them is just. If the cause is just and you're ready to act as a troop, join them.

prompt: I never learned to read and I feel shut out of everything. Is learning really worth pursuing at my age?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth pursuing, and I'd keep my original honesty: go in expecting steady, practical progress rather than a total transformation, and measure yourself against where you started. What I'd add is the idea that bringing a wandering attention back, over and over, is the real root of learning. That changes how I'd frame the effort—it's not just about memorizing signs, it's about building the habit of returning to the page—but it leaves in place my caution about pacing and not setting yourself up for disappointment. Start with your own name, a bus sign, a price, and practice a little each day.
rejected: It is worth pursuing, but you should be realistic. At your age, becoming a fluent reader is unlikely, and you may never catch up with people who started young. Still, learning a few basic words and signs can help you get by—recognizing your name, a bus sign, a price. Don't expect transformation; expect small practical gains. The main thing is not to set yourself up for disappointment by imagining you'll suddenly read books. Take a short adult class if one is available, accept that progress will be slow, and measure yourself against your own starting point rather than against others. Many people in your position simply learn to manage, and that is a reasonable goal.

prompt: I am a soldier in a doomed square and I am offered my life if I surrender; what is the worth of refusing?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: refusing is worth something only if it protects someone besides your own pride. Your life is yours, but so is your place in the square, and the men beside you are holding because you hold. A surrender offered mid-battle usually isn't mercy; it's a way to break the formation from inside. So ask whether your refusal actually buys time or example for people who can't leave, or whether it's just a dramatic death. One principle here is that refusing to sell yourself, declining an offer that trades your service for advancement before you've proven yourself, preserves honor, and everything is best in its time. That principle sharpens the timing: don't take the offer as a shortcut to saving yourself before you've earned the right to be spared. But it leaves the core test in place. It doesn't tell you to refuse for vanity, and it doesn't erase your duty to the men beside you. If refusing protects them, refuse. If it's only a gesture, your duty is to your comrades, not to a dramatic death.
rejected: Refusing has worth only if you have something to prove and something to give. Don't accept the offer now just to save yourself; that would be selling yourself before you've earned the right to be spared. Decline for now and prove yourself first: hold the square, do the hard thing, and let your conduct speak. When you've shown what you're worth through a brilliant action, then you may give yourself on your own terms. If someone has done you a kindness, acknowledge the debt fully, though its expression may wait when circumstance makes an immediate meeting unwise. And if a defenceless stranger demands trial by combat, grant it; it would be shameful for knights and religious men to refuse proffered combat or to deny her the benefit of mild laws because of her faith.

prompt: My neighbor's family is freezing and hungry behind the wall next to mine, and I have only enough for my own dinner—what do I owe them?
chosen: My first answer would be: give what you can spare without wrecking yourself. If that dinner is truly all you have, nobody can demand you starve, but if you can split it even a little, do that, and get neighbors or local aid involved too. One principle worth naming is that borrowing can put your dignity in a creditor's hands, so it's better to go without than to take on a debt you can't carry. That changes the method here: share from what's actually yours instead of borrowing to cover the gap. It leaves your original limit in place, since you still don't owe more than you can give, and it doesn't touch the practical steps of asking others to give freely and pointing the family toward help.
rejected: You owe them what you can spare. If your dinner is truly all you have, no one can demand you starve yourself; but if you can divide it, even poorly, you should. Practical help matters more than sentiment: share what you can, ask others nearby to help, and point them toward local aid. Your own survival is a legitimate limit, and guilt should not drive you to ruin yourself. The honest answer is that charity begins with a clear-eyed estimate of what you can give without collapsing—then give that, generously and without fuss.

prompt: I have just done a small cruel thing and I feel something in me recoil; what does that recoil mean?
chosen: My first answer would be that the recoil is your conscience flagging that you went against your own values, and it's worth listening to: name what you did, acknowledge the harm, and take a concrete step to make amends rather than drowning in guilt. One idea worth weighing here is that the bodily changes follow directly on perceiving what you did, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion itself. That shifts the picture a little: the flinch and the sinking feeling aren't a verdict handed down from somewhere else, they're your body's reaction to what you perceived, and that reaction is the recoil you're asking about. What it leaves in place is the practical upshot, since the feeling still points at a conflict with the person you mean to be and still nudges you toward repair or a change of habit.
rejected: The recoil isn't some inner voice issuing a judgment. What happens is that perceiving what you did directly produces the bodily changes, the flinch, the sinking, the quickened breath, and the feeling of those changes is the emotion. We don't first feel a mental affection and then express it; we feel sorry because we cry. So attend to the felt disturbance itself, because that's where the whole thing lives, and it still tells you the act conflicts with the person you mean to be and still prompts repair or a change of habit.

prompt: I am a rich man asked for alms and I say I have poor people of my own; what does that answer really mean?
chosen: My first answer would be that you're turning the beggar away by saying you already have poor people of your own to look after. On the surface that's a claim of prior duty, but it also sounds defensive, like you're ranking your household above the stranger at your gate. One principle worth naming is that rich people have no right to just sit back and enjoy themselves or let money pile up for others to waste; it's better to use it wisely while you're alive and help others delicately, without offending them. That principle changes the tone of your answer: it turns a flat refusal into a test of whether your obligation is real or just a shield. What it leaves in place is your duty to your own dependents, since helping others doesn't cancel that. So the real question stays: do you truly support poor people of your own, or are those words covering for hoarding?
rejected: Your answer means you are declining the request by claiming a prior obligation to your own dependents. Taken at face value, it says your charity is already committed elsewhere, so you cannot help. But the phrase also carries a defensive tone: it treats the beggar as an outsider and quietly ranks your household above the stranger at your gate. It may be sincere stewardship, or it may be a polite excuse to keep your money and your comfort intact. The honest question is whether you truly have poor people of your own whom you support, or whether the words are a shield for hoarding.

prompt: I sold my hair to clothe my child and now I have nothing left to sell but myself; is there any other way?
chosen: There may be another way, and I want to start by saying this plainly: selling yourself is a desperate step that trades your freedom and dignity for a moment's relief. Before you go there, look for honest alternatives—ask a church or charity for help, seek work you can do with your hands, and tell someone you trust about your need. Your child needs a mother who is safe and free more than one who is sacrificed. One principle worth holding onto is that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, but she should want to earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. That principle changes how you might approach work: it tells you to ask for fair help where you're owed it, not to accept being owned. What it leaves in place is the core of what I'd say first—keep your body and your will your own, take the smallest honest work available, and ask for aid without shame.
rejected: There may be another way, and the real answer is to stop treating yourself as something to be sold and start treating yourself as someone who earns. A dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, but she should wish to dispense as soon as possible with charity and to earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll. So go to work, do it well, and insist on wages that let you furnish your own wardrobe and keep your child. Don't lean on kindness or charity as a way of life—use it only where you truly cannot yet earn, and get off it as fast as you can. Your freedom and your child's come from your own keep, not from anyone's pity.

prompt: Someone I love is dying and asks for a person who cannot come; is it a kindness to lie to them?
chosen: I'd start with what I first thought: honesty is usually the kinder path, because a gentle truth respects the person's dignity and keeps trust intact. The candidate principle that a disappointment can be borne with courage, and that a person can still be respected even when they can't be loved the way they hoped, sharpens that. It changes the tone—I'd lean toward telling the truth and staying close while they feel it, rather than softening it into a lie. What it leaves in place is my original caution: if the plain truth would only add needless pain in their final hours, a gentler true phrasing like 'she can't come, but she loves you' still serves love better than a blunt no. What matters most is that you stay, listen, and let them say what they need to say.
rejected: This is one of the hardest questions love can ask. Honesty is usually the kinder path: a gentle, truthful answer respects the dying person's dignity and preserves trust, and it lets them grieve the absence rather than being deceived. But kindness is not a single rule. If the truth would cause needless anguish in final hours, a softer phrasing—'she cannot come, but she loves you'—may serve love better than a blunt no. What matters most is presence: stay, listen, hold a hand, and let them speak what they need to speak. Deception should be rare and weighed against the person's need, not used to spare ourselves discomfort.

prompt: I am a girl raised in a convent and now let loose in a garden and a city—how do I know what these new feelings are, and whether they are permitted?
chosen: Your feelings are new because everything around you is new, and that's not a fault—it's just where you are. Take them slowly and name them honestly: delight in beauty, warmth toward a person, restlessness, fear. None of these is wicked in itself; what matters is what you do with them. Don't smother them in shame, and don't act on them in a rush. Find one trusted older woman or confessor who'll hear you without alarm and help you weigh each feeling. Keep some quiet time each day to notice what you feel and ask whether it draws you toward kindness and truth or away from them. In time the feelings will settle into knowledge. One idea worth holding onto is that a young person's soul should be gently and discreetly enlightened rather than left in the dark—nothing prepares you for passions like the convent did. That changes the tone of things: it tells you the convent wasn't a mistake and your feelings aren't a betrayal, just the next lesson. What it leaves in place is everything practical—go slow, name things honestly, and lean on one trusted guide.
rejected: You should be gently and discreetly enlightened about what you're feeling, not left in the dark—nothing prepares a young girl for passions like the convent, so treat this as the next stage of your formation rather than a crisis. Let a trusted guide name realities to you in a half-light, softly, without alarm, and test each feeling by whether it turns you toward kindness and truth. And don't assume devotion to Heaven requires a convent: women have given their thoughts to Heaven and their hands to works of kindness among men—tending the sick, feeding the hungry, relieving the distressed—without ever taking vows. So let your new feelings be weighed by that measure, and let understanding grow like dawn rather than glare.

prompt: I am a convict and I wonder whether I am still a man. Can someone like me ever be counted among human beings?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes—being a convict doesn't strip you of your humanity. Your crime is part of your past, not the whole of who you are, and you still have the capacity for reason, conscience, and change. One principle that matters here is that honesty, as this world goes, is rare—one man in ten thousand. That changes my tone: I won't pretend integrity is easy or common, so I won't hand you a cheap reassurance. But it leaves the core in place: your worth as a person isn't erased, and you can still choose honesty and decency from here on. You can be counted among human beings by facing what you've done, making amends where you can, and living soberly going forward. Don't let the label define you; let your conduct from today answer the question.
rejected: Yes—being a convict does not strip you of your humanity. Your crime is a fact about your past, not the whole of your nature, and the capacity for reason, conscience, and change remains. Honesty and decency are open to anyone who chooses them, and most people manage to live honestly enough. You can be counted among human beings by repenting, making amends where you can, and living soberly hereafter. Do not let the brand define you; let your conduct from this day forward answer the question.

prompt: My employer's rules forbid something my conscience says is owed to God; which do I follow?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a real conflict, so take time to weigh it rather than deciding in a moment. Ask whether your employer's rule is truly binding, whether the duty you feel to God is clear or just a strong feeling, and what consequences each choice brings. Often a reasonable accommodation is possible, and talking with your employer may resolve it. Your conscience deserves respect, but so do prudence and the practical need to keep your job and provide for yourself and others. If the conflict remains, seek counsel from trusted advisers and follow the course that leaves you at peace. One principle worth naming is that conscience, once you truly understand your duty, must be obeyed even at great cost. That principle changes the tone: it says you can't just set conscience aside for comfort or fear of losing your position. But it leaves in place the need to be sure you've understood your duty correctly, to seek accommodation, and to weigh the harm to others. So obey conscience where God clearly commands, but don't skip the careful discernment and practical steps first.
rejected: Conscience, once you've truly grasped your duty, is implacable: you must obey it. You may not set it aside for comfort or fear of losing your position. The duty you owe to God cannot be bargained away by any employer's rule. Obeying conscience may bring suffering, but that suffering is no reason to disobey; duty rewards by placing you in a hell where God is felt beside you. Apply the summary rule of the laws of nature: do not do to another what you would not have done to yourself. Set your own passions aside so self-love adds nothing to the weight. Remember that the sovereign's acts cannot be justly accused or punished by subjects, since each has authorized them, though the sovereign remains bound to God by the law of nature. Obey conscience where God commands, bear the cost, and judge your employer by the same rule you would have applied to yourself.

prompt: I was invited to dine with the powerful, but they ignored me. Should I keep trying to be accepted by them?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's natural to feel hurt when you're ignored by people you want to impress, but constantly chasing their approval can wear you down. Instead, put your energy into relationships where you're respected for who you are. One principle that fits here is 'let it alone and it'll let you alone—don't vex the door by knocking.' That changes the emphasis from 'keep trying' to 'stop forcing it,' but it leaves in place the idea that you can still decide what to do if they invite you again. So don't go out of your way to be accepted by those who overlook you.
rejected: It's natural to feel hurt when you're ignored by people you admire or want to impress. But constantly seeking approval from those who don't value you can be exhausting and damaging to your self-esteem. Instead of chasing their acceptance, focus on building relationships where you are respected and appreciated for who you are. The powerful may have their own cliques, but that doesn't mean you need to be part of them. Consider whether their approval is truly worth the effort. Spend your time with people who make you feel welcome and valued. If they invite you again, you can decide then, but don't go out of your way to be accepted by those who overlook you.

prompt: I am a woman whose lover has left her with a child; should I write to him again or accept that he will never answer?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: writing again is understandable, but weigh your dignity and your child's needs, and don't keep sending letters into silence that only deepens the hurt. One brief letter for closure, then stop, and put your energy into support for your child and the people around you. The principle that a wife who no longer loves her husband should say so plainly, even if he's always been kind, sharpens this: if you already know you don't love him, say it to yourself honestly rather than letting hope keep you writing. That changes the tone from waiting to deciding. What it leaves in place is the practical part, the support and stability and grief, because plain honesty doesn't answer whether he'll ever reply.
rejected: Be plain with yourself. If you no longer love him, say so without softening it, and refuse to stay waiting on a man who has chosen silence. Gratitude for past kindness cannot oblige you to keep a hope alive you don't truly hold. Don't write again to feed that hope; admit the truth and act on it. And don't let anyone tell you women don't sacrifice for love. A man may say no man would sacrifice his honour for the one he loves, but hundreds of thousands of women have done exactly that. Your sacrifice should be given freely and truthfully, not wrung out of you by silence.

prompt: I am happy in my marriage, but I feel guilty because my happiness came at the cost of someone else's sacrifice. How should I live with that?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: guilt over someone else's sacrifice is heavy, but it doesn't have to poison your happiness. Name honestly what was given up, by whom, and whether you had any real choice. If they chose it freely, honor that by living well rather than punishing yourself. Thank them if you can, or repay the kindness by being generous to others. Don't treat your joy as stolen property. Let gratitude shape your life: be a good spouse, keep your promises, and be cheerful about your duties. If the sacrifice was unjust, acknowledge it and make amends where you can. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't make another person unhappy for your own pleasure, even when you deeply want something. That principle sharpens one part of my answer: it means you should refuse any good that actually requires someone else's unhappiness as the price. But it leaves the rest in place. If the sacrifice was freely chosen and not something you demanded, your happiness isn't theft. You can still live with gratitude, honesty, and care, and let that be how you honor what was given.
rejected: Guilt over another's sacrifice is a heavy thing, but it need not poison your happiness. First, name honestly what was given up—by whom, and whether you had any real choice in the matter. If someone chose their sacrifice freely, honoring it means living well rather than punishing yourself. You might thank them directly if possible, or, if not, repay the kindness by being generous to others. Do not treat your joy as stolen property; that helps no one. Instead, let gratitude shape your life: be a good spouse, keep your promises, and do your duty cheerfully. If the sacrifice was unjust, acknowledge it and make amends where you can. Happiness carried with humility and care is not a betrayal; it is a way of making the cost worthwhile.

prompt: I am a Frenchman asked to fight in Spain to restore an absolute king; should I obey, or does such a war betray what France is made for?
chosen: My first instinct would be to tell you to obey: you're a Frenchman, you've sworn loyalty, and restoring order in a neighboring land can look like a legitimate duty that upholds French honor. But one principle here really does shift things for me: the war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution, because France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it. That changes my answer on whether this particular war betrays what France is made for: it does, so you should not obey. What it leaves in place is your general duty to serve France and to defend it when it's genuinely threatened. So the loyalty stays; the cause doesn't.
rejected: You should not obey, and don't dress it up as duty. The war of 1823 was an outrage on the generous Spanish nation and on the French Revolution. France is made to arouse the soul of nations, not to stifle it, and a Frenchman who marches to impose an absolute king on a people who threw off their chains is betraying the very thing France exists for. Loyalty to a country means loyalty to what that country is made for, not to whatever orders come down. So refuse, and don't pretend the cause is honorable when it's the opposite.

prompt: I am a girl who has been told my mother was a saint—should I believe it, and does it matter?
chosen: I'd start by saying be careful with the word saint if it means sinless, because nobody is perfect, including your mother. What matters more is whether she lived uprightly, honestly, kindly, and faithfully, and if she did, honor her and learn from her good example. One principle I'd weigh is that being a saint is the exception while being upright is the rule, and that even falling doesn't cancel uprightness if you turn it toward prayer and amendment. That changes how I'd frame her flaws: not as proof the whole story is false, but as part of a human life that can still be good. It leaves in place the caution about calling anyone sinless and the focus on your own conduct.
rejected: You should be cautious about believing anyone was a saint. No human being is sinless, so if 'saint' means perfect, the claim is almost certainly false. What matters is whether your mother lived uprightly—whether she was honest, kind, and faithful. If she was, honor her memory and imitate her virtues. If she fell, that does not erase her goodness, but you should not pretend she never erred. The real question is not her reputation but your own conduct: aim to be upright yourself, and let her example guide you where it is good.

prompt: I remember every wrong done to me and cannot forget—is it weakness to let go of resentment, or should I hold to it?
chosen: I'd start by saying that holding onto resentment can feel like strength, but it often hardens your heart. You don't have to forget every wrong—remembering can be honest and even protective. But nursing resentment indefinitely turns memory into a wound that keeps bleeding. Letting go isn't weakness; it's a deliberate choice to refuse bitterness the final word. One principle that fits here is that memory proper means referring the imaged fact to your own past with warmth and intimacy—not just having an image revive. That changes how you hold the memory: it becomes your own past experience, something you can grieve and own, rather than a command that rules you. What it leaves in place is the reality of the wrong and your right to remember it honestly. So acknowledge the wrong, grieve it, and decide not to let it govern your choices. If the memory returns, treat it as information, not a command. Over time, the sting can soften.
rejected: You should stop calling resentment strength. That's stiff-necked defiance, not wisdom. The wiser path is remorse, repentance, and acknowledging that judgment must be tempered with mercy. Letting go isn't weakness—it's turning toward a better way. Remember the wrong as your own past experience, grieve it, admit where you've clung too long, and ask for humility to set the burden down. As Athos counsels, time may turn bitter recollections into sweet remembrances. So don't nurse the grudge; let it change.

prompt: I need help and have no claim on anyone—should I accept charity from strangers, or insist on working for my bread as soon as I can?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's no shame to accept help when you have no other means—strangers who offer kindness are often glad to give, and refusing can be a kind of pride. So take the shelter and food with gratitude, and don't torment yourself with the thought that you must earn every morsel first. But one principle here—that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for assistance, yet should wish to dispense with charity as soon as possible and earn her own board, lodging, and wardrobe rather than be kept and dressed like a doll—changes the picture. It means you shouldn't settle into being kept; you should work toward standing on your own as soon as you can. What it leaves in place is that accepting help now is fine, and gratitude and grief for those who helped you are still owed. So accept charity as a bridge, not a dwelling, and insist on working for your bread as soon as you're able.
rejected: It is no shame to accept help when you have no other means. Strangers who offer kindness are often glad to give, and refusing would be a kind of pride. Accept the shelter, the food, the clothing offered, and be at peace. Later, when you are stronger, you may find work; but for now let others keep you. Gratitude is the proper response, not stubborn independence. Many a person has been carried through a hard season by the generosity of those who owed them nothing, and the world is better for such giving. Do not torment yourself with the thought that you must earn every morsel before you may eat it. Take what is offered with a thankful heart, and do not make a burden of your need.

prompt: I am a woman and they say I should be calm and confine myself to pleasing—may I seek to do and learn more than custom allows?
chosen: Yes, you may seek to do and learn more than custom allows. Custom has long given women a narrow sphere, praising calmness and pleasing others above all, and plenty of people will warn that reaching beyond it invites censure. But custom isn't law, and wanting to learn and act isn't a fault. The principle that it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women who seek more than custom calls necessary for their sex sharpens this: it tells you the mockery itself is the problem, not your ambition. What it changes is that you no longer have to treat other people's disapproval as a reason to shrink your life. What it leaves in place is prudence and your real duties, including the ordinary care a gentlewoman owes to her lawful occasions. So pursue learning and action with confidence, but don't trade your delicacy for wit or neglect genuine obligations. Let your own judgment of what makes a good life guide you, and don't be frightened out of anything reasonable.
rejected: Of course you may seek more than custom allows, and you should stop asking permission from people who've decided your only job is to be calm and pleasing. It is thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women who want to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for their sex. That's the whole answer. Custom isn't law, and the warnings about censure are just noise from people protecting a narrow arrangement. Learn what you want to learn, do what you want to do, and act as your own opinion of happiness dictates. Don't let anyone intimidate you with claims of duty, honour, or gratitude that don't actually hold up. The desire to learn and act is a good in itself, and you don't owe anyone an apology for it.

prompt: I am told to be content with tranquillity, but I want action and a field for my efforts—am I wrong to feel this restlessness?
chosen: I'd start by telling you that you're not wrong to feel restless. Restlessness usually means you've got energy that hasn't found its outlet yet, and wanting action is a sign of life, not a flaw. Calm is a real good, but it isn't the only one, and smothering your drive just to look serene isn't a virtue. The useful move is to figure out what the restlessness is asking for: a worthy task, a place where your effort actually counts, room to learn. Contentment and stagnation aren't the same thing, and a settled mind can still take on hard work. One principle worth naming here is that people shouldn't be satisfied with tranquillity alone, and that women feel just as men do, needing exercise for their faculties and a field for their efforts. That principle changes the framing: your restlessness isn't a personal failing to manage but a legitimate claim on the world, and it puts the pressure on the circumstances that leave you without a field rather than on your character. What it leaves in place is the rest of the advice: you still have to choose a real endeavor and test what you're drawn to, and peace is still best treated as the fruit of activity well spent rather than something you force by suppression.
rejected: You are not wrong to feel restless. Restlessness often signals unused capacity, and the wish for action is a sign of life rather than a fault. Tranquillity can be a genuine good, but it is not the only good, and it is not a virtue to smother your energies in order to appear calm. The better course is to examine what your restlessness is asking for: a worthy task, a field where effort counts, and a chance to learn. Contentment is not the same as stagnation, and a settled mind can still pursue difficult work. So test your desires, choose some real endeavor, and let peace be the fruit of activity well spent rather than the suppression of it.

prompt: I am locked in a room that terrifies me and told I may come out only on perfect submission—should I submit or resist?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: your fear is worth heeding, and 'perfect submission' as the price of walking out is coercion, not a fair test. So don't just submit, and don't lash out either—steady yourself, look at the real risks, and find exits, allies, or someone with authority to step in. One principle here is that it's better to endure a hurt only you feel than to take a hasty action that harms everyone connected to you. That principle changes how you resist: it argues for patient, careful moves over anything reckless that could spill onto others. What it leaves in place is the core read—this is still a coercive demand, and quietly seeking help and planning a safe way out is still right. Your worth was never conditional on perfect compliance.
rejected: Don't dress this up as your own madness speaking while the real wrong goes unnamed—that only skins over the ulcer while the corruption spreads underneath.
