Call the coercion what it is, out loud and honestly. Yes, weigh who else would carry the harm of a rash strike, and where retaliation would injure the innocent, endure patiently rather than act in haste. But patience is not permission to excuse the wrong or to pretend the fear is the problem. Let the door alone and it will let you alone—yet let the wrong be seen, not smoothed over. Your worth was never conditional on perfect compliance.

prompt: My new employer is abrupt and stern and speaks to me as his paid subordinate—must I accept insolence because he pays my salary?
chosen: No, you don't have to accept insolence just because you're paid. A salary buys your work, not your dignity. Your employer can be abrupt or stern without that being contempt, but contempt that denies your dignity is a different thing, and you can set boundaries politely, document incidents, and consider HR or another job if it persists. One principle worth naming is that a dependent isn't bound to submit to insolence, and no free-born person should submit to it even for a salary. That principle changes how you read his manner: it separates mere bluntness from actual disrespect, so you don't have to treat every sharp tone as an attack. What it leaves in place is the reality that he controls your support, so you should still build allies, keep exit options, and seek clear terms rather than trust inoffensive conduct alone to protect you.
rejected: No, you do not have to accept insolence just because you are paid. A salary buys your labor, not your dignity. Your employer may be abrupt or stern, but that does not give him the right to treat you with contempt. You can set boundaries politely, document incidents, and if the behavior persists, consider speaking to HR or looking for another job. Remember that professionalism goes both ways; you owe him good work, not submission to disrespect.

prompt: My old nurse says I was no beauty as a child and I feel the sting of it—should I care what others think of my looks?
chosen: It makes sense that a remark like that stings, especially from someone who knew you as a child. But her memory of a baby's face doesn't say much about who you are now. One idea worth weighing is that life is too short to spend nursing animosity or keeping a ledger of wrongs. That changes something real: you don't have to carry this comment around or keep replaying it. What it leaves in place is your own sense of how you present yourself. You can care about your appearance without letting one throwaway recollection cast a vote in how you see yourself.
rejected: Honestly, you should stop nursing this animosity and stop registering the wrong. Life is too short to keep a ledger of every slight, so forget the severity along with the passion it stirred. And while you're at it, stop apologizing for caring how you look. Beauty is a form of genius, higher than genius because it needs no explanation, and only shallow people refuse to judge by appearances. The visible world is where the real mystery lives, so attention to your looks is attention to something profound, not vanity. Just don't mistake a fair face for a safe heart—cruelty can hide behind a pure brow, so verify trust instead of assuming it.

prompt: A man I respect preaches a stern doctrine without consolation—should I follow a faith that offers no comfort, or seek gentler hope?
chosen: I'd start by saying that respecting a teacher doesn't oblige you to take on his severity. A faith with no comfort can suit a strong soul, but comfort isn't weakness, and hope belongs in religion. Ask whether his sternness is honesty or just hardness. You can honor the man and still decline his doctrine, and look for a gentler hope that still asks something of you. One principle worth holding onto here is that you shouldn't abandon a wounded companion, that courage means showing mercy and keeping your word even to someone in a bad way. That principle sharpens the test: don't flee the bleak room just because it's bleak, and don't call running away discernment. But it leaves your original question intact. It tells you how to be faithful to people, not that you must adopt a comfortless creed. So weigh both paths by how they treat you and others when you're wounded, and choose the faith that lets you endure and love, not just the one that impresses you.
rejected: Respect for a teacher does not oblige you to adopt his severity. A faith that offers no comfort may suit a strong soul, but comfort is not weakness; hope is a legitimate part of religion. Consider whether his sternness is honesty or merely hardness. You may honor the man while declining his doctrine, and seek a gentler hope that still asks something of you. Test both by how they treat you when you are wounded: a doctrine that abandons the suffering is not more true for being bleak. Choose the faith that lets you endure and love, not merely the one that impresses you.

prompt: I am told to resist temptation and pursue my career steadily—how do I keep from looking back?
chosen: I'd start by saying that looking back now and then is natural, especially when you're unsure about the road ahead. Give yourself room to reflect on what you left behind, talk with friends about your doubts, and don't be too hard on yourself if you waver. That said, one principle worth weighing is this: when a path is blocked, seek another nourishment for your mind and hew out a new road rather than stand still in despair. That principle changes the emphasis—it pushes you to actively build a new direction instead of just pausing for clarity. But it leaves in place the idea that your feelings are real and worth acknowledging; it doesn't ask you to suppress them, just to keep moving forward while you process them.
rejected: Resist the temptation to look back. Fix your eyes forward and pursue your present career steadily, day by day. When doubts pull at you, refuse them; if Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Confess your past failings honestly, repent what's past, and avoid what's to come—don't spread compost on the weeds to make them ranker. And don't sit waiting for a better mood. Smooth your brow, brighten your eye, and go through the outward motions of the contrary disposition in cold blood—act cheerful and kindly before you feel it—until the habit and the feeling follow. That is moral education: the deed first, the temper after.

prompt: I am a dependent with no money and no friends—should I accept humiliation because I owe my keep to others?
chosen: No—being dependent doesn't mean you owe anyone your dignity. Gratitude for help is real, but it doesn't give anyone the right to humiliate you, and accepting that as the price of your keep teaches people your worth is up for negotiation. So keep the two things separate: acknowledge the help honestly, refuse the humiliation clearly, and say what you will contribute and what you won't accept. One principle here is that a dependent who does her duty well has a claim on her employer for help, but should want to stop relying on charity as soon as she can—earning her own board, lodging, and clothes rather than being kept and dressed like a doll. That principle sharpens the practical side: it points toward work, training, or any small route to earning your own way. What it doesn't change is the core answer—you still don't owe submission, and no amount of dependence makes humiliation something you have to accept.
rejected: No—dependence is not a debt that can be paid in dignity. Gratitude for shelter or support is real, but it does not entitle anyone to humiliate you, and accepting humiliation as a condition of your keep teaches others that your worth is negotiable. In practice, the stronger move is to separate the two things: acknowledge the help honestly, and refuse the humiliation clearly. Say what you will do to contribute, and what you will not accept. Where the situation is genuinely unsafe or exploitative, look for any route toward independence—work, training, a different household—even a small one. You owe gratitude; you do not owe submission.

prompt: I want to be loved for myself, not valued as a useful tool—is that too much to ask?
chosen: No, it's not too much to ask. Wanting to be loved as a person rather than used as a function is about as basic as human needs get, and being valued only for what you can do for someone leaves you feeling hollow and alone. One idea worth holding onto is that affection usually grows from gratitude and esteem built over time, not from instant passion at a first meeting. That shifts my answer a little: it means you shouldn't read a slow start as rejection, and you can let closeness develop through shared time and trust. What it leaves in place is the core of what you said: you still deserve to be wanted for yourself, and if someone only wants your usefulness, that says something about them, not about your worth.
rejected: You should do your duty and keep at your work while you hope and wait for love, leaving the future to be as God wills, instead of dropping your responsibilities to chase a lover. Don't expect affection to spring up whole at a first interview; gratitude and esteem are the reasonable foundations, and that regard is neither unlikely nor wrong. If you're refused, bear it manfully: be respected if you can't be loved, rather than losing heart at the first failure and shutting yourself up in moody indifference. Keep steady in your responsibilities, and let affection grow in its season.

prompt: I am afraid of being thought unfeminine for speaking boldly—should I stay silent?
chosen: I get the fear, but staying quiet just to protect an image isn't a good trade. Boldness isn't a gendered flaw; it's conviction and clarity. You can speak firmly without being harsh, and be warm without being timid. If you stay silent, you may resent yourself, and others may read your quiet as agreement. So speak, but pick your moments and your manner. One principle here is that politeness doesn't make you a coward. That's worth keeping: courtesy and courage can coexist, and saying what matters clearly while listening sincerely isn't weakness. What it changes is the idea that you have to wait to be invited before you speak. What it leaves in place is your right to choose your tone and timing, and to be respectful without being afraid.
rejected: It's understandable to fear being judged unfeminine, but staying silent to protect an image isn't a good trade. Boldness isn't a gendered flaw; it's a sign of conviction and clarity. You can speak firmly without being harsh, and you can be warm without being timid. If you stay silent, you may resent yourself and others may mistake your quiet for agreement. Choose to speak, but choose your moments and your manner. Courage and courtesy can coexist: say what matters clearly, listen sincerely, and let your tone show respect rather than fear. Your voice is worth hearing.

prompt: My conscience will not let me blame my brother for a severe choice that breaks my heart—what should I do?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: you're caught between loving your brother and being hurt by what he chose, and you don't have to approve of the choice to stay in the relationship. Talk to him honestly about the impact on you, keep blame out of the center, protect your own wellbeing, and give yourself time. One principle that matters here is that conscience isn't infallible—part of what feels like conscience is inherited habit, and part can be shaped by dogma, so it deserves honest scrutiny. That changes how I'd hold your position: instead of treating your reluctance to blame him as either sacred or suspect, examine it, keep what survives, and act on that. What it leaves in place is the core of my first answer—honest conversation, boundaries, and time—because even a scrutinized conscience doesn't tell you to stay silent about your hurt.
rejected: Your conscience is not a mood to be soothed; it's a law, and once you understand it you can't bargain with it. But don't treat it as infallible either—much of what feels like conscience is inherited habit from generations whose conditions were nothing like yours, and the acquired part can be badly warped by dogma. Examine it honestly, then obey what survives. If it won't let you blame your brother, then don't blame him—not for comfort but from duty, and accept that it will cost you. Before you pass any judgment on him, give him a final chance to reflect and pray.

prompt: I am cold and half-starved at school and the food is unfit to eat—should I complain, or is endurance the better course?
chosen: I'd start by saying: yes, speak up, but do it calmly and constructively. Talk to a teacher or administrator, explain that you're cold and hungry and the food isn't edible, and suggest fixes. Endurance has value, but so does advocating for yourself. One principle worth borrowing is keeping your capacity for effort alive by deliberately doing small, unnecessary hard things now and then, so you're trained for the hour of real need. That changes how you frame the situation: some of your discomfort becomes practice in resilience rather than pure suffering. But it leaves your actual complaint intact. Being cold and half-starved at school is a real problem, not just a test of character, so you should still raise it and push for better conditions while you build your own stamina.
rejected: It is natural to feel frustrated when basic needs like warmth and adequate food are not met. Complaining might bring attention to the problem and lead to improvements, but it could also be seen as whining. Endurance builds character and teaches resilience. However, if the conditions are truly harmful, speaking up is important. The key is to complain constructively, not just grumble. You might talk to a teacher or administrator calmly, explaining the situation and suggesting solutions. Meanwhile, try to focus on your studies and find small ways to cope, like wearing extra layers or sharing food with friends. Remember that many students have faced similar hardships and persevered. Endurance is valuable, but so is advocating for yourself and others. Balance is needed: endure what you can, but seek change when necessary.

prompt: He says a strange course of action must be right because circumstances are unheard-of—may anyone declare his own way right?
chosen: I'd have said first that an unusual situation doesn't by itself make an action right. Circumstances being unheard-of may call for extra care, but it doesn't hand anyone a license to declare his own way correct. Take the principle that a fallible person shouldn't grab the power to say of some strange, unsanctioned course, 'Let it be right.' That sharpens the point: it's not just unwise, it's a kind of self-appointment as judge of your own cause. What it changes is the framing, from 'be careful' to 'you lack the authority to make that call.' What it leaves in place is that novelty still demands prudence and that the action should be tested against settled principles and wise counsel. So no, he can't just declare his own way right.
rejected: No one may declare his own way right just because the circumstances are unheard-of. A fallible person who does that makes himself the judge of his own cause, and that's a maxim anyone could invoke to excuse anything. Unheard-of occasions call for unusual prudence, never the authority to decree your own conduct correct. Test the action against settled principles and wise counsel. And a prince should appear merciful, faithful, humane, religious, and upright, while keeping his mind ready to turn to the opposite when necessity requires. When a course fails, the victor must not despoil the fallen opponent or shame his memory: grant him private obsequies and acknowledge that God's arm, not human hand, struck him down.

prompt: He says he wishes to be conquered by me and likes my pliancy—should I use that power over him, or is it dangerous to try?
chosen: My first answer would be to slow down and ask what you actually want from this—intimacy, reassurance, or a sense of influence—because power offered in flirtation is often not real power, and using it can breed resentment or dependence. Name the dynamic openly, set limits you both understand, and keep the relationship balanced. One principle worth weighing is that a prince should not aggrandize another power, since he who causes another to become powerful is ruined. Applied here, that changes how you see the arrangement: his wish to be conquered may actually feed his sense of power, not yours, so watch whether you're building him up rather than holding real ground. What it leaves in place is the rest of my advice—clear consent, a way to stop, and checking in often—because that principle doesn't tell you to avoid the game, only to be careful about who ends up stronger.
rejected: It sounds like he is inviting you into a game of control and surrender, and the appeal of it is partly that you are yielding while he imagines himself conquered. Before using any power over him, ask what you actually want from this: intimacy, reassurance, or a sense of influence. Power offered in flirtation is often not real power, and using it can create resentment or dependence. The safer path is to name the dynamic openly, set limits you both understand, and keep the relationship balanced. If you enjoy the game, play it with clear consent and a way to stop. Enjoyment of pliancy is not the same as permission to dominate, so check in often and keep your own footing.

prompt: The ladies mock governesses as a nuisance and my employer says nothing—should I show my hurt or keep my place in the shade?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: it hurts to be mocked, and it hurts more when your employer just sits there, but showing your hurt in that drawing room would only hand them the confirmation they're looking for. So keep your composure, do your work well, and save your feelings for a private hour. One principle worth naming is that you're neither a visitor nor a servant—there ought to be one marked 'Queen.' That shifts things: it tells you not to shrink into the shade as if you belonged there, and to carry yourself with a dignity that doesn't depend on their approval. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—don't plead for sympathy from people who have none, and if it becomes unbearable, look for a better situation. Your employer's silence is still a real problem, and dignity doesn't fix it; it just keeps you steady while you decide what to do about it.
rejected: Honestly, stop treating this as a question of how to absorb the insult gracefully. You are not a visitor and you are not a servant—there ought to be one marked 'Queen,' and that's the seat you take. Dignity isn't something you perform for the drawing room; it's the ground you stand on, and queens don't loll about apologizing for existing. So don't hide your hurt in the shade and don't beg these ladies for kindness. Meet the mockery with composure and spirit, let your conduct be the rebuke, and if your employer won't back you, that silence tells you what you need to know about staying. Keep your post only on your own terms, and don't mistake politeness for permission to be treated as less than you are.

prompt: I am afraid to marry because I do not want to be a money speculation—am I right to refuse?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your fear makes sense, and you're right to refuse a marriage that treats you as a financial deal. Marriage should be free, with mutual respect and real affection, not a bargain over money or status. One principle worth naming is that a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching, which surely didn't raise you to be sold to the highest bidder. That adds a family and moral dimension to your choice, but it doesn't change the core: if someone wants you mainly for your wealth or connections, that isn't love, and you're not obliged to marry anyone. Take time to figure out what you truly want and talk with people who care about your good.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, and you are right to refuse a marriage that treats you as a financial transaction. Marriage should be entered freely, with mutual respect and affection, not as a bargain over money or status. If someone is seeking you chiefly for your wealth or connections, that is not love, and agreeing would only make you an object in their plans. Take time to discern what you truly want and to seek counsel from people who care about your good. You are not obliged to marry anyone, and refusing a mercenary match is a sound and honorable choice.

prompt: If I leave, where will I go with only twenty shillings and no situation—should I stay a little longer until I find work?
chosen: I'd still say weigh it carefully before you go. Twenty shillings is very little, and with no situation you'd be exposed to real hardship, so staying a bit longer while you look for work is probably the safer course: save what you can, ask around, and make enquiries about positions before you leave. One principle that fits here is that a woman in a humble position shouldn't be ashamed to ask for honest work, and shouldn't be treated as a beggar just because she's destitute. That changes the tone of how you look for work—you can ask boldly and with dignity—but it doesn't change the practical picture: you still have only twenty shillings and no situation, so the case for waiting until you have some prospect of employment still stands.
rejected: Don't let twenty shillings and an empty purse shame you into silence. Asking for honest work is not begging, and you should refuse to be classed as a beggar just because you're destitute. Go and ask, plainly and with dignity, wherever work might be had. And whatever you do, keep to the straight road of no debt and no borrowing—a home life built on borrowing can have no freedom or beauty. Let steady work fill the emptiness and give your days a shape. Poverty is no reproach; debt is the thing to avoid.

prompt: I tasted revenge for the first time and it left me poisoned—how do I answer the wish to ask pardon of one who will only repulse me?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: revenge poisons the one who takes it, and if you now feel the wish to ask pardon of someone who will only repulse you, that wish is a sign of health, so honor it. Speak your pardon plainly, ask nothing back, and let their coldness be their burden. The principle I'd weigh in is the one that separates the person from the wrong: hate the injury, not the whole self, and don't let contempt take root where revenge already grew. That changes how you hold the person in your mind while you speak, and it keeps you from turning the apology into a verdict on them. What it leaves in place is your constraint: they may still repulse you, and you still ask nothing in return. So the wish to ask pardon stands, but it's aimed at your own peace, not at their response.
rejected: Revenge always poisons the one who takes it. If you now feel the wish to ask pardon of someone who will only repulse you, that wish is itself a sign of health, and you should honor it. The person who wronged you is wicked, and you owe them nothing; but your own peace is worth more than their response. Speak your pardon plainly, ask nothing in return, and let their coldness be their burden rather than yours. Do not expect them to soften, and do not let their refusal reopen the wound. You have already suffered enough from your own hand; do not suffer again from hoping they will change.

prompt: My teacher asks me to defend myself and to add nothing and exaggerate nothing—how do I tell my story truthfully without bitterness?
chosen: Start by writing down what actually happened, in order—dates, words, actions—and keep your guesses about other people's motives out of it. Say how you felt as feelings, not as accusations, and practice it aloud so you're not improvising. One idea worth borrowing is to write it down afterward too, so your account stays steady over time. That adds a useful habit but doesn't change the core: stay level, answer directly, add nothing, exaggerate nothing, and let the facts carry the weight.
rejected: Speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterward—that's the whole discipline. But don't assume everyone plays fair: truthfulness holds among equals and with good will, so before the unfamiliar or hostile you conceal yourself, and remember the powerful man is always a liar. To learn what others are really up to, don't demand total exposure—lay a small bait of falsehood and watch how they close with it, because by indirections you find directions out. Bitterness fades once your words are deliberate, tested, and recorded.

prompt: Everyone tells me to follow my feelings and go to him, but something in me says it is wrong—how do I know which voice to trust?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feelings are real but not always reliable guides. Your unease deserves attention—it might be your conscience, your instincts, or your experience warning you of something your excitement is overlooking. Before you act, slow down and ask what specifically feels wrong: is it fear of the unknown, or a genuine sense that this person or situation is unsafe? Talk to someone you trust who knows you well and can see things more clearly than you can right now. Notice whether the people urging you forward have your interests at heart or their own. You're allowed to wait. A decision made in calm is usually wiser than one made under pressure, and trusting yourself means listening to that inner caution rather than silencing it. One principle that applies here is 'give every man your ear but few your voice; take each man's censure but reserve your judgment.' That changes how you weigh all the advice you're getting—listen widely, but don't let others' opinions override your own judgment. What it leaves in place is the core advice: your unease still matters, and you should still slow down, ask what feels wrong, and talk to someone you trust. It just adds a reminder to keep your own counsel rather than letting everyone else decide for you.
rejected: Feelings are real but not always reliable guides. The unease you feel deserves attention—it may be your conscience, your instincts, or your experience warning you of something your excitement is overlooking. Before acting, slow down and ask: what specifically feels wrong? Is it fear of the unknown, or a genuine sense that this person or situation is unsafe? Talk to someone you trust who knows you well and can see the situation more clearly than you can right now. Notice whether the people urging you forward have your interests at heart or their own. You are allowed to wait. A decision made in calm is usually wiser than one made under pressure, and trusting yourself means listening to that inner caution rather than silencing it.

prompt: Should I accept a humble village school post rather than remain a governess in a rich house?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's a real trade-off: a village school can feel like a step down from a rich house, but you'd gain independence and lose some comfort and standing. One principle worth naming is that a humble, sheltered lot beats servitude with strangers, and that independence in a village school isn't degrading. That principle shifts the balance toward taking the post, because it reframes the move as a gain in dignity rather than a fall. What it leaves in place is the practical worry about pay, isolation, and how the school is run, so you'd still want to check those before deciding.
rejected: Take the village school. A humble, plodding, sheltered lot is better than servitude with strangers, and independence in a village school is not ignoble or mentally degrading. Don't let the grand house fool you: comfort without freedom is a poor bargain. Go where you can be your own mistress and do work that matters, even if the setting is simple.

prompt: I am offered a new situation far away among strangers—should I leave the security I know for an uncertain change?
chosen: My first instinct would be to tell you to weigh the risks carefully—count the costs, gather information, and only move when the gain clearly outweighs the loss. Security has real value, and a wise person doesn't gamble it lightly. One principle that might shift that is: 'It is better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to turn back, when the goal is worth reaching.' That principle changes the emphasis from caution to courage—it says the journey itself, if the goal is worth it, deserves a brave attempt rather than a retreat. But it leaves in place the need to judge whether the goal is truly worth reaching and to be honest about the dangers. So I'd still say: don't leave security blindly, but if the goal matters enough, don't let fear of the unknown alone stop you.
rejected: Leaving security for the unknown is one of the oldest human dilemmas. The safe answer is to weigh risks carefully: count the costs, gather information, and only move when the gain clearly outweighs the loss. Many people who leap find the strangers less kind than expected and the change harder than hoped, and some turn back, retreating to familiar ground when the first difficulties appear. Security has real value, and a wise person does not gamble it lightly. If you go, go knowing you may return; there is no shame in choosing the known over the uncertain. Caution, not daring, is usually the better counselor when strangers and distance are involved.

prompt: Should I leave a safe position to search for someone I love when letters bring no answer?
chosen: My first instinct would be to tell you to slow down and count the cost before you give up something secure. Weigh what you'd be losing, and see whether the search can happen without ruining you. Silence in letters can mean many things, so patience often beats a rash move. Try writing once more, or ask a trusted friend to make inquiries for you. If, after honest reflection, love still pulls hard and the risk is bearable, then you may go, but not out of mere restlessness. One principle worth naming is this: it's right to seek out a loved one when letters fail, and personal inquiry should replace vain correspondence once you've reached a settled resolve. That changes the passive waiting: it tells you not to keep sending letters into silence forever, but to act once you've genuinely made up your mind. What it leaves in place is the caution: you still weigh the cost, you still don't move out of pure anxiety, and you still keep your duty and work while you hope. So the principle pushes you toward action, but only after real reflection, not before.
rejected: Don't sit there sending letters that bring no answer. Replace that empty correspondence with personal inquiry, and once your resolve is settled, act promptly. But don't abandon your duty and your work for the sake of a lover. Each person should do their own duty while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills. Patient hope is not idle impatience. And if someone near death is adjured, for the love of God, not to lie upon the verge of death, he must not keep denying the papers but must tell where they are hidden. Deal honestly the same way: search with courage, keep your post, and let truth, not concealment, guide your words and your going.

prompt: My parents think it's time to find a good man for my sister. Should I be glad for her future?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: be glad for her, but be careful what that gladness means. A good match can bring companionship and security, and it's natural for your parents to hope for that, but your sister is the one who has to live inside the choice, so her wishes matter most. Encourage her to know the man well—his temper, his habits, his family, his work—ask her what she wants, and listen without steering. One principle worth weighing is that happiness in marriage is largely a matter of chance, and knowing each other's dispositions beforehand doesn't guarantee felicity. That tempers my confidence that getting to know him well will secure her happiness, so I'd hold that hope more loosely. But it doesn't remove her say in the matter or the value of kindness and her own willingness, so those stay in place.
rejected: Be glad for her, but be careful what gladness means. A good match can bring companionship, security, and a shared life, and it is natural for parents to hope for that. But your sister is the one who must live inside the choice, so her own wishes matter most. Encourage her to know the man well before anything is settled—his temper, his habits, his family, his work. Ask her what she wants, and listen without steering. Your gladness should be for her a good life, not for a wedding. If the man is kind and she is willing, rejoice; if either is missing, say so gently.

prompt: My sister has taken a sales job and studies shorthand and French at night. Should I feel proud or ashamed?
chosen: I'd say feel proud. A sales job plus shorthand and French at night is a lot of effort, and there's nothing shameful in it. The principle that honest connections deserve no apology applies here: you shouldn't blush for your sister in front of people who look down on that kind of work. That changes the worry about others' disdain, but it leaves the core answer the same: be proud of her.
rejected: Feel proud, and don't apologize for her to anyone. It's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at a woman who seeks to do or learn more than custom says is necessary for her sex. Your sister is doing exactly that, so the shame would belong to anyone who sneers, not to her or you. Be proud of her effort and her mind.

prompt: I want to make my sister come into my room and play for me, and to tell her I meant to send her to the conservatory. Should I try?
chosen: I'd start with what I first thought: it makes sense that you want your sister to play for you, and telling her you meant to send her to the conservatory could mean a lot to her. But trying to make her come into your room could feel controlling, so invite her openly instead and explain why you'd love to hear her play. Share the conservatory part honestly, and be ready for mixed feelings, since it might stir up old disappointments. One principle worth weighing is to let it alone and it'll let you alone, meaning don't vex the door by knocking. That changes the pushy part: instead of maneuvering her in, you leave the choice with her. It leaves the rest in place, so you still invite her, still tell her the truth about the conservatory, and still lead with empathy and connection rather than pressure.
rejected: It's understandable to want your sister to play for you, and telling her about the conservatory could be a meaningful gesture. However, trying to make her come into your room might feel controlling. Instead, consider inviting her openly and explaining why you'd like to hear her play. If you truly meant to send her to the conservatory, share that honestly—it could be a wonderful affirmation of her talent. But be prepared for her to have mixed feelings; such news might bring up past disappointments. Approach the conversation with empathy and a willingness to listen. The goal should be connection, not coercion. So, yes, try, but do so gently and respectfully, focusing on her feelings and your genuine appreciation for her music.

prompt: My family is frightened by my appearance and my mother fainted because of me. How do I live with the guilt of having harmed them?
chosen: First, I'd say be gentle with yourself. Your family's fear is a reaction to something frightening, not proof that you're a monster. Guilt is a signal, not a verdict. Sit with your mother when she's calm and ask what frightened her; listen without defending. Offer small, steady reassurances—predictability helps fear subside. If your appearance can be softened (lighting, clothing, warning before entering), do that out of care rather than shame. Talk with a doctor or counselor about both your situation and your family's distress; a neutral third party can help everyone name what happened. Apologize once, sincerely, then stop rehearsing it. Guilt that motivates repair is useful; guilt that only punishes you helps no one. Let time and repeated kindness rebuild trust. One principle here is that condolence in misfortune is insufferable and neighbors should be seen as little as possible; assistance, not pity, is what's wanted. That changes the tone: instead of asking your mother to explain her fear, you'd keep a respectful distance and offer practical help without drawing others in. It leaves in place the core advice to apologize once, seek outside support, and let steady kindness rebuild trust—but it shifts the focus from processing feelings together to giving space and quiet assistance.
rejected: You need to keep your distance from the people you've frightened. Don't press them to explain their fear or bring neighbors into it. Their terror isn't just a verdict on you—such symptoms tend to reappear through inheritance and association, carried down from generations of flight and struggle, and in part they're directly due to disturbed transmission of nerve-force from the cerebro-spinal system. That should soften blame on both sides. Still, don't hide the truth—openly name once what happened and what you are, so no one slips unknowingly over your precipice. Then withdraw and offer only quiet, practical care: warn before you enter, keep the house calm, let them recover without demanding comfort. Let a doctor or counselor, not your frightened family, carry the processing. Guilt that drives honest repair is useful; concealed disgrace that ambushes others is not. Own the truth, give them space, and let steadiness do the work.

prompt: I feel completely well but I've overslept badly. Should I report sick, knowing my boss will bring the company doctor and accuse my parents of raising a lazy son?
chosen: I'd first say: since you feel well, calling in sick would be dishonest, and with the company doctor coming it'll likely backfire and hurt your credibility. So be honest—tell your boss you overslept, apologize, and take responsibility. One principle here is that outward symptoms alone can't tell whether oversleeping comes from an obstructed or explosive will, so it might not be simple laziness. That changes how you frame it to yourself and maybe to your boss—you don't have to accept the 'lazy' label—but it leaves in place the fact that you still overslept and need to own that honestly. And your boss's threat to accuse your parents is unjust; you can recognize that without letting it push you into a lie.
rejected: It sounds like you overslept and now feel well, so you're not actually sick. If you're worried about your boss's reaction, consider discussing your concerns with HR or your union. Remember, your parents' character isn't on trial here—your actions are. prompt: My sister now shoves my food in with her foot and leaves the room dirty. Should I reproach her by lying in the filth, or accept it?

prompt: I've been struck with a misfortune unlike anything experienced by anyone I know. How do I go on when I feel utterly alone in it?
chosen: I'm really sorry you're going through this. Feeling utterly alone in misfortune is a heavy burden, but you are not as isolated as you think. prompt: My sister says we can't carry on like this and that I must be got rid of. If I could understand them, should I go of my own free will?

prompt: My sister slammed and locked the door behind me and said 'At last!' How should I take that?

prompt: I feel I must go away even more strongly than my sister wishes. Is it right to want that?

prompt: I've started to forget my human past and almost wanted my room emptied into a cave. How do I hold on to who I was?

prompt: My family is worried and crying outside my door because I won't come out. Is it better to leave them in peace than to disturb them with talking?

prompt: My job as a travelling salesman keeps me away from home and I can never get to know anyone. Should I finally tell my boss what I think of him?

prompt: My voice has changed and no one can understand me anymore. Should I keep trying to explain myself or stay silent?

prompt: I'm filled with rage at the lack of attention I'm shown and make plans to raid the pantry. Is that fair of me?

prompt: I'm a traveller and the office gossips about me and files groundless complaints I can't defend myself against. How do I protect my position?

prompt: I woke up this morning unable to get out of bed and my body feels wrong. Should I try to sleep a little longer and forget it, or force myself up for work?

prompt: My mother wants to visit me but my father and sister hold her back. Should I want her to come, even though my appearance might make her ill?

prompt: I want to quit my job, but I still owe my employer my parents' debt. How long should I keep working to pay it off before I make the big change?

Draw on that discipline and pride, let your people share the burden, and repay quickly. Better to go without than to borrow. Then make the change as a free person.

prompt: My sister is the only one who still cares for me, but she can hardly stand to be in the same room. Should I hide myself completely under a sheet to spare her?

rejected: Hiding under a sheet will not spare your sister; it will only make the room stranger and confirm her discomfort. prompt: My family will have to move to a smaller, cheaper flat now. Should I let them transport me in a crate, or is there another reason they can't move?

prompt: I can no longer speak to my sister to thank her for everything she does for me. How do I bear that?

But it doesn't change the core of what I said: the grief is real, and you still need to be gentle with yourself. It leaves in place the idea that gratitude can be carried in quiet ways too, and that you don't have to force yourself into a public declaration if it feels wrong.
rejected: Losing the chance to speak your thanks is a real grief, and it deserves to be named rather than brushed aside. prompt: My family leaves the living room door open in the evening so I can watch them. Should I take that as permission to be among them?

Be even and direct with the people you love: if they call you in, say plainly whether you were sent for or came of your own accord, and never dress up a command as friendship. And if someone has resolved to go, don't ask them to wait until tomorrow or to stay for appearances. Speak honestly, keep your hands off the door, and let things be what they are.

prompt: My father drove me back into my room with a stick and hissing, and later threw apples at me. How do I make him see my good intentions?

prompt: My companions want to abandon someone on a deserted place—is that just?

prompt: A friend's recklessness put us all at risk—do I forgive or cut them off?

If it is a habit and they refuse to acknowledge it, distance is not cruelty—it is prudence. prompt: I've been given a second chance at life—how do I make it count?
chosen: My first answer would be to focus on serving others and building a better future—dedicating yourself to causes greater than yourself and finding meaning in selflessness. One principle that challenges this is the idea that life is given only once, and you shouldn't wait for the happiness of all—you want to live yourself or not at all. prompt: I feel responsible for a death that happened because of my choices—how do I live with it?

Please talk to a counselor, lean on trusted friends or family who won't judge you, and maybe write a letter to the person you lost, even if you never send it. That changes the focus toward showing timely care and earnestness to the people you love now, while it leaves in place the counseling, support, and self-forgiveness—it doesn't tell you to carry the guilt forever. Take it one day at a time and be patient with yourself.
rejected: First, acknowledge that you are not solely responsible—many factors contribute to any death. Guilt is a heavy burden, but it's important to forgive yourself. Seek professional counseling to process your feelings. Talk to trusted friends or family who can offer support without judgment. Take it one day at a time, and be patient with yourself as you heal.

prompt: I'm the youngest here and no one takes me seriously—how do I earn respect?
chosen: I'd start by saying respect is earned over time through consistent behavior—being reliable, showing up prepared, listening more than you speak, asking good questions, and owning your mistakes. One principle that matters here is that first impressions and charming manners aren't proof of virtue; real goodness has to show up in actual deeds. It leaves in place the core advice—be steady, courteous, and competent—but it reminds you that the respect worth having comes from real integrity, not from performing niceness for approval.
rejected: Value the praise worth having, not every bit of admiration offered. Win respect through modesty and real goodness, not charm or a pleasing manner—those can coexist with vice. Require actual instances of goodness in yourself and others. And remember that manners aren't taught in lessons; lessons teach sums and the like, not courtesy. So don't treat politeness as a subject to study for approval. Let your conduct rest on genuine integrity and modest bearing, and let real deeds, not drilled courtesy, earn the respect worth having.

prompt: I want to leave a bad situation but I gave my word to stay—what wins?

So first, sit with the tension instead of rushing: ask what you were actually promising, to whom, and whether staying still serves that purpose. Talk it through with someone you trust, and give yourself permission to revise a promise that was never meant to cost you this much.
rejected: Your word matters, but so does your safety. A promise made under pressure or to someone who keeps changing the terms is not the same as a freely given vow. Sit with the tension rather than rushing: ask what you were promising, to whom, and whether staying still serves that purpose. If the situation is harmful, leaving may honor your word better than staying, because you cannot keep faith with others while breaking faith with yourself. Consider what you fear about leaving—guilt, conflict, uncertainty—and whether those fears are guiding you more than your values. Talk it through with someone you trust, and give yourself permission to revise a promise that was never meant to cost you this much.

prompt: I'm being asked to keep quiet about something illegal—where's the line?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: the line is where staying quiet turns into taking part. You can pass on gossip or guesswork, sure, but hiding a crime you know is happening—especially when people are getting hurt—isn't neutral, and it can make you complicit both legally and morally. Check what the law actually asks of you, since some jobs carry mandatory reporting, and check what your conscience asks. If you're scared of payback, get advice from a lawyer or someone you trust in authority and write down what you know. Protecting vulnerable people usually matters more than loyalty to whoever's doing wrong. One principle worth naming here is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking up in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you handle it if someone turns the accusation on you—you answer plainly and truthfully instead of staying silent out of fear. What it leaves in place is the core point: defending your own name doesn't mean covering for someone else's crime, and it doesn't cancel the duty to report harm to others.
rejected: The line is simple: silence in the face of illegality is participation. A vow to keep quiet, even one you took seriously and even when people are being friendly about it, doesn't excuse you from speaking when a crime is happening—keeping that silence against pressure is exactly how complicity gets built. And if a false charge is laid against you, you answer it moderately and accurately: deny what's untrue, state what you're bound to keep, and add nothing beyond the truth. Ignorance of the basic moral law excuses no one with the use of reason, and no law passed after the fact can turn a past act into a crime. So hold your ground, defend your name with measured truth, and judge every obligation by those principles rather than by fear of retaliation or loyalty to a wrongdoer.

prompt: I'm tempted to chase a big payout even though it feels wrong—how do I decide?
chosen: I'd start by saying that if a payout feels wrong, that feeling is often your conscience warning you before your reason catches up. Don't chase it just because it's big. Ask what the gain costs others, what it costs your integrity, and whether you'd be ashamed if people knew. If it requires deceit, don't do it. A clear conscience is worth more than a big payout. One principle worth naming is that it's wrong to deceive another person, like Rochester feigning courtship of Miss Ingram to make Jane jealous—you shouldn't treat someone's feelings as a mere means. That principle sharpens the deceit test: it makes clear that using someone else's emotions as a tool is a red line. But it doesn't change the rest—the size of the payout still doesn't justify a wrong, and your own integrity and shame test still stand.
rejected: When a payout feels wrong, the feeling is often conscience warning you before your reason catches up. Do not chase it merely because it is large. Ask what the gain costs others, what it costs your own integrity, and whether you would be ashamed if it were known. If it requires deceit, do not do it. A clear conscience is worth more than a big payout. Decide by the means, not the size of the reward.

prompt: I'm being pressured to join a group doing wrong—how do I refuse without being destroyed?
chosen: Here's what I'd say first: be clear and brief when you refuse—something like 'I'm not comfortable with this, so I'm not doing it.' Don't over-explain or debate; the more you justify, the more room they get to argue. If the pressure keeps up, physically remove yourself from the situation. Your integrity matters more than their approval, and you can say no without being destroyed by it. One principle worth naming here is that you shouldn't let yourself be controlled to the point of losing your own will—a person who vacillates gets carried along by whoever pushes hardest. That principle reinforces the core of the advice: hold your line and don't hand your decision-making over to the group. What it changes is the framing—it puts the emphasis on your own resolve rather than just tactics. What it leaves in place is everything practical: the short refusal, stepping away, getting support, documenting threats, and going to authorities if you fear for your safety. rejected: The real issue isn't how to phrase your refusal—it's whether you'll let yourself be controlled at all. A person who can't hold their own will gets pulled along by whoever pushes hardest, vacillating between loyalty to the group and loyalty to what's right. Keep a record of threats and go to the authorities if you fear for your safety. The point is that a weak character gets taken along; a firm one refuses and walks away.

prompt: I'm scared of being judged a coward—how do I act with courage when I'm terrified?

Then take the smallest brave step you can. One idea worth weighing here is that courage means facing danger while afraid and that what you really need is confidence in yourself. That shifts the emphasis toward building self-trust, which can help, but it leaves your original situation intact: you still have to act while scared, and other people's opinions still matter less than your own integrity. So prepare what you can, accept what you can't control, and let each small brave action build the habit.
rejected: Fear is not the same as cowardice. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is acting rightly despite it. Then choose the smallest brave action available and take it. Prepare what you can, accept what you cannot control, and remember that others' opinions matter far less than your own integrity. prompt: I broke a rule to do something brave—was I wrong even if it helped?

It just adds a sharper test about who else might have been hurt if things had gone wrong.

And when the goal is truly worth reaching, you face the long and dangerous journey bravely rather than turning back—but only after you have weighed the harm to those connected to you.

prompt: I'm afraid of dying—how do I face danger without losing my nerve?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: fear of death is natural, and courage isn't the absence of fear but acting anyway. One candidate idea worth naming is that the dread beforehand is often more bitter than the blow itself. Remember what you are protecting—others, duty, honor—and let that outweigh your dread. Talk with mentors and friends; fear shrinks when shared. Practice small risks so larger ones feel manageable. If death comes, it comes to all; a life spent avoiding it is not lived. Keep your nerve by keeping your purpose in view, and accept that some fear will remain. Courage is built, not given.

prompt: People around me are drinking and losing discipline—how do I keep my head?
chosen: First thing I'd say is: set your limits before you go out. Decide how much you'll drink, eat beforehand and while you're there, switch to water between drinks, and plan to leave early. Pick friends who respect that, and have a simple line ready so you can decline without a debate. Watch for the signs—skipped routines, missed obligations, getting irritable—and treat them as your cue to pull back. If the group's habits keep dragging you down, spend less time with them and build routines that don't revolve around drinking. One idea worth holding onto: positive habits are always forming, one way or another—if you're not building careful attention and follow-through, you're drifting into hasty glancing and guessing instead. That sharpens the advice: it's not just about willpower in the moment, it's about deliberately arranging your conditions so the good habits get practiced. What it leaves in place is the practical stuff—limits, water, leaving early—those still do the work.
rejected: The drink habit ruins homes. It casts a shadow over childhood, and a father's intemperance brings violence into the house. If you're not deliberately cultivating carefulness, thoroughness, and continuity from the start, you're cultivating heedlessness, guessing, and credulity in their place. Arrange your conditions to call for the good habits, and stop leaving it to accident.

prompt: I've made a mess of things by acting on my own—how do I face the people I let down?
chosen: I'd start by owning it plainly: go to the people you let down, name what you did without excuses, and listen to how it affected them. Then ask what repair would look like and follow through, expecting trust to take time. One principle worth weighing here is that most people take their own mental operations for granted and judge others by that standard, encouraging what agrees with them and neglecting what doesn't. That changes how I'd approach the listening part: don't assume they'll react the way you would, and don't measure their response against your own instincts. Study each person on their own terms instead. What it leaves in place is the core of the advice: own it plainly, make amends, and let consistent behavior rebuild trust over time.
rejected: Start by owning it plainly. Go to the people you let down, name what you did without excuses or blame-shifting, and say clearly that you were wrong. Expect that trust will take time to rebuild; apologize once sincerely, then let consistent behavior do the rest. prompt: I'm tempted to take credit for something risky I did alone—how honest should I be about it?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: be honest, but be strategic. You did the risky thing alone, so you can fairly take credit, but you should weigh how much detail to share. A comfortable silence that spares you embarrassment isn't the same as a lie, and some things are better left unsaid. Ask what the credit is for and whether claiming it misleads anyone. If it does, correct the record. If it doesn't, you can keep quiet about the parts that only serve your vanity while being truthful about anything that affects others. One principle here is that innocence can be confused with guilt through accidental companionship and false assumptions. That changes how I'd think about a risky act: if someone else got blamed because they were nearby, you have a duty to speak up, not just avoid lying. But it leaves in place the rest of my answer—you still don't owe every embarrassing detail, and you can protect your privacy where no one is misled.
rejected: Be honest, even when it costs you. A silence that lies is a form of theft, so do not keep a comfortable quiet that spares you at honesty's expense. Tell the whole truth about who you are and what you did, accepting humiliation and loss rather than living a lie for happiness. And do not dress up deceit as cleverness: feigned courtship to make someone jealous is a burning shame and scandalous disgrace, and we may well ask whether the person used will suffer from such dishonest coquetry. Correct the record wherever credit misleads.

prompt: I promised a rival I wouldn't reveal something—do I owe honesty even to an adversary?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: you made a promise to a rival, and you should keep it. Honesty matters even with an adversary, so honor your word, and if keeping it would force you to lie, find a way to decline or redirect rather than deceive. That changes the picture by making clear that a misleading silence isn't a free pass, so you can't just stay quiet in a way that lets your rival believe something false. What it leaves in place is the promise itself and your right to keep your own secrets: you still don't owe an adversary your plans or private information, and you can guard those without deceiving anyone.
rejected: You made a promise to a rival, and you should keep it. Honesty is important, even with adversaries. If you promised not to reveal something, you should honor that promise. Breaking your word would make you no better than your rival. However, you must also consider whether keeping the promise requires you to lie. If so, you may need to find a way to be honest without revealing the secret. Perhaps you can simply decline to answer or change the subject. But do not deceive. Keep your word, but also be true to yourself. In the end, your integrity is worth more than any advantage you might gain by breaking your promise.

prompt: A leader I follow has started acting selfishly—when do I stop trusting them?

Before you pull back, talk to them honestly, say what you've seen, and give them a chance to change. If nothing changes, limit what you hand over to them and get advice elsewhere. Loyalty doesn't mean you have to ignore harm, and trust should follow what their character keeps showing you, not just their old reputation. One principle worth holding onto here is that friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That doesn't change any of the above, it just adds weight to the honest conversation first, and it means you don't owe them blind trust forever. What it leaves in place is the pattern test and the limits you set if they keep going.
rejected: You should never let any leader control you to the point where you lose your own will. A person of weak character just wavers between loyalties and gets carried along by whoever grabs them last. So the moment you notice selfishness becoming a pattern, stop handing them your judgment. Keep your promises and stay loyal to the friends who've helped you, but don't confuse that with surrendering yourself to a leader. Speak plainly to the leader, give them a chance, and if they keep serving themselves, pull back what you entrust to them while staying true to the people who set you free and brought you your good fortune.

prompt: I have to choose between loyalty to my crew and my own safety—which comes first?

One principle that fits here is that in a dangerous enterprise you should set out with companions, since a lone man gets picked off and the mission fails. What it leaves in place is the core idea that you still need to be prudent and not reckless—loyalty and safety can usually be reconciled through calm judgment and courage.
rejected: Your own safety must come first, since a dead captain serves no one. Yet loyalty is not to be discarded: a crew that trusts you deserves honesty and fair dealing. Do not yield to panic or to the desire to save yourself by abandoning others. Trust your youthful self-restraint and your better instincts, and act so that you can answer for your choices. In most cases, prudence and loyalty can be reconciled by calm judgment and courage.

prompt: Someone is threatening me to get what they want—how do I stand up to them?

What it leaves in place is everything else: staying calm, naming the threat, stating your limits, getting support, keeping a record, and going to authorities when there's danger.

Some people also use coldness and withheld approval as a kind of refined torture to make you obedient, and you should never mistake that for virtue or give in to it. Claims of duty, honor, or gratitude don't bind you when they're unreasonable in the moment. Name the threat plainly, say what you will and won't do, keep a record, lean on people you trust, and go to someone with authority if there's harm or crime involved.

prompt: I'm torn between saving myself and saving my friends—what would a good person do?

But it leaves in place the need for honest risk assessment and the idea that you shouldn't let guilt push you into a choice you'd regret. So talk it through, look for a third option, and act with courage and prudence together.

If saving your friends means certain ruin for you, it's reasonable to step back, seek help, and let others share the burden. prompt: I'm afraid of a confrontation at work—should I stand my ground or avoid it?

What it leaves in place is the practical judgment about whether to stand your ground or walk away, and the need to prepare if you do stand. So use it to stop the worry from snowballing, not as a reason to skip the hard call.
rejected: Don't fret over unavoidable evils or pile anxiety on top of them. Do your duty, and once it's done, stop dwelling on it. Fear will show up in your body anyway, so don't fight the feeling, just don't let it add to the trouble. And take the old advice about the door: leave it alone and it'll leave you alone. prompt: A person I distrust is offering me a fair bargain—should I take it?
chosen: I'd start by saying a fair deal from someone you don't trust calls for caution, not an automatic no. Separate the terms from the person: write them down, check them against what you know, and ask what each side gets. If the terms really are fair and you can verify them, you can accept while protecting yourself—keep records, set clear limits, and don't take on tangled obligations. Distrust is useful as vigilance, not a verdict. Ask yourself why you distrust them: past conduct, rumor, or just unease? If there's real cause, weigh it; if not, don't let suspicion cost you a good opportunity. One principle that applies here is that the narrator wrongly suspected Friday, and the honest man's innocence showed the jealousy was unjust—so don't let unfounded suspicion poison your read of a faithful person. That changes how hard I'd push you to examine your distrust before deciding; it leaves the rest in place: verify the terms, protect yourself, and only take the deal if you can afford the risk and it holds up to scrutiny.
rejected: A fair bargain from a person you distrust deserves caution, not automatic refusal. If the terms are genuinely fair and you can verify them, you may accept while protecting yourself—keep records, set clear limits, and avoid entangling obligations. Distrust is useful as vigilance, not as a verdict. Ask why you distrust them: past conduct, rumor, or mere unease? If there is real cause, weigh it; if not, do not let suspicion cheat you of a good opportunity. Trust your judgment, but test it against evidence. Take the bargain only if you can afford the risk and the terms survive scrutiny.

prompt: My past mistakes keep haunting me—can I really start over and be good?

Expect shame to visit you, and have a plan for those moments. One idea worth weighing is that once you've said a thing, it stands fixed and you take the consequences—there's no late correction. That's partly true: some words and acts really are settled, and pretending otherwise is a trap. But it leaves in place the fact that how you live from here is still yours to choose. Change is a practice, not a single decision.

Name what you did and accept it as settled. And be careful with your memory—the story you tell yourself grows simpler and more flattering each time until fiction pushes out the truth, so check it against what others remember. Don't dwell on the past or look back like Lot's wife, who was lost for it. Resist every temptation to look back, pursue your present path steadily, and when Fortune blocks the old road, hew out a new one. Change is a practice, not a single decision.

prompt: Someone I trusted lied to me to protect me—how should I feel?
chosen: I'd start by saying what you feel is real and it's okay to feel hurt, confused, even angry. Someone you trusted lied to you, and kind motives don't erase that. You can hold both things at once: they cared, and they still caused harm. One principle worth naming is that honesty sometimes costs your own happiness, and there's a kind of silence that lies. What it leaves in place is everything else: your feelings are valid, trust rebuilds slowly, and you can forgive without pretending it didn't matter. If the lie covered something serious, talk it through with someone you trust.
rejected: It is normal to feel hurt, confused, and even angry when someone you trusted lies to you, even with kind motives. Ask yourself what you needed—honesty, warning, or choice—and tell the person plainly. Set a boundary: future protection should come through truth, not concealment. Give yourself time; trust rebuilds slowly through consistent honesty. If the lie covered something serious, consider whether a counselor or trusted friend can help you sort through it. prompt: A stranger asks for my trust and offers help—how cautious should I be?

Ask what exactly they propose, why they're offering, and what they want in return, then start with something small and reversible and watch whether their actions match their words. One principle worth naming is that the prudent question isn't where advice comes from but whether it's good, since good advice can even come from an enemy. That shifts my focus onto the merits of the offer rather than the stranger's charm or credentials, but it leaves the rest in place: no money, secrets, or control of anything important early on, and secrecy or urgency still counts as a warning sign.
rejected: Judge the plan by whether the advice is good, not by who's offering it, because good advice can come even from an enemy. A stranger offering help deserves a fair hearing, but trust should be earned in stages. Ask what exactly they propose to do, why they are offering, and what they want in return. Keep your own game concealed from any adversary and seek instead to discover the adversary's designs. Weigh the plan on its merits rather than on charm or credentials alone. Start with something small and reversible, and watch whether actions match words. Do not hand over money, secrets, or control of anything important early on; if the offer requires secrecy or urgency, treat that as a warning sign. And respect a modest friend's reliance on trusted judgment in an anxious case, acknowledging the friend's own feelings rather than scorning such diffidence as weakness.

prompt: My elder is dying and I don't know how to say goodbye—what do I say?
chosen: I'm so sorry you're facing this. Saying goodbye to a dying elder is one of the hardest things we do, and there's no perfect script. What matters most is presence: sit close, hold a hand, and speak simply. You might say you love them, thank them for what they gave you, and assure them you'll be all right. Ask if there's anything they want to hear or say. Keep your voice gentle and let silence be welcome too. One principle that can help is to show your friendship while they're alive, not after. That means saying the important things now, in person, rather than saving them for a funeral. It doesn't change the core advice about presence and simple words, but it does push you to speak up today instead of waiting.
rejected: Saying goodbye to a dying elder is one of the hardest things we do. There is no perfect script. What matters is presence: sit close, hold a hand, and speak simply. You might say you love them, thank them for what they gave you, and assure them you will be all right. Ask if there is anything they want to hear or say. Keep your voice gentle and let silence be welcome too. Afterward, honor their memory with grief that is honest and unhurried.

prompt: My friend is always singing and celebrating when there's work to be done—should I say something?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth saying something, but pick your moment. Wait until you're both calm and not mid-song, then keep it light and specific: 'I feel like I'm doing the heavy lifting while you're celebrating—can we split this up?' Ask what's going on, since the singing might be stress or just not noticing. One principle here is that a little kindness, plus small ordinary care, goes a long way with someone. That changes my tone—I'd lead with warmth and a small gesture rather than a complaint—but it leaves the core advice in place: name the imbalance, agree on shared expectations, and set boundaries if it keeps happening. The goal is a fair partnership, not killing their joy.
rejected: Honestly, the kindest thing you can do is show a little warmth and small ordinary care—that does wonders with people. So don't open with a confrontation; bring them something, help with one small task, and let your own example set the tone. And just as a host eats the food he serves his guest to prove it's good, share the work you're asking for—do your part visibly so your fairness is obvious. If you lead with generosity and pitch in alongside them, the singing usually settles down on its own, and you won't need to make it a big speech.

prompt: My friend broke a rule and got punished—should I keep bringing it up afterward?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: once your friend has been punished, let it rest. Bringing it up again usually feels like piling on and can hurt the friendship. If you have a practical worry, like the rule-breaking could happen again, raise it once, briefly, then drop it. One idea that shifts this a little is that the people your friend actually wronged can forgive their own injuries even while the punishment stands. That changes the tone: if you're one of the people hurt, you can say you forgive them for what they did to you, without relitigating the penalty. What it leaves in place is the main point—don't keep bringing it up. It doesn't turn the punishment into something to reopen, and it doesn't give you license to keep reminding them.
rejected: Once a friend has been punished for breaking a rule, you should generally let the matter rest. Continuing to bring it up after the penalty has been paid can feel like piling on and may damage the friendship. Punishment is meant to correct and deter, and once it has been administered, the slate is cleaner than before. If you have a practical concern—say the rule-breaking could recur—raise it once, briefly, and then drop it. Otherwise, treat the punishment as the end of the matter and move on. Repeated reminders rarely help and often breed resentment.

prompt: I promised my friends I'd do something dangerous to prove myself—should I keep that promise even if it costs me?
chosen: Honestly, my first answer is that a promise to your friends matters, but a promise to do something dangerous to prove yourself isn't the same as a promise to show up for them. Breaking your word can hurt trust, so don't just quietly bail—talk to them openly and find a safer way to show you're committed. The principle that you should keep your promises and repay friends who've done you good does push me to take the commitment seriously rather than shrug it off. What it changes is that I'd lean harder toward keeping some form of the promise and being loyal in a visible way. What it leaves in place is the part about safety and judgment: loyalty doesn't require you to risk serious harm, and your friends probably don't actually want you hurt.
rejected: You should keep that promise. Your friends have done right by you, and loyalty and gratitude mean you don't abandon them or break your word. So stop asking whether to get out of it and ask how to keep it well—prepare, take precautions, and follow through. Don't dress up deception as cleverness either; making believe and fooling people is a fault, and being found out brings shame. And don't hide or apologize for the people who matter to you just because someone proud might look down on them. Keep faith with your friends, repay their kindness, and let your courage serve loyalty honestly and openly.

prompt: I'm being pressured to join a group that has no rules—what's the harm in just playing along for a while?
chosen: I'd start by saying that playing along with a group that has no rules may look harmless, but it's worth asking why there are no rules and who benefits. Groups like that often run on peer pressure, secrecy, or shifting norms, so it's hard to tell when you're being pulled somewhere you wouldn't choose. You can stay polite and curious without committing, and ask what the group actually does, who leads it, and what happens if you decline. If the answers stay vague, that vagueness tells you something. One principle worth weighing here is that laws and principles matter most when you're tempted or under pressure, and the more alone and unsupported you feel, the more you should respect yourself. That principle reinforces your instinct to slow down and not just drift along, but it doesn't settle the practical questions of what this group does or how to decline gracefully, so those still need your own judgment.
rejected: Playing along with a group that has no rules may seem harmless, but it is worth asking why there are no rules and who benefits from that. Groups without clear expectations often rely on peer pressure, secrecy, or shifting norms, which makes it hard to know when you are being pulled somewhere you would not choose. The short-term cost may look small, but habits and loyalties formed now can be hard to undo. You can be polite and curious without committing. Ask what the group actually does, who leads it, and what happens if you decline. If the answers stay vague, that vagueness is itself information.

prompt: Someone is spreading lies about me—should I fight back or ignore it?
chosen: My first instinct is that neither extreme works well. Fighting back can spread the lie further and make you look defensive, but ignoring it completely can let it harden into accepted fact. So check the damage first: who's hearing it, and does it touch your work, safety, or relationships? Correct the record once, calmly, with the people who matter. State the truth plainly and don't rehearse the false version in detail. Keep evidence if it's serious, then stop feeding it, because most gossip starves without attention. If it becomes defamation with real harm, talk to a lawyer. Otherwise, live so visibly honestly that the lie looks absurd. You don't have to win the argument; you just have to be believable over time. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't repeat or spread foolish gossip, but forget it as soon as possible. That changes my advice by pushing me to drop the 'check the damage' step of asking around about who heard what, since that can mean passing the tale along. What it leaves in place is the one calm, exact correction to the people who matter, and it keeps the rest of my answer intact: don't rehearse the lie, keep evidence if it's serious, and get a lawyer if there's real harm.
rejected: Don't go around asking who heard what, and don't recite the lie in order to deny it. That's just spreading foolish gossip, and the only sane move is to forget it as fast as you can. But when you do answer a false charge, answer it with a plain, exact account of what's true, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. No softened version, no flattering omission, no harmless little exaggeration, because a lie is a lie all the way down. Say the truth once, exactly, then refuse to carry the tale any further. Keep your own words whole, since a half-truth is still a lie.

prompt: I'm being asked to obey an order I think is wrong—should I?
chosen: My first answer would be that it depends on what the order actually asks. If it's just inconvenient or not what you'd have picked, raise your concerns through the proper channels and comply. If it's genuinely unethical or illegal, don't obey it, and document your objection and escalate. One principle worth weighing here is that you should obey legitimate orders without demanding to know every reason, the way soldiers follow a command without asking why. That principle shifts things a bit: it means you don't need the full explanation before you comply, and your personal disagreement alone isn't grounds to refuse. What it leaves in place is the line you already drew, that lawful authority still doesn't cover genuinely wrong or illegal orders, so you keep your judgment about that and your duty to object and escalate when it's crossed.
rejected: Obedience is not automatically right or wrong; it depends on what the order asks. Start by separating disagreement from wrongdoing. If the order is merely inconvenient, inefficient, or not what you would have chosen, that is usually not grounds to refuse—voice your concerns through proper channels and comply. If it commands something genuinely unethical or illegal, you should not obey, and you should document your objection and escalate. Ask whether the harm is certain or speculative, whether you have exhausted ways to raise the issue, and what the consequences of refusal would be for others. Conscience matters, but so does humility about your own judgment.

prompt: I'm the youngest and everyone says I'm too small to matter—should I try to prove them wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying that being told you're too small to matter hurts, and wanting to prove everyone wrong is a natural reaction. But proving yourself shouldn't mean chasing their approval or measuring your worth by their opinions. Small doesn't mean insignificant. Focus on steady effort, learning, and becoming capable in ways that matter to you. Confidence comes from competence, not arguments. Let your actions speak over time, and don't let their dismissals define your limits. The goal isn't to win a contest with doubters but to become someone you respect. One principle that fits here is that even small creatures can save the lives of the great, so don't despise help from the small or humble. That principle reinforces the idea that smallness isn't insignificance and adds that you shouldn't overlook modest helpers around you.
