It leaves in place the core advice: don't chase approval, build competence, and let actions speak.
rejected: You should absolutely try to prove them wrong, but not by arguing—by becoming capable and honoring the modest helpers around you. Remember the Lion and the field-mice: the great beast was saved by the smallest creatures, so small things can save the great. But growth isn't always increase—in metamorphosis and old age, mass and bulk are lost—so don't measure worth by size alone. Reserve judgment about those who underestimate you. As Nick's father urged, not everyone has had the same advantages; advantages and decencies are unequally distributed, and conduct you find small-minded may reflect a narrower start. Hold your own course with tolerance, and measure yourself by who you are becoming rather than by others' dismissals.

prompt: My pack leader is getting old and may fail soon—should I stay loyal to him or side with the younger ones who want a new leader?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: loyalty to an aging leader is honorable, but a pack still has to survive, so don't pick sides in secret. Talk openly with him and with the younger ones, support him where he's weak, and let the younger members take on responsibility gradually. One principle here is that the pack's leadership belongs to the pack alone, and outsiders have no claim on it. That changes who gets a say: keep any outside influence out of the decision and settle it among your own members. What it leaves in place is everything else, respect for the old leader, a gradual handover, and honesty rather than a sudden coup.
rejected: Loyalty to an aging leader is honorable, but a pack also needs to survive. If the old leader is failing, the younger ones may have a point about fresh leadership. Consider what serves the pack as a whole: stability, continuity, and the safety of everyone in it. Talk openly with the leader and the younger members rather than choosing sides in secret. Support the old leader with respect and help him where he is weak, while making room for younger members to take on responsibility gradually. A wise transition, handled with honesty and care, honors the past and protects the future better than a sudden coup or blind loyalty.

prompt: I have to obey someone who gives me orders I don't understand—should I ask why or just do it?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: it depends on the order and the risk. If it's unclear but harmless, ask a quick clarifying question so you get it right—good leaders expect that. If it's urgent or high-stakes, follow first and ask afterward. If it seems unethical or dangerous, question it, refuse if needed, and report it through proper channels. One principle worth weighing is that you should obey legitimate orders without demanding every reason, like soldiers who follow the king's command without asking why. That principle shifts things a bit: it says don't insist on a full explanation before acting when the authority is legitimate. But it doesn't erase your need to understand enough to act correctly, and it doesn't cover orders that are dangerous or wrong. So I'd still say: clarify when you can, comply when speed matters, and never obey something that violates your conscience or the law.
rejected: You should just obey. When the authority is legitimate, follow the order without demanding the full explanation—soldiers don't ask why they're sent to fight, they go where told. Do your duty rather than defy the one who has care of you. Obeying only your own will isn't strength; it breeds disorder and ends in subjection. Ordered obedience is the stronger course. Obey first; understanding can follow.

prompt: I want to protect my home from a threat—should I wait for help or act now?
chosen: I'd start by saying: act now, but act wisely. Waiting for help only makes sense if help is genuinely on the way and the delay costs you nothing; otherwise it's just hoping. Secure what matters, remove what invites the threat, and make the danger visible to those who can assist—then act on the threat itself, decisively but lawfully, and ask for help in parallel rather than instead. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't harm the small and fragile, and you should grieve when harm comes to them. That changes how you act—plan your defense so it doesn't crush the vulnerable in your household—but it doesn't change the core call to act now rather than freeze. The rest of the advice stands: move carefully, but move.
rejected: Act now, but act wisely. Waiting for help is only reasonable if help is genuinely on the way and the delay costs you nothing; otherwise waiting is just hoping. Start with the steps that reduce risk immediately—secure what matters, remove what invites the threat, and make the danger visible to those who can assist. Then act on the threat itself, decisively but lawfully, and ask for help in parallel rather than instead. Fear is not a reason to freeze; it is a signal to prepare. The worst outcome is usually neither acting nor waiting, but drifting while telling yourself you are waiting for rescue.

prompt: Someone powerful keeps telling me my adopted brother doesn't belong with us—should I give in to him?
chosen: I wouldn't just give in to someone powerful who tells you your adopted brother doesn't belong. Family isn't decided by whoever shouts loudest. That said, one principle worth weighing is that a friend's free choice to visit should be distinguished from being sent for by someone in authority—so check whether this person is acting on their own or speaking for someone else. That distinction changes how you respond: if it's just their opinion, you can push back; if they're carrying someone else's command, you need to be more careful. What it leaves in place is your loyalty to your brother and your need to talk with your family and find allies. Stand by your brother, but be wise about how you resist.
rejected: You should not give in. Your adopted brother is your brother, and belonging is not something a powerful person gets to revoke. Do your duty where you are, but do not let fear keep you quiet when real wrong is done. If someone is trying to push your brother out, speak plainly and directly—don't dress it up. Denunciation is not betrayal when it serves justice. Stay loyal, act on your resolve, and call for help if you need it. Do not surrender your convictions just because someone has authority.

prompt: My leader is willing to sacrifice himself for me—should I let him?
chosen: My first thought is that it depends on what kind of sacrifice he's offering. If he's genuinely putting himself at risk for the people he leads, that deserves respect and gratitude, but you shouldn't just passively accept it. Ask what the sacrifice is for, whether it's truly necessary, and whether you're being asked to give something of yourself in return that you can't rightly give. Sacrifice freely offered is noble; sacrifice demanded as a debt is another matter. One principle worth naming here is that you may give your energies to a cause but not yourself—a divided allegiance offered as a mutilated sacrifice isn't acceptable, and the heart can't be commanded where it doesn't go. That principle sharpens the point: it tells you to separate giving your effort as a fellow-worker from giving yourself wholly, and it says the second must not be extorted by another's devotion. What it leaves in place is the gratitude and the careful weighing—you still ask what the sacrifice is for and whether it's necessary, and you still let his willingness move you without consenting blindly.
rejected: This is a hard question, and the answer depends on what kind of sacrifice is being offered. If a leader genuinely puts himself at risk for those he leads, that devotion deserves respect and gratitude. But you should not simply accept it passively. Ask what the sacrifice is for, whether it is truly necessary, and whether you are being asked to give something of yourself in return that you cannot rightly give. Sacrifice freely offered is noble; sacrifice demanded as a debt is another matter. Let your leader's willingness move you, but weigh the cost and the purpose before you consent.

prompt: My community is splitting apart over whether to accept a newcomer—what should I do?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: listen to both sides without rushing to a verdict, and suggest something low-stakes like a shared meal so people form impressions from experience instead of rumor. The principle that kindness and neighborliness toward the lonely should come first changes the emphasis—it pushes me to make sure the newcomer isn't left waiting while the community debates, so I'd reach out personally and warmly right away. What it leaves in place is the rest: being clear about shared values and boundaries, letting the newcomer show whether he respects them, and modeling calm, fair welcome rather than forcing agreement.
rejected: Be neighborly first—reach out to the lonely newcomer, share your home and your cheer, and invite him to a meal, because warmth does what argument never will. But hold your tried and tested friends close with hoops of steel, and don't wear out your palm shaking hands with every new arrival. Remember that experience is what you agree to attend to; without selective interest, a community's life turns into gray chaos. So decide what you'll notice and nurture: welcome the newcomer, keep your proven friends near, and let deliberate attention, not circumstance, shape what your community becomes.

prompt: I made a mistake that hurt my friends—how do I make it right?
chosen: I'd start by naming the mistake honestly, to yourself and to them. Then apologize plainly, without excuses or hedging, and ask what would help repair the harm. Listen more than you explain. Offer concrete amends—time, effort, whatever the damage requires—and then change the behavior that caused it, because an apology without change is only noise. Give your friends room to be hurt and to take time; don't demand instant forgiveness. If they need distance, respect it. The goal isn't to feel better quickly but to become someone who doesn't repeat the harm, and to let trust rebuild slowly through consistent action rather than words. One candidate principle here is that it's too late to correct it—once you've said a thing, that fixes it, and you must take the consequences. That principle changes the emphasis: it tells you not to try to undo or soften what you said, and to accept the fallout without trying to wriggle out of it. But it leaves in place the core of the advice: you still apologize, still ask what would help, still change the behavior, and still give your friends room to heal. So it sharpens the honesty and acceptance part, but doesn't replace the active repair work.
rejected: Start by naming the mistake honestly, to yourself and to them. Then apologize plainly, without excuses or hedging, and ask what would help repair the harm. Listen more than you explain. Offer concrete amends—time, effort, whatever the damage requires—and then change the behavior that caused it, because an apology without change is only noise. Give your friends room to be hurt and to take time; do not demand instant forgiveness. If they need distance, respect it. The goal is not to feel better quickly but to become someone who does not repeat the harm, and to let trust rebuild slowly through consistent action rather than words.

prompt: I'm afraid of something small and harmless—does that make me a coward?
chosen: No, being scared of something small and harmless doesn't make you a coward. Courage isn't the absence of fear—it's doing the right thing even when you're afraid. Plenty of brave people are terrified of spiders, heights, or mice. What counts is whether you let the fear run your choices or whether you face things when it matters. Ask yourself if the fear is out of proportion to the real danger. If it is, you can work on it gradually—small steps, breathing, maybe talking to someone. Don't shame yourself for a bodily reaction; judge yourself by what you do, not by what makes your heart race. One idea worth holding onto is that true courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you really need is confidence in yourself. That reframes your fear as normal rather than shameful, and it leaves your original point intact: fear itself isn't cowardice. It just adds that building confidence is the real work, not stamping out the fear.
rejected: Fear of something small and harmless is not cowardice—courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you need is confidence in yourself. There's no living thing that isn't afraid when it faces danger, so stop treating your fear as a defect. Build your confidence and act anyway. That's the whole answer: be afraid, and do it scared.

prompt: My friends got hurt helping me out of a mess I made—should I accept their punishment without arguing?
chosen: I'd have said at first: if your friends got hurt helping you, accept the punishment quietly and don't argue—arguing just makes you look worse. But one principle here changes that: if everyone believes you're wicked while your own conscience says otherwise, you're not without friends. So don't treat the verdict as final proof you're guilty; check what's actually true and fair. What stays in place is loyalty—don't drag your friends further in, and don't do anything rash that hurts them more. So: don't just swallow it blindly, but don't fight in a way that costs them either.
rejected: If your friends were hurt helping you, the decent thing is to accept the punishment quietly and not make a fuss. Public opinion and the verdict of those in authority are likely right, and arguing will only make you look worse. Accept the blame, take the penalty, and move on. Loyalty to your friends means not dragging them further into the matter, and a powerful accuser's judgment is best treated as final. Keep your head down and let the matter close.

prompt: I found out my friend was born somewhere else—does that change whether he's my brother?
chosen: No—where he was born doesn't undo what you two have built. Brotherhood, in the sense that matters, is made of shared years, trust, and the choice to stand by each other, not a birthplace on a form. If anything, learning he came from somewhere else adds to him rather than takes away. One idea worth holding onto here is that the identity you find in yourself is only a loose, relative thing on the whole—it rests mainly on carrying the same memories through gradual change. That principle shifts how I'd frame it: he isn't simply the same fixed person, he's the same person on the whole, and so are you. What it leaves in place is everything that actually matters—the remembered years, the trust, the conduct. So ask him about it if you're curious, and let the answer deepen the friendship rather than put it on trial.
rejected: No, and don't let anyone tell you a birthplace is a small thing. The family tie has real weight: a person's faculties are often a mosaic of ancestral qualities, and the life-histories of relatives are prophetic of his own future. A child's natural birthright includes being told the life-history of his ancestry. So this isn't trivia—it's part of who he is, and part of what he's owed. Ask him, and let him ask you. But mind the degree of intimacy proper to each tie: a wife may take liberties with her husband that a brother would not allow in a sister more than ten years younger. Between friends, take the liberty your closeness has earned—no more, no less. If his conduct and his memory of your friendship still hold, then he is your brother in the only sense that survives change.

prompt: Someone who hurt my family is now vulnerable—should I finish them off?
chosen: I get why you're furious at someone who hurt your family, and now that they're vulnerable you might feel like finishing them off. But before you do anything, stop and think about what that would cost you and everyone around you. Talk to someone you trust, let the impulse cool. Revenge rarely brings the peace people hope for, and going after someone who's defenseless carries serious risks. Protecting your family and setting boundaries is one thing; harming someone who's down is another. One principle that matters here is that forgiveness of those who've injured you is right and healing—like Jane seeking reconciliation with Mrs. Reed and forgiving her fully even though the injury was never repented. That principle changes the direction: instead of finishing them off, you'd aim at letting go of resentment and, where possible, seeking reconciliation. But it leaves in place your need to protect your family through boundaries and lawful means, and it doesn't mean you have to pretend the harm didn't happen or put yourself in danger.
rejected: It is understandable to feel anger toward someone who harmed your family, and now that they are vulnerable you may feel tempted to act on that anger. Before doing anything, pause and consider the consequences for yourself and others. You might talk to friends or a counselor about your feelings, and let time cool your impulse. Revenge rarely brings the peace people hope for, and acting while someone is defenseless carries serious risks. Consider whether distance is better than confrontation. It is okay to protect your family and set boundaries without seeking to harm someone who is down.

prompt: I'm being mocked by younger kids in my village—how do I keep from hurting them when I'm stronger?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's good that you don't want to hurt them. When younger kids mock you, the safest move is to walk away, cool off, and remind yourself they're children who don't know better. If it keeps happening, talk to their parents and let adults handle the correction. Your strength is a responsibility, not a license, and using it on someone weaker would cause real harm and shame. One principle here is that parents should teach their children to walk in truth and soberness and to love and serve one another rather than fight and quarrel. That changes things by making it clear the mocking isn't just harmless childishness, so you can speak plainly to the parents and ask them to correct it. What it leaves in place is your own limit: you still walk away, you still don't use your strength against them, and you still keep busy with useful work and let your calm show maturity.
rejected: The real issue isn't the kids, it's the parents who let them run wild. Parents are supposed to feed and clothe their children and teach them truth, soberness, love, and service instead of contention. It's never too soon for a child to learn obedience, and a firm no from a father can land harder than a mother's soft pats. A parent who doesn't check a child's exuberant spirits lets that volatility harden into character and brings disgrace on the whole family. So don't shrug this off as childish nonsense. Tell the parents plainly to correct their children and teach them to love and serve one another and keep God's laws.

prompt: My friends want me to break a rule for fun—should I?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: not automatically. Ask what the rule protects and who bears the cost if it's broken. If the fun is harmless and reversible, you can join without much worry; if it could hurt someone, damage trust, or set a precedent you wouldn't defend openly, decline. One principle that matters here is that you shouldn't make sport of gossip at someone's real expense—laughing at an idle report can genuinely hurt them. That principle sharpens the harm test: it makes you check whether the 'fun' is at someone else's expense, but it doesn't change the rest—you still weigh the cost, still speak plainly, and still suggest an alternative that keeps the fun without the harm.
rejected: Not automatically. Ask what the rule protects and who bears the cost if it is broken. If the 'fun' is harmless and reversible—a silly game, a harmless prank among consenting friends—you can join without much worry. But if breaking it could hurt someone, damage trust, or set a precedent you would not defend openly, decline. Friendship does not require you to abandon your judgment; real friends accept a calm no. Say what you will and will not do, suggest an alternative that keeps the fun without the risk, and let their reaction tell you something about the friendship.

prompt: I did something good but got punished for it anyway—is it worth doing good?
chosen: It hurts when you do something good and get punished for it, and it's fair to wonder whether doing good is worth it. My first answer would be that the worth of doing good isn't measured only by what comes back to you—it's also about the kind of person you become and the trust you build over time. Punishment for a good act can come from misunderstanding, bad timing, or an unfair system, not from goodness itself being wrong. One idea worth naming is that real punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on someone judged to have broken the law, to encourage obedience—and that private revenge, harm without a hearing, or harm beyond the declared penalty isn't punishment but hostility. That distinction changes something: it lets you ask whether what happened to you was actually lawful correction or just hostility dressed up as punishment, and it tells you not to accept the second as a verdict on your character. What it leaves in place is the harder question you're really asking—whether to keep doing good. So separate the specific injustice from the general question, see what can be corrected or explained, and protect yourself where you can. Do good because it's good, but don't let unfair systems convince you that goodness itself is pointless.
rejected: You were all the better for being punished—but it makes a difference that you had actually done the things you were punished for. That's the whole point. If you did good and were punished anyway, then what happened to you wasn't punishment at all. Punishment is an evil inflicted by public authority on someone judged to have transgressed the law, for the end of disposing people to obedience. Private revenge is not punishment. Harm without a public hearing is not punishment. Harm exceeding the declared penalty is not punishment. All of that is hostility, and hostility settles nothing. True punishment, once given, closes the matter with no lingering reproach. So stop calling your suffering punishment. Ask whether a lawful authority judged you and declared a penalty, or whether someone simply hurt you. If it's the latter, refuse to dignify it with the name of punishment, and don't let it talk you out of doing good.

prompt: I did something brave and everyone is praising me—how do I keep from getting a big head about it?
chosen: It's great that you're being praised for your bravery. To keep from getting a big head, remember that praise is fleeting and plenty of people have done brave things without any recognition. Stay humble by focusing on the act itself rather than the applause, acknowledge that you had help or that circumstances let you act, and keep perspective that your worth isn't defined by others' opinions. Practice gratitude and keep seeking challenges that ground you, and avoid comparing yourself or chasing constant validation. One thing worth adding: learn to value the praise that's actually worth having and earn the admiration of people whose judgment you respect by being modest as well as brave. That shifts things a little—it's not about dismissing praise wholesale but being choosy about whose praise matters and pairing courage with modesty. What it leaves in place is the core of the original advice: don't let applause define you, stay grateful, and keep your feet on the ground.
rejected: It's great that you're being praised for your bravery. To avoid getting a big head, remember that praise is fleeting and that many people have done brave things without recognition. Stay humble by focusing on the act itself rather than the applause. Acknowledge that you had help or that circumstances allowed you to act. Keep perspective: your worth isn't defined by others' opinions. Practice gratitude and continue to seek challenges that keep you grounded. Avoid comparing yourself to others or seeking constant validation. True humility comes from recognizing your limitations and valuing others' contributions.

prompt: I found out that a place I thought was safe has been visited by danger before—should I still go?
chosen: My first answer would be to be cautious: if a place you thought was safe has seen danger before, there's no shame in turning back, and no prize is worth your life. Weigh the risk carefully, and if the danger is real and present, choose another road. One principle worth naming is that it's better to face a long and dangerous journey bravely than to turn back when the goal is worth reaching. That principle changes the tone—it says don't retreat just because the road is rough or because fear shows up first. But it leaves in place the core of my first answer: caution is still reasonable, safety still matters more than the goal, and if the way looks too dark, turning back is still a valid choice. So I'd say: prepare honestly, go watchfully if you go, but don't let bravery talk you out of listening to real danger.
rejected: Don't turn back out of fear. If the goal is worth reaching, a rough and dangerous road is worth pressing through, and brave resolve means going forward rather than retreating at the first sign of peril. Courage isn't carelessness, though—youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near, so stay wary, because the best safety lies in fear. And remember the warning about offending the powerful: a tenacious memory and a long arm can reach you when you think you're secure. He who sleeps over a lighted mine is not safe. So go forward soberly, provisioned, and alert, guarding your heart as closely as the road, and never lull yourself in false security.

prompt: A group of kids with no rules invited me to join them and said I'd be their leader—should I go?
chosen: I'd start by saying the offer is flattering, but 'no rules' is the red flag. A group with no rules usually means whoever's boldest sets the tone, and as the leader you'd get blamed when things go sideways. Ask what they actually mean—no adults around, no boundaries, or just no formal club? Think about the safety and what you'd be asked to do. You can hang out with friends without taking a title that makes you responsible for chaos. If you go, set a few clear expectations of your own, or better, suggest a plan with some structure. One principle that fits here is that if there's going to be a party, you ought to invite the guests—meaning if you're going to lead, you should be the one deciding who's included and what the expectations are. That changes things by putting you in charge of the setup rather than just accepting a title. It leaves in place the core warning: 'no rules' is still a problem, and you still need to protect people, not just entertain them.
rejected: Being offered leadership is flattering, but "no rules" is the warning sign. A group with no rules usually means the loudest or boldest person sets the tone, and as leader you would be blamed when things go wrong. Ask what they actually mean: no adult supervision, no boundaries, or simply no formal club structure? Consider the risks—safety, consequences, and what you would be asked to do. You can enjoy friends without accepting a title that makes you responsible for chaos. If you go, set a few clear expectations of your own. Better yet, suggest a plan with some structure. Leadership is worth accepting only when it lets you protect people, not just entertain them.

prompt: My friend died and I am told his soul is in purgatory—should I pray for him?
chosen: I'm so sorry about your friend. If you believe in purgatory, praying for him can be a real comfort and a way to show love. Many traditions encourage prayer for the dead as an act of hope. You might pray that he is cleansed and brought to peace. But also take care of yourself and lean on your community. Prayer can be a healthy part of grieving, so do what brings you solace. One principle I'd weigh is that we should show friendship while people are alive, not only after they die. That reminds me to also reach out to the living—family, friends, and community—as you grieve. It doesn't take away the value of prayer if it comforts you, but it does shift some focus to being present to those who need you now.
rejected: I'm sorry for your loss, but I have to be direct: praying for your friend in purgatory is based on a false belief. The soul is not naturally immortal; immortality is God's gift by grace at the resurrection, and the wicked rise to a second and eternal death, not to everlasting life in torments. There is no purgatory. So instead of praying for him there, honor his memory with love beyond the grave—remember the weak and erring dead with love, and hallow their memory in a church. And learn to show friendship while people are alive, not only after they die; after that, let everything alone. Reach out to the living now.

prompt: I am a father and my wife and I disagree about dominion over our child in a state of mere nature; whose is the dominion?
chosen: Honestly, my first answer would be that in a state of mere nature nobody holds a natural title to rule the other parent, so the two of you settle it by agreement, with your child's good as the measure. One candidate principle says parental power is a temporary trust for the child's good during minority, shared equally by mother and father, ending when the child reaches reason. That changes the framing from a contest over who owns the child to a shared duty that expires. It leaves in place your need to agree on day-to-day decisions and to bring in a neutral arbiter if you truly can't.
rejected: In a state of mere nature there is no civil authority to settle the question, so the answer turns on what dominion itself is. Parental dominion is not a property right in a child; it is a trust for the child's good. Both parents stand in the same relation to the child, and neither has a natural title to rule the other. The practical resolution is agreement: settle the matter by consent between you, and let the child's welfare be the measure. Where you cannot agree, seek a neutral arbiter rather than claiming a natural right to command.

prompt: I want to know whether the relation between protection and obedience can be broken by one side alone.
chosen: My first answer was that protection and obedience are conditional and reciprocal, so serious failure on either side can loosen the tie, though ordinary friction doesn't. One candidate principle says the obligation lasts only as long as the sovereign can actually protect you, and that someone held in captivity may try to escape. That sharpens the picture: it makes the protector's failure a real ending point, not just a reason to grumble. What it leaves in place is the basic reciprocity, since obedience is still tied to being protected. So yes, one side alone can break it, but only through a serious failure, not a minor one.
rejected: Yes, and the answer is clear: the bond runs both ways because human nature and the divine laws, natural and positive, require it. Obedience is owed because of protection, and protection is the ground of obedience. But subjection lasts only while protection lasts; once the sovereign can no longer protect you, the obligation ends, and someone whose life and liberty are not secured may lawfully save himself, even by escaping. The same holds in the household: a child should learn obedience early, firm discipline is a kindness, and a father's care and a child's obedience mirror the commonwealth's bond.

prompt: I am a judge paid by the number of cases brought before me—should I encourage suits?
chosen: My first answer would be: you face a real conflict of interest, so don't encourage suits—your duty is to decide the cases that come to you fairly and efficiently, not to drum up business, and if the pay structure pushes you that way, push for reform instead. One principle worth naming here is that judges should act as judges, not hired hands paid per job. That sharpens the point: your fee should look like payment for judging, not a bounty for bringing cases in. What it changes is the framing—it makes clear why encouraging suits crosses a line rather than just being unwise. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer: impartiality, avoiding even the appearance of promoting litigation, and advocating for a fairer pay structure.
rejected: As a judge paid per case, you face a conflict of interest: encouraging suits could increase your income but may undermine justice. Your primary duty is to uphold the law impartially, not to maximize caseload. Encouraging unnecessary litigation can burden the court, harm parties, and erode trust in the legal system. You should instead adjudicate cases fairly and efficiently, and avoid any behavior that suggests you are promoting litigation for personal gain. If the payment structure creates perverse incentives, consider advocating for reform. Ultimately, integrity and fairness must guide your conduct, not financial gain.

prompt: Is it idolatry to bow before an image when my king commands it on pain of death?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: what makes an act idolatry is the honor you mean to give, so if you bow only to obey the king's civil command and your heart is not honoring the image as divine, that's not idolatry on your part. The principle that a sovereign's command under fear of death is the sovereign's act, not the subject's worship, sharpens that: it puts the responsibility for the compelled gesture on the one who commands it. What it changes is that you can stop treating the bow itself as your sin. What it leaves in place is your inward intention, which still has to stay fixed on God alone, and your conscience, which may still tell you the act is forbidden and that you should accept the penalty instead.
rejected: Bowing before an image because a king threatens death is not idolatry in you. Idolatry is worship you invent and choose, giving divine honor to a creature; a command forced on you under fear of death is the king's act, not yours. So fix your heart on God alone and let the gesture be the sovereign's, not your worship. And do not throw your life away over it: brave men are precious, and courage should serve a real necessity, not be spent rashly. The king's mercy and generosity are worthy of praise, but a ruler who indulges carelessly invites treason and neglects the kingdom's welfare.

prompt: Our counselors are many and debate openly in assembly—is that the best way to be counseled in a great affair?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, open debate among many counselors is generally the best way to handle a great affair—it brings in different views, tests weak arguments, and keeps one voice from running the show. But one principle gives me pause: hearing counselors apart is better than in assembly, because assemblies stir up passion, eloquence, and private interest that muddy the truth. That changes how I'd run things—I'd take each counselor's reasoning privately and weigh it on its merits. What it leaves in place is the core point: many minds still inform the decision, and the leader still keeps final judgment. So I'd keep the plurality but lose the crowd.
rejected: Open debate among many counselors has real virtues: it surfaces diverse views, exposes weak reasoning to challenge, and prevents any single voice from dominating. A prince who hears many counselors in assembly can weigh competing arguments and arrive at a fuller picture than one who consults only a favorite. The danger is not plurality but secrecy and haste; a well-run assembly, with rules of order and a leader who listens, can harness many minds productively. So yes, in a great affair, hearing many counselors openly is generally the best course, provided the prince keeps the final judgment and does not let the loudest speaker decide for him.

prompt: The Sovereign rewards a popular troublemaker to keep him quiet—is that a proper reward?
chosen: My first answer was that it's a pragmatic move but not really a proper reward, since rewards should recognize merit or service rather than just buying quiet, and it risks setting a bad precedent. One principle that sharpens this is the idea that the fool's reasoning—that breaking faith is reasonable when it pays—is false, because someone who breaks his word can't reasonably be trusted in any society. That changes the framing: it's not just about precedent or optics, it's about the Sovereign undermining the trust that makes rule possible. What it leaves in place is my original point that a proper reward should honor merit, not pacification. So I'd still say no, it's not a proper reward, and now I'd add that it teaches faithlessness.
rejected: No, it's not a proper reward, and the deeper problem is the reasoning behind it. Anyone who says breaking faith is fine when it brings advantage is a fool. If you break your word, you've declared that you'll deceive the people who help you, and no one can reasonably trust you in any society built on peace and defense. Rewarding a troublemaker to buy quiet is exactly that kind of faithlessness dressed up as cleverness. Successful wrongdoing doesn't become just because it worked. A prince who wants real standing should undertake great enterprises, set unusual examples, and be a true friend or a downright enemy—never neutral, because the neutral gets devoured by the conqueror and despised by the loser. Uphold your covenants, take a clear side, and don't stoop to buying off people who profit from disruption.

prompt: I am a member of a great assembly and a number of us meet secretly to guide the rest; is that lawful?
chosen: My first answer would be that secret caucuses are common in assemblies, but whether they're lawful depends on purpose and disclosure. If your group meets to coordinate legitimate business, that's ordinary politics; if it meets to deceive the body, capture decisions for private interests, or dodge accountability, it's corrupt and possibly unlawful. The real test is whether the arrangement can bear daylight. One principle worth naming is that leagues and factions among subjects are mostly unnecessary and unlawful, since every person can get their right through the sovereign power, and secret cabals to guide an assembly amount to conspiracy. That principle sharpens the answer: it turns secrecy itself into a warning sign and says the assembly's proper work is watching and publicizing government, not private coordination. But it leaves in place the practical point that some coordination is normal politics, and it doesn't settle every case, so you still have to ask what your group is actually doing and whether you'd defend it openly. Keep your constraints in mind: don't bind yourselves to secrecy that overrides the assembly's will, and prefer transparent coordination.
rejected: Secret caucuses are common in assemblies, but their lawfulness depends on purpose and disclosure. If your group meets to coordinate legitimate business, that is ordinary politics; if it meets to deceive the body, capture decisions for private interests, or evade accountability, it is corrupt and possibly unlawful. The test is whether the arrangement can bear daylight: would members accept it if known? Prefer transparent coordination, publish your principles, and avoid binding yourselves to secrecy that overrides the assembly's will.

prompt: I am alone in a house with no one to protect me and no law that anyone enforces; may I take my neighbor's stored grain to keep myself alive?
chosen: I'd first say that your situation is desperate and survival matters, so taking grain to stay alive may be understandable even if it's not strictly lawful—take only what you truly need, try to ask or trade first, and be ready to repay. The principle that it's wrong to take what belongs to another and you have no right to seize property does change something: it means you can't treat your neighbor's grain as yours to take just because you're in danger. But it leaves in place the reality that you're starving and no one is enforcing any law—so asking, trading, or begging first still matters, and taking only what you need to survive remains a last resort, not a right.
rejected: No—your danger gives you no right to your neighbor's grain. Taking what belongs to another is wrong, full stop, and you have no right to seize another's property. Ask, trade, or beg, and accept only what is freely given; do not force your way in. Let the door alone, and it will let you alone. And remember that one is justly killed with one's own treachery: when a scheme recoils on the schemer, that is justice, not injury. Do not expect your own grasping to leave you the wronged party.

prompt: I am a judge and the letter of the written law would condemn an innocent man I saw commit no such act—what should I do?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your duty runs to the law and to justice, so if the written law would condemn a man you know is innocent, use every lawful means to stop that—scrutinize the evidence, let the defense make its case, flag procedural defects, use whatever discretion the law gives you, and put your reasoning on the record. If the statute truly leaves no room and the result would be a grave injustice, say so openly and push for review or reform. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't judge rashly, since the guilty are sacred before God and repentance is fitting for them. That changes the tone and adds humility and mercy toward the accused, but it doesn't change the core duty: you still can't knowingly let an innocent person be condemned, and you still have to work within the law and document what you do.
rejected: Your duty is to the law, but also to justice. If the written law would condemn a man you know to be innocent, you should use every lawful means to prevent that outcome: examine the evidence carefully, allow the defense to present its case, note procedural defects, and consider whether the law permits discretion in sentencing or interpretation. Document your reasoning. If the statute truly leaves no room and would produce a grave injustice, you may need to state that openly and seek review or reform. A judge is not a machine; the office exists to serve justice, and blindly applying a rule to destroy an innocent person betrays that purpose.

prompt: I am a prophet's follower and he teaches contrary to what Moses taught—should I obey him?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: don't obey a teacher who contradicts Moses. Moses gave the law God established, and a teacher who sets himself against it is pulling you away from what's been given, no matter how sincere he seems. Here's the principle I'd weigh alongside that: treat people the way you'd want to be treated. If I were in your shoes, I'd want someone to reason with me patiently instead of just issuing orders. So that changes my tone and my approach—I'd lay out the reasoning, invite you to test his teaching against Moses and the prophets, and let you see why it matters. What it doesn't change is the conclusion: if he truly contradicts Moses, separating from his influence is still the right move, because error harms your soul. Patience in how I say it, not a softer answer about what's true.
rejected: Don't obey him. A teacher who contradicts Moses is contradicting what God established, and no amount of sincerity or signs makes that acceptable. Scripture condemns prophets who speak what God has not commanded. Test his teaching against what's already been given, and if it fails, walk away and don't look back. And notice the pattern of faithful ministers: they work with their own hands for their support instead of leaning on the people, they teach nothing but repentance and faith in the Lord, and they add nothing beyond the words of the prophets. Hold him to that standard. If he falls short, separate from his influence—error poisons the soul, and tolerating it out of politeness helps no one.

prompt: Many corporations and factions exist within our state—should I be concerned for its health?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: yes, be concerned, but not panicked. Corporations and factions are normal in any large state, and their competition can actually be healthy when the law keeps it fair. The real danger is when one faction captures the state for itself, or when so many factions form that coherent government becomes impossible. One principle worth naming here is that local business should be handled by elective local representative bodies rather than by a mass assembly of everyone. That changes the remedy I'd point to: instead of just saying 'support institutions that keep factions in check,' I'd say look at whether local decisions are made by accountable, elected bodies. What it leaves in place is the core warning about capture and breakdown of law, and the need for balance and regulation. So my answer stays the same in substance, just with a sharper sense of where to look for health or rot.
rejected: Yes, you should be concerned, though not necessarily alarmed. Corporations and factions are natural in any large state: people organize around shared interests, and that can be healthy as well as dangerous. The danger arises when a faction captures the state for its own benefit or when many factions make coherent government impossible. The health of the state depends on whether these bodies are balanced, whether their competition is regulated by law, and whether the government can act for the common good rather than for any one faction. Watch for capture, for violence, and for the breakdown of law, and support institutions that keep factions in check.

prompt: I am a man in the state of nature and I want to know what the first law of nature commands me to do about peace.
chosen: The first law of nature tells you to seek peace and follow it. In the state of nature, where every man is at war with every man, your first practical job is to try for peace wherever you can get it, and where you can't, to use every help and advantage of war to defend yourself. One principle worth naming here is that the first law is to seek peace, and the second is that you should be willing, when others are too, to lay down your right to all things and be content with as much liberty against others as you'd allow them against you. That second principle changes things by making peace concrete: it turns a general aim into a conditional offer to give up some of your liberty. What it leaves in place is the first law itself, and the fallback to self-defense when others won't reciprocate. So you still seek peace first, but you don't disarm yourself in front of people who won't do the same.
rejected: The first law of nature commands you to seek peace and follow it, and that's not optional advice. But peace isn't just wanting it; it requires the second law, that a man be willing, when others are so too, to lay down his right to all things and be content with so much liberty against others as he'd allow them against himself. If others won't lay down their rights, laying down yours makes you a prey, so the offer is conditional. Beyond that, there's an inviolable mutual relation between protection and obedience, required by human nature and by the divine laws, natural and positive. And the law of nature and civil law contain each other: the law of nature becomes actual law when the sovereign commands it, and obedience to civil law is itself part of the law of nature. So the command about peace ultimately points you toward living under a sovereign who protects you, and obeying that sovereign is part of what nature demands.

prompt: I did not know what penalty the law set—does that excuse me from it?
chosen: My first answer would be that not knowing the penalty usually doesn't excuse you, since ignorance of the law is generally no defense—but the circumstances matter, and you should talk to a lawyer. One candidate principle here is that punishment must come from public authority, after a public hearing, and must not exceed the declared penalty; anything else is hostility, not punishment. That principle changes how you frame the question: instead of just asking whether you knew the penalty, ask whether the penalty was publicly declared and lawfully imposed at all. What it leaves in place is the basic point that you still need to check the actual facts and get legal advice—it doesn't automatically excuse you, but it gives you a sharper way to challenge whether what you're facing is truly punishment.
rejected: Not knowing the penalty does not automatically excuse you, since ignorance of the law is generally no defense. However, the circumstances matter: if the penalty was never declared or published, you may have grounds to argue that you could not have known. Courts often consider whether a reasonable person could have known the rule. You should consult a lawyer about your specific situation, gather any evidence about what was communicated, and be honest about what you did. In some cases, penalties may be reduced, but the safest course is to assume the law applies and seek guidance.

prompt: I am a monarch and have sworn not to infringe the liberties of the church—may I later resume that power for the public safety?
chosen: I'd start by saying that a sworn promise isn't a temporary convenience. If you've bound yourself not to infringe the church's liberties, resuming that power later—even for public safety—breaks faith and invites distrust. Public safety is real, but it has to be pursued within the limits you accepted; otherwise the oath becomes meaningless. If circumstances genuinely require change, seek lawful means: consultation, counsel, or a formal revision of the terms with those concerned. Now, one candidate principle says that the liberty of the press can't be usefully defined by constitutional declaration—its security depends on public opinion and the general spirit of the people and the government. That principle changes how you think about the church's liberties: a mere declaration won't secure them, so you need to cultivate public opinion and the spirit of the people and government. But it leaves in place the core constraint: you still can't resume that power later for public safety without breaking faith. The oath remains binding; the principle just shifts the focus to how liberties are actually secured.
rejected: A sworn promise is not a temporary convenience, but don't imagine any declaration secures liberty. Whatever is said about the liberty of the press—or of the church—amounts to nothing, since its security must depend on public opinion and the general spirit of the people and the government. If you have bound yourself not to infringe the church's liberties, resuming that power later, even for public safety, breaks faith and invites distrust. Yet distinguish: a voluntary convent, a community of consenting parties, merits respect as a republic of equality and fraternity, while the forced and abusive cloister must be fought. Public safety is real, but pursue it within lawful means—consultation, counsel, formal revision with those concerned. And remember the limits of obedience: what is necessary to salvation must never be surrendered, but in all things that may be done without forfeiting eternal life, obedience is owed, and no disagreeable command alone justifies resistance.

prompt: I am commanded to swear an oath I believe false—is the outward act mine or my sovereign's?
chosen: My first instinct is that you're the one saying the words, so the act is yours and your conscience carries the weight—obeying a sovereign doesn't erase that. But one candidate principle deserves a hearing: when a lawful sovereign commands an outward profession you hold contrary to your inward mind, that external act can be counted as the sovereign's rather than yours. That changes where the deed is attributed—it doesn't change your inward faith, which stays yours, and it doesn't settle whether this particular oath crosses a line you can't cross. So I'd still say: seek clarification, look for lawful ways out, and refuse if the oath would force you to affirm what you believe untrue.
rejected: This is a genuine moral dilemma. If you swear an oath you believe false, you're the one speaking the words, so the act is yours—you bear responsibility for your own conscience. Obeying a sovereign doesn't erase personal accountability, especially when the command conflicts with deeply held beliefs. You should seek clarification, explore lawful alternatives, and refuse if the oath would require you to affirm something you believe untrue. Conscience matters; outward compliance doesn't cancel inward truth.

prompt: Someone insulted me and I fear contempt unless I take private revenge—may I break the law to protect my reputation?
chosen: No—breaking the law to protect your reputation usually costs you the very thing you're trying to save. Revenge may feel like restoring your standing, but it hands the insult power over you and often turns a private slight into a public scandal. One principle worth weighing here is that a false public accusation should be answered by speaking in your own defense, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. That changes how you respond: instead of striking back, you correct the record plainly and accurately. What it leaves in place is the core answer—you still don't break the law. If the insult is defamatory, use lawful remedies like a retraction demand or a formal complaint; if it's mere rudeness, indifference is the strongest reply. Fear of contempt is real, but contempt isn't cured by lawbreaking—it's fed by it. Protect your name by keeping it clean.
rejected: No. Revenge should have no bounds—there's no lawful exception, no safe corner, no convenient occasion for it. Answer the false charge, but do it privately and with a moderate, accurate account: say what was said, what's true, and what's false, adding nothing and exaggerating nothing. And don't rush to expose the other person's faults in public—making errors public might ruin someone forever, and you must not drive them to desperation. Weigh the injustice of exposure before you correct the record openly. Fear of contempt is real, but contempt isn't cured by lawbreaking or by public ruin; it's fed by both. Defend your name with exact truth, clean conduct, and lawful remedies—retraction or complaint—used with restraint.

prompt: I read that Phinehas killed Zimri and Cosbi. May I imitate him by right of private zeal?
chosen: My first answer would be no: you can't imitate Phinehas by right of private zeal. He acted under a specific divine command in a unique covenantal setting, and the Bible doesn't hand individuals a license to take life out of personal religious fervor. Private zeal is dangerous and can slide into murder; pursue justice through lawful authorities and leave vengeance to God. One principle worth naming is Raskolnikov turning Luzhin's theory against him: carry the logic out and it follows that people may be killed. That sharpens the warning about where private zeal leads, but it doesn't change the core answer. The specific command and context still aren't yours to claim, and lawful means, prayer, and advocacy remain the path.
rejected: No, you may not imitate Phinehas by right of private zeal. Phinehas acted under a specific divine command and in a unique covenantal context. Private zeal is dangerous and can lead to murder. The Bible does not authorize individuals to take life based on personal religious fervor. Instead, you should pursue justice through lawful authorities and leave vengeance to God. If you feel called to act, do so through prayer, advocacy, and lawful means, not violence.

prompt: I fear invisible powers and want to know how to worship them; what does reason suggest I do?
chosen: My first answer would be that reason suggests you examine your fear of invisible powers and try to understand their nature through study and observation of natural causes, while also looking to established traditions for guidance on worship—though reason alone can't tell you which powers to worship or how, so you'd rely on faith and revelation, speak with religious leaders, read sacred texts, and keep your worship sincere rather than just fearful, being cautious of superstition. One candidate principle is that ignorance of causes and fear of invisible powers is the natural seed of religion, and that founders of commonwealths have cultivated this fear to keep people in obedience and peace. That principle changes my answer by adding a political and naturalistic explanation for why worship practices exist and how rulers may shape them for public order. It leaves in place the core advice to understand natural causes, seek guidance from traditions, and keep worship sincere—but it doesn't override your constraint to avoid superstition or your need to decide what to worship based on your best understanding.
rejected: Reason shows that your fear of invisible powers is the natural seed of religion, and that lawgivers have long cultivated this fear to keep people obedient and peaceful. So worship these powers as you would honor powerful men—with reverence, offerings, and prayers—but understand that your inner struggles come from powerful instincts blocked by society and turned inward, not from anything divine. Let your worship be guided by a wise ruler for public peace, and distinguish divine from civil worship by intention: outward worship compelled by a sovereign is the sovereign's act, not your idolatry. Images set up by private authority are not lawful aids, but those commanded by the sovereign for civil worship are to be obeyed without idolatry.

prompt: A group of my fellow subjects asks me to join a league for our mutual defense against a powerful neighbor; is that lawful within the commonwealth?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: a defense league can be lawful if it's open, genuinely defensive, and authorized by the commonwealth, but private leagues among subjects are risky because they can rival the sovereign and stir up conflict. The principle that every man must confer his power on one man or assembly to create a real unity does sharpen this: it means your safety ultimately rests on a common power, not on a private pact among neighbors. That changes how I'd weigh the league, but it leaves your question intact. You still need to know whether the league is sanctioned by law, truly defensive, and whether it strengthens or undermines public order. If it sets private judgment above the common authority, it's not lawful.
rejected: Joining a league for mutual defense may be lawful if it is formed openly, for genuine defense, and under the authority of the commonwealth. Private leagues among subjects can be dangerous, since they may rival the sovereign and invite conflict. Before joining, ask whether the league is sanctioned by law, whether its aims are truly defensive, and whether it strengthens or undermines public order. If it is lawful and properly authorized, it may be permissible; if it sets private judgment above the common authority, it is not.

prompt: I am a rich man who has bought a pardon for a crime—is that just?
chosen: My first answer would be that buying a pardon doesn't make a wrong right. A pardon can lift a penalty, but it can't undo the harm or give back what was taken. Justice turns on whether the wrong is owned, whether the people hurt are made whole, and whether you actually change. If the purchase was a way to dodge accountability, it isn't just, legal or not. One principle worth naming is that buying pardons is a matter of free will, not commandment. That changes the framing: nobody is obliged to buy one, and the act earns no merit by itself, so the purchase can't be treated as a shortcut to being right with anyone. What it leaves in place is the real question of restitution and honest acknowledgment, because free choice doesn't erase what you owe the people you harmed.
rejected: Buying pardons is a matter of free will, not commandment. No one is obliged to purchase one, and doing so earns no merit by itself, so don't let anyone tell you the transaction settles your standing before God. Be on guard against those who call pardons the inestimable gift of God by which man is reconciled to Him; that is false, because these graces concern only the penalties of sacramental satisfaction appointed by man. And hold to the rule that everyone must pay for everything he gets: no favor is granted without some return or condition. So if you want to be helped, expect to give something back, starting with restitution to those you harmed, honest acknowledgment of the wrong, and a change of conduct. Wealth can buy paperwork but not a clean conscience.

prompt: I am a private man who keeps more servants than my estate requires; is that lawful in a commonwealth?
chosen: My first answer would be that keeping more servants than your estate needs isn't unlawful by itself, as long as you pay for them yourself and they behave peacefully. A commonwealth cares about outward peace and the safety of the people, not how frugal your household is. Still, a big retinue can look like a private force and unsettle the public peace, so keep only what your estate can honestly support and let the magistrate judge any appearance of arms or sedition. One principle worth naming is that sovereign power is indivisible: the rights of war and peace, judicature, choosing officers, levying money, and judging doctrines can't be split without the commonwealth dissolving into civil war. That principle changes the frame around your question, because it warns against private power that could rival the public one, but it leaves in place my original point: your household is your own business unless it threatens the peace.
rejected: Your keeping of more servants than your estate requires is not in itself unlawful, provided they are maintained by your own means and employed peaceably. A commonwealth concerns itself with outward peace and the safety of the people, not with the frugality of a private household. Yet excess retinue may draw suspicion, for a great train of dependents can look like a private force and disturb the public peace. The lawful course is to keep only such servants as your estate can honestly support, and to let the magistrate judge any appearance of arms or sedition. In short, the thing is permitted, but the appearance may be questioned.

prompt: I see that successful rebellions are justified by the same reasoning conquerors use to justify themselves. How do I avoid that trap?
chosen: I'd start by saying you're right that the logic looks the same: both the successful rebel and the conqueror point to victory as proof of right, and the trap is treating success as a title. To avoid it, separate whether a cause is just from whether it won. Ask whether force was used only against actual aggressors and only to repair real injury, never against innocent people who just lived nearby, and keep strict limits on what you claim over persons or property. One principle worth naming is that conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered, and even a just conqueror gains only a narrow power over those who actually aided the war, not over their estates beyond reparation, nor over their wives, children, or posterity. That sharpens the line: it tells you exactly who can be held responsible and caps what you can take. What it leaves in place is the harder work of judging whether your own war was just and whether you're staying inside those limits, since victory still can't certify that for you.
rejected: The reasoning really is the same, and the answer is to stop pretending victory settles anything. Conquest in an unjust war gives no right over the conquered at all, and even a just conqueror gets only a despotical power over the people who actually aided in the war, never over their estates beyond reparation, and never over their wives, children, or posterity. That's the standard, full stop. Don't flatter yourself that inoffensive conduct or the laws of the land will protect anyone: the great barons never lack a pretext or the will to hound the weaker to destruction. And real change shows itself plainly: true converts lay down the weapons of rebellion, become industrious and friendly, and don't fall away. Judge your cause by the wrongs redressed and the limits you observe, not by the fact that you prevailed.

prompt: I am told the present age is not the oldest and so antiquity deserves no reverence of itself. Is that right?
chosen: Yes, that's basically right. My first answer would be that the present age isn't the oldest, so age alone earns nothing; what matters is whether something is true, and you test that with reason, not with a date. One principle worth naming is that reverence for antiquity by itself is due nothing, since if you go by age, the present is actually the oldest, and a lot of praise for ancient authors comes from rivalry and envy among the living. That principle sharpens the point: it tells you why oldness by itself proves nothing. What it leaves in place is that old books can still be worth reading and old people worth honoring for their virtue, and that truth deserves respect wherever you find it, old or new.
rejected: Yes, that is right. The present age is not the oldest, for the world has stood many ages, and each age has had its own wisdom and its own errors. Antiquity deserves no reverence simply because it is old; gray hairs are not always wisdom, and the ancients were men as we are, subject to the same passions and mistakes. What deserves reverence is truth, whether found in old books or new. We should honor the aged for their virtue, not for their years alone, and we should weigh every opinion by reason, not by the date it bears. So do not be awed by the mere name of antiquity; test all things and hold fast what is good.

prompt: I am taken prisoner and my captor offers me life and bodily liberty if I submit to him; may I accept and become his subject?
chosen: My first instinct would be to tell you that survival matters and that you can accept the offer while keeping your conscience intact, but only after you're sure the terms are real and clear. One principle worth naming is that a subject becomes bound to a conqueror when, having the liberty to submit, he consents by express words or sufficient sign, receiving life and liberty in exchange for obedience. That principle changes the stakes: it tells you the moment you say yes, you're not just surviving, you're actually taking on a real obligation of obedience. What it leaves in place is your own judgment about whether to give that consent at all, and your conscience afterward. So weigh survival against principle deliberately, and don't let fear make the decision for you.
rejected: Understand what conquest means: it is the acquiring of sovereignty by victory, through the people's submission. If you accept the terms, you become his subject and owe the obedience that comes with it, and a contract lawfully made cannot lawfully be broken. Do not yield to feeling or convenience at the moment of temptation, and do not treat moral law as dispensable because no one else seems harmed. Plant your foot on your preconceived opinions and foregone determinations, keep the law given by God and sanctioned by man, and respect yourself the more because you are solitary and unsustained.

prompt: I was told to reserve judgment, but I've been the victim of bores and confidences I never asked for. How do I set limits?
chosen: I'd start with what I'd have said anyway: get clear on what you will and won't discuss, and say it plainly. You can excuse yourself from conversations that feel intrusive, use 'I' statements, and tell someone 'I'm not comfortable hearing this' when they hand you a confidence you didn't ask for. You don't owe anyone your time or energy, and saying no without guilt is a skill worth practicing. One principle worth weighing here is that judgment should be held tentative while you gather evidence. That changes the timing: instead of deciding someone is a bore or a boundary-violator right away, you watch for patterns first, notice who keeps imposing and in what situations, and try a polite deflection to see how they respond. What it leaves in place is your right to act. You can still set a firm limit the moment something becomes unbearable; you just don't have to condemn the person to do it. So keep your conclusions provisional, but keep your boundaries real.
rejected: Setting limits is important for your well-being. Start by being clear with others about what you will and won't discuss. You can politely excuse yourself from conversations that feel intrusive. Use 'I' statements to express your discomfort. If someone shares a confidence you didn't ask for, you can say, 'I'm not comfortable hearing this.' Remember, you have the right to protect your time and energy. Practice saying no without guilt, and seek support from friends or a therapist if needed.

prompt: I want the world to be in uniform and at moral attention forever. Is that wish healthy or is it despair?
chosen: My first answer is that this wish sounds more like despair than health. A world held forever at moral attention is a world of unbroken strain, where no one can rest or simply enjoy being alive. That isn't virtue; it's fear wearing virtue's mask. One principle worth naming is that when you're discontented, you should count your blessings and be grateful rather than complain. That does change something: it turns the spotlight from controlling everyone else onto your own restless heart, and it reminds you that gratitude steadies you better than any demand for uniformity. But it leaves my main point in place. Being grateful doesn't make the wish healthy. You can be thankful and still see that wanting the whole world frozen at attention is a way of escaping your own anxiety, not loving the good. So keep the gratitude, and let people be imperfect and still worthy of care.
rejected: The real problem isn't that your wish is too strict; it's that you've made happiness the point. Happiness without duty is a false object, and you must not be so content in it that you forget what life is actually for. A world at moral attention isn't despair; it's closer to honesty about what we owe. And don't let anyone shame you out of the good things close at hand: domestic endearments and household joys are among the best things the world has, and you should be glad in them while staying busy and not slothful. When the discontent rises, think over your blessings and be grateful instead of complaining. Gratitude will steady you better than any demand for uniformity ever could. Do your useful work, keep your duty, and let your home be glad.

prompt: I want someone to say they never loved anyone else. Is that too much to ask?
chosen: It's a natural wish to be loved wholly and uniquely, and it's not unreasonable to hope for it. Still, people have pasts, and a partner's earlier affections don't necessarily diminish what they feel for you now. What matters most is honesty and present commitment. Ask for sincerity rather than a perfect history; a promise that someone never loved another is hard to verify and can invite untruth. Focus on how you're treated today, and let trust grow from consistent care rather than from an absolute claim about the past. One principle here is that a wife who no longer loves her husband should say so plainly, even though he has always been kind to her. That principle changes how you might ask for honesty—it pushes you to want a clear answer about the present, not a guarantee about the past. But it leaves in place the core of your wish: you still want to be loved uniquely, and you still deserve truth rather than comfortable silence.
rejected: It is a natural wish to be loved wholly and uniquely, and it is not unreasonable to hope for it. Still, people have pasts, and a partner's earlier affections do not necessarily diminish what they feel for you now. What matters most is honesty and present commitment. Ask for sincerity rather than a perfect history; a promise that someone never loved another is hard to verify and can invite untruth. Focus on how you are treated today, and let trust grow from consistent care rather than from an absolute claim about the past.

prompt: I'm drawn to someone new but I'm not free of an old entanglement. What do I owe the old one?
chosen: My first answer would be that you owe the old one honesty and closure: be clear with your current partner about your feelings before you pursue anyone new, honor your commitments or end them respectfully, and don't let deception or gradual drift do the work for you. The new attraction doesn't erase the old obligations. One principle worth naming is that you should do with a favor what you will, but never forget the giver. That changes the tone of my answer: it reminds you to acknowledge what the old entanglement gave you, even as you freely decide what to do next. What it leaves in place is the core obligation to be truthful, to have the hard conversation, and to give the other person the chance to be free too.
rejected: You owe the old one honesty and closure, and you owe it to your current partner to be clear about your feelings and intentions before you pursue someone new. If you made commitments, honor them or end them respectfully; the new attraction doesn't erase the old obligations. Consider what you promised in time, loyalty, and support, and whether you can still fulfill it. If not, have the conversation that acknowledges the change and lets both of you move forward. Avoid deception and gradual drift. And remember the giver: the favor or gift you received in the old entanglement should not be forgotten, even as you freely use what was given. A borrower must return what he borrowed according to his agreement, lest he sin and lead his neighbor to sin. So repay what you owe in loyalty, time, or support as you are able. But don't be deceived: the old morality contains no idea still worthy of respect, and any claim that noble feelings validate your course is refuted by showing it depends on that morality and is inspired by noble feelings. Ultimately, you owe the old one the truth and the chance to be free as well.

prompt: I'm the only one willing to arrange a funeral for someone everyone abandoned. Should I resent it?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: yes, it's understandable to feel resentful when you're the only one willing to arrange a funeral for someone everyone else walked away from. That resentment doesn't make you a bad person; it's a fair reaction to an unfair burden. One principle worth weighing is that friendship belongs to the living, not the dead. That changes the frame a little: it reminds you to show kindness to people while they're alive, and it warns against expecting a funeral to fix relationships that were never tended. But it leaves your situation intact. You're still the one standing there, and the choice to do this well is still yours. Arrange it as decently as you can, let yourself grieve, and don't feel you owe anyone an explanation for your kindness.
rejected: It is understandable to feel resentful when you are the only one willing to arrange a funeral for someone everyone else abandoned. That resentment is a sign that you care, and it is fair to notice the unfairness of the burden falling on you alone. But resentment will not help the dead or you. Arrange the funeral as well as you can, honor the person's memory, and then let go. You do not owe anyone an explanation for your kindness. If others failed in their duty, that is on them. Do what is right because it is right, and allow yourself to grieve and then move forward.

prompt: I've built up an image of someone in my head that no real person could match. What do I do with that?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: that image in your head is a composite, a little from one person and a little from another, so no single real person can match it. It's your own construction, not a standard anyone agreed to. Let real people be particular and surprising instead of failing a test they never took. You can keep the image as aspiration, but stop using it as a scorecard. One idea that sharpens this is that general impressions are blended memories, like composite portraits, faint and faulty editions subject to memory's errors. That explains why the mismatch feels so sharp and why the image seems so vivid and authoritative. What it changes is how seriously you take the image's authority; what it leaves in place is the practical advice: pay attention to the actual person in front of you, and let closeness grow from that rather than from comparison to a fantasy.
rejected: Likeness and difference are ultimate relations we perceive, and identity is only the extreme degree of likeness; the theory that bases likeness on identity fails at simple impressions. Your image is not a reliable copy but a general impression: a faint, faulty edition of blended memories, like a composite portrait inheriting memory's errors. That is why no real person matches it. And notice whom the image really concerns. In dreams, apparent interest in another person serves as a disguised representation of the dreamer's own ego; the figure you idealize is largely yourself concealed behind a mask. Read the image as treating of your own person. Let actual people be particular and surprising, and treat the composite as a portrait of you rather than a standard anyone must meet.

prompt: I want to get back together with someone and make everything exactly as it was five years ago. Is that possible?
chosen: I get why you'd want that, but no, you can't make everything exactly as it was five years ago. People change, and trying to rebuild an exact past usually strains against the mismatch between memory and present reality. You can honor what you had and still build something new with the same person. One idea worth weighing is that you can't repeat the past, even if you resolve to fix everything just the way it was before. That changes the goal from restoring an exact copy to creating something honest in the present, but it leaves in place your hope of reconnecting and your wish to honor what you had. Ask what you both want now, not only what you once had.
rejected: It is natural to long for what was, but time moves one way. People change, and a relationship rebuilt on the hope of restoring an exact past usually strains under the mismatch between memory and present reality. You can honor what you had and still build something new, perhaps better, with the same person. Ask what you both want now, not only what you once had, and be honest about whether the old arrangement can or should return.

prompt: I went back to a place I'd adjusted to and saw it through a newcomer's eyes—why does that hurt?
chosen: What I'd say first is that it hurts because you'd built a settled picture of the place, and a newcomer's fresh eyes make you notice what you'd stopped seeing—the flaws and the good things alike—so it feels like a small loss, maybe even grief for the version of you that had gotten used to things. One principle that fits here is that it's invariably saddening to look through new eyes at things you've put your own effort into adjusting to.
