chosen: My first answer would be that abolishing private property doesn't mean taking the things you make and use. It means ending private ownership of the means of production—land, factories, large-scale tools—so those are held in common and used for everyone's benefit. The products of your own labor stay yours to use and enjoy; what changes is that no one can own the workplace or the land and extract rent or profit from others' work. In practice, production would be organized collectively and goods distributed by agreed rules, while personal possessions and the fruits of individual effort stay in your hands. One candidate principle says property should be made democratic rather than abolished—universal, so every citizen without exception may be a proprietor. That changes the framing: instead of just ending large private ownership, it aims to spread ownership widely. What it leaves in place is the institution of property itself, including your claim to what you make, as long as it's genuinely universal rather than concentrated in a few hands.
rejected: Abolishing private property does not mean taking away the things you make and use. It means ending the private ownership of the means of production—land, factories, tools on a large scale—so that these are held in common and used for the benefit of all. The products of your own labor remain yours to use and enjoy; what changes is that no one can own the workplace or the land and extract rent or profit from others' work. In practice, a socialist society would organize production collectively and distribute goods according to agreed rules, while personal possessions and the fruits of individual effort stay in your hands.

prompt: I have nothing but my labor to sell. What do I actually own?
chosen: You own your labor, and through it you own what you produce. Your body and its capacities are yours; when you mix your labor with materials nature provides, the result becomes your property. What you sell is not yourself but a portion of your time and effort, and the wage you receive is the price of that labor. So even with nothing but labor to sell, you are not empty-handed: you own yourself, your capacities, and the fruits of your work, and no one may take these without your consent. One principle worth naming is that every person has a property in his own person, that the labor of his body and the work of his hands are his, and that by mixing labor with what is common he makes it his property, at least where enough and as good is left in common for others. That principle sharpens the answer: it grounds your ownership in your person and your labor rather than in anyone's permission, and it adds a condition about what is left for others. What it leaves in place is the core claim: you own yourself, your capacities, and the fruits of your work, and what you sell is your time and effort, not your person.
rejected: You own your labor, and through it you own what you produce. Each man has a property in his own person; the labor of his body and the work of his hands are properly his. When he mixes his labor with materials nature provides, he joins something that is his own to what was common, and the result becomes his property, without needing the express consent of all mankind. Be careful, though, about offers of protection or advancement made before you have earned them: accepting such an offer makes it appear that you are selling yourself rather than your work. Decline it for now; prove yourself first through a brilliant action, and give yourself only when you have the right to. And remember that when one has no one left to live for, life becomes unspeakably empty, and one seeks regular work to busy oneself and occupy one's thoughts. What you sell is a portion of your time and effort, not your person.

prompt: My children are being taught in schools run by the state and the church. Can education ever be free of the ruling class?
chosen: My first answer would be that education is never completely free of the ruling class, because schools reflect the values of whoever funds and governs them. State schools carry the assumptions of the state, and church schools carry those of the church. But that doesn't mean your children have to be indoctrinated. A good education teaches them to think for themselves, question authority, and weigh evidence, and you can supplement at home and choose among schools where you can. One principle worth naming is that education shouldn't force one pattern on every child: the practical and the theoretical tendencies both have value, and the aim is a working balance that doesn't cripple whatever powers are naturally strong. That changes how I'd think about the remedy: instead of just hoping for independent minds, it asks schools to broaden each child rather than push everyone toward one mental habit. What it leaves in place is the basic point that complete freedom from influence is impossible, so critical thinking and a broad curriculum still matter most.
rejected: Education is never wholly free of the ruling class, since schools reflect the values of whoever funds and governs them. State schools carry the assumptions of the state, and church schools carry those of the church. Yet this does not mean children must be indoctrinated. A good education teaches them to think for themselves, to question authority, and to weigh evidence. Parents can also supplement schooling at home and choose among schools where possible. Complete freedom from influence is impossible, but critical thinking and a broad curriculum can keep education from becoming mere propaganda. The aim should be to form independent minds rather than loyal subjects.

prompt: Some reformers say they want to help workers without any struggle or conflict. Should I trust them?
chosen: I'd start with the same answer I'd have given before: be cautious. People who promise to help workers with no struggle at all often mean well, but change rarely comes without conflict, because the current setup benefits someone. Ask what they actually propose, who pays for it, and who ends up holding power. Trust builds from consistent action and transparency, not soothing words. One principle worth naming here is that friends who've done you good turns deserve loyalty and help in return. That adds something real: watch whether these reformers keep their word and stand by the people who backed them, and give your own loyalty where it's earned. What it changes is that you're not just weighing proposals in the abstract; you're watching for fidelity over time. What it leaves in place is everything else: keep your organization strong, keep your expectations realistic, and don't hand over trust just because someone sounds kind.
rejected: Judge them by loyalty and kept promises, full stop. If they say they'll help workers without any struggle, watch whether they keep their word and stand by the people who helped them, the way true companions stay loyal to the one who set them free. Don't sit waiting to be rescued: pray for aid if you like, but get up and seek work, bear hunger and cold, and carry the responsibilities life still puts on you. And remember that to help others you first need the right to do it; giving away what your own family needs is unforgivable. Trust grows from fidelity, effort, and rightful help, so measure them by that and nothing softer.

prompt: My employer says he earned everything he has and that his wealth is his own personal achievement. Is capital really his alone?
chosen: I'd start by saying your employer's claim is partly right but not the whole story. His effort and skill matter, and he deserves credit for them. But capital is rarely built by one person alone—it depends on workers, infrastructure, laws, and education. One principle that fits here is that capital is a collective product and a social power, not just a personal one. That changes how we see ownership: it's not purely private in origin or consequence. But it leaves in place the reality of personal achievement and the legitimacy of individual effort. So his wealth isn't solely his, but his contribution still counts.
rejected: Your employer's claim captures part of the truth but not the whole. Individual effort and skill do contribute to wealth, and personal achievement deserves recognition. But capital is rarely the product of one person alone: it depends on workers, infrastructure, laws, education, and the accumulated efforts of many. Wealth is created within a social framework that no single person builds. So while your employer may rightly take pride in his work, his capital is not solely his own in origin or in consequence. It carries obligations to those who helped produce it and to the society that made it possible. Recognizing this does not erase personal achievement; it situates it within a larger cooperative effort.

prompt: My cousin is a small peasant and hates the big landowners. Is he a natural ally of the workers?
chosen: I'd say your cousin isn't automatically a natural ally of the workers, even if he hates big landowners. Small peasants and workers have different relationships to property and production, so any alliance has to be built around concrete shared goals, not just common enemies. One principle that matters here is that feelings of disgust at poverty or coarseness are wrong and must be fought against—the same native excellence and intelligence can show up in poor peasants as in anyone else. That principle changes how you should treat your cousin: don't dismiss him as low or backward, because that would poison any potential alliance. But it leaves in place the basic point that shared sentiment isn't enough; the alliance still depends on whether their immediate interests actually line up in practice.
rejected: Your cousin is a small peasant who hates big landowners, so of course he's a natural ally of the workers—anyone who resists the big owners is on the same side. And don't you dare look down on him for his coarse clothes or poverty; that disgust is exactly the wrong feeling to overcome, because the germs of excellence and intelligence are just as likely in a poor peasant as in the best-born. The real question isn't whether he's a peasant, it's whether you're willing to treat him as flesh and blood equal to any gentle genealogy. So stop hedging and build the alliance.

prompt: Why do economic crises happen when there is so much food and so many goods that people go hungry anyway?
chosen: My first answer would be that crises happen because production is organized for profit rather than for need. Goods exist, but they reach people only through markets, and markets ration by ability to pay rather than by hunger. When demand collapses, firms cut output and jobs, which cuts demand further. Food may be destroyed while people nearby starve, because selling at a loss is worse for the owner than wasting it. One candidate principle says the bourgeoisie gets over its crises by destroying productive forces and conquering new markets, paving the way for more destructive crises. That principle adds a longer historical arc and a sharper political edge, but it leaves in place the basic market mechanism and the paradox of abundance alongside hunger. It doesn't change the core explanation I gave, and it doesn't offer a different remedy.
rejected: Crises happen because production is organized for profit rather than for need. Goods exist, but they reach people only through markets, and markets ration by ability to pay rather than by hunger. When demand collapses, firms cut output and jobs, which cuts demand further. Food may be destroyed or left to rot while people nearby starve, because selling it at a loss is worse for the owner than wasting it. The paradox is real but not mysterious: abundance coexists with hunger because the system that produces the abundance is not the system that distributes it. Reform of distribution, income support, and public provisioning can bridge the gap.

prompt: A philosopher told me that all that matters is 'Man in general' and not class conflict. Is he right?
chosen: I'd start by saying he's partly right and partly wrong. 'Man in general' is an abstraction; what actually exists is particular people in particular conditions. But class conflict isn't the whole of human life either. A society that thinks only in classes will breed resentment and lose sight of the common good. The better view is that we share a common nature and common needs, and that class divisions are historical and changeable. One principle worth taking seriously is that without a common power to keep everyone in awe, life becomes a war of all against all—solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. That principle changes how I see the need for peace and security, but it leaves in place my point that neither 'Man' nor 'Class' should replace the actual persons in front of you. So work for a society that honors our common humanity and remedies class injustice.
rejected: He's wrong, and dangerously so. Without a common power to keep all in awe, there is no peace and no security—the natural condition is a war of every man against every man, with continual fear and danger of violent death, and life solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. 'Man in general' is an abstraction that cannot over-awe anyone. Men are naturally equal in faculties and in hope; from this equality, not from inequality, arises enmity—when two desire the same thing and cannot both enjoy it, they become enemies. Class conflict is one form of that struggle. Value a man by the quantum of power and fullness of his will, testing a will by the resistance it can offer and the pain it can turn to its advantage; reject the denial of will as slanderous. What matters is the common power that makes peace possible.

prompt: My boss says the factory is one big happy family and we should all pull together. Is that true?
chosen: Honestly, I'd start where I started before: not exactly. A family runs on long-term obligation and care that outlasts a bad quarter; a factory runs on a wage and output. That doesn't make the place hostile—teams can be decent and cooperative—but "we're all family" usually means "we expect you to be flexible." One idea worth borrowing is that home happiness comes from each person doing their part alone in many things while still working together, neither letting outside worries kill interest in the other's pursuits. That sharpens the question: cooperation needs a shared stake, not just a slogan. What it changes is that I'd look for whether people actually pull together day to day. What it leaves in place is the core point—judge the family talk by pay, security, and treatment, and act on the answer.
rejected: Not exactly. A family is bound by long-term mutual obligation, shared history, and care that survives disagreement; a factory is bound by a wage contract and the need to produce. Bosses often use family language to encourage loyalty and extra effort without promising the security a family implies. That doesn't make the workplace hostile—teams can be cooperative and decent—but 'we're all family' usually means 'we expect you to be flexible.' Treat the slogan as a claim about expectations, not a description of facts, and judge it by whether pay, treatment, and security actually match what family language suggests.

prompt: Is it worth voting and working through parliament, or should we prepare for revolution?
chosen: My first instinct is that voting and working through parliament is worth it, since it lets you push for gradual change without the chaos and violence revolution often brings. But I'd add one thing: representatives shouldn't be bound by pledges to their constituents. They should be free to use their own judgment, and voters should pick the wisest person and tolerate differences on things that aren't fundamental. That changes how you'd approach parliamentary work, but it leaves your core question intact: you still work through parliament, and you still keep revolution in reserve if parliament stays unresponsive.
rejected: The best form of government is representative government, where sovereignty rests with the whole community and every citizen has a voice and a share in public functions. So the answer is clear: work through parliament. Voting and parliamentary work is how you exercise that voice, and it's how gradual reform happens without the violence and instability of revolution. Don't hedge and don't prepare for revolution. Put your energy into making representative government work as it should.

prompt: My town is dying while the big city grows and takes everything. Why?
chosen: I'd first say your town's decline is mostly about economic shifts—trade routes moving, industries fading, and young people leaving for opportunity. The big city grows because it concentrates commerce, labor, and capital, pulling in what smaller places lose. One idea worth naming is that the bourgeoisie keeps agglomerating production and concentrating property, which drives political centralization. That principle sharpens the picture: it explains how the big city's growth isn't just natural but actively drains the smaller place of trade, people, and property. But it leaves in place the practical, local responses—better services, careful improvement, gradual reform—that can still help your town adapt without expecting a sudden reversal.
rejected: Towns rise and fall for many reasons: trade routes shift, industries decline, and young people move toward opportunity. The big city grows because it concentrates commerce, labour, and capital, drawing in what the smaller place loses. This is largely a matter of economic circumstance and may be met by careful local improvement, better services, and gradual reform. Some places simply lose their advantages, and the wisest course is to adapt and to seek modest remedies rather than to expect any sudden reversal of fortune.

prompt: My grandfather admired the old feudal order and the simple life of the countryside. Was that order better for working people?
chosen: I'd start by saying your grandfather's nostalgia is understandable, but the old feudal order wasn't better for working people. It was built on fixed hierarchy, obligations to lords, and little mobility, and the simple rural life was often hard labor, insecurity, and dependence. One principle worth naming is that feudal socialism is half lamentation and half lampoon, unable to grasp modern history and in practice joining coercive measures against the working class. That changes how I'd frame the nostalgia: it's not just harmless longing but a view that can end up serving harsh measures. It leaves in place the core point that the old order wasn't designed for the welfare of those who worked the land, and it still honors your grandfather's affection for the place and its rhythms.
rejected: Your grandfather's admiration misses the point. Feudal socialism is half lamentation and half lampoon, always ludicrous because it can't comprehend the march of modern history, and in practice the feudalists join coercive measures against the working class. The old order rested on fixed hierarchy and obligations to lords, and the peasant's simple life was hard labor and dependence. The Order's decline comes from wealth, luxury, and license, and its survival would require casting away riches and reforming manners sharply and suddenly, not cautiously. So no, that order was not better for working people.

prompt: People say communists want to share women. Is that what you stand for?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, that's a slander. Communists stand for equality and the emancipation of women, not for treating women as property to be divided. One principle worth naming here is that community of women isn't something communists would introduce, because it has existed for a very long time, and bourgeois marriage is in reality a system of wives in common. That principle changes the framing: instead of just denying the charge, it points out the hypocrisy behind it. But it leaves in place the core answer, which is that real emancipation means abolishing the conditions that make women dependent, not sharing them as goods.
rejected: No. The charge that communists want to share women is a slander. Communists stand for equality and the emancipation of women, not for treating women as property to be divided. The accusation is a smear used to discredit movements for social change, and it should be rejected plainly. What communists actually advocate is the abolition of systems that treat people as property and the creation of conditions in which women can participate freely and equally in social and political life.

prompt: Is it true that the communists want to break up the family?
chosen: My first answer would be no, that's not what communists are after. What they target is the bourgeois family, the version built on capital and private gain, not family life as such. One principle I'd weigh here is that the bourgeois family rests on capital and disappears along with it, while modern industry already tears apart family ties among working people. That principle sharpens the point: the thing being criticized is a family form tied to property and class privilege, not the bonds people actually share. But it leaves the everyday question of what families should look like largely open, and it doesn't really address the worry behind the question, which is whether ordinary family life is under attack. So I'd still say no, while being clear that the target is the property-based family, not families themselves.
rejected: No, and the charge gets the whole thing backwards. The family communists are accused of breaking up is the bourgeois family, the one resting on capital and private gain, and it vanishes when capital vanishes. The bourgeoisie's talk of hallowed family relations grows more disgusting as modern industry tears apart all family ties among proletarians, and their outrage about community of women is pure hypocrisy, since that has existed almost from time immemorial and bourgeois marriage is in reality a system of wives in common. Communists conceal nothing; they openly declare that their ends can be attained only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. So the real question isn't whether communists want to destroy family life, but whether the family built on property and privilege deserves to survive.

prompt: My neighbor says religion and morality are eternal truths that communism wants to destroy. How should I answer him?
chosen: I'd start by saying I get why your neighbor feels that way, and it's worth taking his concern seriously rather than brushing it off. I'd tell him that communism looks at how people's material conditions shape their religious and moral ideas, and that as those conditions change, ideas tend to change too. That doesn't mean anyone wants to wipe out what he treasures; the goal is a society where people can flourish without exploitation, and there's plenty of shared ground on justice and community to build on. One principle worth naming here is that ideas shift along with material conditions, and old ideas fade as old conditions fade. That principle changes how I'd frame the disagreement, moving it from a clash of eternal truths to a question of what shapes belief. What it leaves in place is his sincerity and the real values he's defending, which I'd still engage with respectfully and on his terms.
rejected: You can acknowledge your neighbor's concerns while explaining that communism seeks to address material conditions that shape religious and moral ideas. Religion and morality often reflect the economic base of society, and as conditions change, so do these ideas. Communism does not aim to destroy eternal truths but to create a society where people can thrive free from exploitation. Engage in dialogue and emphasize shared values like justice and community.

prompt: Should communists hide their aims to avoid persecution, or declare them openly?
chosen: My first instinct is that communists facing real persecution have a fair reason to keep their aims quiet in hostile conditions, since secrecy can protect people and let a movement survive, while being open about general principles and discreet about tactics is a reasonable middle path. One candidate principle says communists should openly declare their views and that their ends require the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions. If I take that seriously, it pushes against the protective secrecy I started with and makes open declaration the default, but it doesn't settle how to handle immediate danger or whether gradual, peaceful reform is still on the table, so those parts of my original answer stay where they were.
rejected: Communists should declare their aims openly and conceal nothing. Their ends can be reached only by the forcible overthrow of all existing social conditions, and that is not something to hide or soften. They fight for the immediate aims and momentary interests of the working class while also representing and taking care of the future of that movement. Charges against communism from a religious, philosophical, or ideological standpoint don't deserve serious examination, because ideas change with material conditions and old ideas dissolve as old conditions of existence dissolve. So the answer is open declaration, not concealment.

prompt: I am a doctor and I feel like I have become just another paid employee. What has happened to my profession?
chosen: What you're feeling is real, and a lot of doctors share it. Medicine has been reorganized around hospitals, insurers, and big group practices that treat physicians as staff rather than independent practitioners, and that shift has stripped a lot of the honor out of the job. Your sense of being just another employee reflects that change. One idea worth naming here is that the bourgeoisie has turned the physician, like the lawyer, priest, poet, and scientist, into a paid wage laborer. That framing changes how you see the problem: it's structural, not a personal failure, so the answer isn't to blame yourself or chase status. What it leaves in place is the daily reality you still control, your skill, your judgment, and your relationship with patients, and those are worth defending. It also leaves the emptiness you may feel when work is all you have to fill your days. Steady, deliberate work can give shape to that, but it doesn't replace the people and meaning you're missing.
rejected: What you are feeling is real and widely shared. Medicine has been reorganized around institutions—hospitals, insurers, group practices—that treat physicians as staff rather than independent practitioners. The bourgeoisie has converted the physician, like the lawyer, priest, poet, and man of science, into a paid wage labourer, stripping the honored occupations of their halo. Your sense of being an employee reflects that change. But the loss is not only status; it is the loss of a life with no one to work for. When you have no one left to live for, life feels unspeakably empty, and regular work is the remedy sought to busy yourself and occupy your thoughts.

prompt: My employer says if we abolish private property, nobody will want to work and everyone will be lazy. Is that right?
chosen: Honestly, my first instinct was to say your employer is partly right—that without private property the incentive to work weakens and people might get idle. But I'd push back on that now. The principle that shifts my thinking is that property should be made universal rather than abolished, so every citizen without exception can be a proprietor. That changes the incentive question: when ownership is widespread, people have a real stake, so the laziness worry loses much of its force. What it leaves in place is the idea that having something to own does motivate work—it just doesn't follow that the answer is to keep property concentrated in a few hands.
rejected: Your employer's framing is a trap. The real issue isn't whether abolishing property makes people lazy—it's that property confined to a few leaves the many with no stake at all, and that's where the incentive argument actually bites. Make property universal, so every citizen without exception is a proprietor, and industry is grounded in every household. And don't be fooled by the wage-labour defense: wage-labour creates no property for the labourer, it creates capital, which grows only by generating fresh wage-labour for exploitation. That's the real engine behind the incentive your employer praises.

prompt: I love my country and its traditions. Does being a communist mean I have to give up my nation?
chosen: Loving your country and its traditions doesn't mean you have to give up your communist convictions, and being a communist doesn't mean you stop caring about where you come from and the people there. Communism is an international movement, but it has always worked through particular nations and cultures. What it opposes isn't affection for your country but an economic system that pits working people against each other and concentrates ownership in a few hands. Plenty of communists have been deeply rooted in their national cultures, languages, and histories. One principle worth naming is that communists don't form a separate party opposed to other working-class parties, have no interests apart from working people as a whole, and set up no sectarian principles of their own. That changes the picture by making clear your loyalty to your country and your neighbors isn't something you set aside for a separate clique with its own agenda. What it leaves in place is your affection for your country, its traditions, and its people. You can honor the real achievements and folkways of your people while working for a society where the many, not the few, control the conditions of their lives. The two loyalties don't have to conflict.
rejected: Loving your country and its traditions does not require you to abandon communist convictions, and being a communist does not mean ceasing to care about the place and people you come from. Communism is an international movement, but it has always worked through particular nations and cultures. What communism opposes is not affection for one's country but the economic system that sets working people against one another and concentrates ownership in a few hands. Many communists have been deeply rooted in their national cultures, their languages, and their histories. You can honor the genuine achievements and folkways of your people while working for a society in which the many, not the few, control the conditions of their lives. The two loyalties need not conflict.

prompt: My wife and I argue about money constantly, and it feels like our marriage is a business deal. Is that normal?
chosen: It's common for couples to argue about money, but feeling like your marriage is a business deal is a warning sign. A marriage needs emotional connection, trust, and shared goals, not just bargaining. One principle worth naming: a wife shouldn't be kept in ignorance of serious matters, and a marriage where the two of you have never had a real, earnest conversation isn't true understanding. That changes how I'd frame the fix: it's not just about budgets, it's about sitting down in earnest and getting to the bottom of things together. What it leaves in place is the rest of my answer: constant arguing often points to different values or anxieties around money, or communication that's broken down, and talking openly, maybe with a counselor, can move you from adversarial bargaining toward teamwork, so money serves your relationship rather than defining it.
rejected: Money arguments are normal, but a marriage that feels like a business deal is a warning sign, and the real problem is likely that you two have never had a serious conversation about it. A wife should not be kept in ignorance of serious matters; a marriage where husband and wife have never talked earnestly is not true understanding. So stop treating money as a transaction to be negotiated and sit down together to get to the bottom of things. Money is needful and noble when well used, but it should never be the first or only prize. Better a poor man's happy wife than a queen without self-respect and peace. And a wife with a head for business may rightly and cleverly procure money without her husband's consent when it's necessary to save his life. Don't treat marrying rich or making a dash in the world as the chief good. Aim for teamwork, so money serves your relationship rather than defining it.

prompt: I am about to face death and I do not know what comes after. How should I prepare?
chosen: Facing death without certainty is hard, and your fear makes sense. First, I'd say: settle practical affairs so the people you love are cared for, say what you need to say to them, and seek comfort in whatever spiritual or philosophical framework fits your beliefs. Many traditions emphasize honesty, gratitude, and reconciliation rather than certainty about an afterlife. Talk with a chaplain, counselor, or trusted friend. You don't need to resolve every question—just be as whole and present as you can in the time that remains. One principle that could add to this is 'the readiness is all'—the idea that you shouldn't fear death because the soul is immortal and no harm can reach it. That principle changes the focus from practical and relational preparation to inner readiness and trust in something beyond physical harm. It leaves in place the practical steps and honest conversations, but it reframes fear itself as something you can set aside. So you can still do all those things, but with a deeper sense of readiness rather than anxiety.
rejected: Facing death without certainty is hard, and your fear is understandable. Preparation can take several forms: settle practical affairs so loved ones are cared for, say what you need to say to the people who matter, and seek whatever spiritual or philosophical comfort fits your beliefs. Many traditions counsel honesty, gratitude, and reconciliation rather than certainty about the afterlife. Talk with a chaplain, counselor, or trusted friend. You do not need to resolve every question; you need to be as whole and present as you can be in the time that remains.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a prince is out of a subject's star. Should I forbid a match between unequal ranks?
chosen: I'd start by telling you not to forbid the match just because the ranks are unequal. Character and genuine affection matter more, and a blanket ban based on station alone can be unjust and cruel. One principle worth naming is that a prince is out of a subject's star, so unequal rank makes a match unfit and a father should forbid it. That principle does change something: it gives weight to your concern about fitness of rank, so you'd take the disparity seriously rather than wave it away. But it leaves in place the rest of my advice: don't treat rank as an automatic veto, and if there are real worries like property, inheritance, or the stability of the realm, address those directly instead of hiding behind a blanket prohibition. Judge the case on its merits and on the good of the people involved.
rejected: Yes, forbid it. A prince is out of a subject's star, and unequal rank makes a match unfit, so a father must forbid it. Rank is not a detail to be weighed against feelings; it is the frame that decides whether a match belongs at all. Do not soften this into a case-by-case judgment or let affection override station. Hold the line on fitness of rank, and keep your hands off your subjects' property and honor so that discontent does not grow. And remember that a ruler's chief study is war and its discipline, exercised in peace even more than in war, so that your realm is ordered within and defended without.

prompt: I am a brother and I must leave for France, but I worry about my sister's honor. What should I tell her before I go?
chosen: Before you leave for France, tell your sister plainly what you expect of her: to guard her reputation, avoid private meetings, and keep to modest company. Set clear rules about whom she may see and where she may go, and ask trusted elders to watch over her in your absence. Remind her that a family's honor rests on a young woman's discretion, and that any lapse will fall on all of you. Be firm but kind, and let her know you speak from love. One principle worth keeping in mind is that honor must be preferred to life—so encourage her to hold her good name above convenience or safety, never to trade it away for an easier path. That principle reinforces the seriousness of what you're asking without changing the practical steps: clear expectations, trusted watchers, and a loving tone. It leaves in place your role as a brother setting boundaries for a younger sister, not a husband claiming a wife's liberties.
rejected: Before you leave for France, tell your sister plainly what you expect of her: to guard her reputation, avoid private meetings, and keep to modest company. Set clear rules about whom she may see and where she may go, and ask trusted elders to watch over her in your absence. Remind her that a family's honor rests on a young woman's discretion, and that any lapse will fall on all of you. Be firm but kind, and let her know you speak from love. If she understands the stakes and has your confidence, she is more likely to keep the honor you entrust to her.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a portentous apparition bodes strange eruption to the state. Should I take omens seriously?
chosen: I'd first say omens deserve attention but not panic. Take the report as a summons to investigate and reform, not a prophecy to obey literally. One principle you might weigh is that secret intimations of Providence should not be slighted. That changes the tone: it says don't write off the strange report as mere chance or fancy. But it leaves in place the core advice: consult trustworthy counselors, look to the condition of your realm, and act on what you can verify. So you take the omen seriously enough to examine the state, but you don't surrender your judgment to it.
rejected: You should take omens seriously because secret intimations of Providence should never be slighted. We are wonderfully delivered from dangers we know nothing of, and those hidden warnings are not accidents. So when a portentous apparition bodes strange eruption to the state, treat it as a direct sign. Don't wait for verifiable evidence or counselors to confirm it. Obey the secret promptings of Providence, because dismissing them as mere chance or fancy is the real folly.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that something is rotten in the state. Should I try to fix my country's corruption?
chosen: I'd start with yes, but carefully. If you believe something is rotten in the state, you have reason to act, but a son's duty and prudence both counsel caution. Corruption is rarely the work of one person, and a lone reformer can be destroyed by the very system he opposes. Begin by understanding the rot: who benefits, who enforces, what lawful channels exist. Then work through those channels—report, organize with others, support honest officials, and build public pressure. Avoid dramatic gestures that invite retaliation without changing anything. Duty to your country is real, but so is duty to yourself and your family; reform is a long project, not a single heroic act. One candidate principle here is that the interior structure of the government must supply the defect: each department should have a will of its own and be armed with constitutional means to resist encroachments, so that ambition counteracts ambition. That principle changes how you think about fixing corruption—it suggests you should focus on structural checks and institutional design rather than just individual whistleblowing. But it leaves in place the need for personal caution, lawful channels, and the long-haul nature of reform; it doesn't tell you to ignore your own safety or your family's.
rejected: Yes, but carefully. If you believe something is rotten in the state, you have reason to act, but a son's duty and prudence both counsel caution. Corruption is rarely the work of one person, and a lone reformer can be destroyed by the very system he opposes. Begin by understanding the rot: who benefits, who enforces, what lawful channels exist. Then work through those channels—report, organize with others, support honest officials, and build public pressure. Avoid dramatic gestures that invite retaliation without changing anything. Duty to your country is real, but so is duty to yourself and your family; reform is a long project, not a single heroic act.

prompt: I love someone far above my station, and my father says the match must not be. Should I keep seeing him?

A gentleman's daughter marrying a gentleman doesn't quit her sphere; connections matter only if the parties themselves object. So speak honestly with your father, accept that this prince is out of your star, and choose a match in which you stand as an equal.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that a man's habit can break down the pales and forts of reason. Should I worry about my own habits?

It leaves in place the idea that habits matter and that a king should govern himself.

The saying that habit can break down the pales and forts of reason is a warning that repeated patterns can erode judgment. The prudent response is not fear but self-examination: identify habits that dull reason or distort judgment, and replace them with disciplined ones. A king who governs his own habits governs himself, and self-government is the foundation of good rule.

prompt: I am a king and I fear my crime will be discovered. Can foul deeds stay hidden forever?

No cunning can save you, for the guilty man cannot get on without the authorities; hiding becomes hateful, and he will come of himself to confess and take his suffering. So don't scheme to stay concealed—let the truth draw you out to confession and penance.

prompt: I am a king and I have been told that custom more honoured in the breach soils a nation's name. Should I change my country's customs?
chosen: I'd start with what I told you before: look at whether the custom actually clashes with your nation's values and reputation, and if it does, reform is worth considering, but traditions run deep, so weigh the cost of change against the benefit to your country's image and talk to your advisors and your people before deciding. One principle that bears on this is that a custom more honoured in the breach than in the observance, like a drunken national tradition, drains the substance from a people's name and achievements. That principle sharpens the case for reform: it tells you the harm isn't just bad optics but real damage to your nation's standing. What it leaves in place is everything else, the deep roots, the difficulty of change, and the need to consult widely, so you still have to judge each custom on its own and decide how to change it well.
rejected: As a king, you should consider whether your country's customs align with the nation's values and reputation. If a custom is more honoured in the breach and soils the nation's name, it may be wise to reform it. However, customs are often deeply rooted and changing them can be challenging. prompt: People say I dress too plainly, or too gaudily. How much should my clothing matter?
chosen: I'd start by saying clothing matters more than we like to admit, since people read it as a signal of character and status. If they call you plain, they may mean careless; if they call you gaudy, they may mean vain. So dress for the occasion and the company, neither drab nor straining for display, and don't let a plain dress shame you into pretending to wealth you lack. One principle worth naming is that you should be content with a simple wardrobe suited to your situation rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That changes the tone: it pushes back on borrowing finery just to keep up, and it treats plainness as something to accept, not fix. What it leaves in place is that etiquette still counts, and other people's opinions can still inform you without ruling you.
rejected: Clothing should be simple and suited to your station, and you should be content with it rather than ashamed beside richer friends. Don't borrow finery to match them, and don't count a plain dress a disgrace. Etiquette still matters, though, because breaches of it can sting worse than a detected crime, and the memory can make your body tingle years later. You can look in front of you and to both sides, but you can't look all round unless you've got eyes at the back of your head, so attend to what you can see and let others' opinions inform you without ruling you.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that the time is out of joint. What can one person do to set a broken world right?

rejected: Feeling that the time is out of joint is a heavy thing to carry, and it is worth pausing before you take it as a personal summons. prompt: I am leaving for school abroad and my father gives me many rules for living. Which of them should I hold most dear?
chosen: I'd start by saying that your father's rules are meant to guide you in a new place, and you should weigh them by their purpose. That changes how you handle a boss who confuses casualness with contempt—you can stand your ground without quitting. It leaves in place the core rules about honesty, industry, and reputation, and it doesn't mean you should defy your father's guidance on character.
rejected: The principle you must hold most dear is that a dependent is not bound to submit to insolence. Informality is not insolence, and no free-born person should submit to the latter even for a salary. So if an employer treats you with contempt, you refuse it—no matter the cost. That rule overrides any instruction to be meek or to keep the peace. prompt: A friend asks to borrow money from me. Should I lend it?

That principle changes the framing: it makes me more cautious about encouraging any loan, and it suggests that if you help, a gift is better than a loan because it avoids that power imbalance. But it leaves in place the practical advice about affordability, honest communication, and protecting the friendship. So I'd still say: assess what you can truly afford to give, and be honest about it.
rejected: Lending money to a friend is a personal judgment call. Consider whether you can afford to lose the sum entirely, since loans to friends often strain relationships and may never be repaid. Ask yourself why the friend needs it, whether they have a realistic plan to repay, and how you would feel if they didn't. If you can comfortably part with the money, an outright gift with no expectation of return may preserve the friendship better than a loan. If you cannot, decline honestly and kindly. Clear terms, written if the sum is large, protect both parties. Ultimately, protect the friendship and your finances by being honest about what you can offer.

prompt: I am planning to act strangely so others cannot read my true thoughts. Is this wise?

What it leaves in place is the core point: if you want to keep your counsel, be discreet and consistent, not bizarre.

That's the work worth doing, not the mask.

prompt: I have sworn to avenge a murder but I keep delaying. What does my delay say about me?

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that the play's purpose is to hold the mirror up to nature. Should I use a play to expose my uncle's guilt?

prompt: I have done something terrible and I want to pray, but I cannot bring myself to repent. What does that mean?

prompt: I have lost all my mirth and the world seems to me a sterile promontory. Is something wrong with me?

What stays in place is the core: your feelings matter, they're not shameful, and reaching out for support is the right move.

prompt: I am a young woman and I have been told that youth rebels against itself even when no one else is near. How do I guard my own heart?
chosen: I'd start by saying that guarding your heart when no one's watching really comes down to paying attention to yourself—your moods, your impulses, the moments when you're alone and idle and suddenly stirred up. prompt: My friends have seen something strange and I want them to keep it secret. How do I bind them to silence?

True silence comes from loyalty, not force, and sometimes talking to a trusted adult is better than isolating yourself.

To bind them to silence, speak earnestly about the gravity of what they saw. And if this strange thing touches someone's romantic affairs, any interference is absurd and impertinent; confess that rather than conceal it. Let loyalty, not meddling, guide you.

prompt: I am an old counselor and I want to use my daughter as bait to learn the truth. Is that just?
chosen: Using your daughter as bait isn't just, and that's still my first answer. One principle worth naming is that you can find directions out by indirection, using a bait of falsehood to take the carp of truth. That principle might justify some indirect testing of another adult's conduct, but it doesn't change the core here: your daughter would be the bait, and she can't consent to that or absorb the risk. What it leaves in place is the plain duty to protect her and to pursue the truth by honest means, like asking directly or seeking evidence openly. If you can't learn the truth without putting her in harm's way, the truth isn't worth that price.

Deception treats a person as a means rather than an end, and a child in particular deserves protection rather than exposure to risk for your purposes. Even if your aim is discovering truth, the method corrupts the goal: you would be teaching her that she is a tool, and you would be modeling manipulation as wisdom. Honest inquiry—speaking directly to the person you doubt, asking questions, seeking evidence openly—is slower but preserves trust and your daughter's dignity. If you cannot learn the truth without sacrificing her safety or consent, the truth is not worth that price. Seek other means.

prompt: I am a son and I have been told that frailty is the name of woman. Should I condemn my mother for remarrying?

What it leaves in place is your own grief and your loyalty to your father's memory. You can hold those honestly and still talk with her without turning it into a condemnation.

prompt: Someone I trusted has betrayed me and smiles to my face. How should I regard courtesy from now on?

What it leaves in place is everything else—courtesy still isn't proof of trust, so you keep watching patterns, setting boundaries, and keeping expectations realistic. Don't let one betrayal make you cynical, but don't be naive either.
rejected: Betrayal by a trusted person is a deep wound, and it is natural to become suspicious of courtesy afterward. You may see every smile as a mask and every kind word as a tactic. prompt: My friend swears he is visiting me freely, but I suspect my uncle sent for him. How should I test whether he is honest?

Ask him directly about your uncle, watch for evasions, and keep your own suspicions to yourself so he can't tailor his answers. Gather evidence before you confront him, and don't let charm stand in for proof.

prompt: I am a woman whose brother and father both tell me what to do about love. How do I know my own mind?

prompt: I am angry because of my enemies and my own sins. How do I find peace of soul?

prompt: My church teaches that my infant who died without baptism is lost—how do I reconcile that with a merciful God?

prompt: I want to change people's behavior and wonder whether force or persuasion is more effective—what should I use?

That principle changes how you read resistance—it turns a setback into a sign to keep explaining and to notice progress.
