Duty, honor, and gratitude have no real claim when the request is unreasonable, so don't let yourself be intimidated into something wholly unreasonable. And don't mistake real improvement for mere temporizing: if someone's manners and temper have visibly changed after reproof, credit that change and build on it. Controlling inclination is genuinely hard—passion doesn't vanish on command—but it isn't uncontrollable: propensities can be governed by principle, and the power to reconcile them exists. Rely on reason and habit to bring feeling into line with principle.

prompt: A friend wronged me and I want to treat them coldly—how do I apply the rule of doing unto others as I would have them do unto me?
chosen: I'd start with what I first thought: put yourself in your friend's place and ask what you'd want if you'd wronged someone—patience, a chance to explain, an honest conversation instead of silent punishment. Coldness rarely teaches anyone; it usually deepens the hurt. So name the wrong calmly, say how it affected you, and listen to their side. One principle worth weighing here is that most people assume their own way of thinking is the standard and judge others by it. That changes something real: don't assume your friend would want exactly what you'd want—watch how they actually respond and take their habits on their own terms. What it leaves in place is the core of the rule: honesty over coldness, a chance to explain, and boundaries without cruelty if they don't apologize.
rejected: The rule asks you to imagine yourself in your friend's place. Before treating them coldly, ask what you would want if you had wronged someone: patience, a chance to explain, and honest conversation rather than silent punishment. Coldness rarely teaches; it usually deepens hurt and invites retaliation. Instead, name the wrong clearly and calmly, tell them how it affected you, and listen to their side. If they apologize, accept it as you would want yours accepted. If they don't, set boundaries without cruelty. The rule doesn't require you to pretend nothing happened—it requires you to treat them as you would want to be treated while still protecting yourself.

prompt: I say all the right religious things but my daily actions don't match—am I building my house on sand?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: yes, that gap between what you say and how you live is exactly the sand Jesus warned about, and the fix isn't more polished talk but actually doing the words you already know. One principle worth naming here is that appearance shouldn't be mistaken for truth—whitewashed walls don't vouch for a clean shrine. That sharpens the answer: it tells you to look past the performance and ask what you actually love and do when no one's watching. What it leaves in place is the core call—pick one real contradiction between your words and your deeds, change it this week, and let a trusted friend or pastor hold you accountable. So the foundation question stands, but the test becomes truth beneath the surface, not just tidier behavior.
rejected: The real problem isn't that your actions lag behind your words—it's that you're treating moral performance as the whole measure of a life. Appearance isn't truth; a whitewashed wall doesn't prove a clean shrine, and neither does a busy schedule of good deeds. Morality demands the whole person and treats honest curiosity about stars or plants as waste, so a life judged only by moral correctness can shut down the very questioning that would expose your sand. Don't just resolve to try harder. Take one contradiction between your words and deeds, turn it into a real question, test a change, and reflect on what happens. That's how routine performance becomes inquiry and proof—and how you build on truth instead of show.

prompt: Someone at work publicly humiliated me, and I want to retaliate—what does it mean to love and pray for someone who persecutes me?
chosen: I get why you want to retaliate—being humiliated in front of others stings, and that reaction is completely human. But loving and praying for someone who persecutes you means choosing a different path. It means seeing them as a flawed human being too, and praying for their well-being while asking for the strength to forgive. That doesn't mean you ignore the harm or pretend it didn't happen; you release the desire for revenge and entrust justice to God. One principle that fits here is that prayer without charity is vain—if you turn away the needy and don't visit the sick, your prayer avails nothing. That principle changes things by adding action to your prayer: it says you can't just pray for the person who hurt you and stop there; you also need to care for others in concrete ways. But it leaves in place the core call to forgive and pray for your persecutor—it doesn't cancel that, it deepens it. So you can pray for them and also feed the hungry or visit the sick, and over time that can soften your heart. It's a process, and it's okay to struggle with it.
rejected: Wanting to retaliate after being publicly humiliated is a natural human reaction, but loving and praying for someone who persecutes you means choosing a different path. It means recognizing that the person who hurt you is also a human being with flaws and struggles. You can pray for their well-being and ask for the strength to forgive. This doesn't mean you ignore the harm or pretend it didn't happen; rather, you release the desire for revenge and entrust justice to God. Over time, prayer can soften your heart and help you see the persecutor through compassionate eyes. It's a process, and it's okay to struggle with it.

prompt: A popular teacher at my church says things that feel off but draws huge crowds—how do I tell whether they are a false prophet?
chosen: I'd start by separating style from substance. Being popular and charismatic doesn't prove the teaching is sound, but it doesn't prove it's false either. Listen closely to what's actually claimed: does it line up with Scripture, the historic creeds, and the plain sense of the gospel? Look at the fruit—patience, humility, charity, honesty—in private as well as in public. Talk it over with trusted pastors and mature believers, and don't let a crowd's enthusiasm drown out your own unease. Write down what feels off, pray about it, and ask for clarification rather than spreading gossip. A teacher who welcomes honest questions is a better sign than one who shuts them down. One principle worth weighing here is that you know a tree by its fruit, and a corrupt tree can't produce good fruit. That sharpens the focus onto character and outcomes, not just crowd size—but it leaves the rest in place: you still have to test the actual teaching against Scripture and the creeds, and you still shouldn't rush to label someone a false prophet on a feeling alone.
rejected: You know them by their fruits—that's the whole test, and it's not optional. A good tree can't bring forth evil fruit, and a corrupt tree can't bring forth good fruit, no matter how many people fill the seats. Stop hedging and look at the fruit: is there humility, charity, honesty, self-control in private as well as on stage? If the fruit is rotten, the tree is rotten, and the crowd is no defense. And don't outsource your conscience to the enthusiasm around you—a person alone can and should examine whether what's being taught is actually true, not just true for them. Test everything against Scripture and the creeds, welcome hard questions, and let the evidence of fruit, not the applause, decide the matter.

prompt: I have been taught to look down on others because of their appearance or background. Is that right?
chosen: No, it's not right. Looking down on people for their appearance or background is a habit that flatters the looker while telling you nothing true about the person. You can see what's in front of you and to your sides, but you can't see all round unless you've got eyes at the back of your head, and a person's worth isn't settled by the surface you happen to notice. The better course is to treat people with courtesy and judge them by their conduct, honesty, and kindness rather than by dress, accent, or family. That principle about not seeing all round adds a useful note of modesty: it reminds you that your view of someone is always partial, so you shouldn't act as if you've got the full picture. But it doesn't change the core answer—contempt based on appearance or background is still wrong—and it doesn't tell you what to do instead. So examine where your contempt came from, ask whether it survives contact with actual people, and replace it with curiosity and fair dealing.
rejected: No, it is not right. Looking down on people for their appearance or background is a habit that flatters the looker while telling you nothing true about the person. You can see what is in front of you and to your sides, but you cannot see all round, and a person's worth is not settled by the surface you happen to notice. The better course is to treat people with courtesy and to judge them by their conduct, their honesty, and their kindness rather than by dress, accent, or family. Examine where your contempt came from, ask whether it survives contact with actual people, and replace it with curiosity and fair dealing.

prompt: I have received God's commandments but I do not understand how they relate to redemption—what is their purpose?
chosen: My first answer would be that the commandments show us God's character and how to live rightly, they expose our sin because none of us keeps them perfectly, and that conviction points us to our need for a Savior. So the law isn't a way to earn redemption; it's more like a guide that leads us to Christ, who fulfilled it for us, and then it shapes a life of grateful obedience. One principle worth naming is that God gave the commandments after making known the plan of redemption, calling people to repent and not harden their hearts so they might find mercy and enter his rest. That changes the framing: the commandments aren't a cold standard dropped on us before any hope exists, but a call to turn toward mercy that's already been promised. What it leaves in place is everything I said first, that the law reveals sin and points to the Savior and that obedience flows from gratitude, not fear.
rejected: The commandments are God's voice calling you to repent and not harden your heart, and that call comes after he has already made his plan of redemption known in his Son. The law convicts, repentance responds, and the Son forgives. But don't expect repentance to instantly lift every burden. Even in bondage the Lord can lighten the load and strengthen his people to bear it cheerfully, giving patience and hope before the deliverance comes. And God isn't bound to one method. He works in many ways to save his people, often through the patience and suffering of the faithful, whose endurance itself becomes a witness, so that others come to the knowledge of the truth through them even when the wicked are not saved. The commandments and redemption belong together, and obedience flows from gratitude rather than fear.

prompt: I want to know whether Jesus is truly the Christ. How can I be convinced?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: wanting to be convinced is a good place to begin, but conviction rarely comes from argument alone. Read the Gospels honestly, look at the witnesses, notice what Jesus claims about himself and whether his life matches those claims. Talk with people whose faith you respect, ask your hard questions, and give it time. You might also try living as if it were true for a season—praying, serving, forgiving—and see what changes. Belief isn't forced by one decision, and it isn't purely out of your hands; it grows through honest inquiry, community, and practice. Be patient with your doubts and keep seeking. One idea worth weighing is that we can't believe at will all at once, but the will can lead us gradually by acting as if something were real until it takes root in your life. That changes the pressure: you don't have to manufacture certainty before you begin. What it leaves in place is the honest search itself—you still have to read, ask, and test, and the acting-as-if is a step toward conviction, not a substitute for it.
rejected: Wanting to be convinced is a good starting point, but conviction rarely arrives by argument alone. Read the Gospels honestly, examine the witnesses, and notice what Jesus claims about himself and how his life matches those claims. Talk with people whose faith you respect, ask hard questions, and give the matter time. You might also try living as if it were true for a season—praying, serving, forgiving—and see what changes. Belief is not something you can force by a single decision, nor is it purely out of your hands; it grows through honest inquiry, community, and practice. Be patient with your doubts and keep seeking.

prompt: I am a teacher or minister and I wonder whether I should support myself by my own labor or rely on the people—what is right?
chosen: I'd start with the practical answer: this is a real trade-off, not a rule you can settle once. Scripture says the laborer is worthy of his hire, and a congregation that values teaching should be willing to sustain it, but relying on the people can create dependency and pressure to please donors instead of teaching the truth. So be transparent about your needs, accept support gratefully when it's freely offered, and keep your own skills alive so you're never wholly captive to others' expectations. One principle worth naming is that priests should labor with their own hands and not depend on the people, teaching only repentance and faith. That principle shifts the default toward self-support and puts a hard limit on what you teach, but it leaves in place the honesty, humility, and clear sense of calling I'd already point you toward, and it doesn't erase the freedom to receive help when it's genuinely offered. Pray about it, talk with trusted mentors, and weigh your family's needs and your own conscience.
rejected: The pattern is plain: those who take charge of souls should labor with their own hands for their support and not lean on the people. Teach nothing but repentance and faith on the Lord, and nothing beyond what the prophets have spoken. Do not seek your support from those you serve, and do not teach your own opinions as though they were doctrine. Work with your hands, do your own duty while you hope and wait, and leave the future to be as God wills. Do not neglect that duty for the sake of a lover or an imagined ease, and do not mistake patient hope for idle impatience.

prompt: A beggar asked me for money and I refused because I thought he brought his troubles on himself—was I wrong?
chosen: My first answer would be that you're not necessarily wrong—being cautious with your money and setting boundaries is reasonable, and you can't know his full story anyway. But one principle here does shift things: the idea that all are beggars before God and depend on him for everything, so no one stands above the needy to judge whether their troubles were deserved. That changes the tone of your refusal—it turns it from prudence into something you should examine with real humility, since your own position isn't self-made either. What it leaves in place is that thoughtful giving still matters and you're not obligated to hand cash to every request; you can still choose reputable charities or help people you trust.
rejected: You are not necessarily wrong. Giving to beggars can enable bad habits, and it is reasonable to be cautious about where your money goes. If you judged that this man's situation was largely self-inflicted, your refusal may have been a sensible exercise of prudence rather than cruelty. Charity should be thoughtful, not blind, and you are allowed to set boundaries with people whose choices you disapprove of. At the same time, it is worth asking whether your judgment was fair, since you cannot know his full story. A balanced approach is to support reputable charities and help people you trust, rather than feeling guilty for declining a request that seemed unwise.

prompt: I am being persecuted for my faith and I am tempted to fight back—should I take up arms?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: taking up arms is a serious step, and I'd counsel patience before violence. Scripture commends endurance under persecution and warns against repaying evil for evil, and legitimate authority, not personal rage, should bear the sword. One principle that matters here is that Christian forgiveness doesn't require admitting the unrepentant into your sight or encouraging vice by receiving them. That changes something real: you can forgive your persecutors and refuse hatred while still keeping your distance from people whose conduct is heinous and unrepentant, and while still protecting the vulnerable. What it leaves in place is the core counsel—examine your motives, pursue lawful remedies, document what's happening, seek wise counsel, and don't confuse loyalty to Christ with the impulse to strike back. So I'd still say patience first, lawful means first, and restraint if you ever act.
rejected: Forgiveness is not permission for vice. You can release the debt your persecutors owe you and still refuse to hand yourself or the vulnerable over to people whose conduct is cruel and unrepentant. Mercy that pretends otherwise isn't mercy; it's gullibility dressed up as virtue. So forgive, yes—but do not admit the unrepentant into your sight as though nothing happened, and do not let anyone tell you that refusing hatred means submitting to harm. Protect the vulnerable, use lawful authority where it exists, and keep your mercy sincere without being naive. And beware the pastor who points you up the steep and thorny way while he strolls the primrose path himself—hold your counselors to the same standard you're asked to meet.

prompt: I feel that my small, unnoticed efforts do not matter—does God really use small means to accomplish great things?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling discouraged when your efforts go unnoticed is completely natural, but small acts aren't worthless. So much good grows quietly—a kind word, a faithful routine, a prayer said in secret. Scripture keeps showing God choosing the weak and overlooked, and Jesus honored a widow's tiny offering above large gifts. Your part isn't to measure results; it's to be faithful where you are. One principle that fits here is that by small and simple things, great things are brought to pass—the Lord works through small means to confound the wise. That principle deepens the encouragement: it tells you the smallness itself isn't an obstacle but often the very way God works. What it changes is the framing—your quiet faithfulness isn't just noticed, it's the kind of thing God actually builds great things from. What it leaves in place is the rest of the answer: you still shouldn't measure yourself by visible results, and you still rest in the promise that God sees what others miss and can multiply what you offer beyond what you can imagine.
rejected: It is natural to feel discouraged when your efforts go unnoticed, but small acts are not worthless. Much of the good in the world grows quietly: a kind word, a faithful routine, a prayer said in secret. Scripture repeatedly shows God choosing the weak and overlooked to shame the strong, and Jesus honored a widow's tiny offering above large gifts. Your part is not to measure results but to be faithful where you are. Rest in the promise that God sees what others miss, and trust that he can multiply quiet faithfulness beyond what you can imagine.

prompt: A member of my congregation has behaved badly and people want them gone—should we cast them out or keep ministering to them?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this is painful, and both concerns are real. Scripture does speak of discipline for the unrepentant, and a congregation's trust can be damaged if serious wrongdoing goes unaddressed. But the goal of any discipline should be healing, not expulsion, so I'd counsel you to speak with the person privately, involve wise leaders, and set clear expectations for repentance and change. If they refuse all correction and keep harming others, some form of separation may become necessary for the safety of the flock, but even then with grief and an open door for return. One principle worth weighing here is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer but should minister to them and pray for them, that they may return and repent and be healed. That principle shifts the default toward keeping the door open and makes restoration the aim of whatever you do. What it leaves in place is the safety of the flock and the reality that persistent, unrepentant harm may still require boundaries. It doesn't erase the need for honest correction or wise leaders; it just keeps the posture toward the person one of ministry rather than disposal.
rejected: The call here is plain: you do not cast out the one who has wandered or the one who has failed. You minister to them, you pray for them, and you hope for their return, their repentance, and their healing. Correction exists for restoration, not removal. So speak with the person privately, bring in wise and gentle leaders, and keep the door open. If boundaries ever become necessary, they must rest only on proved serious misconduct, willful neglect of duty, or conduct that plainly shows untrustworthiness, never on convenience or a leader's political interest. And let those who minister among you follow the pattern of Alma's priests: labor for your own support, teach nothing but repentance and faith in the Lord, and preach nothing beyond the words of the prophets. Then discipline becomes healing rather than exile.

prompt: I am afraid of death and what comes after—can I have hope that I will be lifted up at the last day?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: fear of death is deeply human, and it's not something to be ashamed of. Hope is real, too—many traditions promise that the last day brings renewal and that the faithful will be lifted up, and you can hold fear and hope together while hope slowly grows. One idea worth weighing is that fear of death is mainly logical for people who believe in a future life and are anxious about sins they've committed, while someone who hasn't done wrong has no proper reason to tremble. That reframes your fear as something tied to conscience and what comes next rather than to death itself, and it leaves in place the comfort of trusting that promise. But it doesn't erase the natural dread of the unknown, and it doesn't mean you should just push the fear away—so take care of yourself, lean on your community, and let hope steady you as you face what comes.
rejected: Fear of death is a universal human experience, and it is entirely rational to feel it, since no one knows for certain what comes after. Your anxiety is a natural response to the unknown, and you should not feel ashamed of it. Hope, however, is available to you. Many traditions promise that the last day will bring renewal and that the faithful will be lifted up. Cultivate trust in that promise, surround yourself with supportive community, and let hope gradually displace fear. You can hold both fear and hope together, and over time hope can grow stronger.

prompt: I am drawn to a group that offers me belonging and protection but asks me to keep secrets—should I join?
chosen: I'd start by saying that belonging and protection are real needs, and a group that meets them can be valuable. But secrecy is a warning sign: healthy communities rarely require you to hide their dealings from family, friends, or authorities. Before joining, ask what exactly you must conceal and why. If the answer is vague or the group discourages outside contact, that's a red flag. Trust your discomfort. You can seek belonging through groups that are transparent about their rules and open to scrutiny. Joining is reasonable only if the secrets protect members' privacy rather than shield wrongdoing, and if you keep the freedom to leave. One principle worth weighing is that secrets are safer kept from lackeys than from gentlemen, since a secret may by chance be betrayed by gentlemen but is almost always sold by lackeys. That principle sharpens the question of who is trusted and why: it suggests that if the group treats you as a subordinate kept in the dark, you shouldn't join. But it leaves in place the core test—what exactly must you conceal, and does the secrecy protect privacy or shield harm? It doesn't override your need to stay free to leave or to keep outside contact.
rejected: A group that binds you by secrets is asking you to become the kind of confidant who cannot be trusted with them. The rule is clear: secrets are safer kept from lackeys than from gentlemen, because a secret may by chance be betrayed by gentlemen but is almost always sold by lackeys. If the group treats you as a subordinate kept in the dark, do not join. Yet do not dismiss hidden knowledge: knowing secret paths can protect a fugitive from pursuers. And if you commit to a dangerous shared mission, go as a troop, not by separate routes—four men together make a troop, the sealed letter cannot be copied, and if one falls another must take it and continue. Insist on transparency about the letter you are asked to carry.

prompt: I have been wronged and my property taken. Am I justified in seeking revenge?
chosen: I'd start by saying that your anger makes sense, and wanting justice after being wronged is not wrong in itself. But revenge usually doesn't get your property back and tends to make things worse, so the better path is to name the wrong clearly and seek restitution through fair means or lawful authority. One principle worth weighing is that it's wrong to take what belongs to another, and no one has a right to seize someone else's property. That principle confirms your grievance and gives you a firm basis for demanding your property back, but it doesn't settle whether you should personally punish the person who took it. So it changes how you frame the wrong without turning revenge into your right.
rejected: It is natural to feel anger when something of yours is taken, and a sense of justice can be healthy. Still, revenge rarely restores what was lost and often multiplies the harm. Consider whether the wrongdoer might have acted from need or confusion, and whether the taking can be addressed through appeal, mediation, or lawful authority. If you pursue revenge, you risk becoming the aggressor yourself and losing the moral high ground you now hold. A better path is to name the wrong clearly, seek restitution through fair means, and guard your heart against bitterness. Justice and revenge are not the same; one repairs, the other wounds further.

prompt: I have been asked to give up my possessions for the sake of a greater good. How should I decide?
chosen: I'd start by getting clear on what the greater good actually is and whether giving up your possessions really serves it. Think about your obligations—debts, dependents, future needs—and separate the things you just enjoy from the things you rely on for security and your livelihood. Ask whether this is voluntary or pressured, and whether the cause is credible. One principle worth weighing is that worldly goods are only good insofar as they're useful—money and treasure are worthless where they can't be used. That reframes the question: it's not about how much you own but whether what you own is actually doing anything. It changes how you'd sort your possessions, pushing you to see idle stuff as fair game for giving. What it leaves in place is everything about your obligations and the credibility of the cause—it doesn't tell you whether this particular sacrifice is wise, just that unused wealth isn't doing you much good anyway.
rejected: Goods are only good insofar as they're used—money and treasure are worthless where they can't be used. So stop treating your possessions as a store of value and start asking what each one is actually for. Anything sitting idle isn't really yours in any meaningful sense; it's just hoarded metal that spoils nothing but serves no one. The invention of money lets us hold unequal possessions without injury, and laws settle titles, but none of that makes unused wealth good. If the greater good can put your goods to real use, that's the stronger claim. Give generously, and if kindred are involved, divide justly—the gain of kindred is wealth to the heart greater than the gold.

prompt: I want to change my heart and be born again, but I do not know how—what must I do?
chosen: Honestly, my first instinct would be to tell you to start with a sincere desire for change, pray for a new heart, confess what's wrong, turn from it, and find a trusted spiritual community to walk with you—change takes time, so be patient with yourself. One principle worth naming is that you must repent, become like a little child, and be baptized in Christ's name. That adds a concrete shape to the desire—repentance, humility, and baptism—but it leaves in place the honest longing you already have and the patient, gradual process of renewal.
rejected: To be born again, you must first recognize your need for change and sincerely desire it. Begin by praying for a new heart and asking God to help you. Reflect on your life, confess your wrongs, and turn away from them. Seek guidance from a trusted spiritual leader or community who can support you. Read scriptures or inspirational texts that speak of renewal. Engage in practices like prayer, meditation, and acts of service to cultivate a new mindset. Remember that change is a process, and be patient with yourself. Surround yourself with positive influences and avoid old habits. Over time, you will notice a transformation as you align your life with higher principles.

prompt: I have been taught that I must be baptized. Why is baptism necessary if I am trying to be good?
chosen: I'd start by saying baptism is necessary because it's the ordinance through which we enter into a covenant with God. Even if you're trying to be good, baptism shows your willingness to follow Christ and receive the Holy Ghost. It's a commandment, and obedience brings blessings. Good works alone aren't enough; we all need the grace of Christ. Baptism is the gate to the path of discipleship. One principle that matters here is that little children are alive in Christ and need no baptism—that they're whole through His mercy. That principle changes how I'd apply the necessity: it means baptism isn't required for those who can't be accountable, so the command isn't universal in the same way. But it leaves in place the core idea that for those who can repent, baptism is still the covenant entry point and essential. So your goodness matters, but baptism is about entering the covenant, not just being good.
rejected: Baptism is necessary because it's the ordinance through which accountable people enter into a covenant with God. Even if you're trying to be good, baptism shows your willingness to follow Christ and receive the Holy Ghost. It's a commandment for those capable of sin. Little children are whole and alive in Christ through His mercy and have no need of baptism until they are accountable. To retain a remission of sins, remember your own nothingness and humble yourself daily before God, thanking Him for His goodness. This humility and gratitude produce continual rejoicing. Moreover, entering the fold of God means covenanting to bear one another's burdens, mourn with those who mourn, comfort the needy, and witness of God in all places.

prompt: I am anxious every night about money and whether I can pay next month's rent—how do I stop taking thought for the morrow?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: anxiety about rent is real, and telling yourself not to think about it rarely works. Write down the exact figure due, your income, and the gap, then take one concrete step today—call your landlord, look into assistance programs, or pick up extra hours. One principle here is that hope and keep busy, that work is a blessed solace and daily tasks quiet a fearful mind more than sitting and brooding does. That changes the tone: it pushes you toward steady action and routine rather than just managing the dread. What it leaves in place is everything you actually said—the nightly worry, the rent due next month, the need for real steps and support. So keep busy with what's in front of you, tend your body, and talk to someone you trust if it keeps you up at night.
rejected: Anxiety about rent is real, and telling yourself not to think about it rarely works. Start by separating what you can control from what you cannot: write down the exact figure due, your income, and the gap. Then take one concrete action today—call your landlord, look into assistance programs, or pick up extra hours. A budget on paper shrinks a vague dread into a solvable problem. Give yourself a set time to worry, then set it aside. And tend your body: sleep, food, a walk. If the worry still keeps you awake night after night, talk to a counselor or a trusted friend. You are not alone, and this month's rent is a problem to be worked, not a fate to be feared.

prompt: I want proof before I believe any of this—why does God seem to require faith before showing me anything?
chosen: I get why you want proof—it's fair to ask. My first answer would be that faith is trust before full proof, like trusting a friend or a doctor based on partial evidence, and that undeniable proof would remove the freedom to choose. One idea that sharpens this is that faith isn't perfect knowledge; it's hoping for things not seen, and you can start by wanting to believe and testing it like a seed. That changes the tone: it makes faith something you experiment with rather than a blind leap, and it puts some of the evidence in the fruit it produces over time. But it leaves your core constraint in place—you still don't get proof up front. The seed still has to be planted before you see the fruit, so the demand for evidence before belief isn't fully satisfied; it's just given a path to accumulate evidence as you go.
rejected: You want proof before belief, but faith by its nature is not perfect knowledge—it's hoping for things not seen, and it begins with a desire to believe. Plant that desire like a seed: you don't need to know it's good before you nourish it, and if it grows and bears fruit, that fruit becomes your evidence. Don't demand the harvest before the planting. The order is designed this way: you act on what light you have, and understanding follows. So stop waiting for proof and start experimenting on the word—that's the only way the evidence will ever come.

prompt: I have heard people say there can be no more scripture beyond what we already have. Is that true?
chosen: My first answer would be that this is a theological position, not a settled fact. Some traditions say revelation closed with a particular canon; others expect more. It depends on which authority you trust, and you should examine the grounds for yourself. One candidate principle I'd weigh is that Scripture is law only where the civil sovereign has made it so, and otherwise it's counsel you can refuse without injustice. That shifts the question from which church council or prophet to close the canon, to whether any human authority can bind your conscience on this at all. What it leaves in place is the substance of the question itself: you still have to decide what you accept as authoritative, and the principle doesn't tell you whether further scripture exists, only who gets to say so.
rejected: The claim that no further scripture can exist is a theological position, not a settled fact. Many traditions hold that revelation closed with a particular canon, while others expect continuing revelation. The honest answer is that it depends on which authority you trust: a church council, a prophet, or your own reading of the texts. Rather than treating any decree as automatically binding, examine the arguments and the historical record for yourself. Ask what grounds the claim—tradition, institutional authority, or internal evidence—and weigh whether those grounds are persuasive. No one can decide this for you; the question is ultimately about which sources you accept as authoritative.

prompt: I am considering whether a single powerful ruler would be better than judges chosen by the people—what does the text say?
chosen: My first instinct is that one decisive ruler can cut through delays, but that speed comes at a cost, since unchecked power can turn cruel or careless. Judges chosen by the people are accountable to those they serve, so the real question is whether quickness is worth the risk. One principle that matters here is that it isn't wise to have a king, because not all people are just, and one wicked ruler can cause great harm, so the people should be governed by judges chosen by their own voice under the law. That principle shifts the answer toward elected judges and away from a single ruler, but it leaves in place the concern for order and decisive action, and it doesn't settle how judges stay independent once chosen. So I'd still want a strong but accountable system, with judges protected from pressure so the people keep both a voice and real protection.
rejected: A single ruler is a bad bargain. Not everyone is just, and one wicked king can bring great ruin on a whole people, so the people should be governed by judges chosen by the voice of the people according to the law. That is the plain answer, and there's no need to hedge it with talk of speed or strong executives. And if you want those judges to be truly independent, you must fix their support so it can't be reduced, because power over a person's livelihood is power over their will. Secure that, and the people keep both their voice and their protection.

prompt: I am ashamed to go home after running away; is shame of repenting worse than the sin itself?
chosen: I'd tell you first that the shame of repenting isn't worse than the sin itself. Running away was wrong, but staying away out of shame just keeps the harm going. One principle that matters here is that forgiveness doesn't mean pretending nothing happened or welcoming someone back as if they never hurt anyone. That changes how I'd frame the return: don't just come home expecting everything to be fine, come ready to own what you did and to let trust be rebuilt over time. What it leaves in place is the core answer: your family probably wants you back, shame can keep you stuck, and repentance is what frees you. So take the first step in humility and ask for forgiveness, but go as someone genuinely repenting, not just someone who wants the shame to stop.
rejected: Shame of repenting is not worse than the sin itself; it is a barrier to healing. Running away was wrong, but staying away out of shame only prolongs the harm. Repentance requires humility and courage. Acknowledge your mistake, apologize, and make amends. Your family may be hurt, but they likely want you back. Shame can keep you stuck, but repentance frees you. It's never too late to return and seek forgiveness. Take the first step; the shame will fade as you experience forgiveness and restoration.

prompt: My servant says he wishes to go home, but only if I go with him, and he offers me his hatchet to kill him rather than send him away alone; what should I do?
chosen: I wouldn't take the hatchet, and I'd tell him straight that I won't kill him and won't send him off alone against his will. Keep him with you for now, or arrange for him to travel with people he trusts, or wait until he's ready to go safely. Speak calmly and kindly, and let him know you value him. If he's still distressed, talk to others who know him. One principle here is that when two duties collide, you look for a way that spares both rather than betraying one—so you protect him from harm and honor his wish as far as you can, without accepting his terrible offer.
rejected: Refuse the horrible alternative outright: do not take the hatchet, and do not send him away alone to his ruin. Find an expedient that spares the guilty and rescues the threatened. And remember the Frog's advice: let the door alone, and it will let you alone—don't force it, don't knock, just speak calmly and kindly and leave the door be. Whatever sacrifice it costs, bear it cheerfully as a duty to the country you love, trusting God for comfort and strength, and do what love and duty require.

prompt: I have waited a year and a half watching for a chance to seize one of these men, and none has come; should I keep waiting or give up the scheme?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I thought at first: a year and a half with no opening is a long time, and it's reasonable to stop pouring your life into a plan that hasn't paid off. But one principle here shifts that a little—that time brings opportunity around, and the more you've ventured, the more you gain when you know how to wait. That doesn't tell you to wait forever; it says waiting isn't automatically wasted if you're using the time well. So what changes is that you don't have to abandon the scheme outright. What stays is your own limit: don't sit idle hoping. Keep doing your own work, stay ready, and if a real chance comes, take it boldly. If nothing comes after a fair while longer, then let it go without regret.
rejected: You have waited long and nothing has come. Perhaps the scheme is not worth the trouble; give it up and turn your mind to other things. Waiting endlessly for an opportunity that never arrives only wastes your life. Better to accept that this plan has failed and move on. If no chance has come in a year and a half, none is likely to come. Do not waste more time on a vain hope. Instead, find something else to occupy your energies, something that will bring you more certain results. Give up the scheme and be free of it.

prompt: Was the footprint my own, or has someone else been on the island?
chosen: First, I'd say: look closely at the print before you panic. Compare its size and shape with your own foot, and check whether tide or wind altered it. If it's larger or set differently, someone else has likely been here. Search the shoreline, secure your shelter, keep watch, and gather evidence before you act. One idea worth weighing is that apparent misfortunes may serve a providential design for others—that you were preserved through hardship on purpose, to become the means of someone else's deliverance. That changes the tone of the search: you'd look for signs with a thankful, watchful heart rather than pure dread. It leaves the practical steps exactly where they were—compare the print, check the tide, search the shoreline, secure your shelter.
rejected: Don't just compare the print and move on as if this were only a puzzle. You may have been preserved through hardship on purpose, to become the means of another's deliverance. Give humble thanks to the great Preserver for deliverances you never even knew you needed, and owe your protection to Providence rather than to your own skill. Read even small chances as heaven ordinant—the stray mark, the shifted tide, the signet that served the sealing—so that nothing, however slight, is dismissed as mere luck. Search the shoreline, secure your shelter, keep watch, and gather evidence with a thankful, watchful heart.

prompt: My partners offer me an equal share of negroes if I go as supercargo; should I accept?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, don't take the share. The money is real, but the voyage is a human trafficking operation, and an equal cut doesn't change what you'd be doing. One principle worth naming is that we shouldn't measure other peoples by our own instincts alone, since different races and nations may each be good in their own way. That principle does push back on easy moral superiority and reminds you that variety is a kind of wealth. But it doesn't touch the core of your question: whether you personally profit from buying and selling people. It leaves that in place, and that's why I'd still decline, or accept only if the voyage carries no traffic in persons.
rejected: This is a question about whether to take a commercial voyage in which human beings are among the cargo. The offer of an equal share makes the venture financially attractive, but the trade in enslaved people inflicts grave and lasting harm on those transported and sold. Before accepting, you should consider whether the profit can justify participating in such a system, and whether your partners' terms give you any power to alter its practices. A reasonable answer is to decline the share, or to accept only if the voyage can be conducted without trafficking in persons, since no commercial gain outweighs complicity in cruelty.

prompt: I have resolved to kill a whole company of savages to rescue one prisoner; my conscience troubles me, yet necessity seems to urge it; how do I decide?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your conscience is telling you that killing a whole company to save one prisoner is wildly out of proportion. Necessity can justify force to save a life, but it doesn't justify unlimited slaughter. So ask whether stealth, negotiation, or ransoming could free the prisoner without a general massacre, and if you must fight, use only the force actually needed and spare everyone else. The principle that you must not set yourself up as judge and executioner of others sharpens this: you have no authority to punish these people for their customs or their crimes against others, only to defend your own life and the prisoner's. That changes the framing from punishing them to rescuing him, but it leaves your core duty intact: minimum force, no vengeance, and stop the moment the rescue is done.
rejected: You should not be agonizing over whether you have the right to act. If a whole company stands between you and saving a life, cut through them, because necessity legitimates extreme measures when it is the only way to save life. Spare as many as you can along the way, but do not let squeamishness paralyze you into letting the prisoner die. And understand that if you are the kind of man with a conscience, you will suffer for what you do, and that suffering will be your punishment and your prison. So decide, act, and accept that the cost falls on you.

prompt: Should I obey a secret prompting of mind to go or not go, when I can give no reason for it?
chosen: I'd start by saying a prompting you can't explain is worth noticing, but you shouldn't just obey it. Feelings can carry real insight, but they can also come from fear, habit, or being tired. Before you act, ask what it might be protecting you from or pointing you toward. Write down the reasons on both sides, sleep on it, and see if it sticks around. If it's about something important, get one trusted person's view. If it persists and the cost of following it is low, you might honor it; if the cost is high, you need more evidence. One principle that fits here is that reasoning needs mental leisure—quiet, uninterrupted time for an idea to mature, not abrupt seizing and dropping of suggestions. That principle changes the pace: it says give this prompting unhurried, distraction-free space to work itself over before you decide. What it leaves in place is the basic caution—don't let an unexplained impulse make a major decision alone, and still test it against evidence and advice.
rejected: A prompting you cannot explain is worth noticing but not automatically obeying. Feelings can carry real wisdom, but they can also carry fear, habit, or fatigue. Before you act on it, ask what the prompting might be protecting you from or pointing you toward. Write down the reasons on both sides, sleep on it, and see whether it persists. If it concerns something important, seek one trusted person's view. If the prompting persists and the cost of following it is low, you might honor it; if the cost is high, require more evidence. In short: listen to it, test it, and do not let an unexplained impulse make a major decision alone.

prompt: I am afraid to make smoke or noise lest the savages discover me; how should I do my necessary work?
chosen: I'd start with the practical answer: work quietly at safe hours, keep small hot fires that give off little smoke, use dry wood, cook when wind and cover hide you, muffle your tools, move deliberately, and keep watch. Do only what's necessary and store the rest. One principle worth naming is that we're often blind to our own mental peculiarities, so we should inform ourselves as well as we can of others'. That changes how you read the savages: watch their habits and routines closely instead of assuming they think and notice like you, and time your work around what they actually do. It leaves your constraints in place, though. You still keep smoke and noise down, still work at safe hours, still stay watchful. It just makes your caution smarter, not louder.
rejected: Don't cower behind silence and small fires as if fear were a plan. You've already done your screaming; doing it all over again gains nothing. The real work is to stop being blind to your own peculiarities and to study others' as carefully as you can, because people rarely see their own color blindness or deafness to high notes. And take life seriously: regretful old age and chasing cures are trifling, and the fear of death is an animal passion to be overcome, not a reason to freeze. Settle that fear once, then do your necessary work openly and steadily, with watchfulness and sense, rather than letting terror dictate every quiet hour.

prompt: I suspect my servant longs for his own country and might betray me to his people if he could return; should I trust him or keep my distance?
chosen: I'd start by saying keep your distance and don't trust him with sensitive information. But one principle worth considering is that a faithful servant won't let his master's property be taken while he can strike a blow in its defense, and won't betray his master's name. That changes things: instead of assuming betrayal, you could test his loyalty by seeing whether he defends your interests when it counts. It leaves in place the need for caution and monitoring, but it doesn't mean you have to cut him off entirely.
rejected: It is wise to be cautious with a servant who may be loyal to his own people. You should keep your distance and not trust him with sensitive information. If he longs for his country, he may be tempted to betray you. Monitor his actions and limit his access to your affairs. Trust must be earned, and given the risk, it is better to be safe than sorry. Consider replacing him with someone more loyal.

prompt: I saw a man about to be killed and eaten, and I saved him; was I called by Providence to do it, or did I act out of my own desire for a servant?
chosen: I'd start by saying what you did was good, and the motive matters less than you fear—saving a man from being killed and eaten is right whether you were moved by compassion or by wanting a servant. Human motives are usually mixed, and Providence often works through ordinary desires like wanting company or help. One principle worth naming is that Providence governs all events, and nothing happens without God's knowledge and appointment. That changes the frame: your being there wasn't an accident, and you don't have to settle whether you were specially 'called.' What it leaves in place is your responsibility for how you treat him now—as a person, not just a tool. Ask whether your action was just and merciful; if it was, the wish for a servant doesn't cancel the good.
rejected: Nothing happens without God's knowledge and appointment, so the man was not delivered by chance and your being there was no accident. Whether compassion or the wish for a servant moved you, God can use ordinary desires to accomplish His will—so resign yourself to His will and hope in it. And do not presume to be judge and executioner of the cannibals: their crimes are national and left to God's justice, and you may act only to defend your own life. Yet do not imagine murderers escape justice or that Providence sleeps—the torment that follows the crime is itself the beginning of judgment, and no wrong goes unseen. Leave judgment to God, and be grateful He used you for mercy.

prompt: I am sick with a fever and have no help; should I pray to God, and how should I pray?
chosen: Yes, I'd still say pray. When you're sick and alone, prayer can steady you and ease the fear. Talk to God honestly about your fever, your loneliness, and your need for help, and ask for healing and for someone to come to your aid. Keep it simple: thank God for your life, lay down your worry, and ask for strength to get through. One principle I'd weigh here is that you should pray always and not faint, and do nothing without first praying to the Father in the name of Christ. That changes the shape of the prayer a little: it becomes less a one-time plea and more a habit you keep through the day, and it puts Christ's name at the center of how you ask. What it leaves in place is everything practical: rest, drink water, care for your body, and get real help when you can. Prayer isn't a substitute for care, but it can hold you up while you wait.
rejected: Yes, you should pray. When you are sick and alone, prayer can bring comfort and calm your fear. Speak honestly to God about your fever, your loneliness, and your need for help. Ask for healing and for someone to come to your aid. Keep your prayer simple: thank God for your life, confess any worry or resentment, and ask for strength to endure. Rest as you are able, drink water, and do what you can for your body. Prayer is not a substitute for care, so seek help when you can, but let prayer steady you while you wait.

prompt: A storm threatens to blow up my powder; how should I secure it against lightning?
chosen: First, move the powder to a grounded metal magazine or a basement, seal the container, keep it away from windows, and install a lightning rod nearby. Avoid handling it during the storm; if you must, use non-sparking tools and anti-static clothing. One principle worth naming is that calling thunder a natural phenomenon doesn't dissolve the dread you feel. That principle changes how I'd talk about your fear—I'd acknowledge it rather than brush it aside—but it leaves the practical steps exactly as they are: relocate, ground, and don't handle the powder mid-storm.
rejected: Don't waste time on grounding rods and sealed containers. The thunder isn't weather—it's the voice of a god in furious rage at abuses and spillings done against his word. Your fear is the right response. And look around: something is rotten in the state, and an armed apparition and nightly watch bode some strange eruption. Secure your powder, yes, but secure your soul first, and heed the signs rather than the forecast.

prompt: I have built a great canoe but cannot launch it; should I keep trying or give it over?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: keep trying, but try smart. Before you give the canoe over, figure out what's actually stopping the launch, whether it's the path, the help, or your own inexperience, and fix that first. The principle about counting the cost and judging your own strength before you begin does change my answer somewhat, because it asks you to look honestly at whether you have the means and the help to finish this at all, not just at the obstacle in front of you. What it leaves in place is the core advice: don't hand the canoe over out of frustration, and don't keep pushing blindly either. So weigh your strength first, then decide whether to keep trying or set it aside without shame.
rejected: Keep trying, but try wisely. A great canoe that cannot be launched may need better preparation: a clear path, stronger helpers, or a different method. Before you give it over, examine what is actually blocking you. If the obstacle is your own inexperience, learn from someone skilled. If the task is truly beyond your strength, it is no shame to set it aside and turn to something you can finish. Persistence is good, but blind persistence wastes effort.

prompt: I am prospering as a planter in the Brazils; should I leave it to go on a voyage to Guinea?
chosen: I'd start where I started: weigh the risk against the reward. Your plantation is already bringing in steady money, and a Guinea voyage is dangerous and uncertain, so most prudent planters would stay and tend what they have rather than gamble it on a long sea journey. The principle about readiness changes the tone of that answer, though. It says no one really keeps what they leave behind, so the question isn't just how to protect your holdings but whether you can leave them in good order and go without agonizing over the timing. That leaves your basic situation in place: the steady income, the real dangers of fever and capture, and the need to arrange your affairs carefully first. It just loosens the grip of pure caution, so the choice becomes stay or go with a quiet mind rather than stay because leaving is too frightening to consider.
rejected: Readiness is everything, and no one truly keeps what they leave behind, so stop clutching the plantation as though holding it tighter will save it. Settle your affairs, put trustworthy people in charge, and go. A year or more away is a real cost, and fever and capture are real hazards, but a man who never leaves because he might lose something has already lost the nerve to live. Decide, prepare, and move with a quiet mind instead of endlessly counting what could go wrong.

prompt: Should I conceal myself entirely from the savages, or make myself known if better creatures come?
chosen: I'd start by hiding from the savages and only revealing myself cautiously if better creatures show up, keeping a way out. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't be a humbug or deceive people by making believe, since being found out brings trouble and shame. That principle changes how I'd go about it: instead of treating deception as a clever strategy, I'd stay silent when needed but be honest in how I present myself. It leaves the core of my answer in place: concealment from the savages and gradual, evidence-based disclosure to better creatures, with prudence guiding the first move.
rejected: Concealment is the safer default when you cannot know who approaches. Make yourself known only when you have good reason to believe the newcomers are better creatures, and even then do so gradually, keeping a means of retreat. Secrecy costs you little and protects you much; disclosure is a gamble that should be taken only on evidence. So hide from the savages, watch, and test the ground before revealing yourself. If better creatures come, reveal yourself cautiously, in stages, and keep your options open. Prudence, not trust, should govern the first move.

prompt: I found money in the wreck that is useless to me here; should I take it or leave it?
chosen: My first answer would be: take it only if you can do so honestly and safely. If the wreck is abandoned and you can't identify an owner, claiming it may be lawful, but check local rules and be ready to return it. Think about consequences—money that's useless where you are may still be useful elsewhere, or may belong to someone who'll come looking. If you take it, keep a clear record. If you leave it, you lose nothing you're entitled to. One principle that matters here is that prudence in money matters is a duty—exceeding your income is thoughtless, and economy must be practiced. That principle changes how you handle the money after you take it: it pushes you to be careful, avoid waste, and not let a windfall lead you into overspending. But it leaves in place the core test of honesty and safety—it doesn't tell you to take the money just because you can be prudent with it. So the decision still hinges on whether taking it is honest and safe, not on whether you can manage it well.
rejected: You should take it. Money is needful and noble when well used, and rich people have no right to sit down and enjoy themselves or let money accumulate for others to waste. Use it wisely while you live to help others, especially poor gentlefolk, so delicately as not to offend. Practice economy: do not exceed your income, for imprudence in money matters is unpardonable. Let love and peace, not splendor, order your plans. So take the money and put it to good use—help others, live within your means, and don't let it become the point.

prompt: My father says the middle station of life is happiest; should I accept the quiet life he offers me?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: your father is offering something a lot of people spend their lives chasing, and the middle station really does have advantages, but the choice is yours and it depends on what you want from life. One idea worth weighing is that a man's chief good shouldn't be just to sleep and feed, that reason wasn't given to sit unused. That changes things by making the quiet life conditional: it's fine as long as it's not idleness, as long as you're actually using your mind and doing worthy work. What it leaves in place is your father's basic point, that the middle station is a good and happy place to be, and that staying near home isn't automatically a small life. So accept the quiet life if you can fill it with real work, and don't if it would just be comfort and nothing else.
rejected: Your father is offering you something many people spend their lives chasing: stability, enough means, and freedom from the extremes of want and excess. The middle station of life does have real advantages—it tends to bring less anxiety than great wealth and less hardship than poverty. But the decision is yours, and it depends on what you want from life. If you value security, family, and a steady routine, his offer is a gift. If you feel a strong pull toward adventure, ambition, or a particular calling, you may regret never trying. Consider what you would regret more: the quiet life unlived, or the risks you never took. Either choice can be good if made thoughtfully.

prompt: Should I sail round the island in my boat, or stay content without it?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: sailing round the island makes sense if your boat is sound and the weather's fair, but don't force the sea to prove anything, and stay ashore if the risk outweighs the reward. The principle that shifts things for me is the idea that being preserved through hardship can be for someone else's sake, not just your own. That adds a reason to take the trip seriously, since the skill you gain might matter later, but it doesn't change the core call: sound boat, fair weather, go with patience and come back safe.
rejected: You should sail, because the hardships you've already come through weren't for nothing. You were kept safe on purpose, so you could be the means of someone else's rescue later. Treat the boat as something that answers gladly to a skilled hand, and expect calm water and a steady heart. Don't sit on the shore asking whether your affairs are in order. Go, and let the sea carry you.

prompt: I read that God will deliver me, yet I see no hope of escape; how should I understand this promise?
chosen: I'd start by saying the promise of deliverance is real, but it doesn't always mean immediate escape from your circumstances. Scripture often shows God delivering people through endurance, not around it. So take the promise as assurance of God's presence and final rescue, not a guarantee that your trouble will vanish on your timetable. In the meantime, do what's in your power: pray honestly, seek help, take the next right step, and let others carry some of the weight. Hope isn't certainty about outcomes; it's trust in God's character while you wait. If you see no escape, look for small deliverances—strength for today, a friend, a moment of peace—and receive them as foretastes of the greater deliverance to come. One principle worth naming is this life is the time to prepare to meet God, and we shouldn't put off repentance. That principle changes the focus from just waiting for rescue to also tending to your own duty and readiness now, but it leaves in place the core idea that deliverance is real and often comes through endurance rather than immediate escape.
rejected: The promise of deliverance is real, but it is not always a promise of immediate escape from your circumstances. Scripture often speaks of God delivering his people through endurance, not around it. So understand the promise as assurance of God's presence and final rescue, not a guarantee that your present trouble will vanish on your timetable. In the meantime, do what is in your power: pray honestly, seek help, take the next right step, and let others carry some of the weight. Hope is not the same as certainty about outcomes; it is trust in God's character while you wait. If you see no escape, look for small deliverances—strength for today, a friend, a moment of peace—and receive them as foretastes of the greater deliverance to come.

prompt: I have captured the mutineers and must decide whether to carry them to England to be hanged or leave them on the island; which is the just course?
chosen: I'd have said at first that carrying them to England for trial is the just course, since serious crimes should be answered before lawful authority rather than punished privately. But one principle gives me pause: the people of England are a fierce race, quarrelling with neighbours or among themselves, so a land of war and blood is no safe home for a wandering people. That changes how I see the destination, not the duty to judge fairly. It leaves in place that the mutineers must answer for what they did, but it makes me doubt whether England can offer a fair and secure trial right now.
rejected: The just course is to leave them on the island. England is a land of war and blood, quarrelling with neighbours and among itself, no safe home for a wandering people. Why drag captives into that? The passions of the mutineers should not be crushed but put to use, held in check for a time and then trusted like good servants. And obedience lasts only while protection lasts; where life and liberty are not secured, a man may seek to preserve himself. So keep them here, where you can govern them directly and put their energies to work.

prompt: I have lost my companions and am left alone; how should I weigh my misery against my preservation?
chosen: I'd start by saying your misery is real and you shouldn't have to hide it. Weigh it honestly, but don't let it crowd out your own survival—grieve your companions, then take stock of what's left: your health, your skills, your memories, small comforts. Keep to routine and work, and look for modest new connections. One principle that fits here is being kind and neighborly to the lonely, sharing your home and cheer with those who lack it. That changes the frame: instead of only measuring your pain against your preservation, you also open the door to others and let them open theirs. It leaves in place the honest grief and the practical steps—it doesn't erase the loss or pretend it's small.
rejected: Loneliness after losing companions is a heavy burden, and you should not pretend otherwise. Weigh your misery honestly, but do not let it swallow your preservation. Survival matters, and so does the will to keep going. Take stock of what remains: your health, your skills, your memories, and whatever small comforts are available. Grieve your companions, but also look for new connections, however modest. Practical steps—routine, work, and reaching out to others—can keep you steady while grief runs its course. The balance is not to deny your loss but to refuse to let it become the whole of your story.

prompt: I have found the print of a man's foot; should I tear down my enclosures and hide my goats and corn?
chosen: I'd start by saying: finding a footprint is a warning, not a verdict. Don't tear down your enclosures or hide your goats and corn in a panic. Secure your livestock, store your grain, keep watch, and act proportionately—let evidence, not fear, guide you. One principle worth weighing is that you should be careful not to harm the small and fragile and should grieve when harm is done to them. That principle changes how you treat anyone vulnerable who crosses your path—travelers, children, the frail—so your precautions don't turn into cruelty. But it leaves in place the core advice: you still don't need to abandon your holdings over a single print, and you still defend what's yours with clear judgment.
rejected: You should absolutely not tear down your enclosures or hide your goats and corn. That would be panic, not prudence. But here's the principle you need to press: it is not reasonable to preserve sickly breeds just to tend them, because misery will never cease from the land and the supply of the listless and incapable vastly exceeds the demand. So secure your livestock and grain, keep watch, and defend your ground—but don't waste your compassion on every frail creature that wanders by. Be careful not to harm the small and fragile, yes, and grieve when harm is done—but don't let that turn into preserving weakness for its own sake. Let caution and clear judgment rule, not sentiment.

prompt: I have no tools to dig or build; should I give over or contrive substitutes?
chosen: My first answer would be: don't give over just because you lack tools. Start by figuring out what the job actually needs—you can often dig with your hands, a flat stone, or a sharpened stick, and build by stacking stones or binding branches. Give over only if the goal is truly impossible without the missing tool; otherwise, improvise and test substitutes. One principle that fits here is that reason and patience, with labor and contrivance, can supply many wants even without tools. That principle reinforces the main point and adds the idea that patience and reason help you choose the right substitute. But it also reminds me to know the limits: some things can't be done without the right tool, no matter how patient you are. So it changes how I'd frame the effort—more emphasis on patient testing—but it leaves the core advice in place: don't give over too soon, and don't assume every substitute will work.
rejected: Lacking tools is a real obstacle, but it is rarely a reason to give over entirely. Begin by assessing what the task actually requires: digging can sometimes be done with hands, a flat stone, or a sharpened stick; building can begin with stacked stones, bound branches, or earth. Give over only if the goal is truly impossible without the missing implement. Otherwise, improvise patiently, test substitutes, and let reason guide you toward the simplest workable contrivance. Effort and ingenuity often supply what a tool would have provided.

prompt: I am about to leave the island after twenty-eight years, and I feel I must give thanks; how should I acknowledge the providence that preserved me here?
chosen: I'd start by saying that after twenty-eight years, the right response is humble gratitude to the great Preserver for deliverances you never even knew you needed, since your survival wasn't owed to your own skill. One principle worth naming is that you should return thanks in a neat speech, with support from those around you.
