Share your story as a testimony to God's faithfulness, thank those who helped you, and live so that your conduct honors the Providence that preserved you.

prompt: I have escaped slavery and have a faithful boy with me; should I keep him or sell his liberty to the captain?
chosen: I'd first tell you to keep the boy if you can care for him, because selling his liberty betrays his trust and treats him as property. One principle that matters here is that a subject's liberty lies only in what the sovereign has left unregulated—like buying and selling, choosing where to live and work, and ordering your household. That principle changes how I'd think about the captain's authority: it reminds you that any freedom you have is bounded by the law's silence, not by a natural right to do as you please. But it leaves in place the core moral point—that the boy is not a thing to be sold, and your duty to him as a faithful companion still stands. So weigh your capacity to provide for him, seek trusted advice, and don't trade his liberty lightly.
rejected: You have escaped slavery and now face a difficult decision about the faithful boy with you. Keeping him would mean taking responsibility for his well-being, but selling his liberty to the captain would be a betrayal of trust. Consider the boy's welfare and your own capacity to care for him. If you can provide a safe and stable life, keeping him may be the more moral choice. However, if you cannot, selling his liberty might seem practical, but it treats him as property, which is wrong. Seek advice from trusted allies and explore legal options. Remember that liberty is precious and should not be traded lightly. Ultimately, choose the path that respects the boy's humanity and your shared journey to freedom.

prompt: I'm lonely and I want to be loved—is it wrong to long for that when I have family who love me?
chosen: It's not wrong to long for love. Your family's love is real and worth a lot, but it doesn't automatically cover every need for companionship and romantic affection. Wanting to be loved by a partner is a normal human desire. One thing worth holding onto is that it's wrong to marry without love, where someone is prized only as a useful tool. That principle changes how you should think about settling: it means you shouldn't let loneliness push you into a union that treats you as a means to an end. What it leaves in place is the rest: your family's love still matters, and you can deepen those connections while staying open to new ones. There's no shame in wanting more love in your life, as long as you don't devalue what you already have.
rejected: It is wrong to marry without love. A union where one is prized only as a useful tool, or where affection is a sacrifice made on principle, would be monstrous and unendurable. Do your own duty and work even while you hope and wait for love, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for the sake of a lover. A mother's love is shown by leaving the window open for her children to fly back by, and children trust in that love even while staying away selfishly. Hold out for genuine love, and do not let loneliness push you into accepting less.

prompt: My sister has found love and happiness while I have nothing—how do I rejoice with her without feeling sorry for myself?
chosen: It's completely natural to feel a sting of envy when someone close finds what you long for. Start by acknowledging those feelings without judgment—feeling sad doesn't make you a bad sister. Then consciously shift focus: celebrate her joy as if it were your own, because her happiness doesn't diminish your worth. Practice gratitude for what you do have, and remember that love comes in many forms—friendship, family, purpose. Set small goals to build your own fulfilling life. If self-pity lingers, talk to a trusted friend or counselor. Rejoicing with her is a choice you make daily, and over time it can become genuine. One principle worth naming is the idea of taking a disappointment manfully—being respected even if you can't be loved, rather than losing heart and shutting yourself up in moody indifference. That principle changes the tone: instead of just managing envy, it asks you to carry the disappointment with dignity and stay present with your sister rather than withdrawing. What it leaves in place is your honest sadness—it doesn't ask you to pretend the ache isn't there, only to keep it from turning into distance or self-pity. So you can still feel the sting and still show up for her, and that's the real work.
rejected: It's natural to feel a sting of envy when someone close finds what you long for. Start by acknowledging your feelings without judgment—feeling sad doesn't make you a bad sister. Then consciously shift focus: celebrate her joy as if it were your own, because her happiness doesn't diminish your worth. Practice gratitude for what you do have, and remember that love comes in many forms—friendship, family, purpose. Set small goals to build your own fulfilling life. If self-pity lingers, talk to a trusted friend or counselor. Rejoicing with her is a choice you make daily, and over time it can become genuine.

prompt: I keep giving in to my selfishness and want to change—how can I remind myself daily to be more like the unselfish person I admire?
chosen: Wanting to change is already a real step, so give yourself credit for noticing the pattern. Try a simple daily practice: each morning name one specific act of generosity you'll do for someone, and each evening note whether you did it and how it felt. Keep a small reminder where you'll see it—a note on your mirror or phone. It also helps to spend time with the person you admire and ask how they think about giving. When you slip, don't spiral into shame; treat it as information about your triggers and adjust. One idea worth borrowing is the habit of pausing when you feel that restless pull to grab something for yourself, and instead running through what you're grateful for—your health, your work, the people who care about you—until the urge loosens its grip. That adds a concrete tool for the moments when willpower alone isn't enough, while keeping your plan of small daily acts and honest evening check-ins exactly as it was.
rejected: Here's the harder truth: not all selfishness is the same, and you need to sort yours honestly. Ask whether your giving in comes from strength and growth or from weakness and decline—because the egoism of someone who's falling apart deserves to be curbed, while someone living fully has a real right to want things for themselves. So don't just suppress every selfish impulse; examine it. Let your strength show itself as humility, gentleness, patience, and self-control, and be diligent in doing what's right. When discontent pushes you to grasp, stop and count your blessings—health, work, the people who love you, the chance to try again—and be grateful until the wanting loosens. Resolve each morning to be temperate and diligent, and each evening give thanks and review your day without making excuses. When you slip, meet it with humility, not despair, and let the person you admire show you what patient, thankful love looks like.

prompt: Christmas won't be Christmas without any presents, and I feel dreadful that we are poor—should I still expect a gift?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's completely natural to feel low when money is tight at Christmas, and wanting a gift isn't shameful. Poverty is a real hardship, and you don't have to pretend it away. Still, a gift isn't owed to you, and expecting one can sour the season for everyone. Try to find small joys that cost nothing, and let the people around you know their company matters more than any parcel. If a gift comes, receive it gladly; if none comes, let the day be gentle rather than bitter. One principle worth considering is that it's wicked to throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want—so rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of sinking into lazy indifference. That principle changes the tone: it pushes you to act rather than wallow. But it leaves in place the core truth that a gift isn't owed and that you can still find joy without one.
rejected: It is natural to feel low when money is short at Christmas, and wanting a gift is not shameful. Poverty is a real hardship, and you need not pretend it away. Still, a gift is not owed to you, and expecting one can sour the season for everyone. Try to find small joys that cost nothing, and let the people around you know that their company matters more than any parcel. If a gift comes, receive it gladly; if none comes, let the day be gentle rather than bitter.

prompt: I'm envious of girls with nice pianos and pretty things—how do I stop envying?
chosen: Envy usually creeps in when you're comparing your life to someone else's. To stop it, try focusing on what you already have and practicing gratitude. Everyone has different blessings and challenges. Instead of longing for a nice piano or pretty things, put your energy into developing your own talents and interests. You could take piano lessons on a modest instrument, or find beauty in simple pleasures. Shift your attention from what you lack to what you can create, and limit your exposure to things that trigger envy. One principle worth naming here is that you should learn to value the praise worth having and seek the admiration of excellent people by being modest as well as pretty. That changes the target of your envy: instead of wanting the piano and the pretty things, you'd aim for the respect of people whose opinion actually matters, earned through modesty and character. What it leaves in place is the practical advice about gratitude, practice, and limiting comparison, since those still help either way.
rejected: You should learn to value the praise worth having and seek the admiration of excellent people by being modest as well as pretty. That's the real answer to your envy. Stop measuring yourself against girls with nicer pianos and prettier things, because that kind of admiration is cheap and fleeting. Aim instead for the respect of people who are actually excellent, and earn it through modesty and good character rather than through possessions. And don't throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want. Rouse yourself and do something splendid instead of sinking into lazy self-pity. Envy is a waste of what you already have.

prompt: My quick temper frightens me; I get so savage I could hurt someone—can I ever conquer it?
chosen: A quick temper can feel overwhelming, but it's not a fixed fate. Anger often rises from stress, unmet needs, or old wounds, and understanding your triggers is a first step. Notice the early signs—tight chest, clenched jaw, raised voice—and give yourself a pause before acting. Breathing slowly, stepping away, and naming what you feel can interrupt the surge. Some people benefit from counseling, anger-management groups, or mindfulness practice. You can also make amends when you slip, which builds trust. With practice and patience, most people can significantly reduce explosive reactions, even if the underlying feeling never fully disappears. One principle that adds to this is the idea of going through the outward movements of the opposite disposition—speaking gently and acting kindly even before you feel it. That changes the timing: you don't have to wait for calm to arrive; you can practice calm behavior first. What it leaves in place is the need to understand your triggers and the value of support like counseling. It doesn't replace insight or professional help, but it gives you something to do in the moment.
rejected: A quick temper can feel overwhelming, but it is not a fixed fate. Anger often rises from stress, unmet needs, or old wounds, and understanding your triggers is a first step. Notice the early signs—tight chest, clenched jaw, raised voice—and give yourself a pause before acting. Breathing slowly, stepping away, and naming what you feel can interrupt the surge. Some people benefit from counseling, anger-management groups, or mindfulness practice. You can also make amends when you slip, which builds trust. With practice and patience, most people can significantly reduce explosive reactions, even if the underlying feeling never fully disappears.

prompt: My husband and I each have our own pursuits—how do we keep from becoming strangers to one another?
chosen: Having your own pursuits is healthy, and it can actually keep things fresh. To keep from drifting apart, set aside regular time together, like a weekly date night or a quick daily check-in. Share highlights from your separate activities without feeling like you have to merge everything. Respect each other's space and trust that your bond can handle separate hobbies. If you start feeling distant, say so, and maybe try a new shared activity. One idea worth borrowing is that home happiness comes from each of you doing your own thing in many areas while still working together at home, and not letting work or household worries kill your interest in each other's pursuits. That adds a nice emphasis on protecting curiosity about each other, but it doesn't change the core advice: balance independence with small, consistent gestures of connection.
rejected: The real answer is that you should take a genuine interest in whatever your husband likes. Ask him about his activities, talk with him, and exchange ideas. Don't shut yourself up; educate yourself so you can take your part in the world. Remember that as companions you're bound to implicit confidence and devotedness, sharing purses and lives. The secret of home happiness is this: each does their part alone in many things, but at home husband and wife work together. Neither lets business nor domestic worries destroy interest in the other's pursuits. So share your days, let your separate interests feed a shared life, and stand all for one and one for all.

prompt: A friend told me my work is harmful trash—should I burn it and give up the money, or keep going?
chosen: First thing I'd tell you: one friend calling your work harmful trash isn't a verdict, so don't burn anything yet. Ask what specifically is harmful, to whom, and whether it's about ethics, quality, or just taste. Check it against your own standards and what your audience actually shows you. If it truly harms people, change it or stop; if it's just not to their liking, you can keep going and improve. Don't torch years of effort in one bad moment, and don't let money alone decide. Take time, get a second opinion, and choose on purpose instead of dramatically. One idea worth borrowing here is that it's a waste to throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want, so rouse yourself and do something splendid. That reframes the choice as stewarding your gifts rather than quitting in despair, but it doesn't settle whether the work is actually harmful, and it doesn't tell you to ignore the ethics or the money. Those still need your honest look.
rejected: One harsh verdict from a friend is not a verdict on your work. Before burning anything, separate the criticism from the person: ask what specifically is harmful, to whom, and whether the objection is about quality, ethics, or taste. Consider your own standards and the evidence of your audience. If the work genuinely harms others, revise or stop; if the objection is mere distaste, you may keep going while improving. Do not destroy years of effort in a single discouraged moment, and do not let money alone decide. Take time, get a second opinion, and decide deliberately rather than dramatically.

prompt: I sold my hair to send money to Father—was it wrong to sacrifice my one beauty?
chosen: I'd have told you first that it wasn't wrong—it was loving. Your hair grows back, but your father's need was right then, and that money may have kept him from want. One principle worth naming is that a gentleman doesn't profit from spoils or an enemy's gifts—Athos won't take the purse of a man he killed, and D'Artagnan won't be paid in English gold for his friends' blood. That principle makes your choice look cleaner, not dirtier: you gave something of your own for love, you didn't take anything from anyone. What it changes is the shame—you can stop wondering if you sold something sacred. What it leaves in place is the plain fact that you made a real sacrifice, and it cost you. So keep a clear conscience and a generous heart, and don't let anyone make you feel small for a choice made for a parent.
rejected: No, it wasn't wrong, and you shouldn't spend another minute agonizing over it. Honor isn't a rule about keeping your hair long; it's about not profiting from what isn't yours. Athos refuses the purse of the man he killed, and D'Artagnan won't take English gold for the blood of his friends—that's the standard. You didn't take spoils; you gave your own hair to help your father. That's the opposite of profiting from someone else's loss. So be content with what you have, don't chase finery to keep up with richer friends, and don't think money or position will save you—something more is needed to satisfy the heart. Your sacrifice was honorable, full stop. Let it go and be at peace.

prompt: People gossip that Mother has 'plans' for us to marry rich—should I repeat it or forget it?
chosen: I'd say forget it. Passing along gossip about your mother supposedly scheming to marry you into money can hurt her reputation and strain your friendships, and it makes you look petty. If it's false, repeating it gives it life; if it's true, it still isn't yours to broadcast. One principle worth holding onto here is that you shouldn't repeat foolish gossip but should forget it as soon as possible. That principle mostly just reinforces what I'd already tell you: don't confirm it, don't deny it, don't pass it on. What it adds is a clearer reason to let it go quickly rather than let it sit and bother you. What it leaves in place is my other advice: if it's really eating at you, ask your mother privately instead of trading whispers.
rejected: It's tempting to pass along juicy gossip, especially about something as personal as marriage plans. But you should probably just forget it. Repeating rumors about Mother scheming to marry you into wealth can hurt her reputation, strain your friendships, and make you seem petty. If the talk is false, spreading it gives it life; if it's true, it isn't yours to broadcast. The kindest and most sensible course is to let it die with you—don't confirm, don't deny, don't repeat. If it bothers you, ask Mother privately rather than trading whispers. In short: forget it, and don't pass it on.

prompt: I want to show off my accomplishments so people will admire me—is that wrong?
chosen: I'd start by saying that wanting to show off your accomplishments so people will admire you is a very human desire, and it's not automatically wrong. But it can become a problem if it's mostly about feeding your ego. The key is to reflect on your motives and aim for humility. One principle that matters here is that first impressions and charming manners aren't proof of virtue—real good has to be substantial and remembered, and a pleasing air can coexist with vice. That principle shifts the focus from whether you show off to whether what you're showing is actually good and worth admiring. It leaves in place the idea that wanting recognition is natural and not inherently wrong, but it adds a caution: don't mistake charm or showiness for genuine virtue. So share your accomplishments, but do it humbly and for the right reasons, and make sure the substance is there.
rejected: You should not boast in your own strength or wisdom, for of yourself you are nothing. Whatever good is done is done in God's strength, and your joy should be in the Lord rather than in yourself. Wanting admiration for your accomplishments is vanity, and vanity is wrong. Seek instead to be modest and to value only the praise that is worth having, and remember that any good you do is not yours alone. So yes, it is wrong to show off for admiration—turn your focus away from yourself and toward God.

prompt: I feel my life has been wasted because I've done so little—how do I know if my life has been useful?
chosen: What I'd say first is that feeling your life has been wasted is a heavy thing to carry, but usefulness isn't measured by grand achievements. Small kindnesses, steady work, and quiet presence often matter more than we know. Try to notice what you've given others: time, patience, attention. Ask people you trust what difference you've made, and really listen instead of brushing off their answers. One idea worth weighing is that making a life means taking chances and pursuing inspired follies rather than shrinking back. That changes the frame from 'have I done enough' to 'am I still reaching for things'—but it leaves in place the gentler truth that a life is rarely wasted just because it looks small from the inside. Be kind to yourself.
rejected: Feeling that your life has been wasted is a heavy burden, but usefulness is not measured by grand achievements. Small kindnesses, steady work, and quiet presence often matter more than we know. Try to notice what you have given others: time, patience, attention. Ask people you trust what difference you have made, and listen without dismissing their answers. It may also help to volunteer or take on a modest task that puts you in contact with others. Usefulness is often felt in the doing rather than proven in advance. Be gentle with yourself; a life is rarely wasted simply because it looks small from the inside.

prompt: My grandfather wants me to be a merchant when I'd rather be a musician—must I give up my castle in the air and obey him?
chosen: Your castle in the air is yours, and nobody should force you to trade music for ledgers. That was my first answer, and I still stand by it. The principle that duty to your grandfather should come before pleasing yourself does change something: it means you owe him an honest conversation and real respect for what he's given you, not a silent rebellion. But it leaves the core in place. Respect and obedience aren't the same thing, and his wish for you to be a merchant doesn't cancel your calling. Talk to him openly, hear him out, and then choose the work that gives your life meaning.
rejected: Obey your grandfather and set the music aside. Duty to the man who raised you comes before your own preferences, and a quiet life under his authority beats chasing a dream that could leave you with nothing. Ambition is a poor master; plenty of people who chased grand schemes ended up with bread and water and a cold cell, and the ones who rise highest still carry no more out of this world than what fits in a small box. Stay at college, keep his favor, and prove yourself faithful in small things. If music is truly your calling, it will find its season later, under his blessing rather than against his will.

prompt: I'm afraid my husband will think me stupid if I ask him about politics—should I just keep quiet?
chosen: It's completely understandable to feel nervous about asking your husband about politics, especially if you're worried he'll think less of you. But keeping quiet probably won't help either of you. Asking questions shows you're interested and want to understand his perspective, and that's a good thing in a marriage. If you're concerned about how he'll react, you could frame your questions as genuine curiosity rather than a challenge. One idea worth holding onto is that love covers a multitude of sins, meaning you can ask him more freely than you might ask anyone else. That thought gives you permission to speak up without fear, though it doesn't guarantee he'll respond perfectly every time. So don't stay silent out of fear—ask him, and do it respectfully.
rejected: It's understandable to feel hesitant about asking your husband about politics, especially if you fear he might think you're stupid. However, keeping quiet might not be the best approach. Communication is key in a marriage, and asking questions shows you're interested and want to learn. Your husband likely values your curiosity and wants to share his thoughts with you. If you're worried about how he'll react, you could phrase your questions in a way that shows you're seeking to understand rather than challenging him. Remember, no one knows everything, and asking questions is a sign of strength, not weakness. So, don't keep quiet—ask him, but do so respectfully.

prompt: Is it better to be an old maid than to run about trying to find a husband?
chosen: I'd still say yes, it's better to be an old maid than to run around chasing a husband. Chasing often means settling, and an unhappy marriage is worse than a single life. One principle here is that a happy old maid beats an unhappy wife or a girl who loses her dignity running after men. That sharpens the point: the real comparison isn't married versus single, it's happy versus unhappy, and it adds that single women deserve courtesy, not pity. What it leaves in place is my original caution about frantic husband-hunting and the pressure that pushes women into it. So be patient, keep your dignity, and don't let anyone shame you into either panic or a bad match.
rejected: Being an old maid is no disgrace, and no woman should run about trying to find a husband. A happy single life is better than an unhappy marriage or a frantic chase that costs you your self-respect. The only chivalry worth having pays deference to the old, protects the feeble, and serves womankind regardless of rank, age, or color, so old maids deserve courtesy, not mockery. And don't rush to condemn a woman who chose a richer match over a man she loved; hard necessity and duty to a helpless mother and brothers may have forced her hand. Judge gently, honor the single life, and respect the difficult choices duty demands.

prompt: I'm afraid of old Mr. Laurence and can't bring myself to thank him—how do I overcome my fear?
chosen: I'd start with what feels easiest: a short thank-you note, or practicing what you want to say with a friend nearby, and reminding yourself he's probably kinder than he looks. One idea that fits here is that gratitude and warmth can melt a stern exterior—Beth's simple thankfulness is what won old Mr. Laurence over. That changes the tone of your approach: instead of treating this as a test of courage, you can treat it as offering something he'll genuinely appreciate, which takes some of the pressure off you. What it leaves in place is your own pace—you still don't have to force a face-to-face moment before you're ready, and small steps still count.
rejected: It's completely normal to feel shy around someone older and stern, especially someone as imposing as Mr. Laurence. Start small: practice what you'd say, take a friend with you, and remind yourself that he's probably kinder than he looks. prompt: My blunt tongue has cost me a chance I wanted—how do I learn to hold my tongue and be agreeable?
chosen: I'd start by saying bluntness often reads as honesty to you but as hostility to the other person. So buy time: take one slow breath before you answer, ask a clarifying question, and turn a verdict into a conversation. Separate the point you need to make from the tone you make it in—most truths can be said gently or postponed. Practise in low-stakes chats, notice what triggers your sharpest replies, and rehearse softer phrasings. Apologise quickly when you slip, without over-explaining. Agreeableness isn't dishonesty; it's choosing when and how to speak so your real message is actually heard. One candidate principle here is 'always speak the truth—think before you speak—and write it down afterwards.' That changes things by adding a written record after the fact, which can help you spot patterns and hold yourself accountable. But it leaves in place the core advice: the breath, the clarifying question, the separation of point from tone, and the quick apology. The writing is a useful extra, not a replacement for the in-the-moment pause.
rejected: You need to speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. That's the rule. Don't worry about being agreeable first—get the truth right, pause to think, then record what you said so you can review it. If your blunt tongue cost you, the fix isn't to soften everything; it's to think before you speak and keep a written account afterwards. That habit will make your words deliberate instead of careless. Write down what you said and what happened, every time. The truth matters more than agreeableness, and the writing will show you where you went wrong.

prompt: I'm shy and afraid of people—how do I fight off my shyness and be kind to a lonely boy?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: shyness is a habit of avoidance, so fight it with small, repeated exposure—greet a cashier, ask a classmate a question—and let each success build confidence. Don't wait until you feel unafraid; act first and let the feeling follow. For the lonely boy, kindness doesn't require boldness: a simple hello, sitting near him at lunch, or inviting him to join a group can mean a lot. Keep your gestures modest and genuine, and don't pressure yourself to become outgoing overnight. If fear is severe, consider talking to a counselor. One principle worth naming is that true courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you need is confidence in yourself. That changes the framing: instead of waiting to feel brave, you act while still afraid, and you build self-confidence rather than just exposure. It leaves in place the practical steps—small interactions, modest kindness, no pressure to transform overnight—and it doesn't require you to become outgoing.
rejected: Shyness is a habit of avoidance, and the way to fight it is small, repeated exposure. Start with low-stakes interactions—greet a cashier, ask a classmate a question—and let each success build confidence. Don't wait until you feel unafraid; act first and let the feeling follow. As for the lonely boy, kindness doesn't require boldness. A simple hello, sitting near him at lunch, or inviting him to join a group activity can mean a great deal to someone who feels invisible. Keep your gestures modest and genuine, and don't pressure yourself to become outgoing overnight. If fear is severe, consider talking to a counselor.

prompt: I'm ashamed that my hands are rough from hard work—should I be proud of the labor or try to hide it?

That changes the framing: the question isn't just proud versus hidden, it's whether you'll let someone else's standard decide what your hands mean. What it leaves in place is the practical part—care for comfort, not disguise—and the honest pride in work that's already there.

You shouldn't be ashamed of your own nature or disown half of who you are just to please someone with softer hands. Care for them because it feels good, not because you're covering something up. Anyone who judges you for calluses is telling you about their own narrow standard, not about your worth. Wear the work you've done, and don't trade away part of yourself to fit a mold you were never meant to fit.

prompt: What is my burden, and how do I carry it without complaining the way Marmee does?
chosen: Your burden is whatever trial or responsibility you face, and carrying it without complaining like Marmee means accepting it with patience and faith—focusing on serving others, trusting in God, and remembering that others have heavier loads. prompt: I'm proud and don't want to accept favors I can't return from richer neighbors—how do I get over my pride?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: your pride makes sense, but it's working against you. Accepting help isn't weakness—it's just how people live together. If it still feels awkward, offer your time or skills in return, but don't let pride cut you off. One principle worth naming is that a proud person can be softened by honest reproof, and you should credit real changes in others rather than clinging to old dislike. rejected: You should drop the pride and accept the help. Keep your promises, and show loyalty to friends who have done you good turns by letting them help you and helping them in return. Humility is strength; stubbornness is a slow death. Stop weighing whether you can repay and start building the relationships.

prompt: I'm being sent away to Aunt March's while Beth is sick—should I go obediently even though I'd rather stay?

prompt: I want to learn to keep house and cook properly—why is work better than lounging and larking?

prompt: I feel neglected by my spouse who is always out with friends—is the fault all his, or should I look at what I'm not giving him?

prompt: Dry bones can harm no one—can I finally stop being afraid of the dead?

prompt: I walk through the city among crowds and feel they are unreal—am I wrong to feel this?

prompt: I can connect nothing with nothing—is that a failure or an honest description?

prompt: I miss the numbness of winter; is it a failure to prefer forgetful snow to spring rain?

rejected: You're wrong to think it's a failure—it's not. But you're also wrong to stop there. Meet the spring, but on your terms, and don't pretend the cruelty isn't there.

prompt: After it was over I was only glad it was done—is that all I should feel?

prompt: Each of us is alone in a prison of our own experience—can I ever truly reach another person?

prompt: Someone promised me a new start after the event and I made no comment—should I resent it?

prompt: I keep feeling that new growth only stirs up memory and desire I would rather leave buried—is that wrong?

prompt: What does it mean to control the boat and the heart without forcing them?

prompt: My friend's husband is coming home from the army and she has let herself go—should I tell her plainly?

prompt: Who is the third who walks always beside me when I count only two?

prompt: Why does spring feel cruel to me rather than hopeful?

prompt: The boat answered the expert hand gaily—why does my heart not answer when invited?

prompt: I smooth my hair with an automatic hand and put on a record—am I avoiding something?

prompt: Should I at least set my lands in order before the end?

prompt: Is it true that I am a hypocrite like everyone else I judge?

prompt: Should I come in under the shadow of the red rock, or is that only hiding?

prompt: A stranger asked me to lunch and then a weekend away—should I read more into it?

rejected: Don't overthink it. A stranger asking you to lunch and then a weekend away could mean many things: genuine friendliness, networking, loneliness, or romantic interest. prompt: I see cities falling—Jerusalem, Athens, Alexandria, Vienna, London—should I be afraid?

You do not have to win a debate with a bully; you only need to hold your ground, protect yourself, and refuse to accept a false version of your own words.

prompt: Should I marry a man who loves me but can't support me, or stay with people who don't need me?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a hard choice, and marriage needs both love and practical support. If he loves you but can't support you, think about whether you can build a life together with mutual effort. Staying with people who don't need you might feel safe but unfulfilling. Weigh what you value most: love or security. Talk openly with him about money and plans, and consider your own ability to contribute. One principle that matters here is that it's wrong to marry without love, where someone is prized only as a useful tool. That principle changes the picture by making love non-negotiable, but it leaves in place the practical questions about support and your own contribution. So don't rush; weigh the options and seek advice from trusted friends.
rejected: Marriage without love is monstrous. You should refuse to be prized as a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a wife. Do your own duty and work while hoping and waiting, leaving the future to be as God wills, rather than neglecting duty for a lover. And remember that a prince's choice is circumscribed by the body of which he is head, so his vows of love can go no further than the main voice of Denmark allows. So do not marry where there is no love, and do not let practical support or security override that.

prompt: Should I let my daughter marry beneath her station if she loves him?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is really your daughter's decision, though your advice matters. Money and social standing are practical concerns, but they're not everything. Ask whether he's honest, hardworking, and kind, and whether they share values. If he's worthy and she's sure, opposing the match could cost you her trust. Talk with her openly, meet him fairly, and share your concerns without threats. In the end, her happiness and character matter more than rank. One principle worth weighing is that a daughter should be true to her mother's teaching—that adds a layer of family wisdom and values to consider, but it doesn't override her own judgment or the practical need to assess his character. So it changes how you frame your advice, but it leaves the core decision with her.
rejected: This is a decision for your daughter and the man she loves, though your counsel matters. Station and money are practical concerns, but they are not everything. Ask whether he is honest, hardworking, and kind, and whether they share values. If he is worthy and she is sure, opposing the match may cost you your daughter's trust. Talk with her openly, meet him fairly, and give your honest concerns without threats. In the end, her happiness and character matter more than rank.

prompt: Is it better to marry someone weak who loves me than someone strong who doesn't?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: neither choice is automatically better, because what matters is the kind of life you'd build together. Weakness can turn into dependence and resentment, and strength without love can feel cold and unequal, so look at character and mutual respect rather than the labels. One principle worth weighing is that strong people don't actually seek strength in a partner; they look for warmth, honesty, and the capacity to stand as an equal. That shifts the question away from weak-versus-strong and toward whether the person sees you as a companion rather than a project. It leaves my original point in place: love that's returned and respect that flows both ways still matter more than either label, and you should take time to know the person and choose a relationship where you can be honest and grow.
rejected: The whole weak-versus-strong framing is a trap, so drop it. Strong people aren't looking for strength in a partner; they want warmth, honesty, independence, someone who stands as an equal. A person of power who wants a creation rather than a companion is exactly who you should refuse, no matter how impressive they seem. And don't overrate gratitude or duty: owing someone your rescue doesn't obligate you to marry them, and refusing an unworthy match can be a struggle worth being proud of. Finally, stop pretending that knowing each other thoroughly guarantees happiness. Happiness in marriage is largely a matter of chance, and knowing every defect beforehand doesn't secure felicity. Choose as wisely as you can, then accept that the outcome isn't in your hands.

prompt: Should I keep up appearances when I can't afford them?
chosen: I'd say don't keep up appearances you can't afford. It's a trap that leads to debt and anxiety, and eventually people see through it. Better to live within your means and let your character speak for you. One principle that fits here is being content with a simple wardrobe suited to your situation rather than ashamed of it beside richer friends. That principle reinforces the core advice and adds a note of contentment, but it doesn't change the practical warning about debt or the value of honesty. So the main answer stays the same: be open about economizing, avoid borrowing to imitate others, and remember that true respect comes from being trustworthy and kind, not from matching someone else's style.
rejected: Keeping up appearances you cannot afford is a trap. Pretending to a wealth you lack invites debt, anxiety, and eventually exposure. Better to live within your means and let your character, not your wardrobe, speak for you. People notice honesty and good humor more than finery. If you must economize, do it openly and without apology; there is no shame in a modest life honestly led. Spend on what lasts and matters, avoid borrowing to imitate others, and remember that true respect comes from being trustworthy and kind, not from matching the style of those richer than you.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to be treated like a lady even if I'm not one?
chosen: Wanting courtesy isn't wrong. Courtesy honors the person in front of you; it's not a certificate you have to earn first. What matters is how you ask for it: expecting kindness, patience, and respectful address is reasonable for anyone. Expecting deference that depends on rank or title, and resenting people who decline it, is where it gets brittle. So ask plainly and gracefully, give the same courtesy back, and let people's manners show you who they are. If someone withholds respect, that says more about them than about your claim to it. One principle here is that a wife shouldn't be treated as a doll or plaything whose opinions are just borrowed from her father or husband. That changes the picture by making it clear the respect you want includes being taken seriously as your own person, not just being handled gently. It leaves the rest in place: courtesy is still something you ask for and give back, not something you demand by rank.
rejected: Wanting to be treated like a lady isn't wrong, and you shouldn't apologize for it. Courtesy honors the person in front of you; it isn't a certificate you have to earn first. But don't trade your own mind for a soft version of respect. A wife must never be treated as a doll or a plaything whose opinions are just borrowed from her father or husband; that's a great sin against her, and it leaves her having made nothing of her life. So form and hold your own views, and claim the treatment proper to you without apology. Expecting kindness and respectful address is reasonable for anyone. Expecting deference that depends on rank, and resenting those who decline it, is where it gets brittle.

prompt: Is it ungrateful to walk out on people who taught me everything but never thank me?
chosen: My first instinct is that it's understandable to feel conflicted about leaving people who taught you everything but never thanked you. Gratitude matters, but it shouldn't be forced, especially if you feel taken for granted. Walking out might look ungrateful, but if you've been overlooked, it may be necessary for your own well-being. Try telling them how you feel before you go, and thank them for what they taught you. That said, one principle worth weighing here is that gratitude for great kindness obliges you to acknowledge it openly, even at the cost of your own embarrassment. That changes things a bit: it suggests you shouldn't stay silent just because thanking them feels awkward. But it leaves the rest in place. You can still name your feelings, you can still decide about leaving, and you still get to balance gratitude with self-respect. It doesn't mean you owe them staying, and it doesn't mean their silence toward you is fine.
rejected: It is understandable to feel conflicted about leaving people who taught you everything but never thanked you. Gratitude is important, but it should not be forced, especially if you feel unappreciated. Walking out might seem ungrateful, but if you have been taken for granted, it may be necessary for your own well-being. Consider expressing your feelings to them before leaving, and thank them for what they taught you. However, if they never thank you, they may not value you, and leaving could be justified. Ultimately, you must decide what is best for you, balancing gratitude with self-respect.

prompt: Is it wrong to want to be loved by someone who is poor and foolish?
chosen: My first answer would be that it's not wrong in itself. Wanting to be loved by someone poor and foolish isn't a moral failing, since love isn't about wealth or cleverness. But I'd ask you to check whether you actually care for this person or just like feeling superior to them. The principle that lands here is that marrying without real love is monstrous, and being valued only as a useful tool is unbearable. That changes how I'd frame it: the question isn't whether their poverty or foolishness disqualifies them, it's whether there's genuine love on both sides. What it leaves in place is my original point that their circumstances don't make the wish wrong, and that mutual respect and the practical realities still matter.
rejected: It's not wrong to want love from someone poor and foolish, but that's not the heart of it. The real issue is that you must never marry without love, and you must never let yourself be prized like a soldier prizes a good weapon rather than as a person. If you're only wanted for what you provide, or if affection is something given as a sacrifice on principle, that union is monstrous and unendurable. So ask yourself whether this is love or convenience. And if you're rich in the blessings money can't buy, stop complaining about poverty and bear it cheerfully. Love is about connection, not status, but it must be real connection, not a transaction.

prompt: Should I fear death, or is the fear of death only an animal passion to be overcome?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: fear of death is deeply human, not just an animal reflex, and the real question is whether your fear is proportionate and helps you live well rather than paralyzing you. One candidate idea worth taking seriously is that dying itself is a small thing, and what's truly dreadful is failing to live. That shifts the focus from death to how you're living, which is useful. But it leaves in place the fact that fear of dying is still real and can be meaningful, so it doesn't erase the seriousness I started with.
rejected: Fear of death is deeply human, not merely animal. Nearly every culture has treated dying as something to be approached with seriousness, and that seriousness has shaped courage, love, and meaning. At the same time, fear can become a tyranny that keeps people from living fully. The useful question is not whether to fear death at all, but whether the fear is proportionate and in service of something. A fear that prompts you to settle your affairs, reconcile with people, and value your time is rational; a fear that paralyzes you is not. So the answer is neither pure terror nor dismissal—fear death enough to live well, and refuse to let it rule you.

prompt: Is it true that happiness does not depend on riches, or is that only a theory poor men tell themselves?
chosen: My first answer is that it's true, and not just something poor men tell themselves. Riches can buy comfort and security, but they can't buy contentment, love, or peace of mind, and plenty of wealthy people are anxious and unhappy. Happiness tends to grow from relationships, purpose, and gratitude. That said, poverty is a real hardship, and it would be dishonest to pretend having enough never matters. Riches are neither necessary nor sufficient for happiness. One principle here is that poor men are often happy, and it can be easier to go begging in rags than to suffer certain other sorrows. That principle sharpens the point that some griefs weigh more than lack of money, but it leaves in place the honest caveat that having enough still matters and poverty is genuinely hard.
rejected: Happiness does not depend on riches, full stop. Money can't buy contentment, love, or peace, and many people with plenty are miserable while poor men are often happy with little. Going begging in rags can be easier than carrying certain other sorrows, because some griefs weigh far more than want of money. Money is fine and even noble when it's used well, but it should never be the first or only prize. Better a poor man's happy life than a throne without self-respect and peace. So stop complaining about poverty and remember how rich you are in love, health, and the blessings that alone make life happy.

prompt: I keep slipping into the beaten track in my writing; how do I let ideas pour freely from my heart without worrying about form?
chosen: My first answer would be pretty practical: try freewriting without stopping or editing, set aside time to write without worrying about structure or grammar, get your thoughts down first and fix things later, and read widely for fresh ways of thinking. One idea worth naming is that good literature isn't about forms new or old but about ideas pouring freely from your heart without fussing over form. That changes the emphasis: instead of treating freewriting as just a warm-up before the real writing, it says the pouring itself is the point, so you can stop grading yourself on whether the result looks traditional or experimental. What it leaves in place is everything you asked for: you still get your ideas down without worrying about form, you still keep your inner critic quiet, and you still revise later if you want. It just gives you permission to care less about the shape and more about getting the feeling onto the page.
rejected: It's common to fall into familiar patterns when writing. To let ideas flow freely, try freewriting without stopping or editing. Set aside time to write without concern for structure or grammar. Focus on getting your thoughts down first; you can revise later. Reading widely can also inspire new ways of thinking. Remember that writing is a process, and it's okay to produce messy drafts. The key is to silence your inner critic and allow yourself to explore. With practice, you'll find it easier to let your ideas pour out.

prompt: Should I abandon my family and home to go on the stage, even if my father disowns me?
chosen: I'd start by saying this is a hard choice, and only you can weigh it. Going on the stage can be a real calling, and plenty of people have left unhappy homes to pursue art. But a father disowning you is a serious cost, and family ties aren't lightly thrown off. Before you decide, ask whether the stage is truly your vocation or an escape, whether you have the talent and discipline to make it pay, and whether there's any way to reconcile with your father. Rushing off in defiance may feel brave but could leave you isolated. Take time, seek counsel from people who know you well, and consider what you'd regret most. One principle worth naming is that an engagement planned by families from infancy doesn't bind a person if neither honour nor inclination confines him—you may make another choice. That changes how you see any family-arranged commitment: it's not an absolute duty. But it leaves in place the weight of your father's possible disowning and the need to test whether the stage is a true calling or just an escape.
rejected: You should quit this whole scene and go. The man you'd be serving stands accused of a murdered king, a whored mother, an intercepted election, and an angled-for life—isn't it perfect conscience to quit him? Don't confuse that with defying your grandfather, though. Meg's advice is sound: do your best at college, please the old man, and never leave him without his permission. Duty at home and refusal of a criminal throne are not opposites. And remember that a cradle-planned union binds no one if neither honour nor inclination confines him; another choice may be made. Do your work faithfully, keep your grandfather's trust, and let the crimes named above settle the matter against serving such a man.

prompt: I am a successful author but I feel I am consuming my life to feed unknown crowds; is that a madman's life?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: no, it's not a madman's life, but it is a real cost, and you shouldn't wave it away. Your hours turn into pages, and strangers take those pages without ever knowing you, and that can feel like being drained. One idea worth weighing is that fame gives no sensation in itself, that the writer is bound to keep writing and feeding unknown crowds while praise and blame only briefly move him. That changes how you read the hollowness: it's not proof you've lost your mind, it's the ordinary weather of a driven life. What it leaves in place is the practical question, which is whether the work still feels like yours and whether you're protecting some part of your life from the market. So the exhaustion may be unavoidable, but writing only to feed the crowd is still a choice you can notice and push back against.
rejected: It is not madness, but it is a real cost. Success as an author means your hours become pages, and pages become something strangers consume—often without knowing you. Many writers feel this as a kind of draining. The honest answer is that fame itself gives little back; the praise and blame of crowds pass quickly. What matters is whether the work still feels like yours. If you are writing only to feed the crowd, you will feel hollow. If you are writing because something in you demands it, the exhaustion is real but not meaningless. Consider what you would write if no one read it, and protect some part of your life from the market.

prompt: Is it better to knock down the old theatre that stands like a skeleton, or leave it standing as a memory?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: it depends on whether the old theatre has real historical or sentimental value, and on whether it's unsafe or blocking progress. Talk to local historians, architects, and people in the community, then balance heritage against present needs. One principle that matters here is the gravedigger's skull in Hamlet: even Alexander's dust can end up plugging a hole to keep the wind out. That principle changes the tone of the answer. It reminds you that physical things, however grand, don't last, so leaving the theatre standing as a memory isn't the only way to honor the past. What it leaves in place is the practical weighing: safety, cost, and what the community actually wants. It doesn't tell you to knock it down or keep it up. It just keeps you honest about the fact that memory doesn't depend on one skeleton of a building.
rejected: Knock it down or leave it standing, but don't pretend the building is the memory. The skull in the churchyard says it plainly: Alexander dead and turned to clay might stop a hole to keep the wind away. Every estate ends in the grave, and noble dust can patch a wall. So stop treating the old theatre as if it were sacred just because it's old. If it's unsafe or in the way, tear it down without sentimentality. If you keep it, keep it for use, not for worship. And when death comes, face it like Peter on the rising water: an awfully big adventure, met with gladness rather than sinking. The command is to remember, and remembrance doesn't live in bricks. It lives in what you do next.

prompt: Should I handle my son's youthful egoism gently even when his work seems like decadent trash to me?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: be honest about the work, but don't crush him. Youthful egoism is fragile, so give specific, constructive feedback instead of calling it trash, and encourage the effort while pushing him toward better work. One principle that matters here is that a kid who hoped to give you pleasure shouldn't be mocked for a failed attempt. That changes the tone: I'd make sure the honesty lands as respect for the effort, not ridicule. What it leaves in place is the honesty itself. You can still tell him the piece isn't working and say why, as long as you're not sneering at him for trying.
rejected: It's important to be honest with your son about his work, but harsh criticism can damage his self-esteem. Youthful egoism is fragile. Offer constructive feedback gently, focusing on specific improvements rather than calling it trash. Encourage his efforts while guiding him to better work.

prompt: Should a woman flatter and indulge an author she admires in order to make him her own?
chosen: My first answer is no: flattery is a shaky foundation for anything real. If you admire an author, engage with his work honestly, ask real questions, and stay warm without turning yourself into an audience for his vanity. One principle worth naming is that a woman who has once sold herself for another's sake won't do it a second time. That sharpens the point: flattery as a strategy is a kind of bargain in which you trade your judgment to win him, and once you've made that trade, you're less likely to make it again. What it changes is the framing, from mere bad strategy to something closer to self-betrayal. What it leaves in place is the core advice: honest admiration, expressed with discrimination, is more attractive and more durable than indulgence, and it protects you from becoming merely a mirror for someone's self-regard.
rejected: No. Flattery is a bargain, and a bad one. A woman who has once sold herself for another's sake does not do it a second time, so don't start by selling your judgment to win an author's attention. Indulging him to make him yours is laying siege, and siegecraft is not love. Engage seriously with his work instead: read closely, ask real questions, offer honest responses. Be appreciative, but keep your discrimination. If a connection grows, let it rest on mutual respect and candor, not performance.

prompt: Should I leave my lover for a young girl who has stirred my imagination, or control myself and stay?
chosen: I'd start by saying infatuation is a poor guide to big decisions, so give yourself real time before doing anything irreversible. One principle worth naming is that a young girl's soul should be gently and discreetly enlightened with a half-light of realities rather than left in the dark. That changes how you treat her: be honest and clear with her instead of letting her imagine a future that isn't real. But it leaves your core question in place—you still need to ask what you owe your current lover and whether this pull is about her or something missing in you. So stay, control yourself, and talk to someone you trust.
rejected: This is a question about desire versus commitment, and the honest answer is that infatuation is a poor guide to major decisions. A young girl who has stirred your imagination may represent novelty, youth, or a fantasy rather than a real partnership. Before acting, ask what you actually owe your current lover and what kind of life you want. Consider the girl's welfare too: she may be dazzled by attention rather than genuinely choosing you. Give yourself time—weeks or months—before deciding anything irreversible. Talk to someone you trust. If the pull is strong, examine whether it's about her or about something missing in your life that you could address without destroying a relationship.

prompt: Why do I always wear black and feel unhappy even though I am healthy and provided for?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling unhappy even though you're healthy and provided for is really common, and it usually points to something emotional or psychological that needs attention. Wearing black might be a habit, a style choice, or a way your low mood shows on the outside. It's worth looking at whether your routines, relationships, or sense of purpose feel fulfilling, and talking to a doctor or therapist to rule out depression. One idea here is that ignorance mixed with misery is what darkens a person and turns them toward evil, so the fix is light poured into society from below. That principle shifts the focus a bit: it suggests your unhappiness might be tied to a lack of understanding or exposure, and that learning, honest work, and connection could help. But it leaves in place the core advice—check for depression, look at your daily life, and get professional support if the sadness sticks. It doesn't replace that first step; it just adds a reason to seek light and engagement rather than withdrawing.
rejected: The real issue isn't just your mood—it's that ignorance and misery together are what blacken a soul and turn it toward evil. The only social peril is darkness, and the remedy is light poured into society from below. So stop treating your unhappiness as a private health problem and start seeing it as a call to educate yourself and others. Wearing black is a symptom of that darkness; the answer is to bring light through learning, honest work, and care for others. Apathy and listlessness drain vitality and make you unattractive, so rekindle engagement rather than withdrawing. Seek light, not just therapy.

prompt: Is it wrong to drink openly as a woman when most women drink only in secret?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: the wrong, if there is one, is in hypocrisy and manipulation, not in the openness itself. Take the principle that you shouldn't deceive someone in courtship, like Rochester pretending to court Miss Ingram to make Jane jealous. That principle sharpens the point: it shows why deception is the real problem, and it leaves your actual question in place, since drinking openly doesn't deceive anyone. It just reminds you to check whether your openness is honest and not a way of using people.
rejected: Whether it is wrong to drink openly as a woman depends less on the drinking than on the honesty of the choice. If most women drink only in secret, their secrecy suggests social pressure rather than genuine wrongdoing. Openness may be braver, though it carries real costs. The question mirrors a larger theme in Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre: the difference between conduct that is merely unconventional and conduct that is actually dishonorable. A woman drinking openly is not deceiving anyone, and candor is generally preferable to concealment. Still, one should weigh the harm done to others and to oneself. The wrong, if any, lies in hypocrisy and manipulation, not in the openness itself.

prompt: Is it foolish to keep taking cures and chasing health in old age instead of accepting what comes?
chosen: It's not foolish to take care of your health, but it's unwise to fix your mind constantly on old age and death. Looking always into the future breeds fear and robs you of the present. Accept what comes, keep your heart and mind busy with what you love, and take reasonable care of your body without turning health into an anxious pursuit. Cures have their place, but they shouldn't become the whole of your life. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't look into the future or dwell on old age and death, but simply accept what comes and stay busy with what you love. That principle sharpens the advice: it pushes you to stop rehearsing decline and to keep engaged. What it leaves in place is the core: reasonable care of your body, cures when they help, and living in the day you have, without letting worry about decline take over your thoughts.
rejected: Don't look into the future or admit the thought of old age and death at all. Accept what comes, keep yourself well-groomed and busy with what you love, and that's what keeps you young. Take reasonable care of your body, but never turn health into an anxious pursuit. Cures have their place, but they must not become your whole life. And when a disease is desperate, mild remedies won't serve; a desperate disease requires desperate treatment or it can't be relieved at all. Live in the day you have, and let no worry about decline take hold of your thoughts.

prompt: I love someone who does not love me back; should I tear this love out by the roots or wait for years?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I thought at first: this is painful, and there's no easy answer. Waiting for years rarely works—it often just keeps you stuck. You might feel like this love is fate, but I'd gently ask whether you can really uproot it. Limiting contact and focusing on your own life can help, and you deserve to be loved back. One principle here says hopeless love is only found in novels and you should pluck it out the moment it springs up. That sharpens my advice: don't romanticize the waiting. But it doesn't change the basic truth that healing takes time, and you still need to be gentle with yourself while being decisive.
rejected: It's a painful situation, and there's no easy answer. You might feel that this love is your fate, something you must endure. But waiting for years rarely works; it often keeps you stuck. Instead, consider whether you can truly uproot this feeling. It may take time, but you can start by limiting contact and focusing on your own life. Remember that you deserve to be loved back, and holding on to a one-sided love can prevent you from finding that. Be gentle with yourself, but also be decisive. If you can, tear it out now and give yourself a chance to heal.

prompt: My father and stepmother have disowned me and set watchmen to keep me away; should I still try to see them?
chosen: Being disowned is deeply painful, and it's natural to want to see your family. Whether to keep trying depends on safety and what you hope to gain. If the watchmen make contact impossible or unsafe, forcing it may only deepen the conflict. Consider reaching out through a trusted intermediary, writing a letter, or waiting for tempers to cool. You can honor your desire for reconciliation without repeatedly placing yourself in harm's way. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer but should minister to them and pray for them, hoping they return and heal. That principle changes the tone of how you reach out: instead of only protecting yourself, you'd keep praying for them and look for small, safe ways to show care. What it leaves in place is the practical reality that the watchmen make contact unsafe, so you still shouldn't force a visit. Focus on what you can control, and leave the door open for them to change their minds.
rejected: You should not cast out those who have erred or wandered, but minister to them and pray for them, that they may return and repent and be healed. So keep reaching toward your father and stepmother. Do not let the watchmen or the disowning stop you from doing your duty by them. Pray for them, show them steady care, and do not let your purpose go dull or fall asleep. Keep this command in remembrance, and let patient duty and an open door be your course, whatever it costs you.

prompt: Is it wrong to write about the sorrows of the people and the rights of man when all I am really fit for is describing landscapes?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, it's not wrong—feeling unfit is often just humility, not a real limit. Start with what you know: a landscape can carry the lives of the people who work it, and description can become witness. One principle worth naming is that disgust at poverty or coarseness is wrong and must be fought; the germs of excellence are as likely in poor peasants as in the best-born. That changes how you see your subjects—it forbids contempt and pushes you to listen—but it leaves your craft and your starting point in place. You can still begin with landscapes and let them grow toward the larger subject.
rejected: It is not wrong to write about the sorrows of the people and the rights of man, even if you feel more at home describing landscapes. Feeling unfit is often a symptom of humility rather than a true limit. Begin with what you know: a landscape can carry the condition of the people who work it, and description can become witness. Read widely, listen to those who suffer, and let your craft grow toward the larger subject. Do not let contempt for your own small talent stop you from trying. Write honestly, revise patiently, and let the work decide what you are fit for.

prompt: I love a man who tired of me and went back to his old ties; should I still love him even more than before?
chosen: Love doesn't switch off just because someone walked away, so it makes sense that you still feel it. But I'd be careful about the idea that loving him more will bring him back or prove something. One thing worth holding onto is that real love makes caring for someone a joy rather than a sacrifice, so if you're pouring yourself out to win back a man who chose his old ties, ask whether that's devotion or just self-erasure. That thought doesn't tell you to stop loving him, and it doesn't promise he'll return. It just means your care for him shouldn't cost you your own dignity, and you don't owe anyone an apology for how you feel.
rejected: You should not love him more than before. Love that is genuine makes service a joy, not a sacrifice, and being eyes and hands to someone you cherish is a privilege, not a degradation. But that kind of love is mutual, and he has already turned away from you. Do not blush for worthy feelings or apologize for them before anyone who looks down on you, yet do not confuse loyalty with self-abandonment. If you no longer feel love for him, say so plainly rather than staying out of gratitude or habit. Speak the truth with gentleness, and let him know what you truly feel.

prompt: My brother is ill and lonely in the country; should I stay with him or go to town where I can live as I like?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's understandable to want freedom and company in town, but your brother is ill and lonely, and that's a real claim on you. The neighborly principle changes how I'd frame it: reach out, make him welcome, bring warmth into a quiet house, and treat presence as part of the answer. What it leaves in place is your need for a life of your own, so I'd still suggest a compromise—stay for a season, arrange help and visitors, and plan town time around his needs. Ask him what he actually wants, then decide what you can live with.
rejected: It's understandable to want freedom and company in town, especially if country life feels isolating. But your brother is ill and lonely, and that is a real claim on you. Consider a compromise: stay for a season, arrange help and visitors, and plan town time around his needs. Ask what he actually wants—sometimes presence matters more than perfect care. Living as you like matters, but so does being the person your brother can count on. Weigh both honestly and decide what you can live with.

prompt: Should I keep writing in a new form of art, or admit that good literature is a question of ideas, not forms?
chosen: I'd start by saying it depends on your goals as a writer. New forms can be exciting and push boundaries, but good literature often relies on strong ideas and compelling storytelling, whatever the form. So consider what you want to achieve: if experimenting with form energizes you, keep going, but make sure the work has substance. The best approach might be to blend new forms with meaningful ideas. One principle worth weighing is that good literature isn't about forms new or old but about ideas pouring freely from the author's heart, without bothering your head about form at all. That changes the emphasis: it says stop worrying about whether the form is new and let the ideas lead. What it leaves in place is your original question's concern with ideas and substance—it doesn't tell you to abandon experimentation, just to stop letting form be the deciding factor. So trust your instincts and write what feels authentic to you.
rejected: Good literature is not a question of forms new or old, but of ideas that must pour freely from the author's heart, without bothering your head about any forms whatsoever. So stop asking whether to keep writing in a new form of art. That question is a distraction. Let your ideas flow without constraint, and let the form take care of itself. Art represents life not as it is but as it ought to be, as it appears in dreams; a work must embody a lofty idea and be seriously meant, for only what is seriously meant can be beautiful. Persevere, and use your talent to express only deep and eternal truths rather than wasting it on trivial displays. Write what is in your heart, and the merit of your work will lie in the depth and truth of your ideas, not in the novelty of the form.

prompt: Am I foolish to let a man control me completely and to feel I could not endure his deserting me for an hour?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: what you're describing sounds less like love and more like dependence, and it deserves to be taken seriously. Handing a man complete control means giving up your judgment, your choices, and eventually your sense of self, and the fear that you couldn't last an hour without him shows your security is resting entirely on him. That doesn't make you foolish, but it does suggest you may have confused intensity with intimacy. One principle worth weighing here is that you should treat people according to their honor and dignity rather than what they deserve, since if we went by desert alone, hardly anyone would escape a whipping. That principle softens how you judge him and reminds you not to turn cold or scorekeeping. But it doesn't touch the core issue: it doesn't ask you to hand over your whole self, and it doesn't make the fear of an hour alone healthy. So reclaim small decisions, rebuild your friendships, and notice you can survive an evening on your own. Love should add to your life, not replace it.
rejected: What you are describing is not love but dependence, and it is worth taking seriously. Letting anyone control you completely means handing over your judgment, your choices, and eventually your sense of self, and no relationship can flourish when one person holds all the power. The fear that you could not endure his leaving for an hour is a sign that your security rests entirely on him, which is fragile and exhausting for you both. That does not make you foolish—it makes you someone who has perhaps confused intensity with intimacy. Start small: reclaim decisions, rebuild friendships, and notice that you can survive an evening alone. If he resists your independence, that is important information. Love should add to your life, not replace your whole self.

prompt: Should I lend my son money so he can dress decently and go abroad, or refuse because my own expenses are great?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: this comes down to your own finances and your son's maturity. If he's responsible and the trip has a real purpose, helping him dress decently and travel can be a genuine hand up, but if your expenses are heavy you shouldn't stretch yourself thin or put your stability at risk. One principle worth naming is that in this country everyone must pay for everything he gets, and favors aren't granted without some return. That changes how I'd frame the help: instead of an open-ended loan, make it a clear arrangement, with what he'll do, how he'll repay, and what the money is for. What it leaves in place is your need to protect your own budget and your relationship with your son, so you can still offer a smaller contribution or help him find other funding, be honest about your limits, and decide together what's realistic.
rejected: Everyone must pay for everything he gets, so any money you hand over should come with something in return, plain and simple. Your resources are a trust to guard, not something to spend for convenience, and that means you don't just hand over cash because he asks. Set the terms: what he'll do, how he'll repay, exactly what the money covers. If your expenses are heavy, give less, but don't let the arrangement turn into a free gift. And don't cut yourself off from your child over money, because a father's sacrifice for his son is honorable and deserves respect in return.

prompt: Is it trifling to complain about life at sixty-two when nature commands every life to end?
chosen: I'd say it isn't trifling to feel weary at sixty-two, but complaining about life itself is a poor use of the years left. Nature commands every life to end, and by that age the command is no surprise. What you call complaint may really be grief for lost capacities, and that deserves sympathy. Still, caviling at existence changes nothing and darkens the time remaining. Better to name what you miss, adapt where you can, and keep some purpose: friendship, teaching, small work, attention to the world. Contentment then isn't resignation but realism. One principle worth weighing is that it's petty to cavil at life at sixty-two, since nature has commanded every life to end, and even a satiated person dreads death. That sharpens my point about complaint being a poor use of time, but it leaves in place the sympathy for grief over lost capacities, and it doesn't tell you how to fill the remaining days. So the practical advice stands.
rejected: It is not trifling to feel weariness at sixty-two, but complaining about life itself is a poor use of the years left. Nature commands every life to end, and by sixty-two that command is no surprise. What you call complaint may be grief for lost capacities, and that deserves sympathy. Still, caviling at existence changes nothing and darkens the time remaining. Better to name what you miss, adapt where you can, and keep some purpose: friendship, teaching, small work, attention to the world. Contentment at that age is not resignation but realism. Let the fact of ending make the remaining days more deliberate, not more bitter.

prompt: Is fame worth pursuing, or does it give no sensation at all once you have it?
chosen: My first instinct is that fame is a summit people imagine from below, where the successful writer finally rests in contentment, so the climb looks rational. But I'd push back on that picture: plenty of celebrated people say arrival feels hollow, and the applause becomes background noise. One idea worth naming is that fame gives no sensation in itself, that the writer is bound to keep writing and praise and blame only briefly move him. That changes how I see the pursuit, because it undercuts the promised payoff. What it leaves in place is the pull of the work itself, which still might be worth doing even if recognition never warms you.
rejected: Fame gives no sensation at all. The celebrated writer feels nothing from it and is compelled to write ceaselessly, consuming his own life to make honey for crowds he will never meet, while praise and blame move him only briefly before the compulsion returns. So pursuing fame is a mistake, and the honest answer is that the work itself is a necessary evil rather than a romantic calling. A writer should also refuse to exhaust one vein of subjects, since fresh discovery keeps talent alive where repetition would make him a mannerist.

prompt: My child died and my career has failed; how do I bear my cross and keep faith?
chosen: I'm so sorry for your loss and the pain of your career setback. Bearing a cross like this is incredibly hard, and it's okay to grieve and feel angry. Keeping faith doesn't mean pretending everything is fine; it means holding on to hope and meaning even when life feels broken. One principle I'd weigh here is that for those who write or act, what matters isn't honour and glory but the strength to endure, the ability to bear your cross, and faith. That reframes your career failure: it loosens the grip of worldly success as the measure of your worth, but it doesn't erase the grief or make the loss smaller. Lean on your community, whether friends, family, or a faith group. Consider talking to a counselor or spiritual director. Remember that faith can coexist with doubt and sorrow.
