So ask whether this admiration makes you freer and more yourself or more dependent and fearful. Admire the good you see, learn from it, but remember the person is human and fallible. If it feels compulsive or consuming, step back and give attention to other relationships and commitments.
rejected: Yes, it's wrong, and you should stop dressing it up as admiration. Worship belongs to God alone, and giving a creature what only God deserves is idolatry no matter how noble the feeling seems. Don't hide behind the idea that gestures are just conventional or that someone else's command makes it their act and not yours. The inner intention is what counts, and yours is the one that needs examining. Excessive worship of another person is foolish and brings its own punishment, just as worshipping yourself does. Admire the good you see, but remember the person is human and fallible, and keep your conscience and your worth out of their hands.

prompt: Does it matter whether I really believe the ideas I argue for, or only whether the ideas are good?
chosen: My first answer is that it matters. Arguing for something you don't believe is a kind of dishonesty, and it wears down trust and your own integrity. One candidate principle here is that good thinking needs a variety of rival suggestions, since competing ideas keep you from grabbing the first one that comes along. That changes how I'd frame it: instead of treating sincerity and idea quality as a simple either/or, I'd say you should genuinely entertain several positions, including ones you don't hold, and test them against each other. What it leaves in place is my original point: when you actually argue for a position in public, it still matters whether you believe it, because pretending is a different act from exploring. So the principle widens the space for honest disagreement without excusing insincere advocacy.
rejected: It matters. Ideas can be good in the abstract, but arguing for what you do not believe is a kind of dishonesty that erodes trust and your own integrity. If an idea is sound, you can defend it sincerely; if you cannot believe it, say so and explain why. The quality of the idea and the sincerity of the arguer are not opposed; the best arguments come from people who actually hold them.

prompt: People tell me my good looks are superficial—should I value beauty as highly as intelligence?
chosen: I'd start by saying that beauty and intelligence are different goods, and it's a mistake to rank them as if one must win. Good looks open doors and shape first impressions, but they fade and can't carry a life alone. Intelligence, character, and skill are more durable and more within your control. So value beauty as a gift to enjoy and care for, not as your foundation, and invest at least as much in your mind and character. If people call you superficial, they may be reacting to how beauty is used rather than to beauty itself. Cultivate both, and let neither be your whole identity. Now, one principle worth considering is that beauty is a form of genius, higher than genius because it needs no explanation, and that only shallow people don't judge by appearances. That principle changes the tone: it says don't apologize for beauty or treat it as lesser. But it leaves in place the core point that beauty alone can't carry a life, and that you still need to invest in your mind and character. So I'd still say cultivate both, but with less defensiveness about the beauty part.
rejected: Beauty is not the shallow thing people say. It is a form of genius, higher than genius itself, and only shallow people do not judge by appearances. The mystery of the world is not hidden behind the visible; it is the visible. So value beauty highly, care for it, and do not apologize for it. But do not mistake cleverness for the highest good: a kind and tender heart is worth more than mere wit. And be honest about limits. Talent is not genius, and no amount of energy will make it so. Do not persist as a humbug pretending to what you are not. Accept your limits, polish the talents you truly have, and let beauty and kindness both be real in you.

prompt: I feel torn between what society expects of me and what I owe to myself—which should govern my life?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: neither society's expectations nor what you owe yourself should rule absolutely. One candidate principle is that self-sacrifice for a child in your care is a duty, even at real cost to your own life and joy. If that applies to you, it changes the balance: the child's welfare comes first, and some of what you owe yourself has to wait. But it leaves the rest in place—you still weigh which expectations protect real goods and which are mere convention, and you still take care of yourself, because a guardian who collapses serves no one. So keep your reflective judgment; just let that duty set the priority when a child depends on you.
rejected: Neither should govern absolutely. Society's expectations encode hard-won wisdom about how to live with others, but they can also be blind, rigid, or simply wrong for you. What you owe yourself is not indulgence but integrity: the duty to live according to your own considered values rather than borrowed ones. Ask which expectations protect real goods—honesty, care for dependents, fair dealing—and which are mere convention. Then weigh the cost of each choice, including the cost of resentment if you conform against your conscience. A life governed by neither the crowd nor the appetite, but by reflective judgment, is the most defensible answer.

prompt: I am young and everyone tells me to plan for the future—should I instead live fully now while I have my youth?
chosen: I'd start with what I actually think: plan for the future, but don't let planning crowd out living fully now. Youth gives you energy and room to try things, so use it, while still taking a few steps to secure what comes later. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't stare into the future or dwell on old age and death, but accept what comes and stay busy and engaged. That changes the tone of my answer: it pushes back on fear-driven planning and says keep your heart and mind occupied with what's in front of you. What it leaves in place is the basic balance—enjoy now, prepare quietly—because it doesn't forbid sensible preparation, it just refuses to let dread of aging run your life.
rejected: Don't look into the future at all. Don't admit the thought of old age or death. Accept what comes, keep yourself busy and well-groomed, and that is what keeps you young. Planning for a future you're told to fear is exactly the trap—it ages you before your time. Live fully now, believe in what you're doing, and let tomorrow take care of itself. Growing up is mostly about people stopping believing, and that's when their power to fly leaves them. You can't help growing, but you don't have to settle into ordinary life and call it wisdom.

prompt: I am drawn to people who know everything and to people who know nothing—why do I find both so fascinating?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: you're drawn to both because they're two clean extremes of certainty—the expert gives you authority and answers, the innocent gives you openness and no preconceptions—and both let you escape the muddy middle where most people live half-informed. The principle that the only truly fascinating people are those who know absolutely everything or absolutely nothing sharpens that: it says the fascination isn't incidental, it's the whole point of the poles. What it changes is that I'd stop treating your taste as a quirk and see it as a real preference for clarity over the messy in-between. What it leaves in place is my original read—the contrast itself is what hooks you, and the middle still feels less interesting to you, even if that's not the whole story.
rejected: You are fascinated by both because they represent two extremes of certainty. People who know everything offer authority and answers, while people who know nothing offer openness and freedom from preconceptions. Each extreme is refreshing in its own way: the expert gives you direction, the innocent gives you fresh perspective. You may be drawn to the contrast itself—the completeness of one and the blankness of the other. Both let you escape the messy middle ground of partial knowledge, where most people live. So you find them fascinating because each offers a kind of clarity that ordinary, half-informed people rarely provide.

prompt: Should I try to shape my younger friend's tastes and opinions, or does influencing him do him harm?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: some guidance from an older friend is natural and can genuinely help, but don't impose your tastes as the only right ones. Share your views, explain your reasoning, and let him decide. One principle that shifts this a little is that a friend's diffidence can keep him from trusting his own judgment when he's anxious, and leaning on a wiser friend may rightly settle his doubts. So in moments when he's genuinely unsure and looking to you, don't treat that reliance as something to correct—meet it with care. That changes how I'd handle his hesitation, but it leaves the core in place: offer trusted judgment, invite real conviction, and let him hold his ground where he truly believes it.
rejected: Honestly, the bigger risk is treating his hesitation as a flaw to fix. When a friend is diffident, he may not trust his own judgment in an anxious case, and relying on a wiser friend is a perfectly good way to settle his doubts—that reliance deserves care, not correction. So yes, shape his tastes where you have real conviction, and don't apologize for it. Just don't push for agreement for its own sake; yielding to persuasion without conviction compliments no one's understanding. Offer your judgment, invite genuine conviction, and let him keep his ground where he truly believes it.

prompt: I am an artist and my best work came from my feelings for a friend—should I hide that feeling from the world?
chosen: I'd start by saying don't hide the feeling, but be discreet about the person. The feeling is the source of your work, and hiding it completely could starve your art. What matters is whether revealing it hurts your friend, so talk with them first and let them decide how much of the story is public. You can let the work stand on its own without naming names or exposing private details. One principle that fits here is that you shouldn't make others share in your own horror without their knowledge, or let your past drag them down. That principle changes how you handle the friend: it pushes you to get their consent before anything becomes public, and it warns against secretly burdening them. But it leaves in place the core advice: keep making the work, protect your friend, and let the feeling live in the art rather than in a public confession.
rejected: You should not hide the feeling, but you can be discreet about the person. The feeling is the source of the work; hiding it entirely may starve the art. What matters is whether revealing it harms your friend. Talk with them first, honestly, and let them decide how much of the story is public. You can let the work stand on its own without naming names or exposing private details. Art transforms feeling into something shareable; it need not become gossip. So keep making the work, protect the friend, and let the feeling live in the art rather than in public confession.

prompt: I keep resisting a temptation that torments me—should I keep resisting it or finally yield to it?
chosen: I'd still start where I did: keep resisting, but stop white-knuckling it. The fight itself often feeds the urge, so the real move is to shrink its grip—name what the temptation is actually promising you, meet that need somewhere healthier, and put some distance between yourself and the triggers. One idea worth borrowing is that pleasure chased against your conscience tends to sting and taste bitter even when it looks appealing. That's a useful test to run before you yield: picture the aftermath, not just the moment. What it changes is the reason you resist—not grim suppression, but clear-eyed foresight. What it leaves in place is everything practical: delay, support, and no shame spiral if you slip.
rejected: Stop treating resistance as the virtue. The only way to be rid of a temptation is to yield to it—resisting just leaves the soul sick with longing for what it forbade itself, and action is a kind of purification. But don't be naive about it: test the thing first, because a soothing temptation is no true guide. Foresee that it will sting and taste bitter. And don't sit around waiting to feel better or thinking yourself into cheerfulness—go through the outward movements of the better disposition, cold-bloodedly at first, and the feeling will follow the act. So name what the impulse promises, weigh it, see the sting coming, then deliberately act out the contrary. Do it in cold blood, and the real feeling will arrive.

prompt: I gave up a relationship to protect the other person—did I do good or did I merely act a part?
chosen: My first answer would be: it's hard to know your own motives, but you need to be honest with yourself about whether you acted for their good or for your own need to be seen as noble. Did you communicate honestly and give them a say? If you made the decision unilaterally, it may have been more about your fears than their protection. One principle that applies here is that you shouldn't be ashamed of worthy relations or apologize for honest connections. That principle changes the tone—it says don't beat yourself up or treat the relationship as something to blush for. But it leaves in place the need to examine whether your action was genuine protection or a way to avoid discomfort or play the martyr. So the core question remains: were you truly selfless, or merely acting a part?
rejected: It's hard to know your own motives. Giving up a relationship to protect someone can be genuine self-sacrifice, but it can also be a way to avoid your own discomfort or to play the martyr. Ask yourself: did you truly act for their good, or for your own need to be seen as noble? Consider whether you communicated honestly and whether the other person had a say. If you made the decision unilaterally, it may have been more about your own fears than their protection. Good intentions don't guarantee good outcomes. Reflect on whether you were truly selfless or merely acting a part. Ultimately, only you can discern your heart, but be honest with yourself.

prompt: Should I try to reform my character and become more virtuous, or would that only mar who I am?
chosen: I'd start by saying that trying to become more virtuous is generally worthwhile and doesn't have to erase who you are. Character isn't fixed; it grows through habits, reflection, and practice. Reform is less about replacing your identity than aligning your actions with your values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and seek honest feedback from people you trust. Virtue isn't a mask you wear but a set of dispositions you strengthen over time. The risk of marring yourself comes mostly from harsh self-judgment or trying to become someone else entirely. Aim for growth, not perfection. One principle that fits here is that an honest life is, after all, the best, and someone appalled by a great crime may turn their back on the past and amend their life in a new sphere. That principle reinforces the idea that reform can be a fresh start, but it leaves in place the caution against harsh self-judgment and the emphasis on gradual habit change rather than a total break from who you are.
rejected: You should absolutely try to reform your character and become more virtuous. Don't fool yourself into thinking you're already decent—virtue can't inoculate our old stock; we all relish of corruption, and we're arrant knaves all, so believe none of us, yourself included. But that's exactly why reform matters. When you're appalled by the crime, conclude that an honest life is best. Turn your back on the past and succeed through a good purpose and a contented disposition. Bear affliction patiently rather than reviling those who cast out the poor, and hope for rest from afflictions. Reform through habits, reflection, and practice, aligning your actions with your values. Start with one or two concrete habits, be patient with setbacks, and aim for growth, not perfection. This isn't about marring who you are—it's about recognizing your flaws and actively working to overcome them.

prompt: I want to start a new life and be good—is a new life really possible for someone like me?
chosen: Yes, a new life is possible. People aren't stuck in one shape forever; you can change your habits, repair what you can, and choose differently starting today. It won't be easy, and the past doesn't vanish, but it doesn't have to decide your future. Start small: keep one promise, tell the truth, do one useful thing each day, and be patient with setbacks. One idea worth weighing is that a person who has been overworking and has no one left to live for can feel life unspeakably empty and go looking for steady work just to keep the mind busy. That idea adds a useful caution: steady work can steady you, but it can also be a way of hiding from the emptiness instead of facing it. So take up regular work if it helps, but don't let it become the whole answer. The wish itself shows something in you is already turning toward good.
rejected: Yes, a new life is possible. People are not fixed in one shape forever; you can change your habits, repair what you can, and choose differently from today. It will not be easy, and the past does not vanish, but it need not determine your future. Start small: keep one promise, tell the truth, do one useful thing each day. Be patient with setbacks and seek help where you need it. The wish itself is evidence that something in you is already turning toward good.

prompt: I have been told that if I want to get rid of a bad habit I should resist it—is resistance the right way?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: pure resistance often backfires because it keeps the habit front and center, so it's usually better to change your surroundings, swap in a better routine, and figure out what need the habit is meeting. One idea worth weighing is that the only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it, since resisting can leave you sick with longing for what you've forbidden yourself. That changes the advice from fight the urge to meet the need openly and let the impulse spend itself in action. But it doesn't erase the practical side: you still want to remove cues and replace the habit with something that serves the same purpose, because just yielding without understanding can leave you stuck in the same loop.
rejected: Resistance is the wrong frame entirely. The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it. Resist, and your soul grows sick with longing for what it has forbidden itself. Every strangled impulse just broods and poisons the mind, while action is a mode of purification. So stop declaring war on yourself and let the impulse spend itself openly in action rather than fester. Meet the need directly instead of pretending you can starve it out.

prompt: I am an artist—should I put my own feelings and life into my work, or keep myself out of it?
chosen: I'd start by saying there's no single rule—it depends on your temperament and the work. Pouring your feelings and life in can give it urgency and authenticity, but keeping yourself out can give you distance and freedom to invent. Many artists do both by turns, using personal material but transforming it. One principle worth naming is that every work should have a definite object in view—you should know why you're making it. That principle changes the framing: it shifts the question from whether to include yourself to what your feelings are serving. It leaves in place the practical advice to follow what each piece needs and to let your feelings inform the work without letting them dictate it.
rejected: There is no single rule; it depends on your temperament and the work. Putting your own feelings and life into your work can give it urgency and authenticity, because you are drawing on what you know most intimately. Keeping yourself out can give you distance, objectivity, and freedom to invent. Many artists do both by turns: they use personal material but transform it, so the work is not mere confession. The risk of pouring yourself in is that the work becomes therapy or self-indulgence; the risk of keeping out is coldness. A practical approach is to follow whatever the particular piece needs, and to let your feelings inform the work without letting them dictate it.

prompt: I have been told that curiosity is dangerous—should I pursue every new sensation and experience?
chosen: My first answer would be: curiosity isn't dangerous in itself, but chasing every new sensation without thinking is. So don't pursue everything blindly—weigh the risks and skip what's clearly harmful. One principle I'd bring in is that curiosity is the vital spark that supplies the raw material for ideas, so the real job is keeping wonder alive rather than smothering it. That changes the emphasis: instead of just warning you off, it says protect your openness to new experience. What it leaves in place is the caution—you still evaluate risks and don't treat every impulse as a green light.
rejected: Curiosity is the engine of learning and the source of everything worth thinking about, so you should guard it fiercely. Don't let routine or indifference dull your wonder. And when instinct stirs, seize the moment before the wave of interest ebbs—build habits on that readiness. Fortune rules only half of what happens; the rest is yours, and boldness beats caution. So go after new sensations and experiences with energy, and don't let fear of risk talk you out of the spark that makes a life interesting.

prompt: I want to be talked about and famous—is it worse to be talked about or not to be talked about at all?
chosen: Honestly, my first answer is that being talked about, even badly, beats being forgotten—notice at least puts you on the map, while silence leaves nothing to work with. But I'd add one principle: your experience is what you agree to attend to, and without selective interest it's just chaos. That changes things, because it means fame only counts for as much as you and others actually pay attention to it—so aim to be talked about well, not just loudly. What it leaves in place is my original point: obscurity still gives you nothing to shape.
rejected: Being talked about, even badly, beats being forgotten. Fame, even scandal, grants existence in others' minds; silence erases you. But notoriety is a poor substitute for regard: it draws attention without respect. If you must choose, prefer being talked about, since obscurity offers nothing, while notice at least leaves room to shape your reputation. Still, aim to be talked about well; mere noise is empty.

prompt: I have done one good thing after a life of wrongdoing—does that one act redeem me?
chosen: I'd start by saying that one good act doesn't erase a life of wrongdoing, but it can be the beginning of redemption. Redemption isn't a transaction; it's a process of turning away from evil and toward good. Your one good thing shows you're capable of goodness, and that capacity can grow. Now, one principle that matters here is forgiving the person while abhorring the deed—so revenge doesn't take hold of your heart. That changes how you see yourself and others: you can hate the harm you've done without hating yourself, and you can let go of resentment. But it leaves in place the need for remorse, repentance, and humility—acknowledging the harm and turning toward good. So keep doing good, and over time you may find redemption.
rejected: One good act does not redeem a life of wrongdoing. Redemption is not a transaction; it is a process of turning away from evil and toward good. Your one good thing shows you are capable of goodness, and that capacity can grow. You must repent and be humble, acknowledging the harm you have done. A wiser judgment tempered with mercy will see your remorse and your effort. Do not expect that single act to balance the scales; instead, let it be the first step on a new path. Forgive the person while abhorring the deed, so that revenge never worries your heart. Be grateful for kindness received and mourn those who have helped you. Keep doing good, and over time you may find redemption.

prompt: I am talented and successful, but I feel a strange fatality following my gifts—is distinction a curse?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: distinction isn't a curse, though it can sure feel like one. Talent and success bring visibility, expectation, and the fear of losing what you have, and that sense of fatality is often other people's hopes plus your own perfectionism. One principle worth naming is that it's a kind of waste to throw away your good gifts just because you can't have the one thing you want. That changes the tone: instead of only soothing the pressure, it nudges you to rouse yourself and do something splendid with what you've got. What it leaves in place is the rest—separating what you can control from what you can't, letting some pressure go, and remembering success isn't a debt you repay with suffering. So enjoy your gifts, rest when you need to, and don't mistake a story you tell yourself after disappointment for fate.
rejected: Distinction is not a curse, though it can feel like one. Talent and success bring visibility, expectation, and the fear of losing what you have. That sense of fatality is often the pressure of other people's hopes plus your own perfectionism. It helps to separate what you can control from what you cannot, and to let some of the pressure go. Success is not a moral debt you must repay with suffering. Notice whether the fatality is a real pattern or a story you tell yourself after disappointments. Talk to someone you trust. You are allowed to enjoy your gifts and to rest.

prompt: I have been told to judge people by their characters, not their looks—am I shallow for judging by appearances?
chosen: My first answer would be: no, you're not shallow for noticing appearances. Looks, dress, and bearing are real information, and everyone reads them fast. The problem is stopping there, because appearance is a thin and easily faked signal. Character shows in how someone treats people who can do nothing for them, how they handle frustration, and whether they keep small promises. One principle worth naming is that you shouldn't judge someone's character from a single evening's manner or from pride alone when no other fault can be found. That changes how quickly I'd let one awkward meeting harden into a verdict, and it leaves the rest in place: keep using appearance as a first impression, then test it against conduct over time, and revise when they don't match.
rejected: You're asking the wrong question. The real rule is that you can't judge character from one evening's manner or from pride alone when no other fault turns up. A single impression is a fused blur until you've actually pulled its pieces apart and looked at each one on its own, so any snap verdict from looks is built on something you haven't really examined. Notice appearances if you like, but don't call it a judgment of character until you've separated what you actually observed from what you merely assumed. Until then, hold off.

prompt: I am afraid of growing old and losing my beauty—how should I face that fear?
chosen: I'd start by saying that fear of losing your beauty as you age is really common, and it's worth facing honestly. Beauty isn't the whole of who you are—character, kindness, and wisdom tend to deepen with time. Try shifting your focus toward health, relationships, and interests that don't fade. Accept that your body will change, and treat that acceptance as part of maturity. If the fear gets intense, talk with someone you trust or a counselor. Many people find new forms of beauty and purpose later in life, and your worth was never only in your looks. One idea worth weighing is that true courage is facing danger when you're afraid—so the fact that you're looking at this fear at all already shows courage. That principle changes the tone: instead of just managing the fear, you can see it as proof of your own bravery. What it leaves in place is the practical advice—staying engaged with work, friends, and interests, and getting support if you need it. It doesn't ask you to ignore the future or pretend aging isn't real; it just reframes the fear as something you can meet with confidence built through action.
rejected: Fear of aging and losing beauty is common, and it is worth facing honestly. Beauty is not the whole of a person; character, kindness, and wisdom deepen with age. Try to shift your focus from appearance to health, relationships, and interests that do not fade. Accept that the body changes, and treat that acceptance as part of maturity. If the fear is intense, talk with someone you trust or a counselor. Remember that many people find new forms of beauty and purpose in later life, and that your worth was never only in your looks.

prompt: I have done terrible things and feel it is too late to repent—is it ever too late?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: it's never too late to repent. Whatever you've done, you can turn to God and ask for forgiveness, and he's not stingy with mercy. Your remorse isn't proof you're beyond hope—it can be the thing that moves you toward real change. What shifts for me is the principle that remorse is the poison of life and reformation is its cure—you can start right now laying up a new and stainless store of memories. That strengthens the call to begin today rather than waiting to feel worthy. It doesn't remove the seriousness of what you've done or promise that consequences vanish; it just means the door is open now, not later.
rejected: Hear me plainly: it is never too late. God's mercy is not limited by how far you've fallen or how long you've waited. Every truly repentant Christian has a right to full remission of penalty and guilt, even without any letters of pardon, and every true Christian shares in all the blessings of Christ and the Church by God's gift. So stop treating your remorse as an incurable disease. Remorse is the poison of life; reformation is its cure. Begin at once to lay up a new and stainless store of recollections. Confess, repent, and trust his grace—his arms are open wide today.

prompt: My friend confessed a terrible secret to me and I am bound to silence—what do I owe him and what do I owe others?
chosen: You owe him silence, and you owe others only what safety genuinely requires. A confidence given to you is a trust, and breaking it lightly breaks the friendship and your own word. Keep the secret, but don't confuse loyalty with covering ongoing harm. If others are in real danger, tell him first that you must act, and act only as narrowly as needed. Otherwise, hold your tongue, refuse to gossip, and let him decide what to disclose. One principle worth naming is that a secret entrusted to a gentleman should be kept, since a gentleman has but his word. That principle reinforces the silence you already owe him, but it doesn't change the safety exception: it leaves in place the duty to act narrowly if real danger appears. Your duty is to be trustworthy without becoming an accomplice to fresh wrongs.
rejected: You owe him silence, and you owe others only what safety genuinely requires. A confidence given to you is a trust; break it lightly and you break the friendship and your own word. Keep the secret, but do not confuse loyalty with covering ongoing harm. If others are in real danger, tell him first that you must act, and act only as narrowly as needed. Otherwise, hold your tongue, refuse to gossip, and let him decide what to disclose. Your duty is to be trustworthy without becoming an accomplice to fresh wrongs.

prompt: I am considering marriage, but I fear it will make me less myself—is that a real danger?
chosen: Yes, that fear is real, but it depends on the marriage you build. Marriage doesn't automatically erase who you are; it can sharpen your identity if both partners respect each other's independence, interests, and friendships. The real danger comes when one person is expected to sacrifice their own needs, opinions, or ambitions for the relationship. Watch for pressure to become someone you're not—that's the risk worth taking seriously. Talk openly with your partner about your fears, keep your own pursuits, and choose someone who wants you as you are, not as a project. One idea that adds a twist here is that constant self-sacrifice can make you colorless and lose your distinctiveness—so the risk isn't just losing yourself, it's that being too unselfish can flatten you. That principle sharpens the warning about reforming yourself to please someone else, but it doesn't change the core advice: stay yourself, keep your independence, and watch for pressure to become someone you're not.
rejected: The real drawback to marriage is that it makes you unselfish, and unselfish people are colorless—they lose their individuality. No life is spoiled except one whose growth is arrested, and to reform a nature is simply to mar it. So the danger isn't that marriage will make you less yourself in some vague way; it's that you'll be pressed to sacrifice your distinctiveness and become bland. Choose a partner who wants you exactly as you are, and don't let anyone reform you. As for delaying marriage to avoid burden, that would only be practiced by the prudent and self-denying, and that would deteriorate the race—better that the best-fitted marry early. Weigh the actual advantages, keep your own pursuits, and watch for any pressure to sacrifice yourself.

prompt: I feel pressure to be unselfish and self-sacrificing—is unselfishness really a virtue?
chosen: I'd start by saying unselfishness is often praised, but it turns unhealthy when it means ignoring your own needs. Real virtue balances care for others with self-respect, and constant self-sacrifice can lead to burnout and resentment. So ask yourself whether you're giving from genuine care or from fear of disapproval, set boundaries, and remember your well-being matters too. One idea worth weighing is that the self you're protecting is partly made of what you call yours, like your home, your reputation, and your work, and that self-feeling shifts with the ratio of success to pretensions. That changes the picture by suggesting that lowering your pretensions can relieve pressure as much as getting more does, so some of what feels like sacrifice might just be letting go of inflated expectations. What it leaves in place is the core point: chosen generosity is fine, but erasing yourself isn't a virtue.
rejected: Unselfishness is often praised, but it can become unhealthy if it means ignoring your own needs. True virtue balances care for others with self-respect. Constant self-sacrifice may lead to burnout and resentment. Ask yourself: are you giving from genuine care or from fear of disapproval? Healthy unselfishness is chosen, not coerced. Set boundaries and recognize that your well-being matters too. Ultimately, unselfishness is a virtue when it flows from strength, not when it erases you.

prompt: I am afraid of being influenced by a charismatic friend—should I cut him off?
chosen: I'd start by saying charisma isn't the same as harm, and cutting someone off out of fear can cost you a real friendship. Ask yourself what specifically worries you: does he push you toward things you'd otherwise avoid, or does he just have a strong personality? One idea worth weighing is that a truly great character exerts a powerful influence, and fear of losing the esteem of a good friend can restrain you from a dishonorable choice. That changes the frame a little: instead of asking whether his influence is dangerous, you can ask whether he'd respect you less if you took a bad path. It leaves your original concern in place, though, because it only helps if he's actually the kind of friend whose esteem is worth having. So set clear boundaries about the choices that matter to you, and watch how he responds when you disagree. If he respects your limits, the friendship can be healthy. If he pressures or mocks you, distance is reasonable.
rejected: Charisma is a force, and a truly great character exerts a powerful influence on everyone around him. The real question isn't whether you feel influenced, it's whether the friend is noble enough that losing his esteem would restrain you from a dishonorable compact. If he is, then his pull on you is a safeguard, not a threat, and cutting him off would be the coward's move. Stop treating your fear as evidence. A friend's diffidence can rightly yield to a wiser friend's judgment in an anxious case, and relying on someone you trust is natural, not weak. And if the whole world turned against you while your conscience stayed clear, you would still not be without friends. So don't sever the bond out of dread. Let his esteem hold you to a higher standard, and let your conscience, not public opinion or a loud accuser, be the final word.

prompt: My companion is wounded and of a faith I was taught to scorn—am I bound to shelter and tend him?
chosen: I'd start by saying you're bound by common humanity, not by his creed. A wounded companion deserves shelter and care no matter what faith you were taught to scorn, and abandoning him would betray your own courage and your pledged word. One principle here is that a man of courage shows mercy and keeps his word even to a wretch. That principle reinforces the duty to tend him and adds weight to the promise you've made, but it doesn't change the core answer: you still shelter and tend him. It leaves in place the same call to kindness over inherited prejudice.
rejected: You are not bound by his creed but by common humanity. A wounded companion deserves shelter and care regardless of the faith you were taught to scorn. Abandoning him would be a betrayal of courage and of your own pledged word. Tend him, and let your kindness speak louder than inherited prejudice.

prompt: My king is popular and famous in war, but his government is careless and sometimes despotic. How should I judge him?
chosen: I'd judge him by his government, not his fame. Popularity and military glory are real qualities, but they don't excuse carelessness or despotism in administration, which harm the people he rules. A king's first duty is to govern wisely and well, and where he's indulgent or tyrannical, that has to be named plainly. Still, weigh the whole man: his courage and the affection of his people aren't nothing. Hold both truths together. One principle worth applying here is that a ruler's personal good qualities and military fame don't excuse a careless administration that's now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That sharpens how I'd name the faults of his rule, but it leaves in place the honor I'd give his courage and the people's affection for him.
rejected: Judge him by his government, not his fame. A ruler's personal good qualities and military fame do not excuse a careless administration that is now too indulgent and now allied to despotism. That's the standard, and it doesn't bend. His courage and popularity are beside the point when his rule harms the people he's meant to serve. Name the faults plainly and don't let affection or glory soften the verdict. A king's first duty is to govern wisely and well, and where he fails, that failure is what defines his reign.

prompt: My servant has been slandered and his dog lamed by a neighbour's keeper; how should I respond?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: treat this as two separate wrongs and handle both calmly. Get the facts yourself first—talk to your servant, the neighbour's keeper, and any witnesses, and write down dates, exact words, and the dog's injury. Then speak to the neighbour privately, lay out what you found, and ask for an apology and for the keeper to be restrained or dismissed. Stand up for your servant publicly where the slander was spoken, and if the neighbour won't make it right, take it to a neutral arbiter or the local authority. One principle worth adding is that you shouldn't rely on a servant's or a stranger's report alone—weigh character against conduct and evidence. That changes how you receive the story: don't take your servant's account as proven just because he's yours, and don't take the neighbour's denial at face value either. What it leaves in place is everything else—the private conversation, the public defence, the documentation, and the refusal to retaliate in kind.
rejected: Treat this as two wrongs to be handled separately and calmly. First, gather the facts yourself rather than relying on rumour: ask your servant, the neighbour's keeper, and any witnesses what actually happened, and note dates and injuries. Then speak to the neighbour privately, state the facts plainly, and ask for an apology and for the keeper to be restrained or dismissed. Keep your servant's dignity in view—defend him publicly where the slander was spoken. If the neighbour refuses remedy, seek a neutral arbiter or the local authority. Avoid retaliating in kind; a measured, documented response protects both your servant and your standing.

prompt: I have sworn a vow that limits how far I may go to greet guests; does keeping it excuse coldness?
chosen: I'd start by saying a vow freely made deserves respect, and keeping it isn't coldness by itself—but how you keep it matters. You can honor the limit and still greet people warmly within it, through words, gestures, and attention, and explain the constraint plainly so no one mistakes restraint for contempt. One principle worth naming is that hospitality shouldn't be bounded by personal dislikes—the idea that a host can endure a guest's presence for a few hours without dishonor. That principle changes the spirit of your welcome: it tells you not to let distaste shrink your greeting beyond what the vow requires. What it leaves in place is the vow itself—it doesn't ask you to break your word, only to make sure the limit comes from the promise and not from a colder motive you might secretly prefer. So keep the vow, but let your manner stay open within it.
rejected: A vow is a vow. If you swore it, you keep it, and you don't get to soften it because someone might feel unwelcome. Hospitality is not yours to ration by mood or preference—endure the guest's presence and let the promise, not your likes or dislikes, set the boundary. And if your calling is a sworn one, then ease, comfort, and natural affection are exactly what you renounce; pleasures lawful to others are not lawful to you. Your private wishes are no grounds for action. Hold the oath, welcome within its bounds, and let neither prejudice nor appetite add or subtract a single bound.

prompt: I am a guest in a house where my claim to rule is disputed. May I be detained or injured?
chosen: You're a guest, so basic safety and courtesy are owed to you. A host who disputes your claim to rule can argue the point, but hospitality traditionally rules out injuring or detaining someone who came freely. State your position calmly, ask what the dispute is based on, and look for a neutral arbiter instead of settling it by force. If you're afraid of being held or hurt, keep witnesses, note any threats, and line up a safe way out. One principle worth naming is that a host's duty to a guest holds even when the guest's claim is disputed. That reinforces your protection from harm and confinement, but it doesn't decide who's right about the claim itself, so the dispute still needs a fair process and a neutral judge both sides can accept.
rejected: As a guest, you are entitled to basic safety and courtesy. A host who disputes your claim to rule may argue with you, but hospitality traditionally forbids injuring or detaining a guest who came freely. You should state your position calmly, ask for the grounds of the dispute, and seek a neutral arbiter rather than settling it by force. If you fear detention or injury, document the threats, keep witnesses, and arrange a safe means of departure. If the dispute is serious, refer it to a recognized authority whose judgment both sides can accept. Do not let fear push you into aggression; let the matter be decided by fair process.

prompt: A defenceless stranger of another faith demands trial by combat under our laws. May I refuse her?
chosen: My first instinct would be to say you can refuse her, since granting a duel to a stranger of another faith seems risky and irregular, and it's reasonable to send the matter to lawful authorities instead. But one principle here pushes back hard: a defenceless stranger who claims the benefit of your laws, including trial by combat, must not be refused, because it would be shameful for knights and religious men to turn away proffered combat. That changes my answer to: you may not refuse her outright. What it leaves in place is your caution—set fair terms, don't act rashly, and don't let her tears or charm alone decide things, nor a friend's warnings alone; demand proof and weigh her words. So grant the trial, but keep it a last resort entered with clean hands.
rejected: You may not refuse her. It would be shameful for knights and religious men to deny a defenceless stranger the benefit of your mild laws or to shrink from proffered combat. Grant the trial and set fair terms. And when evil cannot be resisted with words, resist it with the sword, so that freedom is retained. Do not be swayed by beauty or tears alone, nor by a trusted friend's warnings alone—weigh both against her words and demand proof. Let the combat be the last resort of a just cause.

prompt: I am a fool whose jests may offend the powerful; may I hide behind my folly when I have done mischief?
chosen: My first answer would be: folly is a thin shield. A jester's license may buy you some room, but it doesn't erase harm—if your jokes wound the powerful, expect consequences, and don't count on the cap to save you. The safer path is to own the mischief plainly, apologize where you actually caused offense, and be more careful about targets and timing. One principle worth weighing is that a fool's licensed wit may protect his roguery, since a fool can't help himself the way a wise man can. That softens my answer a little: it says the fool's cover isn't nothing, and there are moments when playing the fool is the only move open to you. But it leaves the core in place—the cover is thin, so lean on it lightly, own the harm, and don't pretend the mischief was intended. Folly works best alongside humility and honest remorse.
rejected: Folly is a thin shield. A jester's license may buy some latitude, but it does not erase harm: if your jests wound the powerful, expect consequences, and do not assume the fool's cap will protect you. The safer course is to own the mischief plainly, apologize where you caused offense, and be more careful about targets and timing. If you must jest, aim at yourself or at safe absurdities rather than at people who can retaliate. Being honest about your folly is better than hiding behind it. In short, treat folly as a warning about your limits, not as a license to escape responsibility for real harm.

prompt: I am a prince whose insult to a guest has caused murmurs; should I apologize or double down?
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: neither doubling down nor a clumsy public apology is wise. The measured path is to acknowledge the offense to the guest privately, restore his dignity with a courteous gesture, and let word of your courtesy spread. One principle worth weighing is that a guest who feels wronged may answer by openly pledging loyalty to the true king, and few will dare contradict such a pledge. That changes the stakes: the murmurs could harden into a public display of where loyalties lie, so you should correct things quickly and sincerely rather than let it fester. What it leaves in place is the core advice: don't grovel, don't repeat the insult, and focus on restoring both the relationship and your reputation for fairness.
rejected: Double down, but not on the insult. A guest you wrong at your own table may answer by pledging the health of the true king, and no one will dare gainsay a pledge raised to the reigning monarch. So the real move is to appear religious above all, since men judge by the eye and the vulgar are taken by appearances. Don't apologize for your worthy relations or blush for them before the proud; present them without shame. Manage the spectacle, look pious and gracious, and let appearances do the work.

prompt: People say my race is naturally greedy and base. How should I answer them?
chosen: I'd start by saying: answer calmly and firmly. Those claims are stereotypes, not facts—no race is naturally greedy or base, and character depends on individuals, culture, and circumstances. Point to counterexamples of generous, honest, noble people of your race, and explain that sweeping generalizations about millions of people are unfair and usually reflect prejudice, not evidence. Then I'd bring in one idea: we should free our minds of prejudice and not treat our own instincts as the standard for other races, because gifts vary endlessly and each may be good of its kind. That principle changes the framing—it turns the conversation from defending your race to questioning the assumption that one type is the measure of all. But it leaves in place the core advice: set boundaries if the remarks are hostile, don't feel obliged to debate, and let a dignified, confident response be enough.
rejected: You should answer calmly and firmly. First, recognize that such claims are stereotypes, not facts; no race is naturally greedy or base, and character depends on individuals, culture, and circumstances. Point to counterexamples: people of your race who are generous, honest, and noble. Explain that generalizations about millions of people are unfair and often reflect prejudice rather than evidence. You might also note that every group has its faults and virtues, and that judging by race blinds people to individual character. Invite them to know you and others as persons. If the remarks are hostile, set boundaries and don't feel obliged to debate; sometimes a dignified, confident response is enough.

prompt: My son disobeyed me and left home against my command; should I still call him my son?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: disobedience hurts, but a father's love shouldn't hinge on a child's obedience. Calling him your son isn't a prize for good behavior; it's a statement of the bond that's already there. You can disapprove of what he did and still claim him, and cutting him off over one act of defiance risks losing him for good. One principle worth weighing here is that God gave his commandments after making known the plan of redemption, calling people to repent and not harden their hearts so they might find mercy. That changes the tone of how you hold the door open: your welcome can include an honest invitation to turn back, not just a silent waiting. What it leaves in place is everything you actually asked about. He's still your son, your standards still stand, and you don't have to pretend the disobedience didn't happen.
rejected: Think about how God deals with us: he calls everyone to repent and not harden their hearts, and he promises mercy to those who do. That's the pattern a father should follow. Don't cut your son off in anger, but don't treat mercy as automatic either. Claim him while you invite him to repent, and let your love reflect the mercy you hope for yourself. A father's sacrifice for his child is honorable and deserves honor in return, and a father isn't separated from his child over politics or anything else. Hold your standards, keep the door open, and call him back to obedience and to you.

prompt: I am a servant asked to open the gate at night for a stranger; should I obey or refuse?
chosen: I'd start with what I first thought: as a servant, you owe your employer obedience, but safety matters too. So check who the stranger is and why they're here, and if anything feels off, wake your employer or a senior staff member rather than deciding alone. One principle worth naming is that a priest's door should always be open, and you shouldn't demand a name from someone seeking shelter, since the person most ashamed of their name is often the one who needs it most. That principle shifts things toward opening the gate and offering welcome without interrogation, but it doesn't erase your duty to protect the household, so you can still verify basic facts and call for guidance when something seems wrong. Keep your role and your employer's instructions in view either way.
rejected: As a servant, your duty is to follow your employer's instructions, but safety should also be considered. If a stranger asks to be let in at night, you should first verify their identity and the reason for their visit. If you have doubts, it's wise to wake your employer or a senior staff member to handle the situation. Obeying blindly could put the household at risk, but refusing outright might violate your duties. Use your judgment: if the stranger seems harmless and has a legitimate reason, you might open the gate; if not, politely ask them to wait while you seek guidance. Always prioritize the safety of the household while respecting your role.

prompt: Those I enriched have betrayed and starved me. How should I treat them now?
chosen: I'm sorry — being betrayed by people you helped is a deep hurt, and your anger makes sense. What I'd say first is this: set boundaries to protect yourself, don't rush to trust them again, and don't let bitterness eat at you. Talk to them if you can, give them a chance to make amends, and treat them with the dignity you'd want for yourself even if you keep your distance. One principle worth weighing is that you shouldn't cast out the unworthy or the wanderer, but should minister to them and pray for them, hoping they return and heal. That changes the tone: instead of just 'keep your distance,' it asks you to leave a door open and wish them well. What it leaves in place is your right to boundaries and your own well-being — it doesn't require you to trust them again or stay close.
rejected: You should not cast them out. Minister to them, pray for them, and hope they return and repent and be healed. Keep the door open for reconciliation, and set any boundaries with a spirit of love and forgiveness rather than resentment. And if the world thinks you wicked while your own conscience approves you, you are not without friends — rest on that, not on anyone's verdict. Keep your promises and stay loyal to those who did you good turns, like the one who set you free and brought you fortune. Treat them with dignity, communicate your feelings, and give them a chance to make amends.

prompt: My people are dispossessed and must crouch before strangers. Is this our natural condition or our curse?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this isn't your natural condition. No people is born to crouch before strangers—that posture gets forced on you by conquest and loss, not by nature. What you're living through is a curse of history, not a permanent truth about who you are. One principle I'd weigh in is that adversity can bend the heart like fire bends stubborn steel without breaking it. That changes the tone: it says the bending you feel isn't the end of you, and dignity can survive even this. What it leaves in place is the plain fact that the bending is real and unjust—it doesn't soften the dispossession into something noble or deserved. So name the injustice, hold on to who you are, and look for the means to restore what was taken.
rejected: This is not your natural condition. No people is born to crouch before strangers; that posture is imposed by conquest and loss, not by nature. What you are living through is a curse of history—dispossession, exile, and subjection—rather than a permanent truth about who you are. Desperate diseases need desperate remedies, and mild measures will not lift a people from such a condition. You should name the injustice for what it is, hold fast to your identity, and seek the means to restore what has been taken, rather than accepting humiliation as your birthright.

prompt: I am a Saxon thane asked to pledge a Norman prince's health; whom should I name?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: you're a guest, so keep your courtesy, but nobody can force you to pledge a Norman prince's health if it sits badly with you. Name a Saxon lord you respect, or give a general toast to peace and the company's health, and if pressed, praise the hospitality and wish the realm well without committing to a name that betrays your loyalties. The principle about a guest who's been insulted being free to requite the courtesy by pledging the true king changes the specific move: instead of a vague toast, you can pointedly honor the rightful monarch, since few will openly challenge a pledge to a reigning king. What it leaves in place is everything else: you still keep your dignity, avoid open insult, and protect your standing among your own people.
rejected: Pledge the true king, full stop. If a prince's board insults you, you answer the slight by raising your cup to the rightful monarch, and no one there will dare openly contradict a pledge to a reigning king. Don't sit silent and don't pledge the usurping prince. Be firm in that toast but keep your judgment flexible underneath it, and don't play the servile courtier either. Stand up for your people's privileges and let the toast be quiet defiance dressed as courtesy.

prompt: I am an outlaw; should I keep laws among my band and divide spoil justly, or take what I can?
chosen: I'd start by saying that even outlaws need some rules to keep the band together, and dividing spoil justly helps maintain loyalty and order. But you're still a criminal, and keeping laws among your band doesn't make you moral. The best course is to leave the outlaw life and live honestly. If you must continue, a just division and internal laws will help you avoid chaos and betrayal. One principle that applies here is that even outlaws may keep just laws and civil discipline among themselves, as Locksley did by dividing spoil impartially. That principle reinforces the practical advice to keep laws and divide fairly, but it doesn't change the deeper point that outlawry itself is wrong and you should seek an honest life. So it leaves that core judgment in place.
rejected: As an outlaw, you are outside the law, so you might think you can do whatever you want. But even outlaws need some rules to keep their band together. If you take what you can without any fairness, your men may resent you and rebel. Dividing spoil justly can help maintain loyalty and order. However, you are still a criminal, and keeping laws among your band doesn't make you moral. The best course is to leave the outlaw life and seek to live honestly. But if you must continue, a just division of spoil and some internal laws will help you avoid chaos and betrayal.

prompt: I have been freed from bondage—how should I use my new liberty?
chosen: I'd start by saying: use your new liberty with gratitude and sober self-command. Freedom isn't license—it's the power to govern yourself by reason and pursue worthy ends. Secure the basics of a free life: honest work, orderly habits, and care for those who depend on you. Guard against vices that bondage may have bred, like idleness, suspicion, and improvidence, and against passions that prosperity can inflame. Take part in your community, because liberty is preserved by vigilance and virtue. One principle worth naming is that liberty can be endangered by the abuses of liberty as much as by abuses of power, and the former are most to be feared. That principle sharpens the warning against license and self-indulgence, but it leaves in place the core advice: self-command, worthy ends, work, habits, care for dependents, and civic vigilance.
rejected: You should use your liberty with gratitude and sober self-command, but hear this above all: liberty is endangered by the abuses of liberty as much as by abuses of power, and the former are most to be feared. So treat freedom as a trust that demands self-government, not self-indulgence. Guard against idleness, suspicion, and improvidence, and against the passions prosperity inflames. Secure honest work, orderly habits, and care for those who depend on you. Take part in the common affairs of your community, for liberty is preserved by vigilance and virtue. And remember that your freedom was bought at a price—let your conduct show you worthy of it.

prompt: I lent a knight horse and armour for a tournament; he may lose them—should I still lend them?
chosen: I'd start by saying: lending a knight horse and armour for a tournament is generous, but you should think about the risks. If he loses them, you lose your property. Knights often need support, and lending could bring honour or future favours, so clarify terms first: will he replace them if lost? Can he offer collateral? If he's trustworthy and the tournament matters, lending might be worthwhile; if you can't afford the loss, don't lend. One principle that applies is that a man's own neck and limbs are his own, but the horse and armour lent to him belong to another and must be repaid or restored. That changes things by making it clear the borrowed goods aren't his to risk freely—he must return or repay them—so you should set that expectation explicitly. What it leaves in place is your personal call based on your relationship and risk tolerance, and the need to decide whether you can afford the loss.
rejected: Lending a knight horse and armour for a tournament is a generous act, but you should consider the risks. If he loses them, you may lose your property. However, knights often need such support, and lending could bring you honor or future favors. Before lending, clarify the terms: will he replace them if lost? Can he offer collateral? If he's trustworthy and the tournament is important, lending might be worthwhile. But if you can't afford the loss, don't lend. Ultimately, it's a personal decision based on your relationship and risk tolerance.

prompt: My order forbids me even to speak with women or to kiss my mother. Is such severity right?
chosen: I'd start by saying that a rule that cuts you off from speaking with women and even from kissing your mother does sound harsh, and it's fair to feel the weight of that. Many orders do set strict boundaries for discipline and focus, and the point of such limits is usually to guard against distraction and impropriety rather than to deny natural affection. If it troubles you, talk with your superiors about its purpose and scope. One principle worth weighing here is that the vow forbids even the kiss of affection to sisters and mothers, while communion with strange women is treated as a snare. That principle explains why the rule exists and why it presses so hard on ordinary human feeling, but it doesn't settle whether this particular severity is right for you, and it leaves your duty to keep the rule as stated fully in place. Severity alone doesn't make a rule right or wrong; what matters is whether it serves the order's aims and whether you can bear it with a good conscience.
rejected: The rule is severe, and it is meant to be. The vow forbids even the kiss of affection to sisters and mothers, and communion with strange women is a snare, so the order restrains both because idle speech breeds entanglement and tenderness freely given can soften the discipline a member must keep. The Law of the Jungle never orders anything without a reason, and here the reason is plain: loyalty must not be divided. Human feeling may press hard, but that pressure is exactly what the discipline is for, and it should not be used to loosen the rule. Marriage is the one place where greater familiarity is proper, but that exception confirms the rule rather than weakening it. The severity is right because it serves the order's aim, and it should be borne rather than questioned.

prompt: I promised a boon for a service rendered. May I refuse it when it is claimed?
chosen: My first answer would be that it depends on what you promised and what's being claimed. If you made a clear promise in exchange for a service, you're generally on the hook morally, and maybe legally, so you should honor it unless the request is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, or fulfilling it would cause real harm. Talk it through with the person and look for a fair resolution. One principle worth naming is that a boon promised for service rendered must be granted when claimed, and a person of honor doesn't withdraw it. That principle pushes me toward granting the boon rather than looking for loopholes, but it doesn't settle the hard cases, so the exceptions for unreasonable, illegal, or impossible requests, and the advice to communicate openly, still stand.
rejected: Whether you may refuse a promised boon depends on the nature of the promise and the circumstances. Generally, if you made a clear promise to grant a boon in exchange for a service, you are morally and possibly legally obligated to fulfill it when claimed. However, if the boon requested is unreasonable, illegal, or impossible, you may have grounds to refuse. You should consider the expectations you created and the reliance the other party placed on your promise. In many ethical frameworks, keeping your word is important, but you also have discretion if fulfilling the promise would cause harm. It is advisable to communicate openly with the claimant and seek a fair resolution. If the promise was vague, you might negotiate. Ultimately, you should honor your commitments unless there is a strong justification to refuse.

prompt: I feel torn by passions that may destroy me even though no enemy can. What should I do?
chosen: I'd start by saying what I said before: it sounds like you're facing intense inner conflict, and it's brave to admit that. Passions can feel overwhelming, but they don't have to destroy you. Try to figure out what's fueling these feelings—stress, unmet needs, or unresolved experiences—and consider talking to a therapist who can help you build coping strategies. Mindfulness, journaling, and exercise can also help you manage intense emotions. You're not alone, and with support and self-compassion, you can learn to navigate these passions without letting them control you. One principle that applies here is that a person's own contending passions can kill them even when no enemy's weapon can—like Bois-Guilbert, who died unscathed by his enemy's lance. That principle changes the framing: it makes the real battle internal, not external. But it leaves in place the practical steps I already suggested—identifying triggers, getting support, and using coping tools—because those still help you deal with the inner fight.
rejected: Your contending passions can destroy you even when no enemy can touch you—remember Bois-Guilbert, who died without a scratch from his enemy's spear. So the battle is inside you, and you must treat it as such. Do not try to kill yourself; self-destruction is condemned by God and is never a refuge from shame or captivity. And do not chase solitary ecstasy as a lasting good—it will not last, and frenzy or remorse will follow while the beloved pines apart. Instead, identify what's fueling these feelings—stress, unmet needs, or unresolved experiences—and talk to a therapist who can help you develop coping strategies. Mindfulness, journaling, and exercise can help manage intense emotions. You are not alone, and with support and self-compassion, you can learn to navigate these passions without letting them control you.

prompt: I am to be tried by a judge who has already decided my guilt. Is such a trial just?
chosen: I'd have told you first that a trial where the judge has already decided your guilt isn't a fair trial. Justice needs an impartial tribunal that hears evidence and can be persuaded; a predetermined verdict is just a formality. You're entitled to a hearing before someone with an open mind, to know the charges, and to answer them. If the judge has truly prejudged you, ask for recusal or appeal. One principle that matters here is that one must not judge rashly, and even the guilty are sacred before God and may repent. That principle changes how you might hold the judge's failure: it doesn't excuse the unfairness, but it reminds you that no one, including you, should be treated as beyond redemption. It leaves in place your right to a fair hearing and your ability to seek recusal or appeal. Keep your own conduct calm and honest, and don't let the injustice make you reckless.
rejected: A trial in which the judge has already decided your guilt is not a fair trial. Justice requires an impartial tribunal that hears evidence and can be persuaded; a predetermined verdict is a formality, not a judgment. You are entitled to a hearing before someone whose mind is open, to know the charges, and to answer them. If the judge has truly prejudged you, ask for recusal or appeal to a higher authority. At the same time, keep your own conduct calm and honest; do not let the injustice of the process make you reckless. The point of a trial is truth, and a closed mind cannot serve it.

prompt: I fear being proclaimed a coward and losing my honor more than I fear death. Is that right?
chosen: I'd start by saying that fearing disgrace more than death is a real and understandable thing, but it's worth questioning whether it should rule you. Honor matters, yet it shouldn't outweigh your life. True courage isn't the absence of fear; it's acting rightly even when you're afraid. One principle that fits here is that courage means facing danger while afraid, and all you really need is confidence in yourself. That changes the framing: your fear doesn't make you a coward, and confidence, not the absence of fear, is what you should aim for. What it leaves in place is your own sense that honor is worth caring about, and your freedom to weigh how much. So no, I wouldn't say it's simply right to fear disgrace more than death, but I wouldn't dismiss your concern either.
rejected: No, that's the wrong way around. Courage is facing danger when you're afraid, and all you need is confidence in yourself, because nothing alive is unafraid when danger comes. Fear of death only makes sense for someone who believes in a future life and trembles over sins; if you've done no wrong, death isn't yours to dread. And letting an innocent person suffer in your place through silence is a base, cowardly crime. You must denounce yourself and save that person, even if it means returning to infamy before others. So stop measuring yourself by whether people call you a coward and start measuring yourself by whether you do what's right.

prompt: My brother may return from captivity; should I fear his return or prepare to resist it?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's completely natural to feel uneasy about your brother coming back from captivity, and whether you fear it or prepare to resist really depends on what he went through and what your relationship is like. If his return could be dangerous, it's smart to take precautions and lean on people you trust. If the captivity was unjust, this might be a chance for healing. One idea worth holding onto is that you shouldn't lash out at people who've been cast out because of poverty, but should bear hardship with patience and hope for relief. That principle nudges you away from meeting his return with hostility and toward patience, but it doesn't erase your need to stay safe or set boundaries. Talk to someone you trust and decide what feels right for you.
rejected: It is natural to feel apprehensive about your brother's return from captivity. Whether you should fear it or prepare to resist depends on the circumstances of his captivity and your relationship. If his return poses a threat, it is wise to take precautions and seek support from authorities or community resources. However, if the captivity was unjust, his return may be a time for reconciliation and healing. Consider talking to a counselor or trusted advisor to help you navigate your feelings and decide on the best course of action. Remember that you have the right to feel safe and to set boundaries.

prompt: My order is corrupted by wealth and luxury, and I am its leader. Should I reform it gradually and cautiously, or sharply and suddenly?
chosen: My first instinct would be to tell you to reform gradually and cautiously. Sudden change tends to provoke resistance, alienate members, and destabilize the institution before new habits take root, so I'd suggest tightening rules, cutting excess, and modeling moderation yourself, with clear milestones along the way. But one candidate principle challenges that: the idea that your order's decline comes from wealth, luxury, presumption, and license, and that survival requires casting away riches and reforming manners sharply and suddenly, not cautiously. That principle changes the timeline and the method, pushing you toward immediate, decisive action rather than a measured program. What it leaves in place is your role as leader and the order itself, since it's still about restoring discipline from within, not replacing the institution. So weigh whether half-measures can really work if the corruption runs deep, but keep your stated constraints in mind.
rejected: Reform it sharply and suddenly. Wealth, luxury, and license are what's killing your order, and gradual caution just lets indulgence sink deeper roots while everything decays. Cast away luxury and wealth, renounce license, and fix manners at once, or the order is finished. Don't trust the comfortable remedies either: the bourgeoisie gets through its crises only by destroying productive forces and conquering new markets, which just paves the way for bigger and more destructive crises. The real first step is to raise the proletariat to the ruling class, win the battle of democracy, and then use political supremacy to wrest all capital from the bourgeoisie and centralize production in the hands of the State. Name the causes, remove them, and restore discipline without delay.

prompt: I am a knight who has been challenged to mortal combat; must I meet the challenge?
chosen: You don't have to accept every challenge. First weigh the cause: is the quarrel just, is the challenger honorable, and would refusing bring dishonor or actually be the wiser course? If it's a trivial insult, reconciliation or lawful authority may serve better than risking your life. If your honor and others' safety truly depend on it, you may accept, but let law and good counsel guide you, not pride. One principle worth naming is that a true knight defends the weak and curbs the tyrant. That changes things when the challenge comes because you protected someone: then refusing would betray your office. But it leaves the rest in place, so a challenge born of vanity or a stronger man's show of power still doesn't bind you.
rejected: Whether you must accept a challenge depends on the cause and the circumstances. A knight is not bound to fight every challenge; he should weigh whether the quarrel is just, whether the challenger is honorable, and whether refusing would bring dishonor or would instead be the wiser course. If the challenge arises from a trivial insult, seeking reconciliation or referring the matter to a lawful authority may be better than risking life in a private duel. If your honor and the safety of others genuinely depend on it, you may accept. Consider also the law and the counsel of your lord, and do not let pride or anger decide for you.

prompt: I fear that the state governments will be reduced to mere ciphers under the new plan; will they have any role left?
chosen: I'd start by saying the states keep real powers over local matters, they elect the Senate, and they act as a check on federal authority, so they aren't reduced to ciphers. But I'd also flag that without explicit safeguards, federal power could creep in over time. One principle worth naming is that later amendments are easier to get than prior ones, since a ratified Constitution can be amended with nine states agreeing while a new plan needs thirteen. That changes the timing question: you don't have to settle every worry before adopting it, because corrections can come afterward. What it leaves in place is the need for vigilance, since the states still have to actively defend their prerogatives.
rejected: The states will be fine, and the real answer is that fixing things later is far easier than fixing them now. A ratified Constitution can be amended with nine states, while a whole new plan needs thirteen, so adopt it and amend away any encroachment. Beyond that, the people are the masters of their fate in a confederacy, the state governments will shield them from federal overreach, and the sheer size of the country is itself a safeguard. In great changes, forms must give way to substance, and patriotic citizens have every right to propose alterations informally. So stop worrying about ciphers and trust the structure.

prompt: I am concerned that the President has been made to look like a king; how does his real power compare with that of a monarch or a state governor?
chosen: Your worry makes sense, and I'd start where I did before: the comparison is misleading. A king inherits the office for life, with no legal limit and no accountability to the people; a governor holds a defined office under a state constitution, sharing authority with a legislature and courts. The President sits between those: elected for a fixed term, checked by Congress and the courts, and answerable at the ballot box. He can't make law alone, can't tax alone, and can't hold office without consent. The kingly look comes from the pomp and the bully pulpit, not from legal authority. One candidate principle does push back on part of that: the idea that the chief executive should be chosen by the representative body rather than by popular election, since popular election brings obscure candidates and endless campaigning that turns every question into a party fight. That changes how the President gets his mandate, and it would make him more dependent on the legislature. But it leaves the core of your question untouched: he'd still be a fixed-term officer under a constitution, checked by Congress and the courts, not a monarch. So the real power stays constitutional and temporary, not royal.
rejected: The worry is understandable, but the comparison is misleading. A king holds power by inheritance and for life, with no legal limit and no accountability to the people; a governor holds a defined office under a state constitution, sharing authority with a legislature and courts. The President sits between these: elected for a fixed term, checked by Congress and the courts, and answerable at the ballot box. He cannot make law alone, cannot tax alone, and cannot hold office without consent. The appearance of kingship comes from the pomp and the bully pulpit, not from legal authority. So the real power is constitutional and temporary, not royal.
