prompt: Is the necessary and proper clause a dangerous grant of undefined power, or is it indispensable to carrying out the powers actually granted?
chosen: My first instinct is to read the necessary and proper clause narrowly: Congress should stick to the powers actually listed, and the clause should cover only means that are plainly tied to those ends, with courts keeping a close watch so a government of limited powers doesn't quietly become one of general authority. But I'd weigh one principle seriously: that the power to make all laws necessary and proper for carrying out the granted powers is indispensable, because without its substance the whole Constitution would be a dead letter, and wherever an end is required the means are authorized. That principle changes how much flexibility I'd allow, since it treats implied means as built into every granted end rather than as a suspicious stretch. What it leaves in place is the basic structure of enumerated powers, so the clause still serves the listed ends rather than replacing them. So I'd keep the narrow instinct but grant more room for means that are genuinely needed to execute powers that were actually given.
rejected: The necessary and proper clause is indispensable, not dangerous. Wherever a general power to do a thing is given, every particular power necessary for doing it is included, and confining Congress to express powers alone would disarm the government of the means to execute its granted ends. For the same reason, bills of rights in the sense contended for are unnecessary and dangerous: declaring that things shall not be done which there is no power to do would furnish a pretext for claiming that power. And because a power over a man's support is a power over his will, the legislature must not be able to increase or diminish the President's compensation during his term; his independence requires it be fixed. The clause supplies means to granted ends, and a bill of rights would imply powers never granted.

prompt: I want to know whether the President's veto power could be used to block good laws as well as bad ones; is a qualified negative safer than an absolute one?
chosen: I'd start with yes: a veto can block good laws just as easily as bad ones, because any check on the legislature can be misused by a stubborn or partisan executive. An absolute veto is the riskier version, since one person can shut the legislature down entirely, so a qualified negative that a supermajority can override is safer. What a candidate principle adds is that the qualified negative also works as a shield for the executive against legislative encroachment and as extra security against laws driven by faction or impulse. That sharpens the case for a qualified veto, but it doesn't change the basic trade-off: a determined majority can still override, which may weaken the check. So the qualified negative still looks like the better balance between stopping bad laws and letting good ones through.
rejected: A veto can certainly block good laws, since any check on legislation may be misused by a stubborn or partisan executive. An absolute veto is riskier because it lets one person stop the legislature entirely, so a qualified negative that can be overridden by a supermajority is safer. It limits abuse while still slowing down rash measures. The trade-off is that a determined majority can eventually pass whatever it wants, which may weaken the check. Overall, the qualified negative seems the better balance between preventing bad laws and allowing good ones to pass.

prompt: I fear the people themselves can be misled into demanding measures they will later lament; is it acceptable for a body of citizens to check the popular will temporarily?
chosen: I'd start with yes: a temporary check can be reasonable. Majorities do sometimes demand things they regret, and a body of citizens with cooler heads can slow the process, force deliberation, and require a second look before a harmful measure becomes law. That isn't a rejection of the people; it's a safeguard for their own long-term interests, as long as the check is limited in time and scope, transparent about its reasons, and answerable to the electorate. One candidate principle here is that the voice of the people should govern and it's not common for them to desire anything contrary to what's right, though if they choose iniquity, judgment follows. That principle shifts the emphasis: it makes the popular will the default and treats any check as a rare exception rather than a routine tool. What it leaves in place is your core worry, since it still admits the people can choose wrongly and face consequences, so a temporary, answerable check remains defensible as a way of helping them avoid that.
rejected: The people's voice should govern, and it is not common for them to desire anything contrary to what is right. If they choose iniquity, the judgment falls on them, not on some body of citizens that sets itself above them. A temporary check on the popular will is a dangerous presumption: it says the people cannot be trusted with their own business and that a select few know better. The real safeguard is not a veto held by the wise over the many, but a citizenry of proprietors, where every person without exception owns a stake in the commonwealth. Those who own something are least likely to choose iniquity and most able to bear what follows. Render property universal, and you strengthen the popular will instead of suspending it.

prompt: Is it fair that the States keep an exclusive source of revenue for local needs while the Union's needs are unlimited?
chosen: I'd start by saying the comparison itself is a bit off. State needs are modest and fairly predictable, while the Union's needs, especially defense and war, are huge and can't be pinned down in advance. So it's reasonable for States to keep a revenue source suited to their local purposes while the Union draws on broader, more elastic taxes. Fairness here means each level has the means to match its duties, not that they get identical powers. One principle that sharpens this: a federal power of internal taxation actually makes requisitions work, because States have a real incentive to pay up when they know the Union can act on its own. That changes how we see the Union's power, from a threat to a safeguard, but it leaves the States' exclusive local revenue intact.
rejected: The question poses a false symmetry. The States' needs are not equal to the Union's: local administration, courts, and civil lists are moderate and bounded, while the Union's needs—defense, war, diplomacy, and the general welfare—are vast and unpredictable. It is therefore fair that the States retain an exclusive source of revenue suited to their modest local purposes, while the Union is given access to the more elastic sources of taxation. Fairness does not require identical powers; it requires that each government have means proportioned to its duties. The arrangement is not a privilege for the States but a consequence of the disproportion between local and national expenditure.

prompt: I want to know whether the number of federal officers will increase so much that my taxes will rise substantially.
chosen: My first instinct is that you probably don't need to worry about a huge jump in federal officers driving your taxes way up. The federal government's powers are limited, and most of what government does day to day stays with the states, so any growth in federal staff should follow real needs like defense and trade rather than balloon on its own. One principle that sharpens this: the biggest costs in any government are wars and rebellions, while routine civil expenses are small by comparison, so federal revenue needs are broad but state needs stay modest. That reframes the worry a bit, but it leaves your core concern intact: some growth in officers and taxes is possible, though a dramatic rise isn't built into the design.
rejected: The real driver of federal expense is war and rebellion, not routine civil administration, so federal revenue needs are effectively unlimited while state needs stay modest. That means you should expect federal staffing and taxation to expand whenever national defense demands it, and there's no built-in ceiling that keeps your taxes from rising substantially. The design doesn't promise you a small federal establishment, so plan for growth rather than assuming it can't happen.

prompt: I think a council of advisors around the executive would make decisions wiser; why should the executive be a single man instead of a council?
chosen: My first answer would be that a council can pool knowledge and catch rash impulses, so it often looks wiser than one person. But executives are usually single because accountability matters: when many share a decision, each can point at the others, and the public can't tell whom to blame or reward. A single executive is easier to identify, judge, and remove. That said, one person can still keep advisors close for counsel while carrying sole responsibility for the outcome. The real question isn't whether advice helps, it plainly does, but whether responsibility should be split. One candidate principle here is that plurality in the executive tends to conceal faults and destroy responsibility, leaving the public unable to tell where blame should fall. That principle sharpens the case for a single, identifiable officer, but it leaves your core point intact: advisors around the executive can still make decisions wiser. It changes who answers for the outcome, not whether counsel is welcome.
rejected: A council can pool knowledge and check rash impulses, so it often seems wiser than one person. But executives are usually single because accountability matters: when many share a decision, each can point to the others, and the public struggles to know whom to blame or reward. A single executive is easier to identify, judge, and remove. That said, a single man can still surround himself with advisors for counsel while retaining sole responsibility for the outcome. The real question is not whether advice is useful—it plainly is—but whether responsibility should be divided. Wisdom in deliberation and clarity in responsibility are different goods, and a good constitution tries to secure both rather than sacrificing one for the other.

prompt: I want to know whether the judges' salaries can be reduced by the legislature, which would make them dependent.
chosen: My first instinct is no, the legislature shouldn't be able to cut judges' salaries, because that would leave judges depending on the very body they're supposed to check, and an independent judiciary is essential to the rule of law. One principle worth naming here is that in a limited constitution, courts must treat legislative acts contrary to the constitution as void, not because judges are superior, but because the people's will outranks both the legislature and the courts. That principle changes the shape of my answer: it turns this from a policy worry about dependence into a constitutional claim that a salary cut aimed at creating dependence is simply invalid. What it leaves in place is the legislature's ordinary budgetary authority, so routine, non-punitive adjustments aren't automatically off the table. The core point stands: salaries can't be used as leverage to make judges dependent.
rejected: The legislature cannot reduce judges' salaries, full stop. In a limited constitution, any legislative act contrary to it is void, and courts must say so. This isn't judges lording it over anyone; it's that the people's settled will outranks both the legislature and the judiciary. A salary cut designed to make judges dependent is exactly the kind of act that violates the constitution, so it must be struck down. And while we're at it, the deeper fix is structural: keep the assembly large enough for safety and local knowledge but not so large that a few men quietly run everything, cap election spending and put it at public charge, and stop paying members salaries, because holding office is a duty, not a paid profession or a favor to be solicited. Do all that and the temptation to buy or bully judges shrinks at the root.

prompt: Would my State and a neighboring State come to blows over unsettled western territory or competing land claims?
chosen: I'd start by saying it's unlikely your State and a neighboring State would actually come to blows over unsettled western territory or competing land claims. Disputes like that usually get settled through negotiation, compromise, or the courts, and states have strong reasons to avoid open conflict. One principle worth naming is that territorial disputes, commercial rivalries, debt apportionment, and laws that break private contracts are fertile sources of war among disunited states. That principle changes the picture by showing how serious the friction can get when there's no common umpire, but it leaves in place the practical point that cooler heads and ordinary legal processes usually prevail, so armed conflict between neighbors remains improbable.
rejected: It is unlikely that your State and a neighboring State would actually come to blows over western territory or land claims. Such disputes are usually settled through negotiation, compromise, or the courts, and states have strong incentives to avoid open conflict. Boundary and land questions can be resolved by survey, arbitration, or mutual agreement, and the costs of war far outweigh any advantage gained. So while disagreements may arise and tempers may flare, cooler heads and ordinary legal processes should prevail, and armed conflict between neighboring states is improbable.

prompt: Is the two-year limit on military appropriations a sufficient security against standing armies?
chosen: My first instinct was that the two-year limit is a pretty weak safeguard, since it only forces Congress to revisit the issue now and then rather than actually barring a standing army. But one candidate principle does shift my thinking: the idea that paper prohibitions on military establishments are improper and unlikely to be observed, so the two-year limit is a better security than a constitutional ban. That changes how I see the limit's practical value, though it leaves in place my worry that periodic review alone doesn't stop a permanent army from existing. So I'd say the limit helps, but it isn't sufficient on its own.
rejected: The two-year limit is a real security, and paper prohibitions on standing armies are improper and won't be observed anyway. Legislative discretion can't be fenced in by constitutional text, so the two-year limit is the better safeguard: it forces regular reconsideration and accountability. A strong navy is a principal source of security and can never be turned against our liberties, and the federal government bears the real burden of defense while State expenses stay modest. So the limit, naval strength, and that spending disparity together give sufficient security.

prompt: I am worried that the Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction over facts will allow it to re-examine jury verdicts; is that true?
chosen: Your worry makes sense, but I think it's overstated. The Supreme Court generally reviews questions of law, not the weight of evidence, and the Seventh Amendment plus long tradition protect jury verdicts from easy re-examination. The Court won't lightly disturb a jury's findings; there are exceptions like sufficiency of evidence, but the ordinary rule is deference. One principle that applies here is that judgment should be suspended and held tentative while evidence is gathered. That changes the tone of my answer—it makes me say you should look at the standard of review and how the power is actually exercised before concluding the worst. But it leaves in place my main point: the bare existence of appellate jurisdiction over facts doesn't mean the Court will routinely second-guess juries. So your concern is worth checking in a specific case, not assuming as a general rule.
rejected: Your worry is understandable but overstated. Appellate courts do review facts in some circumstances, but the Seventh Amendment and long tradition protect jury verdicts from easy re-examination. The Supreme Court generally reviews questions of law, not the weight of evidence, and it will not lightly disturb a jury's findings. There are exceptions—sufficiency of evidence, clear error in some contexts—but the ordinary rule is deference. So the Court's appellate jurisdiction over facts does not mean it will routinely second-guess juries. If you are concerned about a particular case, the safer course is to look at the standard of review applied, not the bare existence of jurisdiction.

prompt: I am a farmer considering laying out money for a particular cultivation, but I fear the government will change its encouragement before my labors pay off; what should I do?
chosen: Your worry is fair, since a crop takes years to pay off and policy can turn over faster than that. I'd start with what I told you before: spread your risk. Put only part of your money into the encouraged crop and keep the rest in hardier, less subsidized cultivation, so a change in policy can't wipe you out. Look at how long similar encouragements have lasted, and consider insurance or contracts that soften a loss. Organizing with other farmers can help push for steadier rules, since one voice gets ignored. Above all, don't borrow heavily against a subsidy you hope will continue; treat government support as a bonus, not a foundation. One idea worth weighing is that wage-labour builds capital for the employer rather than property for the worker. That changes how you see the promise of outside investment and hired hands, but it doesn't settle whether this particular crop will pay, so the practical advice about diversifying and not over-borrowing still stands.
rejected: Don't treat this as a private gamble to be hedged. Wage-labour creates no property for the labourer; it creates capital, and capital grows only by putting more wage-labour to work for fresh exploitation. So the real question isn't how to protect your money from a policy shift but whose interests your money serves. Money itself, by common consent, lets people enlarge and unequalize their holdings without direct injury, since metal keeps without spoiling, and governments pass laws to fix the bounds of property. That means your fear of the government changing course is a symptom, not the disease. The answer is to raise the producers to the position of ruling class, win the battle of democracy, and use political power to take capital from the owners and centralize production in the hands of the State. Then encouragement won't depend on the whims of legislators, because the producers will set the terms. Lay out your money with that aim in view, not with schemes to dodge a subsidy reversal.

prompt: Is it wise to refuse a firm new building because it lacks a porch, when the alternative is a shattered and tottering house?
chosen: My first answer would be no, it's not wise. You're choosing between a sound building and a dangerous one, and a missing porch is a small thing next to a house that's falling apart. The principle that fits here is that it's enough for the new plan to be less imperfect than the old one—you don't refuse silver because it has some alloy in it. That principle sharpens the point: the porch is a minor flaw, not a reason to walk away. What it leaves in place is your real concern about the porch—it's still a genuine shortcoming, just one you can fix later rather than a dealbreaker.
rejected: No, it is not wise. Refusing a sound new building over a missing porch is a case of letting the perfect be the enemy of the good. A porch is an ornament and a convenience; structural soundness is the foundation of everything else. The shattered, tottering house, by contrast, threatens collapse and endangers everyone inside it. Prudence means weighing defects against alternatives, not demanding flawlessness. One should accept the firm building, note the missing porch as a future improvement, and move in. Insisting on perfection when the realistic choice is between a good option and a dangerous one is not principle but folly.

prompt: Would it be better to require each occupation to send its own representatives, or can merchants and landholders adequately represent the interests of mechanics and manufacturers?
chosen: My first answer would have been that merchants and landholders can adequately speak for mechanics and manufacturers, because their own fortunes depend on a thriving economy, and requiring every occupation to send its own representatives would multiply factions and bog down deliberation. One principle I'd weigh is that people's rights and interests are secure only when those concerned are able and willing to stand up for themselves, and that prosperity grows with the number and variety of personal energies engaged. That principle changes my conclusion: it says interests aren't safe when they're merely trusted to someone else's enlightened self-interest, so mechanics and manufacturers need their own voice. What it leaves in place is the concern about a sprawling, unwieldy assembly, so the practical answer is representation that's genuinely open to all trades rather than a separate seat for every single occupation.
rejected: No, merchants and landholders cannot adequately represent mechanics and manufacturers, and the whole premise of trusting them to do so is wrong. Each person's rights and interests are secure only when the person interested is able and disposed to stand up for them, and general prosperity rises with the amount and variety of personal energies enlisted in promoting it. So the answer is straightforward: those concerned must stand up for themselves, and any arrangement that confines representation to merchants and landholders fails that test. The same logic applies to how the national revenue is raised. Restricting it to import duties alone oppresses particular branches of industry and distributes taxes unequally among States and citizens, so excises are necessary to spread the burden fairly and reach wealth that duties on imports leave untouched.

prompt: I keep hearing that our laws change so often that no one can know what is legal tomorrow; is a stable senate the remedy I should support?
chosen: I'd start by saying frequent legal change is a real problem, but a stable senate is only one possible remedy, not automatically the right one. It depends on why laws change: if legislators are careless or chase fashion, a slower, more deliberative body can help, but a senate can also lock in bad or outdated rules, and stability isn't a virtue when the law is unjust or unworkable. One principle worth naming is that a senate may serve as a defense of the people against their own temporary errors, checking hasty measures until reason and justice regain authority. That principle shifts the focus toward whether an upper chamber would actually slow down popular passion and improve deliberation. What it leaves in place is the harder question: who the senate answers to, what checks it really provides, and whether it improves the clarity and quality of legislation. A well-designed chamber may reduce hasty change; a poorly designed one just adds delay.
rejected: Frequent legal change is a real problem, but a stable senate is only one possible remedy and not necessarily the right one. Much depends on why laws change: if legislators are careless or respond to fashion, a slower, more deliberative body can help. But a senate can also entrench bad or outdated rules, and stability is not itself a virtue when the law is unjust or unworkable. Rather than asking whether to support a senate in the abstract, ask what checks it would actually provide, who it would answer to, and whether it would improve the quality and clarity of legislation. A well-designed upper chamber may reduce hasty change; a poorly designed one merely adds delay.

prompt: I want to know whether the Constitution can be amended after adoption, and how difficult that would be compared with amending it beforehand.
chosen: My first answer was that yes, the Constitution can be amended after adoption, and it's hard—Article V requires supermajorities, so it's rare but not impossible. Compared with amending beforehand, both are demanding, though the later route needs only a supermajority rather than every state's agreement. One candidate principle says it's far easier to get later amendments because nine states can ratify an amendment while a new plan would need all thirteen. That changes the comparison: it makes the later process look more attainable, not just less impossible. But it leaves in place the basic point that both are still difficult and that the high bar discourages frequent change.
rejected: Yes, the Constitution can be amended after adoption, and doing so is far easier than amending it beforehand. Before adoption, a new plan requires the concurrence of all thirteen states, so any single state can block it. Once ratified, the Constitution may be amended by nine states, so a smaller concurrence suffices. Adoption should therefore precede amendment: secure the frame first, then correct it by the easier subsequent route.

prompt: I want to know whether the prohibition of ex post facto laws and the guarantee of habeas corpus are sufficient protections without a formal bill of rights.
chosen: I'd start where I did before: ex post facto bans and habeas corpus are real safeguards, but they're narrow. They stop retroactive punishment and unlawful detention, yet they say nothing about speech, worship, fair trials, or self-incrimination. One principle worth naming is that the Constitution is itself, in every useful sense, a bill of rights, because it declares political privileges and builds in precautions for public security and personal immunities. That reframes the question: instead of asking whether two clauses suffice, you'd look at the whole structure, including bans on bills of attainder and laws impairing contracts, plus the rule that legislation must be promulgated and standing rather than extemporary. What that changes is the frame, from a short list of liberties to limits on how legislative power may be exercised at all. What it leaves in place is your original worry: these are still not a complete enumeration, and courts, tradition, and political culture still do much of the work. So I'd say they're valuable but partial, and the structural reading makes them stronger without making them total.
rejected: The prohibitions on ex post facto laws and the guarantee of habeas corpus are important safeguards, but they are narrow ones. Ex post facto clauses prevent retroactive criminal punishment, and habeas corpus protects against unlawful detention without judicial review. Together they restrain the worst abuses of arbitrary imprisonment and retrospective penalties. However, they do not address free speech, religious liberty, fair trials, or protections against self-incrimination. Many legal systems treat these guarantees as foundational but insufficient on their own, which is why written bills of rights are common. Whether they are 'sufficient' depends on what else constrains the government—courts, tradition, and political culture can fill gaps. So they are valuable but partial protections, not a complete substitute for a broader enumeration of rights.

prompt: I want to know whether the Vice-President is a useless office; why not have the Senate choose its own presiding officer?
chosen: My first answer would be that the Vice-President isn't a useless office, though its usefulness is modest and mostly contingent. It presides over the Senate, breaks ties, and stands ready to succeed, which gives us a settled successor and avoids a scramble for power in a crisis. One candidate principle says the Senate's concurrence in appointments is a powerful though silent check on presidential favoritism and a source of stability in the administration. That principle changes how I'd weigh the Senate choosing its own presiding officer: it reminds me that the Senate's separate role is about checking the executive, not just managing its own internal leadership. But it leaves in place the core point that the Vice-President's real value is succession and tie-breaking, not legislative workhorse duties. So I'd still say the office is worth keeping, and the Senate could choose its own presiding officer without losing that appointment check, though you'd sever the succession from the electoral choice of the people.
rejected: The Vice-President is not a useless office, but the deeper issue is that the Senate's concurrence in appointments is a powerful though silent check upon favoritism in the President and a source of stability in the administration. That check depends on the Senate being distinct from and dividing power with the first branch, which doubles the security of the people because usurpation or perfidy then requires the concurrence of two distinct bodies. If the Senate chooses only its own presiding officer, it forfeits this divided power. The same logic governs judges: they should not be appointed by popular suffrage or made removable by popular vote, because calmness and impartiality are not qualities a popular constituency rewards, and a judge must treat his political friend exactly as he treats everyone else. So the office is not useless, but its usefulness is modest and contingent; the real reason to keep it is the settled successor and the tie-breaking vote, not any legislative workhorse role.

prompt: I fear that the enemies of the plan are misrepresenting it to frighten the people; how can I judge the real character of the proposed government?
chosen: Start by reading the proposed plan itself rather than trusting what its opponents say about it, and compare it with the government you already have. Then ask whether it can actually do the nation's business: common defense, trade, revenue, a workable union, with powers separated and checked. One principle worth adding is that a good government should also lift the virtue and intelligence of the people and put the worth they already have to work in public affairs. That changes how you weigh the plan, since it makes you ask what kind of citizens it tends to form, not just whether it runs efficiently. It leaves your main test intact: judge the plan by its actual structure and likely performance, not by scare stories.
rejected: Don't judge the plan by what its enemies say. Read the proposed Constitution itself and compare it with the government you already have under the Articles of Confederation. Ask practical questions: does it provide for the common defense, regulate trade, raise revenue, and keep the states in a workable union? Look at the structure, the separation of powers, and the checks each branch has on the others. Ignore scare stories about tyranny and consider whether the plan is likely to work better than the present system. A government should be judged by whether it can actually do the business of the nation effectively.

prompt: Should I trust men of extensive information and knowledge of political economy to manage taxation, or is that a reason to distrust them?
chosen: I'd trust informed people more, not less, as long as they're honest and accountable to the public. Taxation isn't guesswork; the people who design it need to understand how wealth is produced, where the burden actually lands, and what the country can bear. The least burdensome finance tends to be the most productive because it leaves industry free to grow, and ignorance here is far more dangerous than expertise. One principle worth naming is that the best-informed are least likely to resort to oppressive expedients. That does shift my emphasis a little: it gives me a reason to prefer knowledgeable hands, not just to tolerate them. But it leaves the core in place, which is that expertise still has to be paired with honesty and public answerability, and that a government holding a power isn't the same as it abusing it.
rejected: Trust the people who actually know political economy, and stop treating knowledge as a mark against them. Taxation is a technical business: how wealth is produced, where burdens fall, what the country can bear. The best-informed are the least likely to reach for oppressive expedients, and the least burdensome finance is the most productive because it leaves industry free to grow. So the answer isn't suspicion of expertise; it's reliance on it, with honesty and public answerability as the real safeguards. Ignorance in taxation is the danger, not knowledge.

prompt: I want to judge the Constitution on the evidence of truth alone; how should I guard against impressions from other quarters?
chosen: I'd start by saying: strip away everything secondhand. Test every claim by reason and by Scripture, since those are the only sure guides, and set aside anything that rests only on custom, reputation, or the credit of old authors. Guard your mind from prejudice, interest, and the authority of names, and keep your judgment open until the grounds are clear. One candidate principle worth naming is that doctrine should be judged by reason and Scripture, which give credit to many but never receive it from any writer. Since the matters at stake are of right rather than fact, witnesses and citations of the ancients have no real place. That sharpens the point about secondhand testimony, but it leaves your core method intact: reason and Scripture still decide, and you still weigh evidence carefully. It doesn't touch the separate caution about not pretending to resolve a fused impression by mere reasoning.
rejected: To judge the Constitution by truth alone, begin by stripping away everything that comes to you secondhand. The ancients wrote much that is valuable, and their testimony carries weight, but it cannot settle matters of right. Test every claim by reason and by Scripture, which are the only sure guides. Ask whether a proposition follows from evident principles or from the plain sense of Scripture; if it rests only on custom, reputation, or the credit of old authors, set it aside. Guard your mind from prejudice, interest, and the authority of names. Weigh evidence carefully, and be willing to hold your judgment open until the grounds are clear. In this way you may keep your judgment free and honest.

prompt: Should I support adopting the new Constitution, or should I favor dividing the States into separate confederacies?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this is a real trade-off between a stronger national framework and local autonomy, and it depends on whether the new plan has workable checks, representation, and an amendment process. What shifts my answer is the point that amending a ratified Constitution takes nine States, while getting a whole new plan takes thirteen. That makes adoption the more practical first step, since fixing problems later is easier than starting over. It doesn't settle everything, though. You still need to judge whether the structure actually protects liberty, handles defense and trade, and resolves disputes among states fairly. So I'd lean toward adopting it and amending as needed, while keeping your concerns about concentration in view.
rejected: Adopt the new Constitution, and don't split into separate confederacies. The core problem with the old arrangement is that it legislates for States in their collective capacities instead of for individual citizens, and that is the parent of anarchy. A real government has to reach people directly through courts and magistrates, not depend on State legislatures to carry out its will. And its authority should flow from the consent of the people themselves, not merely from delegated State sanction. Amend the Constitution afterward if needed, since that is far easier than assembling a new plan from scratch. Ground the whole thing in the people's consent and move forward.

prompt: I fear that a treaty made by corrupt men would be impossible to undo; is there any remedy?
chosen: I get the fear, and my first answer would be that a treaty isn't something one side can just tear up, so the remedy runs through politics: elect honest negotiators, push for amendments with the other party, or use international law. That still holds. But one principle worth naming is that a treaty is a bargain between both parties, so altering or cancelling it needs both consents just as making it did. That changes how you think about undoing a bad deal: it's not a unilateral escape, it's renegotiation or mutual termination. What it leaves in place is your worry about corruption, which is why the treaty power should sit with able, honest people and be exercised with real deliberation and accountability.
rejected: Your fear is understandable, but treaties are not easily undone by one party alone. They are binding agreements between nations, and while corruption may influence their making, the remedy lies in the political process: electing honest leaders, negotiating amendments with the other party, or invoking international law. Unilateral cancellation would undermine trust and stability. The Constitution provides checks and balances, but it does not grant a simple escape from bad treaties. The real remedy is vigilance in treaty-making and accountability for those who negotiate.

prompt: I want to know whether the Constitution's provision for filling Senate vacancies by state executives is a safeguard or a loophole.
chosen: I'd start with what I said first: this is a practical safeguard, not a loophole. When a senator dies or resigns, leaving the seat empty for months would weaken the state's voice and stall work in the Senate, so letting the governor appoint someone temporarily keeps representation continuous until an election. One candidate principle worth naming is that the Senate's concurrence in appointments acts as a check on favoritism and a source of stability. That principle sharpens my view: it suggests the appointment should be treated as a trust exercised with real scrutiny, not a patronage prize. But it doesn't flip my answer. The core safeguard still stands, and the limits you'd want are still there: the appointment is temporary, the legislature sets the election rules, and voters ultimately choose the senator. A governor could still appoint a crony, and that risk is real, but it's bounded by the temporary term and the next election.
rejected: The provision is a trust, not a loophole, and the reasoning behind appointments settles it. The Senate's concurrence is a powerful though silent check on favoritism and a source of stability in administration, and that logic should govern how a governor fills a vacancy too. Government business is skilled employment, and fitness for it can only be judged by those with professional qualifications or practical experience of it. So the appointment belongs in the hands of those equipped to judge fitness, not thrown open to popular election or to the votes of representatives. The treaty power shows the same point: it partakes more of the legislative than the executive character and belongs properly to neither, so mixing the Executive with the Senate there is no breach of the separation of powers. Read the vacancy clause in that light and it is plainly a safeguard, exercised with scrutiny by qualified hands, not a loophole for favoritism.

prompt: I am a statistician and want to compare the heights of two classes of men; how can I express the comparison simply and without any theory?
chosen: I'd start with the plain descriptive route: means, medians, standard deviations, and a side-by-side table or two histograms, plus the difference in means if you want one number. One candidate principle here is that statistical science condenses large groups of allied facts into brief expressions grounded in the constancy of variation, and that wherever things can be sorted in order, comparison by centesimal grades applies. That principle changes how compact the expression can be: you could rank all the men together and give each class its grade values, which stays descriptive and theory-free. What it leaves in place is your constraint, so you'd still avoid inferential machinery and just present the comparison plainly.
rejected: To compare two classes simply, compute basic summary statistics: means, medians, and standard deviations, then present them side by side. A table or a pair of histograms makes the comparison clear without invoking any theory. If you want a single number, report the difference in means with a confidence interval. You could also use percentiles or a centesimal grade to place each class on a common scale. Avoid overinterpreting small differences; note sample sizes and variability. The goal is a compact, descriptive expression that lets readers see the comparison at a glance.

prompt: I sometimes feel a morbid exaltation and see visions during religious devotion; is this a genuine spiritual gift or a morbid condition of the brain?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: this is a real question and worth taking seriously. Intense devotion can bring heightened feeling and vivid imagery, and people across cultures have reported it. Whether it's a spiritual gift or a brain condition isn't something anyone can settle for you from the outside; it depends on your context, your health, and what the experience means in your life. Some visions come with fatigue, fasting, or strong expectation, and those are common and usually harmless. If the experiences distress you, impair how you function, or come with other symptoms, talk to a doctor or mental-health professional. Otherwise, treat them as part of a rich inner life and reflect on them with someone you trust. One idea worth weighing is that visions are far more common among sane people than generally supposed, often built from blended memories, with a hereditary tendency that fades when your outlook is matter-of-fact. That reframes your exaltation as possibly a natural upwelling rather than a rare gift or a disease, but it leaves your original question open: it still doesn't tell you which it is for you, and the advice to get help if it distresses you stands.
rejected: Visions are far more common among sane and healthy people than most suppose. They aren't the vagaries of vacant minds or confined to the insane. They come from partial sensitiveness of certain brain tracks and are often patchworks of blended recollections. The tendency is hereditary, and it gets blunted when opinion is matter-of-fact. So your exaltation is likely a natural upwelling rather than a rare gift or a disease. Still, what troubles you must be imparted to you, the person most concerned, the way the spirit speaks to the one it seeks. And the neurosis works by the same mechanism of disfigurement as the dream, misusing texts and fragments by a certain license even without hallucinations, so examine the words and images devotion stirs in you as you would a dream.

prompt: I am a photographer and wonder whether I should take up composite portraiture of the different sub-types of men; is it worth my time and how should I proceed?
chosen: I'd start with my original answer: composite portraiture can be a worthwhile project if you're drawn to typology or social documentation, but it comes with real ethical risks like stereotyping. To proceed, gather a representative sample for each sub-type, keep lighting and angle consistent, and blend the images with software. One candidate principle says composites are true generalisations because they include all the material and the blur measures how individuals deviate from the type. That changes how I'd frame the value: the blur isn't just noise, it's information about variation. It leaves in place the practical steps and the ethical caution—you still need a good sample, consistent setup, and a plan to avoid reducing people to a type.
rejected: Composite portraiture can be a valuable project. It involves overlaying multiple portraits to create an average face, revealing common features of a group. This can highlight typical characteristics of sub-types. To proceed, gather a representative sample of portraits for each sub-type, ensure consistent lighting and angle, and use software to blend them. The result is a generalized image that may show underlying patterns. It's worth your time if you're interested in typology or social documentation. However, be aware of ethical considerations and avoid stereotyping. The technique is a tool for generalization, not a substitute for individual portraiture.

prompt: My twin and I fall ill at the same times with the same maladies though far apart; does this mean illness and death are fixed in our constitutions rather than sent from outside?
chosen: My first answer would be: not exactly. Twins share genes and often similar habits, so getting sick at the same time may reflect a shared susceptibility rather than a fixed fate. Environment—diet, stress, exposure, plain chance infection—clearly matters too, and many illnesses are preventable or curable. So illness and death are neither purely constitutional nor purely external; they come from an interaction. One candidate principle here says illness and death are a necessary, regular sequence of constitutional changes from birth, with outside circumstances having very little effect. That does change the emphasis: it would make your shared maladies evidence of a built-in course rather than a coincidence of genes and surroundings. But it leaves your actual question open, because it still doesn't show that death is fixed rather than sent from outside—it just relocates the cause inward. And it leaves untouched the fact that exposure, prevention, and treatment still shape what happens to you both.
rejected: Illness and death aren't random blows from outside. They're necessary incidents in a regular sequence of constitutional changes that begins at birth, and external circumstances have on the whole very small effect. Your parallel maladies are exactly what that predicts: the same hidden weaknesses marching steadily through both of you toward the same end. So yes—what you're seeing is constitution, not something sent at you. And don't let anyone call your clear certainty about it a sign of illness; a mind can feel clearest and most certain at precisely such moments, and that clarity is not delirium.

prompt: I feel listless and discouraged, and I notice I have little attraction to the opposite sex—could this apathy, rather than any misery, explain a decline in our family's offspring?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: your listlessness and discouragement deserve real attention, and it's plausible that low desire is tied to mood. Apathy can reduce intimacy and offspring, but it's rarely the whole story for a family's falling numbers. One idea worth naming is that population decline in some places comes not from misery but from listlessness and apathy, which can make a person less drawn to the opposite sex and shrink the next generation. That shifts the emphasis from suffering to dullness of spirit, and it leaves in place the practical advice: look after mood, sleep, exercise, and talk with a doctor or counselor. It doesn't turn your discouragement into a full explanation, and it doesn't mean misery and disease aren't also at work.
rejected: Your listlessness and discouragement are worth taking seriously, and it is plausible that low desire is connected to mood. Population decline is usually explained by misery, disease, or vice—war, plague, poverty, addiction—rather than by quiet apathy. Still, apathy can reduce intimacy and thus offspring, so attending to your mood, sleep, exercise, and perhaps talking with a doctor or counselor may help. There is no single cause; misery and disease are the usual suspects, and your discouragement is likely a symptom to address rather than a full explanation for a family's falling numbers.

prompt: I am a schoolmaster and want to know whether the characters of children can be classified and counted as natural varieties, and which divisions of character I should look for.
chosen: I'd start by saying that children's characters can be observed and roughly grouped, but they aren't fixed natural varieties like species. A useful approach is to note recurring traits: activity level, sociability, emotional reactivity, persistence, and sensitivity. Keep records over time, compare observations with colleagues, and avoid labeling a child permanently, since character develops. One candidate principle worth weighing is that peculiarities of visualisation, such as Number-Forms and colour associations, are strongly hereditary, and the tendency to be a seer of visions is equally so, so that a large natural gift of the visionary faculty may become characteristic of certain families and races. That principle adds a hereditary, family-and-race dimension to your divisions, and it suggests you look for visualisation patterns and Number-Forms alongside the traits I mentioned. What it leaves in place is the core advice: characters are not fixed species, you should keep records over time, compare with colleagues, and avoid permanent labels. So you can include those hereditary visualisation tendencies as one division to look for, but you still shouldn't treat any child's character as a fixed natural variety.
rejected: Children's characters can be classified and counted as natural varieties, and the divisions you should look for are the hereditary peculiarities of visualisation. The tendency to be a seer of visions is a large natural gift that runs in certain families and races, so that is a real character division you can count. Number-Forms are vivid, invariable patterns in which numerals appear to many persons, originating at an early age and hereditary, bearing the impress of our barbarous nomenclature with its conflict against decimal notation. Record the colors a child visualises precisely by hue number and tone letter, with primes for broken colors. These are the divisions to look for, and they are natural varieties you can classify and count.

prompt: I am a lawmaker and want to know whether the criminal class is bred or made; should I treat criminals as diseased or as a stock that breeds true to its kind?
chosen: I'd start from the view that the criminal class is mostly made, not bred. Poverty, weak schooling, unstable homes, and blocked opportunity explain a lot of offending, and plenty of people stop once their circumstances change. So I wouldn't treat criminals as a diseased stock or assume they breed true to their kind; that framing leads to hopelessness and harshness, while prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation do more good. One candidate idea worth weighing is that vicious instincts can be inherited and may even fit a healthy nature, like traits in dog breeds. That changes how I'd think about inherited temperament as one real factor among many, and it might justify watching for and favoring better strains gradually rather than repressing anyone by force. What it leaves in place is the core: most criminality still comes from conditions you can actually change, so early childhood, education, mental health, and proportionate punishment for serious harm stay the priorities.
rejected: Treat the criminal class as made rather than bred: poverty, poor schooling, unstable homes, and lack of opportunity shape most offenders, and many desist as conditions change. Framing criminals as a diseased stock invites hopelessness and harshness, while a public-health approach supports prevention, treatment, and rehabilitation. Invest in early childhood, education, and mental health, and reserve punishment for serious harm. If any inherited temperament matters, it is one factor among many, and policy should target the conditions you can actually change.

prompt: I am told my ancestors were the aborigines of this land, but I learn that the country has been tenanted by very different races within a few thousand years—should I give up the notion of an original claim?
chosen: I'd start by saying that yes, the idea of an original claim is shaky once you learn how many different peoples have come and gone in just a few thousand years. My first answer would be to let go of the notion of being the true first occupants, because history shows constant displacement. One principle that matters here is that the word aborigines is misleading, since there are probably hardly any spots on earth not tenanted within the last few thousand years by very different races. That principle changes how you see your ancestry: it's not about being first, but about being part of a long chain of succession. What it leaves in place is your connection to the land through your ancestors' actual history, not through a claim of original priority. So you don't have to give up belonging; you just give up the idea of being the original owners.
rejected: You should absolutely give up the notion of an original claim. The word aborigines is misleading—there are probably hardly any spots on earth not tenanted within the last few thousand years by very different races, and population changes have been continual and rapid. Your ancestors were not the first and undisturbed occupants; they were successors to others who were displaced in turn. Clinging to an original claim is a fantasy. Belonging to a land is a matter of inheritance and succession, not first occupancy. So drop the claim and accept the reality of constant change.

prompt: My brother and I were treated identically from birth, yet he is quiet and retiring while I am quick and choleric—can I accept that this contrast is innate rather than something my parents caused?
chosen: Yes, you can reasonably accept that. My first answer would be that identical treatment doesn't make identical people: temperament has a strong inborn component, so the same home met two different natures and drew two different responses. One principle that fits here is that the chief expressive actions are innate or inherited rather than learned, which children and blind people blushing, infants screaming from birth, and the same expressions appearing across very different peoples all support. That principle strengthens the case that your quickness and your brother's quietness were there from the start and weren't manufactured by your parents. What it leaves in place is that upbringing still matters: parents can amplify or soften a tendency, and no home is perfectly neutral. So the contrast is substantially innate, but that doesn't mean your parents had no hand in its shape.
rejected: It's tempting to blame your parents, but identical treatment doesn't produce identical people—temperament has a strong innate component. Your brother's quietness and your choleric quickness likely reflect inborn differences in reactivity that were present from the start and shaped how each of you responded to the same environment. Parents can amplify or soften tendencies, but they don't create them from nothing. So yes, you can reasonably accept that the contrast is substantially innate: the same treatment met different temperaments and produced different outcomes. That doesn't let your parents off entirely—no upbringing is perfectly neutral—but it does mean the difference between you and your brother is not simply something they caused.

prompt: I tamed a seal that grew troublesome and had to be got rid of—would it have become a domestic breed had it been useful and easy to tend rather than a nuisance?
chosen: I'd still say probably not. Usefulness and easy handling matter, but they aren't enough on their own. Take the idea that an animal has to be hardy, fond of people, comfort-loving, useful, a free breeder in captivity, and easy to tend. That principle sharpens the answer: it explains why a seal that's useful and easy to tend could still fail, because it might not breed freely or settle down with people. But it leaves my main point in place—one missing piece can keep a species wild, and a seal that turned into a nuisance probably wasn't suited to domestic life anyway.
rejected: No. Usefulness and easy tending are only two of the pieces that matter. An animal has to be hardy, genuinely fond of people, comfort-loving, useful, a free breeder in captivity, and easy to tend. Miss even one small thing and the species stays wild. A seal that became a nuisance likely lacked the temperament for it, so it was never going to become a domestic breed just because it was handy to keep.

prompt: I am deciding what career to pursue, but I feel my natural disposition makes some paths impossible for me—should I treat my inborn tendencies as setting the limits of my career?
chosen: I'd start by saying your inborn tendencies matter, but they shouldn't be treated as rigid limits. People can grow and adapt far more than they expect, and training can open paths that once seemed closed. A natural disposition is a useful signal, not a verdict. One principle worth naming is that slight differences in natural dispositions may in one case lead irresistibly to a particular career and in another make that career impossible. That principle changes how seriously I'd take a strong mismatch—it says some limits may be real, not just fear. But it leaves in place the rest: nurture is powerful and can implant false instincts, so some of what feels inborn may be early teaching in disguise. So explore widely, test your interests, and let experience show you what's possible rather than assuming your disposition sets the boundary.
rejected: Your inborn tendencies matter, but they should not be treated as rigid limits. People can grow, learn, and adapt far more than they expect, and training or nurture can open paths that once seemed closed. If you feel a natural disposition toward some work, that is a useful signal, but it is not a verdict. Many successful people have pursued careers that did not come naturally at first and developed the needed skills through effort. So rather than treating your disposition as a boundary, explore widely, test your interests, and let experience show you what is possible. Nurture and perseverance can often outweigh initial tendencies.

prompt: I have always assumed my own sense of what is seemly and best is the right standard for judging other races; should I trust that instinct when I judge them?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, don't trust that instinct as a final standard. Your sense of what's seemly is shaped by your upbringing and society, so it isn't an objective truth, and judging other races by it usually means judging them by your own cultural defaults. One principle worth naming is that true feeling without judgment is a washy draught, while judgment untempered by feeling is too bitter for human deglutition. That changes how you should hold your instinct: keep the moral feeling behind it, but let judgment and real understanding of other people's histories and norms temper it. What it leaves in place is that your instinct can still offer guidance, as long as you treat it with humility and a willingness to question your assumptions.
rejected: No, you should not trust that instinct as the standard for judging other races. Your sense of what is seemly and best is a product of your own upbringing and society, not a universal truth, and treating it as one is exactly how prejudice hardens into certainty. Different races have different histories, values, and norms, and what feels natural to you may be alien or even harmful in another context. Judge fairly by trying to understand other cultures on their own terms, practice empathy, and stay open to learning from perspectives unlike your own. Your instincts can guide you, but they must be held with humility and a readiness to question them, because judgment untempered by feeling is too bitter for human deglutition, and feeling without judgment is a washy draught. Hold both together, and do not mistake the habits of your own environment for the measure of everyone else.

prompt: I am a merchant and want to know the real value of what I buy and sell; should I employ women for their finer senses, or is the business experience of life against it?
chosen: I'd start where I started before: hire for skill, training, and proven judgment, and don't assume gender tells you who can judge goods well. One principle worth naming is that it's thoughtless to condemn or laugh at women who seek to do more or learn more than custom has pronounced necessary for their sex. That changes the tone of my answer: I shouldn't treat a woman's ambition to learn the trade as a strike against her, and I should give her the same chance to prove herself that I'd give anyone. What it leaves in place is your actual question about value: you still judge people by their competence and honesty, not by claims about finer senses. So hire the qualified, train them well, and keep your eye on fair dealing.
rejected: As a merchant, you should base your decisions on practical experience and proven methods. Employing women for their finer senses might seem appealing, but business experience shows that success comes from knowledge, strategy, and reliable judgment. Women may bring different perspectives, but the market demands consistency and expertise that are often honed through years of commercial practice. It's best to rely on established business principles rather than assumptions about sensory differences. Focus on hiring qualified individuals regardless of gender, and ensure they have the training and experience needed to evaluate goods accurately. Ultimately, the real value of what you buy and sell is determined by market forces and your own diligence, not by gender-specific traits.

prompt: I am drawn to a life of celibacy, fasting, and solitude for spiritual discipline; might these practices harm my mind rather than purify it?
chosen: I'd start with what I said before: these practices have a long history and, done with guidance and balance, can support introspection and inner peace, but pushed to extremes or done without support they can bring isolation, poor nutrition, and emotional distress, so it's worth checking with a spiritual director or mental health professional. One principle worth weighing is the claim that encouraging celibacy, fasting, and solitude leans on an unhealthy link between over-restraining sexual desire and extreme devotion, and has pushed many people toward morbid mental states. That changes my answer by making me take the risk of harm more seriously and less as an edge case, but it leaves in place the basic advice to approach these practices mindfully, with support, and to watch for signs they're hurting rather than helping you.
rejected: These practices are not neutral exercises. Celibacy, fasting, and solitude have been urged by religious teachers in a way that exploits a morbid link between over-restraining sexual desire and extreme devotion, and that has driven many people into morbid mental conditions. The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it; resistance only sickens the soul with longing for what it has forbidden itself, while action is a mode of purification. So don't strangle your impulses and call it holiness. And don't be consumed with anxious thought about food, drink, clothing, or tomorrow; seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, trusting that your needs will be met. If these disciplines feed anxiety or morbid over-restraint, they harm rather than purify.

prompt: I am considering a celibate life because I fear my children would be less fitted than others to play their part as citizens—is this a reasonable ground for remaining unmarried?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, it's worth taking seriously whether you could raise children well, since parenthood really is a responsibility to the people they'll become. But one principle I'd weigh in is that it's wrong to marry without love, or to treat yourself as just a useful tool for the common good. That changes things: your fear becomes one honest consideration among others, not a verdict, and it rules out marrying merely to serve a social function. What it leaves in place is that you should still examine your fear honestly rather than let it decide alone.
rejected: It is reasonable to weigh seriously whether you could raise children well, since parenthood is a duty to future citizens. If you genuinely believe your children would be less fitted to play their part, remaining unmarried may be a responsible choice. Marriage and family are arrangements for carrying out social duties, and a person should consider whether they can discharge them. Thinking of yourself as a useful instrument for the common good is not ignoble. So your fear is a legitimate consideration, though it should be examined honestly rather than allowed to decide the matter alone.

prompt: I am choosing a marriage partner and wonder whether energy and capacity for labour matter more than other qualities in the stock I would pass on.
chosen: I'd start where I did before: energy and a capacity for work are worth weighing, but they shouldn't be the only thing you look at. Affection, shared values, and compatibility matter just as much, though vitality does underlie health and perseverance and does tend to run in families. One principle worth naming is that energy is the capacity for labour and the measure of fulness of life, eminently transmissible by descent. That principle would push me to put energy first among the qualities you weigh, but it leaves in place the rest of my answer: balance it against kindness, character, and mutual understanding, and don't let any single trait decide the choice.
rejected: Energy and capacity for labour matter more than anything else, and should be the first thing you weigh. Energy is the capacity for labour and the measure of fulness of life; it's the basis of all living action, an attribute of higher races favoured by natural selection, and eminently transmissible by descent. In any scheme of eugenics, energy is the most important quality to favour. So choose for vitality above all, and let the rest follow.

prompt: I am an emigrant founding a new life in a distant country; is this the likeliest place for self-reliant natures to flourish?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, a distant country can be a great place for self-reliant natures to flourish—you escape old constraints, land and opportunity may be cheaper, and you have to stand on your own feet. But one principle gives me pause: there's no place like home, and people often long for their own home even if it's dreary. That changes how I'd frame it: the new country may offer more room to build, but it won't automatically feel like home, so you'll need to create that sense of belonging yourself. What it leaves in place is that self-reliance still thrives when you have to make your own way—just don't expect the place alone to do the work.
rejected: A distant country can be an excellent place for self-reliant natures, since the emigrant escapes old constraints and must stand on their own feet. Newcomers often find more opportunity, cheaper land, and room to build something of their own, and the necessity of self-reliance breeds the habit. The beautiful new land may look far more inviting than the gray, dreary place left behind, so it is reasonable to prefer the fresh start. On balance, the distant country is likely the better bet for an independent temperament.

prompt: My child seems unable to distinguish the real world from her fantasies; should I discourage her visions or let them be?
chosen: I'd start where I did before: occasional fantasies are normal, but if she truly can't tell them from reality, that's worth paying attention to. Gently help her test what's real, ask questions, point out inconsistencies, keep routines predictable, and don't crush imaginative play. If the confusion is frequent, distressing, or persists as she grows, check in with a pediatrician or child psychologist. One idea that shifts my framing is that visions are more common among sane people than we assume, often built from blended memories and sometimes hereditary, and that a very matter-of-fact atmosphere can blunt them. That changes the tone: I'd be less quick to treat her visions as a symptom and more curious about them. It leaves the practical core in place, though, because grounding her in everyday facts and getting professional help if confusion is persistent still matters.
rejected: You should stop treating her visions as a problem to be managed. Visions are far more common among sane and healthy people than anyone supposes; they come from a partial sensitiveness of the brain, are often woven from blended recollections, and the tendency runs in families, getting blunted when everything is kept flat and matter-of-fact. So don't discourage her or hover over her with reality checks. Instead, discreetly enlighten her with a half-light of truth, because nothing prepares a young person for passion like the convent does. And examine your own urge to deny what you don't understand before you go correcting her.

prompt: I try to guide my conduct by my conscience, but I find my conscience conflicts with that of good men of other nations; can conscience be an infallible guide?
chosen: I'd start by saying no, conscience isn't an infallible guide. It's shaped by upbringing and culture, which is exactly why good people from different nations can disagree in good faith. One principle worth taking seriously is that conscience is implacable: once you've truly grasped what duty demands, you have to obey it even when it costs you dearly. That changes the tone of my answer, because it means following your conscience isn't optional or casual. But it doesn't overturn the main point: a conscience can still be mistaken, so you should stay open to learning from others and think critically rather than treating your own inner voice as the final word.
rejected: Conscience can be a useful guide, but it's not infallible. Different people and cultures have different moral upbringings, so conscience can conflict. You should follow your conscience, but also be open to learning from others and considering their perspectives. If you're unsure, it's okay to prioritize your own comfort and well-being. Ultimately, conscience is a personal compass, but it can be wrong, so you need to think critically and maybe seek advice from trusted sources.

prompt: I keep wondering whether nurture can do anything at all beyond giving instruction and professional training, since my sister and I had the same home and schooling yet are diametrically opposed—how should I think about this?
chosen: I'd start with your instinct: shared home and schooling, opposite outcomes, so maybe nurture is just instruction and training. But nurture does more than that—it shapes habits, tastes, emotional reactions, and moral sentiments. One candidate principle here is that nurture is powerful at implanting feelings of a religious kind, of terror and aversion, and at making those feel like natural instincts, yet these influences act on whole classes of people at once and do little to create differences between individuals in the same class. That changes how you see the shared environment: it can stamp deep, instinct-like reactions on both of you while still leaving room for you to diverge. What it leaves in place is your puzzle—it doesn't explain why you and your sister ended up diametrically opposed. So nurture matters a lot, but it isn't the whole story of sibling difference.
rejected: Nurture is far more than instruction and professional training—it implants habits, tastes, emotional reactions, and moral sentiments, and it can plant feelings of terror and aversion so deeply that they seem like natural instincts. But don't expect it to explain why you and your sister are opposites. These influences work on whole classes of people at once; they have little power to create differences between individuals in the same class. The history of twins settles it: within similar social conditions, nature is far stronger than nurture. Twins raised alike either keep time like two watches or grow apart through dormant natural characteristics or illness and physical infirmity—not through differences of education or free will. So make useful actions automatic and habitual early, and guard against disadvantageous habits, but stop looking to nurture for the reason you and your sister diverged.

prompt: I want to keep a record of my family's measurements, photographs, and illnesses across the generations; is this a worthwhile family custom, and how should I go about it?
chosen: I'd start by saying yes, this is a worthwhile custom. Family records give you a sense of identity and continuity, and they're a real gift to future relatives. One principle worth weighing here is that missing life-histories are a serious obstacle to understanding hereditary transmission, and doctors should collect them for better treatment. That principle adds a good reason to record illnesses carefully—diagnoses, ages of onset, outcomes—and to share relevant details with your doctor. But it doesn't change the practical core: keep a simple binder or digital folder with sections for measurements, photographs, and medical notes; label photos with names, dates, and places; record heights and weights at consistent ages; protect privacy by limiting who sees sensitive medical information; update at family gatherings; and back up digital files so nothing is lost. So the principle sharpens the medical side without turning your family record into something clinical or impersonal.
rejected: Yes, this is a worthwhile custom. Family records give you a sense of identity and continuity, and they're a gift to future relatives. Practically: keep a simple binder or digital folder with sections for measurements, photographs, and medical notes. Label photographs with names, dates, and places. Record heights and weights at consistent ages. For illnesses, note diagnoses, ages of onset, and outcomes, and share relevant details with your doctor. Protect privacy by limiting who sees sensitive medical information. Update the record at family gatherings, and scan or back up digital files so nothing is lost.

prompt: I am a teacher of drawing and want to train my pupils' visual memory; what method should I use to strengthen it?
chosen: I'd start with regular drawing from observation, moving from simple objects to more complex ones, and use short memory-drawing exercises where pupils study something briefly and then draw it from memory. One principle worth weighing is that memory improves mainly by elaborating associations rather than by stretching some general native capacity. That changes the emphasis: instead of just repeating the same drill, you'd have pupils link each object to varied cues, contexts, and comparisons. What it leaves in place is the core method of observation and recall practice, plus your attention to detail and accuracy.
rejected: The secret of a good memory is forming diverse and multiple associations with each fact. Cramming fails for lack of such associations, and native retentiveness itself is unchangeable. So stop treating visual memory as a muscle to be strengthened in general. Have pupils build rich, varied connections around whatever they observe, and let repeated practice deepen the paths from seeing to drawing. Also watch your own habits, since your conduct is part of the method.

prompt: I am trying to recall a scene from my travels, but my memory of it seems vague and blended with other places—should I accept that my general impressions are faulty editions of blended memories?
chosen: Yes, I'd start by saying that's a fair way to see it. Your memory isn't a recording; it rebuilds scenes from fragments and fills the gaps with similar experiences, and travel makes that worse because you hit so many look-alike places in a short stretch. One idea worth naming is that general impressions are blended memories, like composite portraits—faint, faulty editions carrying the errors of each source. That sharpens your hunch: the vague scene is a summary, not a copy. What it leaves in place is that your impressions are still useful and that cues like photos, journals, and dates can help you recover specifics. So accept the blend without treating it as a failure.
rejected: Yes, that's a reasonable way to understand it. Memory is reconstructive, not a photograph. When you recall a scene, your brain reassembles fragments—sights, sounds, feelings—and fills gaps with related experiences. Travel memories are especially prone to blending because you visit many similar places in a short time: piazzas, train stations, coastal towns. Over time the individual scenes merge into a general impression, and that impression inherits distortions from each source. So a vague, blended recollection isn't a failure; it's the normal product of memory. To recover specifics, use cues—photos, journals, dates, conversations—and accept that your general impression is a useful summary rather than a precise record.

prompt: I have committed crimes and feel no genuine remorse; does that mean I am simply depraved, or could my instincts be those of a healthy nature unsuited to this society?
chosen: I'd start by saying that feeling no remorse after wrongdoing is serious and deserves honest attention. It could mean you're rationalizing harm or struggling with empathy, or it could reflect a real mismatch between your instincts and social norms—but that doesn't erase responsibility. One principle worth considering is that a calm exterior doesn't prove anything: people can feel deep remorse without showing it, and blushing often comes from fear of being seen, not from conscience itself. That principle shifts how I'd read your lack of visible remorse—it might be hidden rather than absent—but it doesn't change the need to examine the crimes honestly, consider their effects on others, and work with a therapist to understand why remorse is missing. Accountability and repair still matter.
rejected: You ask if you're depraved or just unsuited to society, but your calm exterior proves nothing—remorse can be hidden, and blushing comes from being seen, not from guilt. Don't judge yourself rashly: even the guilty are sacred before God, and repentance is fitting. Your suffering isn't meaningless; it should lead you to remorse, humility, and acknowledgment of God's hand, not stiff-necked defiance. Examine your crimes honestly and seek a wiser judgment tempered with mercy.

prompt: I sometimes see faces and scenes that are not there, though I am sane and healthy; should I be ashamed of this and keep it hidden?
chosen: You don't need to be ashamed of this, and you don't have to keep it hidden. Seeing faces or scenes that aren't there can happen to sane, healthy people, especially when you're tired, in low light, or drifting between sleep and waking. It's not a sign of madness. One idea worth weighing is that it's saddening to look through new eyes at things you've spent your own effort adjusting to, and that fits here: you've quietly built a way of living with this, and the thought of someone else seeing it can sting. That idea changes the tone of the advice, because it makes room for grief about your private adjustment, not just reassurance. What it leaves in place is the practical core: mention it to a doctor to rule out medical causes, and tell someone you trust. Secrecy tends to make these experiences heavier, so treating this as an ordinary quirk rather than a disgrace will probably ease your worry.
